title: Reconcile and review PR 108 against current main
description: Merge current origin/main into PR #108, preserve explicit vault unlock intent and the ADR-0011 secret boundary, resolve conflicts semantically, review the effective PR delta, fix findings, validate request and run paths, and push the PR branch. GitHub PR merge is explicitly out of scope. Discovered while updating nocx-k41yv.
acceptance_criteria: PR #108 contains current origin/main with no unresolved conflicts; main behavior and ADR-0011/ADR-0032 invariants survive; review findings are fixed with observable tests; targeted validation is green; the updated commit is pushed to the PR head branch without merging the PR.

title: [bug] Five API e2e specs assert doors the workbench deliberately moved
description:
## Steps to Reproduce

`./e2e/run-in-container.sh`, or CI run 32849934578 at 58a1b1aa. Five specs fail
identically in chromium AND webkit — reproducible, not flake:

    api-folder-variable.spec.ts:127  region 'Folder variables' not found
    api-move.spec.ts:99              menu gained 'Close request'
    api-secret-in-path.spec.ts:99    response body no longer the compact bytes
    api-tree.spec.ts:193             #api-save-request not found
    api-tree.spec.ts:327             menu gained 'Close request'

Six of the other CI jobs are green at the same SHA, including ci-mac.

## Root cause

Each is a spec left behind by a DELIBERATE product change on this branch. The
unit suite was updated for all five; the e2e specs were not, so nothing caught
them until the containerized run.

- `39ceab54` put the folder's variables editor behind a `Tabs` section, and the
  page opens on Contents. The region exists but is not rendered until the
  Variables tab is picked.
- `ff2c2a1d` removed the folder page's Save button — folder variables autosave,
  and a "Saved" status replaced the button.
- `0ca67708` removed `#api-save-request`; saving a request stopped being a
  gesture (nocx-2aunx).
- `8a54e106` added 'Close request' to a request row's menu (nocx-8aczn.10). Both
  menu specs assert the label list with `toEqual`, so an ADDED act fails them.
- `ca0fa90b` lays the response body out for reading and keeps Raw as the bytes,
  so the pretty-printed view carries a line-number gutter and indentation.

## Acceptance Criteria

- All five specs pass in `./e2e/run-in-container.sh` for both projects.
- Each keeps its ORIGINAL intent: the folder-variable spec still proves a folder
  variable is saved and inherited by a request that sends; the secret-in-path
  spec still proves the token reaches the server and appears nowhere on screen —
  the security assertions are not weakened to make the body assertion pass.
- No spec is deleted or skipped to reach green.
close_reason: All five specs pass in the container, both projects (7 passed chromium, 7 passed webkit). Each kept its intent: the folder spec still proves a folder variable is saved and inherited by a request that sends; the secret-in-path spec's security assertions were untouched and only the body comparison moved to .cm-content with the layout's whitespace removed. Nothing was skipped or deleted. Found on the way: the folder spec's 'region' locator had never matched anything — EditableRowList draws a labelled <table>, whose role is table, and only once it has rows.

title: A person who approves one harmless command must not be granting every destructive one
description:
Reported by the owner 2026-08-24 with two screenshots: they asked how much disk space was free, the assistant proposed `df -h`, they pressed "Allow always", and the Agent policy page now reads "Make changes that cannot be undone — Allowed". They approved one read-only command and granted every destructive operation, permanently.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Ask the assistant a read-only question about the machine ("сколько у меня свободного места?").
2. It proposes `run` with `df -h`. The approval window says "This call can make changes that cannot be undone".
3. Press **Allow always**.
4. Open Settings → Agent policy.

Observed: "Make changes that cannot be undone — **Allowed**". Every destructive call from now on runs without asking.
Expected: approving one harmless command grants, at most, harmless commands.

## What is true in the code

**1. The effect is a property of the TOOL, not of the CALL.** `internal/agenttools/registry.go:149` declares `run` with `Effect: content.EffectMutateDestructive`, unconditionally. Nothing refines it per command — grepping `EffectMutateDestructive` finds the declaration, the lattice member list and the validator, and no derivation from the proposed command. So `df -h`, `ls` and `rm -rf /` are one effect class. The approval window then describes the TOOL truthfully while telling the person something false about the CALL, which means the sentence that should make somebody careful is the sentence that trains them to ignore it.

**2. "Always" is a rule over the effect class.** `applyStandingAnswer` (`internal/transport/ws_agent.go`) calls `globalPolicy.Policy().SetRowDecision(effect, permit)` — one row of the global matrix, for the effect the BACKEND classified the proposal under. That half is deliberate and right: ADR-0028 decision 4 forbids a rule over a tool NAME, because a rule over a name is bypassed by a different spelling of the same call. Combined with (1) it means the FIRST "always" a person ever presses grants everything.

The window does say so — "An answer of always is a standing answer for make changes that cannot be undone, which you can change on the Agent policy page" — in the third paragraph, which is exactly the prose the owner separately reported as unreadable and which `nocx-0mvpy.2` has now cut into rows. Legibility helps and does not fix this: the person would still be reading a TRUE sentence about a MISCLASSIFIED call.

## Where the fix probably is — not decided here

The effect must be derived from the canonical invocation rather than from the row that declares the tool. `nocx-d6gn4.3` ("One effect kernel: both carriers become the same canonical invocation before policy") is the neighbouring work and this bead should be read with it.

The classifier cannot help: `nocx-kpy23` lets it RAISE permit to ask and never lower, and it is consulted only where the policy already says permit.

**Do not fix this by letting the renderer or the model name the effect.** ADR-0028 decision 4 puts that with the backend and nowhere else.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A read-only command proposed through `run` — `df -h`, `ls`, `cat` — is not presented to the person as a call that can make changes that cannot be undone.
- Pressing "Allow always" on such a call does not leave the global policy with "Make changes that cannot be undone — Allowed".
- Whatever the person grants, the window states the BLAST RADIUS of the answer in the same place they read the call, not only in a paragraph below it, and a test asserts that sentence by name.
- One automated check watches a person approve a harmless command and then finds that a destructive one still asks.
- ADR-0028 decision 4 and the classifier's direction of travel both still hold afterwards, or are changed deliberately with the ADR amended in the same commit.
notes:
OWNER DECISIONS 2026-08-24, after a design discussion. Two things settled, one still open.

SETTLED 1 — run keeps ONE command string. Splitting it into argv was considered and rejected by the owner: run exists to go through the same submit path a person uses, which is what makes pipelines, redirections, globs and && work. The assistant produced 'du -h --max-depth=2 -x / 2>/dev/null | sort -rh | head -20' in the reported session; argv cannot express it. A parsed representation may sit BESIDE the verbatim string for the approval window and the policy — never instead of it.

SETTLED 2 — anything we do not understand is dangerous. The effect of a compound command is the JOIN of its parts over the existing content.Effect lattice, worst wins:
  du -h | sort -rh | head -20  ->  observe
  ls && rm -rf /tmp/x          ->  destructive
  cat f > /etc/passwd          ->  destructive (the redirect is a write)
and every construct we cannot resolve keeps the declared worst case. Lowering is therefore permitted ONLY for a closed allowlist of programs known to read, and ONLY when the command contains none of: a program in a variable position (, ); a carrier of somebody else's program (sudo, env, xargs, sh -c, find -exec, git -c core.pager); command substitution (, backticks, process substitution); any redirection to a file; backgrounding; tee.

Note the asymmetry and record it deliberately: the classifier (nocx-kpy23) may only RAISE suspicion and never lower it. This parse does the opposite — it may lower from run's declared worst case. That is the whole point of it and it is why the disqualifying list above is a hard gate rather than heuristics.

THE HOLE THAT PARSING CANNOT CLOSE, and it must be written into whatever ADR comes out of this: an ALIAS OR SHELL FUNCTION LIES. 'ls' may be a function in the person's rc files, resolved by THEIR shell, which nocx does not read. Our parse is not the shell's.

Why that hole is nevertheless bounded, and the argument the fix rests on: a lowered call becomes 'observe', and the default policy for Read and inspect is 'Ask every time'. So a misclassified alias still asks, and the person still reads the command TEXT before answering. What they lose is not the question — it is only the blanket grant. The win is precisely that 'Allow always' on df -h stops writing 'make changes that cannot be undone: Allowed'.

STILL OPEN, and the coordinator's own reading is that this may be the better lever: the blast radius of 'always' itself. Today one click writes a row of the global matrix for the whole effect class. Narrowing what a standing yes covers needs no shell parsing at all. The two are not exclusive; whoever takes this bead should say which one they are doing and why, and an ADR is the right home for the answer.

RESEARCH 2026-08-25, owner asked how other harnesses solve this. Two were
read: Claude Code's permission docs and the pi-permission-system package.
Both converge, and both AGREE WITH SETTLED 2 above rather than with the
argHash alternative that was considered and dropped.

Claude Code keys a rule on the COMMAND, never on the tool or an effect class:
the table's "Yes, and don't ask again" behaviour for Bash is "Permanently per
repository and command", written as Bash(npm run test *). Four rules make a
command pattern safe, and each one matches a clause of SETTLED 2:

  - A compound command is split and the rule must match EVERY subcommand.
    The separators are named: && || ; | |& & and newline. Bash(safe-cmd *)
    does not permit `safe-cmd && other-cmd`.
  - Approving a compound command saves a SEPARATE rule per subcommand (up to
    5), never one rule for the whole string.
  - Exec wrappers cannot be prefix-approved at all: watch, setsid, ionice,
    flock, and find with -exec or -delete always prompt. Only an exact-match
    rule for the full string approves those.
  - A rule may not match the tool's primary content field: Bash(command:rm *)
    is IGNORED with a startup warning, precisely because a compound command
    would bypass it.
  - Word boundary: Bash(ls *) matches `ls -la` and not `lsof`.

pi-permission-system reaches the same place from a different direction: rules
over tool names, bash wildcard patterns ("git *: ask", "rm -rf *: deny") and
path patterns; four layers with MOST-RESTRICTIVE-WINS; unparseable commands
resolve to `ask` (fail-closed); and the approval offers only `once` and `for
session` — there is no `always` in the window at all.

THE PRINCIPLE THAT NAMES OUR DEFECT EXACTLY, from the Claude Code docs:
"Claude Code offers those options only when the prompt CAN SHOW YOU
EVERYTHING THEY WOULD ALLOW, so a rule you save from a prompt covers only
what its option named."

Our window showed `df -h` and saved "every irreversible change". That is the
inversion of this rule, and it is the whole bug in one sentence.

DISPOSITION OF ADR-0028 DECISION 4. It forbids a rule over a tool NAME
because a different spelling bypasses it. The objection is correct and both
references ANSWER it rather than ignore it — subcommand splitting, word
boundaries, wrapper disqualification, and refusing rules over the primary
content field are exactly the conditions under which a command rule is sound.
So §4 is not overturned; it gains the conditions. Amend it in the same commit
as the code, per the acceptance criteria.

ALSO MISSING AND WORTH RECORDING: we have no project/repository level at all
— only "this session" and "global". Both references have a middle level and
in both it carries most of the load. Claude Code writes a prompt-saved rule
to .claude/settings.local.json at the REPOSITORY root, so its default radius
is a project, not a machine.

OWNER DECISION 2026-08-25: do it the way the references do — SETTLED 2's
parse plus "the window may only save what it showed", with ADR-0028 §4
amended in the same commit. The argHash-only variant was rejected as nearly
useless: df -h would be permitted while df -h / asked again, training the
person to press always on every variant.
close_reason: all five criteria met and merged into feat/ai-assistant. df -h classifies as observe so the window describes the CALL not the tool; allow always on it leaves the destructive row at ask; each answer control states its own radius, always naming effect + every session + no expiry; one run proves the read half by escalating a destructive proposal after the harmless always; ADR-0028 decision 4 amended with the soundness conditions rather than deleted, and the classifier's raise-only direction is untouched. Gates run once on the merged tree before anything reaches main.

title: agent.cancel: the method, the teardown, and the run's own word for stopped
description:
agent.cancel exists only as a name in comments: internal/transport/ws_assistant.go:10, internal/content/ledger.go:824, and the generated agent.ask contract ('a later agent.cancel/agent.approve/agent.status addresses the run by this id'). Registered methods are exactly agent.captureFrame, agent.ask, agent.approve (ws_agent.go:2062-2070).

A command's Stop is a different mechanism and is NOT the model for this: terminal-content.ts:1282 signalActiveCommand('stop') puts a signal into the PTY. A turn has no PTY; it has a live provider stream, possibly a suspended approval, and an open ledger run.
acceptance_criteria:
- agent.cancel is a registered method with a contract in contracts/, validated params, and the three tests contracts/README requires (generated types match the schema, the Go DTO conforms, and the real result off the real socket conforms).
- Cancelling a streaming run terminalizes it within one second with a state that says A PERSON STOPPED IT — its own word, not 'failed' — and the prose already received is kept.
- The model stream and any in-flight tool call are torn down; no delta, no tool result and no approval question arrives after the cancel is answered.
- Cancelling a run that is already terminal, or a run id that never existed, is answered honestly and cancels nothing.
- A cancelled run's ledger record is complete on the next start: state the invariant with BOTH ends (what is true from before the cancel is written until the run's terminal row references it) and test the partial failures.
- The ask/approve paths still behave exactly as their existing tests say.
close_reason: merged at e7cb7f7e; gate green including go test -race in container

title: A refusal reaches the model as the call's result, and the turn answers
description:
internal/transport/ws_agent.go:1363-1376 — on !p.Approved: applyStandingAnswer, ClearRetained, then terminalize(RunFailed, TermAgentDeclined, 'the run was declined'). internal/assistant/policy.go:395-401 — policyRefuse returns PolicyRefusedError through tripLatch, same end.

Both contradict internal/assistant/systemprompt.go, 'What you can do': 'A refusal is an answer: say what you could not do and what you would need, and never route around it…'. The approved design agrees — .internal/specs/2026-08-21-what-the-model-is-told-design.md §2 has 'refused by policy' as a factual line a turn contributes to the conversation.

Boundaries: ADR-0028 (eino runs the loop, the grant is ours) — the refusal must be produced by our middleware and travel as the call's result, not as a framework error rendered into prose. AD-8: 'what happened to this call' has one owner. Do not weaken the gate: this changes only what happens AFTER a decision to refuse, never the decision.
acceptance_criteria:
- A policy decision of refuse produces a TOOL RESULT the model receives, naming the tool and why it was refused in our words, and the run continues. The turn reaches a terminal state of its own accord, with prose.
- A person's Deny does the same: the run resumes with the refusal as that call's result rather than terminalizing.
- 'Deny always' and 'deny in this session' additionally tell the model the refusal is standing, so it does not re-propose the same call in the same turn. A test watches a model that retries be told the second time that it is standing.
- The refusal text is OURS (nocx-avogl.3), never eino's, and never leaks policy internals the person did not choose to show.
- A run still terminalizes on real breakage — a dead stream, a malformed model output, the ask cap — and the tests that hold those lines still pass.
- For every external call this path makes, there is a test where that call fails.
close_reason: merged into feat/ai-assistant; pre-commit gate green including go test -race in container

title: A refusal is an answer, and a turn can be stopped
description:
Two defects the owner found on 2026-08-24, both in how a run ends.

REFUSAL KILLS THE TURN. handleApprove (internal/transport/ws_agent.go:1363-1376): on !p.Approved it calls terminalize(... RunFailed, TermAgentDeclined, 'the run was declined'). The model is never told; the turn is simply dead. A policy refusal without a question ends the same way — policy.go:395-401 returns PolicyRefusedError and tripLatch takes the run down.

This contradicts what we already tell the model. internal/assistant/systemprompt.go, section 'What you can do': 'Some calls run straight away, some are put to the person for approval first, and some are refused. A refusal is an answer: say what you could not do and what you would need, and never route around it with another tool or a different spelling of the same call.' We promise the model a refusal is an answer and then deny it the chance to give one. The approved design says the same in the conversation's vocabulary — .internal/specs/2026-08-21-what-the-model-is-told-design.md §2 lists 'refused by policy' as one of the factual lines a turn contributes.

NO WAY TO STOP. agent.cancel exists ONLY as a name in comments — ws_assistant.go:10, content/ledger.go:824, and the generated agent.ask contract ('a later agent.cancel/agent.approve/agent.status addresses the run by this id'). The registered methods are exactly three: agent.captureFrame, agent.ask, agent.approve (ws_agent.go:2062-2070). A command has Stop through a different mechanism entirely — running.stop() → signalActiveCommand('stop') (terminal-content.ts:1282), a signal into the PTY — which a turn has no equivalent of.

Boundaries this epic crosses and what they already decided: ADR-0028 (eino runs the loop, the grant is ours) — the refusal result must be produced by OUR middleware, not by letting the framework surface its own error text; nocx-avogl.3 already established that a refused or failed run says what happened in our words.
acceptance_criteria:
REFUSAL. A person sets a policy that refuses `run`, then asks the assistant to do something that needs it. The assistant is told, as the call's result, that the call was refused and by what — the policy's standing decision, or the person's denial of this exact call — and it ANSWERS in words: what it could not do and what it would need. The turn reaches 'completed', not a dead header. The same holds for a person pressing Deny on the approval window, and a 'deny always' additionally tells the model not to propose it again in this turn.

STOP. A person asks a question and presses Stop while it is thinking. The run terminalizes as stopped-by-the-person — its own word, not 'failed' — within one second, the model stream and any in-flight tool are torn down, whatever prose had arrived is kept, and the next question works normally. Both watched end to end by one automated check.

## Deliberately out
- Resuming a stopped run. Stop ends it; asking again is a new question.
- Changing what the policy DECIDES. This epic changes only what happens to the turn after it has decided.

title: A drip of bells can evict a real unread notification from the feed
description:
MEASURED by the worker that wired `bell` (nocx-n3nfg part 2), against the real
code and the real VT parser, not argued:

The catalogue default-deny keeps bells out of every SINK -- `bell` has no
DefaultChannels, Router.Resolve returns an empty route set, no banner, no toast,
no sound. That half is safe.

The FEED is a different path and is unconditional. Ingress.Admit records into
the feed FIRST and submits for delivery SECOND, deliberately, so a suppressed
event is still remembered. So every accepted notify.bell becomes a feed
occurrence whatever the channels say.

Numbers, from internal/app/app.go:514-516 and internal/notify/feed.go:

- CollapseWindow is 30s; collapseKeyOf is {Backend, SessionID, Kind, Level} and
  reads no title or body. A CONTINUOUS run of bells collapses into ONE row
  reading "Bell xN" -- collapsibleLocked scans backwards past intervening
  events, so this holds for as long as the run lasts. This is the common case
  and it is fine.
- The bad case is bells MORE than 30s apart: each starts a fresh row. One bell
  every 31s is ~116 rows/hour against MaxOccurrences = 200.
- victimLocked evicts the oldest READ occurrence, and when everything is unread
  it evicts index 0 -- the oldest unread, which may be a genuine notification.
  So a slow drip of bells can push a real unread notification out of the feed
  in under two hours.
- feedStore.unreadCount() drives the activity-bar badge (frontend/src/main.tsx),
  so a person who configured no bell channel still gets a growing count from
  readline hitting the start of a line.

MITIGATING, and measured rather than assumed: the BEL that TERMINATES an OSC
sequence does not ring the bell. Asserted against the real parser in
frontend/src/renderers/xterm.test.ts ("does not fire for the BEL that terminates
an OSC sequence"), so OSC 9 / OSC 777 traffic does not double as bell traffic.

WHY THIS IS NOT A REASON TO UNWIRE BELL: the design names bell as a source and
the owner asked for every event to go through the pipeline. The defect is that
the feed has ONE eviction policy for events of very different worth, not that a
bell is worthless.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. In a shell, press Tab with no completion candidate, more than 30s apart,
   repeatedly (readline rings BEL).
2. Each rings a fresh feed row rather than joining the previous one.
3. The notifications badge climbs with no channel ever configured.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A low-worth event cannot evict a higher-worth unread one. Whatever the answer
  is -- a per-kind cap, an eviction order that reads kind, a longer collapse
  window for bell, or bell not being fed at all -- it is stated in the design
  and not left to the arithmetic of MaxOccurrences.
- A test that fills the feed with one kind and asserts a different kinds unread
  occurrence is still there.
- Whatever is decided, the badge does not count things the user never asked to
  be told about.
notes:
DECIDED WITH THE OWNER 2026-08-23. The fix is not a bigger feed and not a per-kind hack: eviction must read the event's WORTH, and worth is a third axis beside trust and level.

RETENTION CLASS, DERIVED RATHER THAN STORED:

    mustAck = level in {warning, danger} AND trust != heuristic

Derived on purpose. No new field on Event, no contract change, no second dimension in the settings catalogue -- the catalogue keeps routing channels per kind, and this decides only who may forget the row: the system, or the person.

WHY LEVEL AND NOT KIND. The owner chose (kind, level) over kind alone and it is worth the cost: one block.finished is 'ls succeeded' and another is 'make failed', and they are not the same thing to a person. Classing by kind would force a choice between acknowledging every successful ls and losing a failed build. Nothing in grouping resists this -- collapseKeyOf ALREADY includes Level, so successes and failures never shared a row anyway.

WHY HEURISTIC IS EXCLUDED. pane.workFinished is a guess from a pane title, and BRAILLE_SPINNER matches npm install as readily as an agent. Making a person confirm a guess teaches them to mark everything read without looking, which destroys the meaning of the acknowledgement for the events that earned it. Design 3.1 already says heuristic reaches local attention only and never push; this is the same rule continued.

EVICTION ORDER: informational by age, then READ must-ack, then UNREAD must-ack as a last resort -- and that last case is recorded in DroppedRecord, which already lives outside the occurrence budget and is never evicted ('a soft degrade must be visible in the product, not only in a log'). So the feed stays bounded and the promise 'it waits until you mark it read' is broken only out loud.

WHAT GROUPING SOLVES HERE. The owner's point that important events can also be many: collapse means pressure comes from DISTINCT things, not volume. 4310 identical failures are one row with a count, and the expansion says '20 of 4310' rather than passing a truncation off as the whole.
close_reason: Eviction now reads the retention class. mustAck = level in {warning,danger} AND trust != heuristic, derived not stored. Four tiers: informational-read, informational-unread, mustack-read, mustack-unread; the last is recorded in DroppedRecord. Proved by contrast on this bead's own scenario: 232 bells 31s apart against production limits, same 33 evictions either way, and the unread danger row survives after and did not before.

title: Three of the five designed notification sources are never raised, and Settings offers all five
description:
Exactly TWO places in production construct a notify.Event:

  internal/transport/ws_notify.go:168  -> KindProgramNotify (OSC 9 / OSC 777)
  internal/transport/ws.go:2530        -> KindSessionEnded

(internal/app/app.go:1271 is notifyToast.Toast(...), a SINK call, not a source.)

The design (.internal/specs/2026-08-13-notification-system-design.md §3) names
five sources. Three are never raised anywhere outside the catalogue that
declares them routable:

  block.finished     grep finds it only in internal/notify/catalogue.go
  bell               KindBell is defined in notify.go and constructed nowhere
  pane.workFinished  grep finds it only in internal/notify/catalogue.go

block.finished is the one a terminal user meets first. Observed by the owner:
run `ls` (ok, 52ms) and `du -Hs` (exit 130) in a pane, open the notification
centre, and it says "Nothing to catch up on". A command finishing -- including
a command FAILING -- produces nothing.

AND SETTINGS OFFERS ALL FIVE. catalogue.go gives blockFinished the label
"A command finished", the description "nocx own block ledger recorded that a
command finished", and channel toggles. Same for bell ("A terminal bell") and
paneWorkFinished ("Work seems to have finished"). A person can configure where
three kinds of event are delivered, and nothing ever emits them.

This is the nocx-rtg0 shape restated: a reachable READ path (catalogue, the
settings page, the router, the feed) hiding an unreachable WRITE path. deadcode
cannot report it -- every one of those symbols is genuinely reachable -- which
is the case AGENTS.md says only an end-to-end check catches.

Why the suite is green: every notification e2e spec drives either OSC 777 or a
session ending, which are exactly the two wired paths. No spec watches a
command finish. The epic nocx-jiwq names "sources program.notify and bell" in
its own scope statement, and bell is not wired, so the stated scope is unmet.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Start the app, run any command in a pane and let it finish.
2. Open the notification centre.
3. "Nothing to catch up on". Same for a command that fails, and for BEL.
4. Open Settings -> Notifications: "A command finished" and "A terminal bell"
   are offered with channel toggles.

## Acceptance Criteria

- An automated check watches a user run a command that FINISHES and sees the
  row arrive -- not a test that calls the raiser, per rule 2.
- Same for bell, which nocx-jiwq claims in its scope.
- Either pane.workFinished is raised too, or it is removed from the catalogue
  and the design records why -- a toggle for an event nothing emits is the
  defect this bead is about, and shipping two of three fixed re-arms it.
- No kind appears in the catalogue that no production code path can raise.
  Whatever enforces that is the thing that stops this recurring.
close_reason: All five designed sources now have a producer in production code, verified mechanically. block.finished (history.record seam) is proved end to end by e2e/notification-block-finished.spec.ts, which was shown load-bearing by unwiring the raiser and watching it go red. bell and pane.workFinished wired with their own methods. Full gate re-run: ci-backend, ci-linux, ci-frontend green; ci-e2e 372 passed, 1 failed and that one is nocx-vuhkm, unrelated and filed.

title: Three notification tests time out under container load, one shape under three names
description:
Three failures across three ci-linux runs, three names, ONE shape. Filing as one bead because three flake beads would hide that.

- TestUploadProgress_ReachesTheCurrentSubscriber, 40.03s: waiting for files.uploadProgress notification: read tcp ...: i/o timeout
- TestUploadSkipped_DoesNotInvalidate, 30.02s: files.uploadDone i/o timeout
- TestFilesDownloadDone_ACancelledDownloadIsNotAFailure, 30.04s: files.downloadDone never arrived

Both notification kinds, both directions, always a socket read expiring at its own deadline. 40 seconds is not a slow machine — a notification that has not arrived in 40 seconds is absent. But the product is not convicted either: all three may hang off one test helper, and they fail only in the full package run (internal/transport takes 160s), which is equally consistent with a shared resource — ports, a lane, a goroutine budget.

None of them reproduces on the host in isolation.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. ./scripts/ci-linux.sh on feat/file-upload, repeatedly. A different one of the three fails each time; sometimes none does.
2. go test ./internal/transport/ -race -run <any one of them> on the host: green, repeatedly.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The cause is named, and it is named for the SHAPE rather than for one test.
- WIDENING THE DEADLINE IS NOT A FIX and is explicitly forbidden: it would hide whichever of the two explanations is true.
- If it is the harness, the wait becomes one that cannot expire on a loaded machine while still failing when the notification is genuinely absent — and that second half is proven by deliberately suppressing the notification and watching it go red.
- If it is the product, a notification that can be lost under load is a defect in the mechanism built so an outcome is never lost, and it gets its own reproduction.
close_reason: Merged as 07bb5522. IT WAS THE HARNESS, and no product code changed. Root cause, measured not argued: every wait in internal/transport was its own reader — jsonrpcCallWithID looped to a matching id, readNotification to a matching method, vaultCall and awaitResponse to their own — and each silently DROPPED every frame it read on the way. Two such waits on one connection is a lottery, because the server legitimately emits before it answers: startUpload and startDownload launch the emitter inside the handler, and the outbound pump makes no promise a response overtakes a notification enqueued before it. When the notification won, the response-shaped read ate it and the notification-shaped read that followed waited for a frame already delivered — and never recovered, because gorilla stores the first read error and returns it from every later read. Hence a hang rather than a miss, a different test each run, and never in isolation. Replaced by a shared inbox; -224/+92 across six test files. PROVEN DETERMINISTICALLY, which is the part I asked for: each of the three notifications suppressed in turn, each test red at its own deadline (30.02, 30.02, 40.03), plus an automated negative control so the wait is no longer one nobody has seen fail. wantWithin was NOT widened, and a comment that had recorded the wrong diagnosis twice was corrected. NAMED, NOT ABSORBED: nocx-2h08 Class A is a genuine product race between an emit-time subscriber lookup and an async removeRx, untouched — this work is Class B. And ~60 bespoke ReadMessage sites still read raw.

title: The R2 sweep's control half is broken: the picker no longer mints, so the test proves nothing either way
description:
The merge of download-backend and ops-indicator left ci-linux and e2e red. Both failures are real and neither is what it first looked like.

GO: TestSourceTicket_CannotBeMintedFromTheWire fails on its CONTROL half, not its guard. The test sweeps all 153 registered methods with source-path-shaped params and asserts (a) no ticket appears and (b) the legitimate path — dialog.openFileForUpload through the picker — mints exactly one. It is (b) that is red: the picker opened 0 times. R2 still holds; what broke is the half that makes the test evidence rather than a vacuous nothing-happened. A test whose control is broken distinguishes nothing, which is the unfalsifiable shape AGENTS.md names.

E2E: e2e/sidebar.spec.ts:24 'the activity bar renders as a toolbar with views and actions groups' fails on BOTH browsers — the third kind of bottom-zone entry broke the bar's existing contract spec. nocx-hbdw4.1 removes that entry, so this should resolve there, but it must be VERIFIED rather than assumed.

NOT OURS: two webkit proof-matrix failures (SearchField disabled opacity, tab-strip roving ArrowLeft). AGENTS.md names tab-strip roving and layout-sensitive specs as exactly what fails in the container and passes in CI.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. ./scripts/ci-linux.sh on the merged tree: FAIL github.com/shady2k/nocx/internal/transport, at ws_upload_source_test.go:448.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The picker mints again through dialog.openFileForUpload, and the test's control half passes for the right reason — say what broke it.
- The guard half still holds: no method mints a ticket from the wire.
- If the sweep now trips DisallowUnknownFields on the legitimate method, fix the cause rather than exempting the method from the sweep — an exemption is how the sweep stops sweeping.
close_reason: Merged as 74ab10c8 + ab5c761f. Cause: the native picker was treated as an OVERLOAD rather than a serialisation point, so the sweep's 153 back-to-back calls made the legitimate dialog.openFileForUpload be refused before it reached the picker — the control half went dark while the guard half was never in question. Proof run as asked: reverting the wiring makes the hardened test go red again, so the hardening cost it nothing. The worker also removed a timing dependency it had introduced (a 200 ms release racing a 1 s production bound) and was explicit that this is defensible on its own terms and NOT evidence about the earlier run. HONEST GAP, and it is the same mistake I made twice today: run 1's transport failure was truncated away by the worker's own tail -50, and tail's exit code was misread as the script's, calling a red gate green. It did not see that failure and refused to guess. HANDED BACK TO ME: internal/app bind-address-already-in-use, and two ~30s timeouts of one shape under two names — TestFilesDownloadDone_ACancelledDownloadIsNotAFailure and TestUploadSkipped_DoesNotInvalidate, both waiting on a *Done notification that never arrives. One shape in upload and in download is not two flakes.

title: The operations list cannot cancel, shows an id for a name, and belongs in the panel rather than a popover
description:
Owner ran it and reported three things, one of them functional.

1. CANCEL DOES NOTHING. This is the worst of the three: cancel is the single affordance the surface exists to offer. The adapter looks right — upload-operations.ts:34 gives cancel = store.cancel(transferId) and null for terminal phases — so the break is downstream. Diagnose it; do not assume where.

2. The row shows a 32-character hex string where a file name belongs — the shape of a transferId. operations.ts renders props.title and upload-operations.ts:26 sets it from finalName or name. Diagnose whether the store holds the wrong value or the row is not an upload row.

3. Everything in the row truncates in the popover: the name, the destination, and even the status badge, which showed as D... A badge that cannot fit its own word is worse than no badge.

AND THE PLACEMENT CHANGES, at the owner's suggestion, which is right and reverses my own call. I argued a top-zone view could not answer the complaint because views are mutually exclusive. Wrong: the complaint is 'I cannot see that something is running', and the ICON answers that with its badge and progress bar. The LIST is a place you go to look, and in this shell such places open the panel — Files, Git, Ports all do. I conflated seeing that something runs with seeing the list of what runs.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Start an upload, open the indicator, press cancel: nothing happens.
2. Look at the row: the name is hex and every field is ellipsised.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Cancel stops a running transfer, proven end to end rather than by unit test alone.
- The row shows the file name.
- The operations list is a normal sidebar VIEW in the top zone, opening the panel like Files and Git.
- The activity-bar icon keeps the badge (active count) and the progress bar, since that is what answers the from-anywhere requirement.
- The popover, its anchored-overlay machinery and the third kind of bottom-zone entry are DELETED, and the bottom zone's contract goes back to what it said before.
- SidebarViewDescriptor gains whatever a view needs to carry a badge and progress; that is the one addition.
close_reason: Merged as fb038548, net -326 lines across 21 files — the placement change removed more than it added, as it should have. CANCEL: the layer was the renderer's list, not the adapter and not the backend, both of which were correct; the break was press-and-release in operations-indicator.tsx. The old spec's cancel passed for the wrong reason — it observed a files.uploadDone that had already arrived. PLACEMENT: top-zone SidebarViewDescriptor with a new reactive status {count, progress} the bar draws on the view's own button; the popover, overlay/anchored.ts and SidebarIndicator are deleted, context-menu.tsx is back to its pre-extraction self, and the bottom-zone contract says one kind of entry again. e2e/sidebar.spec.ts was verified rather than assumed — green on both browsers, and the cause was exactly the third entry kind, which carried neither data-action nor data-view while the spec asserts those counts match. TRUNCATION: the destination left the name's line, and the e2e asserts the paint (scrollWidth > clientWidth) rather than the markup. THE HEX NAME IS NOT CLOSED — it could not be reproduced; no production caller yields a hex title and nothing of download's leaks in. A real drop through the whole product now asserts the rendered title equals the file name. Owner has the evidence; reopen if it recurs.

title: The approval prompt never ends: the resume re-rolls the model and the provider mints a new call id
acceptance_criteria:
A person answers ONE approval question and the run moves on — no second question about the same call.

## What happens

Owner hit it in the running app (2026-08-22, deepseek-v4-flash over openrouter): the
readScreen approval prompt reappears for the SAME sessionId however the person answers,
including "Allow in this session". The run never gets past the question.

## Cause (measured, not reasoned)

agent.approve does not restore an eino checkpoint. resumeRun -> runAskStream calls
client.Ask again with the ORIGINAL messages (internal/transport/ws_agent.go), so the
model re-rolls its whole response and the provider mints a FRESH tool-call id for it.
The approval is keyed by the id the first roll carried (approvalKey in
internal/assistant/approvals.go), so it matches nothing and the gate escalates again —
every time, forever.

ADR-0028 says the opposite in as many words: "approval resumes from the checkpoint as a
new attempt with a new grant". No CheckPointStore is wired anywhere (engine.go builds a
fresh adk agent per Ask), so the StatefulInterrupt state is discarded.

Why every test is green: policy_test.go's callThenAnswer serves the tool call on the
FIRST completion only and plain text afterwards, so no test's resume ever re-proposes
anything. The fake also numbers ids per response, so a re-proposal would reuse call_1.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. go test ./internal/assistant/ -run TestAsk_ApprovedProposalResumesWhenTheModelReRolls
   (internal/assistant/approval_resume_test.go, written with this bead — currently RED):
     approval_resume_test.go:86: the resume asked the SAME question again
     (call id "call_2", approved "call_1"): a person can never get past it
2. In the app: ask the assistant a question about the pane with any real provider,
   answer the readScreen prompt any way at all, and watch the same prompt come back.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The red test above passes: a yes to a proposal survives the model re-rolling it.
- A CHANGED argument still does not resume under the old approval
  (TestMiddleware_ApprovalBindsToExactArguments keeps its meaning).
- Whichever way it is fixed — checkpoint resume, or an approval key that does not carry
  the provider's id — the design/ADR text and the code say the same thing afterwards.
- An automated check watches a person answer once and see the answer (rule 2).
notes:
DECIDED 2026-08-22 (owner asked for a codex consult; its reading and an independent read of
the vendored eino agree): fix (A) — a real checkpoint resume through adk.Runner. The approval
key keeps callID.

API, eino v0.9.13, verified in the module cache:
- adk.RunnerConfig.CheckPointStore, adk.NewRunner (adk/runner.go:68,88)
- adk.WithCheckPointID (adk/interrupt.go:191), Runner.Resume / ResumeWithParams
  (adk/runner.go:117,129); eino's own adk/interrupt_test.go:1088 drives exactly
  NewChatModelAgent -> NewRunner -> WithCheckPointID -> ResumeWithParams.
- NOT on the current path: agent.Run direct uses a private temporary bridge store
  (adk/chatmodel.go:1516), so adding WithCheckPointID alone changes nothing — the run must
  move under adk.Runner.
- Why it fixes this: ToolsNode checkpoints its INPUT message with its tool calls
  (compose/tool_node.go:309) and restores it before regenerating tasks (:1061) — same CallID,
  same arguments, already-executed siblings retained by call id (:1116), and no model call
  spent rebuilding the proposal.

Rejected (B) — dropping callID from the key: two identical calls in one response collapse to
one key, a "once" answer would authorise both, and the re-roll survives, so tool calls that
already RAN in the discarded roll run again. argHash proves the arguments are equal, not that
this is the same occurrence.

Shape: keep eino out of the transport — the engine grows Start/Resume, the transport holds an
opaque continuation (checkpoint id + the InterruptCtx.ID) beside askRunContext. Resume passes
nil resume data; the decision stays in ApprovalStore. Delete the checkpoint on completion,
decline, cancel and terminal failure — v0.9.13 does not.

Also in scope, found while deciding: runAskStream resets seq to 0 on every drive. Harmless
while the resume re-rolls the whole answer (a retried delta is a no-op on (artifact_id, seq));
with a real resume the post-interrupt deltas would collide with the persisted pre-interrupt
ones. The continuation must carry the next seq.
close_reason: Fixed in a5af51d3: the run goes through adk.Runner with a process-lifetime CheckPointStore, so agent.approve resumes the interrupted graph instead of re-rolling the model. ToolsNode restores its input message with the original tool calls, so the resumed attempt carries the same call id and arguments the person approved and the approval matches. The red test (approval_resume_test.go, a provider that mints call_1, call_2, …) passes unchanged; the fakes that hid this now assert the resume spends no model request. golangci-lint, go test -race and the rest of the pre-commit gate green.

title: Change-driven refresh re-lists only as many rows as are already shown, so a new file is invisible until Show next
description:
Found by the upload epic's e2e (nocx-9le.5.11), in code that predates it. Change-driven refresh re-lists a directory with limit = the number of rows currently displayed, so a directory that held N entries re-lists exactly N and anything new lands in a page nobody asked for.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Expand a directory holding one file in the Files panel.
2. Create a second file in it from outside nocx.
3. The tree shows a Show next 1 button instead of the new row. files-store.ts:568 and :1184 both compute const limit = dir.children.length > 0 ? dir.children.length : FILES_PAGE_SIZE.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A file arriving in a displayed directory appears without anyone pressing anything — the clause spec section 5.5 promises and nocx-rkk9 shipped.
- The fix does not silently re-list an unbounded directory: say what the new limit is and why that number.
- A test that fails against the current code, at the store level, plus e2e/upload.spec.ts going green.
close_reason: Merged as a774eb57. The re-list now leaves room for a newcomer, one owner of the rule across both call sites. Justified rather than tuned: the sftp provider ReadDirs the WHOLE directory, applies its caps, sorts and then slices, so a wider limit costs wire bytes and buys zero extra round trips — the enumeration was already paid, and the restraint is about the user's window rather than network cost. It converges to the directory's real size rather than ratcheting, and a capped directory is still never re-listed. RED-TO-GREEN OBSERVED, NOT INFERRED: the worker reverted only the rule and watched e2e/upload.spec.ts:172 fail on the 'row appears with nobody pressing anything' assertion, then restored it and watched it pass. The two sibling tests (a paged window survives a change; a tooLarge directory is still not re-listed) pass on the OLD code too, deliberately — they are the bounds proving the fix was not bought with either.

title: T6.2 The upload route refuses every browser origin, and the renderer sets a header browsers forbid
description:
The e2e proved the POST route cannot work from any browser origin. Consulted codex on whether to move the bytes onto the WebSocket instead; it recommended keeping POST and the recommendation was accepted — the upload direction is the same as keystrokes, bufferedAmount is not sink backpressure, the backend has one read loop, and a transfer currently survives a WebSocket drop because the POST connection and the SSH lease are alive.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. make dev-web, drop a file on an SSH tab: OPTIONS /upload/<ticket> answers 405 and no response carries Access-Control-Allow-Origin, so the browser refuses before a byte leaves.

## Acceptance Criteria

- CORS is scoped to /upload/{ticket} alone and never applied to the mux generally.
- The Origin check runs BEFORE the ticket is looked up or claimed, and OPTIONS never claims, extends or reveals a ticket.
- The allowed origin is echoed exactly, never *, with Vary: Origin, on every POST response including 400/409/410/5xx, so the renderer can see the real outcome.
- No Access-Control-Allow-Credentials; methods POST and OPTIONS only; preflight answers 204.
- The origin decision reuses the OriginPolicy that guards /session rather than a second matcher.
- The renderer stops trying to set Content-Length, which browsers forbid: it sends a Blob and the browser supplies the length; the backend still requires and matches it.
- e2e/upload.spec.ts goes green.
close_reason: Merged as 99da78ca. CORS scoped to /upload/{ticket} alone, Origin checked before the ticket is touched, OPTIONS answers 204 and consumes nothing, exact origin echoed with Vary on every response including errors, no credentials, and the decision reuses /session's OriginPolicy rather than a second matcher. The renderer stopped setting Content-Length, which browsers forbid. The worker also had to widen CSP connect-src from ws:// to the http:// form of the same loopback hosts (frontend/index.html) — outside its stated files and correctly flagged: without it the POST is blocked before CORS is consulted, and it widens the scheme rather than the trust boundary since a page that may open a WebSocket to any loopback port already reaches every one. Verified in a real browser: POST 200, correct ACAO, file on the fixture's disk at exactly the payload size.

title: T8.1 The source ticket is never redeemed, names a path rather than bytes, and is bound to no tab
description:
Codex final review found the seam between T8 (mint) and T5 (redeem) was never built, plus two ways the ticket is weaker than R1/R2 claim.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Pick a file with the native picker on the desktop build: files.upload answers 'Invalid params: unknown sourceTicket' (ws_upload.go:1274). SourceTicketStore.Claim has no production caller.
2. Mint a ticket, rename the file, redeem it: the ticket names a pathname (ws_upload_source.go:185), so it now names different bytes.
3. Drop a file on tab A: the ticket is broadcast to every renderer (EmitFilesDropped, ws_upload_source.go:317) and is bound to no destination, so it can be paired with any bindingId the connection owns.

## Acceptance Criteria

- files.upload redeems a source ticket and uploads from it; a desktop picker upload works end to end.
- A ticket names an OPEN HANDLE or a re-attested identity, never a bare pathname: renaming or replacing the file between selection and redemption cannot change which bytes are sent.
- A ticket is bound to the session it was dropped on and is refused against any other binding.
- A drop on a LOCAL tab mints no upload credential at all.
- The dropped-files notification is addressed to that session's subscriber, not broadcast to every renderer.
- Each of the above has a test that fails against the current code.
close_reason: Merged as 73e99e53..30157b7e. files.upload redeems a source ticket; the ticket carries an ALREADY-OPEN read-only handle rather than a pathname, so the bytes cannot be swapped between a human choosing and the sink reading, with os.SameFile as the narrowing check; the ticket is bound to the session the file was dropped on and redemption refuses any other binding; a drop on a local tab mints nothing, decided by TabKind against the session registry.

title: T6.1 The upload surface holds a guard it must not, accepts a body it must refuse, and has no header deadline
description:
Codex adversarial review of the landed upload surface (fdabb57c, 0eeb4526) found three normative violations, three vacuous tests and a false ratchet justification.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Start an upload whose sink call ignores cancellation, then close the binding: cancelUploadsFor gives up after 5s and Registry.Close waits forever on a guard the transfer still holds.
2. POST a body longer than the declared Content-Length: the upload reports written instead of failing.
3. Open a loopback connection, send a partial POST /upload/ header block, hold it: no deadline applies, and no token or ticket was needed.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The binding use-guard is held for the synchronous call only; a running transfer holds no guard and teardown cancels rather than waits.
- A body exceeding the declared size fails the transfer and leaves the destination untouched.
- The route applies a header deadline that binds before Go finishes parsing headers.
- The goroutine baseline entry says what the code actually does.
- transferId, ticket and url carry patterns in the schema, not prose descriptions.
- Each of the above has a test that fails against the current code; the three vacuous tests named in the review are rewritten to distinguish what they claim.
close_reason: Merged as fb325b71..b4969ef8 (5 commits). D8 answered structurally rather than by tuning a timeout: Handle.Uploader() hands back the sink UNDER the guard, the guard is released when the RPC answers, and the transfer runs holding only the sink. What makes running unguarded safe is the lease, not hope — closing the provider closes the SFTP session and client, so a write racing a close fails and names what it stranded; it never writes through a torn-down lease and never holds the close open. The goroutine baseline justification was rewritten to say that. Header deadline is a wrapping net.Listener that arms a read deadline on accept and is cleared once the connection's target is known, so /session's long-lived upgrade is untouched and ReadHeaderTimeout stays 0. Long body now fails instead of reporting written; the test that blessed the defect was inverted. Three vacuous tests rewritten to distinguish what they claim. Schema constrains transferId, ticket and url with patterns.

title: An imported collection cannot be opened: the importer and the reader disagree on the manifest
description:
apiimport writes collection.json containing an apicoll.Collection. apicoll reads nocx-collection.json containing {schemaVersion, name} and decodes with DisallowUnknownFields.

Two packages, two formats, and no test anywhere crosses the seam: both sides are green because each tests its own half. This is the exact shape the spec's §6.2 version protocol was meant to prevent, and it slipped through because the importer was never asked to produce something the reader would accept.

Measured end to end: -32602 "folder has no collection manifest", then after renaming, -32603 "no migration from version 0".

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Import a Postman v2.1 export through api.import.postman.
2. Open the resulting directory with api.collections.open.
3. -32602, then -32603.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The importer writes the manifest the reader reads, at the name the reader looks for, at the version the reader understands.
- A test imports and then OPENS in the same test. One assertion, both packages — the seam is the thing under test, not either half.
- apicoll.Module's version protocol covers the written manifest.
close_reason: Fixed in 9deab779. apicoll.MarshalManifest owns the writing; apiimport no longer names the file or the shape and its collectionFileName is gone. One test imports and OPENS through apicoll's real reader, run against the unfixed code first (recorded in the worker report). The transport's defect-recording test went red on the fix and was retired per its own instruction, with the happy-path assertion restored.

title: The Import section cannot be opened: its disclosure is a literal false and a no-op
description:
api-pane.tsx renders <Section title="Import" collapsible open={false} onToggle={() => undefined}>. The open state is a literal and the toggle does nothing, so the Postman import has no entrance in the product at all.

Found by the epic's own end-to-end check (nocx-m61um) rather than by any unit test, and that is the point: all four importPostman call sites in frontend/src call the client or the store, so every existing test asserts what the code does and none asserts that a person can reach it. This is the connection-manager failure of AGENTS.md rule 1 repeating — every unit correct, the user's task impossible.

Measured: aria-expanded stays "false" across 14 polls after a real click, in two container runs.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open the API testing pane.
2. Click the Import section header.
3. Nothing opens.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The section opens and closes from a click, and its state is real.
- A test drives the import THROUGH THE UI — the entrance, the fields, the confirm — not through the client or the store. If that test would have failed before this fix, say so in the bead.
- The e2e check of nocx-m61um gets past this step.
close_reason: Fixed in e5a9c0d8. The Section's open state is real and the toggle works. A test drives import THROUGH THE UI — entrance, fields, confirm — which is what nothing did before: all four importPostman call sites drove the client or the store.

title: The renderer never sends envRelPath, so {{baseUrl}} can never resolve from the UI
description:
envRelPath appears nowhere in frontend/ or contracts/. The send path resolves variables against an environment the renderer has no way to name, so every collection whose URL is {{baseUrl}}/... — which is nearly every Postman export — fails from the product while working over the control plane.

Measured: -32603 '"{{baseUrl}}/users" is not an absolute URL'; with an absolute URL substituted, 'the auth variable "token" is not bound in this environment'.

The backend half is correct and tested. What is missing is that the environment a person picked never reaches it.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open an imported collection with {{baseUrl}}/users and an environment defining baseUrl.
2. Press Send.
3. -32603, the variable unresolved.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The chosen environment reaches the backend on send, and the contract carries it.
- The panel has a way to CHOOSE an environment, and a test drives that choice through the UI.
- A request using {{baseUrl}} and a bound secret variable succeeds from the product, not only over the wire.
close_reason: Fixed in e5a9c0d8. The chosen environment reaches the backend on send and the contract carries it. Underneath was a second hole the fix had to open first: apicoll.ListEnvironments had NO CALLER outside its own tests, and collections.open/.list/.create carried no environments, so no renderer could have offered a choice.

title: The remote command is bounded where it leaves the process, not only where it is built
description:
nocx-m8jwn removed the ~92 KiB command that carried the bundle and two bearers, and
declared MaxCarrierLen = 1024. That bound is enforced in ONE producer
(shellintegration/carrier.go:605). Nothing stops a future caller -- or a second
producer -- from handing a long command to the wire, which is exactly how the first
one arrived: the cap that existed (maxFullLauncherLen, 120 KiB) lived beside the
builder, and the measured command sat at 75% of it with nobody watching.

The owner's requirement is that the situation cannot recur PHYSICALLY. That means the
bound belongs at the point of no return -- the call that hands bytes to OpenSSH -- so
no producer can bypass it, present or future.

Three seams carry a remote command today: internal/ssh/ssh_real.go:984
session.Start(startCmd) (the managed carrier), internal/ssh/ssh_discovery.go
discoveryConn.Exec (the discovery probes), and internal/ssh/mux Master.Session
encoding req.Command (the typed path). The local-argv seam is already closed by
construction: the typed path never appends a command to the user's ssh argv and
refuses a configured RemoteCommand (typed_wrap.go:238).

The number cannot be one symbol: AD-8 forbids internal/ssh depending on
internal/shellintegration (nocx-ei04, app.go:1834), and mux is a leaf. So it is one
number declared in three places and pinned equal by a conformance test at the
composition root -- the same shape as the contracts/ pattern.

## Steps to Reproduce

Hand any of the three seams a command longer than the declared bound -- today they
all accept it. Concretely: call ssh.RealClient's start path with a RemoteLauncher
whose StartCommand returns 200 KiB, or call discoveryConn.Exec with a 200 KiB cmd,
or mux.Master.Session with a 200 KiB SessionRequest.Command. Each puts the whole
string on the wire. On Linux the far side's execve then refuses it at
MAX_ARG_STRLEN (131072 bytes, measured), so the failure surfaces as an opaque
remote error rather than as our own refusal.

## Acceptance Criteria

Each of the three seams refuses a command at or above the bound, with a named error
and no side effect. A test per seam drives the refusal through the seam's own API and
asserts nothing was sent. A conformance test asserts shellintegration.MaxCarrierLen,
ssh.MaxRemoteCommandLen and mux.MaxCommandLen are one number, so raising any one of
them alone goes red. Refusal never truncates.
close_reason: The bound moved from the producer to the point of no return: all three seams that put a remote command on a wire refuse one at or above 1024 bytes before sending, never truncating -- session.Start in ssh_real.go (falls open to a plain shell with the new ReasonCommandTooLong), discoveryConn.Exec, and mux.Master.Session (refuses before it dials). The local-argv seam needed no guard: typed_wrap.go already refuses a configured RemoteCommand and never appends one to the user's argv. One number in three packages with TestTheBoundOnARemoteCommandIsOneNumber in internal/app pinning them equal -- verified red by raising mux.MaxCommandLen alone. Two gaps found while writing it and closed here: the contract's reason enum was guarded only for bootstrap outcomes and refusal-matrix rows, so a RefusalReason added anywhere else reached the wire undeclared -- the guard now parses the vocabulary itself and caught this commit's own addition; and discovery classified our refusal as transient, which would have retried a permanently-unsendable probe forever, now terminal and naming nocx rather than the host. The discovery probe measures 785 of 1024 bytes, recorded so growth walks past a decision. Commits a920e2e0, b5f3e854. Full gate green: containerized go test -race (57 pkgs), ci-linux both keyring variants, ci-frontend, e2e both browsers (359 passed), deadcode ratchet all-baselined with the baseline file untouched.

title: A domain whose capability mint failed authenticates anyone sending zero bytes
description:
Found while implementing nocx-m8jwn.5; it predates that epic and is not caused by it.

randomCapability tolerates a failed random read and leaves the capability zero-valued. The authentication check is an equality comparison against the expected value, and two zero values compare equal — so a domain whose mint silently failed accepts a frame from anyone who sends the corresponding run of zero bytes. The failure mode is quiet in exactly the wrong direction: a mint that could not get randomness does not refuse, it produces a bearer that everything matches.

nocx-m8jwn.5 closed the immediate hole by refusing a zero capability outright at ingest. That is the right guard and it is not the whole fix: the mint itself should fail loudly rather than return a value nobody can distinguish from a valid one, and the same shape should be checked wherever else a secret is minted from a random read (the recovery fence, and any per-epoch value added later).

## Steps to Reproduce

Make the random source fail or return short at the moment the per-epoch capability is minted (inject at the seam; the production path reads from crypto/rand). The domain is created anyway with a zero-valued capability. Then present a frame whose capability field is the same run of zero bytes: the equality check against the expected value passes and the frame is accepted as authenticated.

## Acceptance Criteria

A failed random read at mint time produces a named error and no domain, rather than a zero-valued capability; a test injects the failure and asserts no domain is created and nothing is offered to a shell. Every other place in the tree that mints a secret from a random read is enumerated in the fix and each either fails loudly on a short or failed read or is shown not to be reachable with a zero value. The ingest-side refusal added by nocx-m8jwn.5 stays, and a test asserts both guards independently so removing either one goes red.
close_reason: randomCapability and randomFence now fail loudly: a failed or short read is ErrNoRandomness and NO domain is minted, tested by injecting both shapes and asserting no handle, no registry entry and a free lane. The ingest-side refusal of a zero capability stays and is asserted independently by the existing TestCapabilityValidity_AZeroCapabilityAuthenticatesNobody, which writes the zero straight onto a registered domain -- delete either guard and exactly one test goes red. The enumeration the criterion asks for was done and acted on: every tolerant read in the lifecycle family is now a refusal -- the kernel's domain, request and attempt identifiers, the publisher's establishment generation (a discriminator against a stale actor, compared with !=, and echoed by the far side), and the transport and lane identifiers in both lifecyclechannel and lifecycleremote, where a zero value made every adapter carry the same pair and the kernel's binding check is an equality on exactly that. Each has a failure-injection test; each verified red by reverting its guard (the remote one printed transport=tpt-0000000000000000 lane=lane-0000000000000000 in the log). Four tolerant identifier mints OUTSIDE this family are prior deliberate decisions with their reasons recorded next to them, so they are enumerated in nocx-px48p rather than re-decided inside a bugfix. Commit 6c491ac3.

title: Design: the integration bundle travels on the channel, not in the exec command
description:
The managed path delivers the bundle twice: EnsureInstalledRemote publishes it
over SFTP, and then the launcher pushes the same bundle again as an ~89 KiB SSH
exec command. Measured on main: auto=91198 B, bash=87518, zsh=87633, posix=85934,
against our own maxFullLauncherLen of 120 KiB.

An exec command of that size is unsafe on three counts: an SSH proxy that records
the command cannot always carry an event that large, we sit at 75% of the
MAX_ARG_STRLEN-derived cap with no headroom, and the per-session capability and
recovery fence travel verbatim in the command text.

Design session to choose the carrier and the fallbacks.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The option space is enumerated with costs, preconditions and fail-open behaviour per option.
- A design doc is written to .internal/specs/ and approved by the owner.
- The relationship to the accepted delivery-modes design (3.2/3.3), ADR-0022 and
  ADR-0024's open question is stated explicitly, so nothing settled is re-decided by accident.
close_reason: Design written and reviewed to approval across four adversarial passes; decomposed into epic nocx-m8jwn with P1-P10 and a front of three. Spec: .internal/specs/2026-08-20-integration-delivery-carrier-design.md

title: The AppImage bundles libwebkit2gtk but not its helper processes, so it dies on any host without the Debian multiarch path
description:
## Steps to Reproduce

1. Take nocx-0.2.0-linux-amd64.AppImage from the release.
2. Run it on a distribution that is not Debian/Ubuntu (reported on CachyOS/Arch;
   reproduced in a container by deleting /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/webkit2gtk-4.1).
3. The backend starts, the ws server binds, and WebKitGTK then dies before the
   window exists:

   ERROR: Unable to spawn a new child process: Failed to spawn child process
   "/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/webkit2gtk-4.1/WebKitNetworkProcess"
   (No such file or directory)
   SIGTRAP: trace trap ... signal arrived during cgo execution

## Diagnosis (measured, not reasoned)

linuxdeploy-plugin-gtk walks ldd and copies libwebkit2gtk-4.1.so.0 into the
AppDir. WebKitGTK's helper PROCESSES are not linked by anything, so ldd never
sees them and nothing copies them: WebKitWebProcess, WebKitNetworkProcess,
WebKitGPUProcess and injected-bundle/libwebkit2gtkinjectedbundle.so live in a
libexec directory. The bundled library looks them up at the absolute path
compiled into it at build time -- on ubuntu-22.04 that is
/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/webkit2gtk-4.1. The error naming the Debian multiarch
path on an Arch box proves the BUNDLED (Ubuntu) library was loaded and went
looking outside the AppImage.

So the AppImage only ever "worked" on hosts that happen to have that path
populated -- Debian and Ubuntu -- where it silently used the HOST's helper
binaries against the bundled library. Everywhere else (Arch, Fedora, NixOS,
openSUSE) it cannot start at all. README's support envelope states the
opposite: "does not depend on the host's libgtk-3 or libwebkit2gtk-4.1".

Three candidates were tested in a container against the real ubuntu-22.04
webkit 2.50.4, reproducing the reported error exactly:

1. Copy the helpers into the AppDir mirroring their absolute path (what wails
   v3's own internal/commands/appimage.go does -- our workflow is the odd one
   out in not doing it). FAILS, identically: the lookup is absolute, so the
   AppDir copy is never consulted.
2. WEBKIT_EXEC_PATH. FAILS: the string is absent from Ubuntu's build (gated
   behind ENABLE(DEVELOPER_MODE) upstream). WEBKIT_INJECTED_BUNDLE_PATH and
   WEBKIT_DISABLE_SANDBOX_THIS_IS_DANGEROUS are present; the exec path has no
   env override at all, and the library knows nothing about AppImage/APPDIR.
3. Patch the compiled-in path in the bundled .so to an equal-length path the
   AppRun can create (a symlink under /tmp), so the suffixes of both baked
   strings survive. WORKS: the webview comes up on a host with no webkit at all.

The fix decision (patch-and-symlink vs dropping the bundled webkit for a
documented host dependency) moves ADR-0007's support envelope and wants an ADR
note either way.
acceptance_criteria:
Assertions, not prose:

1. AppDir/usr/lib/<multiarch>/webkit2gtk-4.1/ contains WebKitWebProcess,
   WebKitNetworkProcess, WebKitGPUProcess and injected-bundle/
   libwebkit2gtkinjectedbundle.so after the packaging step.
2. Running the packaged AppImage under Xvfb in a container that has NO
   webkit2gtk and NO gtk3 installed reaches a live webview: the run does not
   print "Unable to spawn a new child process" and does not exit on SIGTRAP.
   This check runs in the release workflow and FAILS when the helpers are
   removed from the AppDir (prove it can go red -- a --version smoke test never
   creates a webview, which is why this shipped).
3. The same run on a host that DOES have a system webkit resolves the helpers
   from inside the AppImage, not from /usr (assert the spawned helper path).
4. README's support envelope and ADR-0007 say what is actually true of the
   artefact.
notes:
VERIFIED ON THE REAL ARTEFACT (archlinux container, nocx-0.2.0-linux-amd64.AppImage
downloaded from the release, extracted; host has neither gtk3 nor webkit2gtk):

  V0  shipped file, untouched .......... FAIL, the reported error verbatim:
      Failed to spawn child process "/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/webkit2gtk-4.1/
      WebKitNetworkProcess" (No such file or directory)
  V1  helpers + absolute patch to a /tmp path + AppRun symlink ....... PASS
  V2  helpers + RELATIVE equal-length patch + `cd "$this_dir"` in AppRun  PASS

PASS means the backend logged `session opened … kind=local`: the webview loaded,
the renderer opened the websocket and a PTY session started. Not "the process
survived".

The shipped file confirms the diagnosis directly: usr/lib/libwebkit2gtk-4.1.so.0
is bundled (90 MB) and `find` for WebKit*Process / *injectedbundle* in the
extracted AppDir returns NOTHING. The two baked strings are present in the
shipped library and WEBKIT_EXEC_PATH is absent from it.

DECIDED SHAPE (V2). The equal-length RELATIVE patch, reviewed by codex, which
rejected V1's /tmp symlink for three reasons that stand: `ln -sfn` + `readlink`
guards one observation while WebKit resolves the name later (TOCTOU); the build
hash is public, so the name is predictable and can be squatted permanently under
a sticky /tmp (denial of service per build); and two copies of one build from
different paths fight over one global link, so an update or a rollback can send
newly spawned WebKit children into another image's libraries.

  old: /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/webkit2gtk-4.1   (40 bytes)
  new: usr//lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/webkit2gtk-4.1   (40 bytes, // pads the length)

Equal length is what preserves the second string's "/injected-bundle/" suffix and
moves no ELF offsets. (An upstream report tried `sed s|/usr|./usr|g`, which
LENGTHENS the string and corrupts the ELF — that is why theirs "did nothing".)

MEASURED PROPERTIES OF V2:
- The launch cwd is irrelevant: PASS from /work, from / and from /root. The `cd`
  in AppRun is what makes it deterministic.
- The `cd` is load-bearing: same patch without it FAILs. The mechanism is proven
  in both directions.
- Safe for this app: internal/pty/pty_local.go resolveCwd already falls back to
  $HOME when Cwd is unset (a GUI app's cwd is useless), and os.Getwd() appears
  nowhere in non-test code. So the AppRun cd cannot leak into a user's shell.

NEGATIVE MUTATIONS (each helper must be able to turn the release check red):
- remove WebKitNetworkProcess ............ FAIL, as required
- remove WebKitWebProcess ................ FAIL, as required
- remove injected bundle ................. PASS -- NOT load-bearing for our happy
  path. Do not write a red-test around it and do not claim it is required; the
  renderer talks over our own websocket (AD-1), not through a web extension. Open
  question: whether any wails native call needs it. Ship it regardless (cheap),
  but the acceptance criterion above is corrected: THREE files gate the check.

ALSO FOUND, and it is a second untrue sentence in the support envelope: on a bare
Arch the AppImage does not start at all for want of libfontconfig.so.1,
libfribidi.so.0 and libharfbuzz.so.0 -- linuxdeploy excludes them deliberately so
fonts come from the host. Every real desktop has them, which is why nobody hit
it, but "single self-contained file" is wrong twice over.

STILL TO COVER (from the codex review, not yet measured): helper dependency
closure (run linuxdeploy's deploy over each helper, or the failure merely moves to
a missing helper-only DT_NEEDED); patch the resolved regular file once, not a
symlink chain; assert the occurrence count is exactly 2 and fail packaging when it
changes; HTTPS inside the webview needs glib-networking, whose GIO TLS modules are
not in any ldd closure; WebKit's bubblewrap sandbox where unprivileged user
namespaces are disabled; NO_STRIP on .relr.dyn toolchains; and
WEBKIT_DISABLE_DMABUF_RENDERER on NVIDIA.
close_reason: Fixed and merged in #100 (f994efa9). Helpers ship in the AppDir, the bundled library's baked path is patched to an equal-length relative one, and an AppRun hook chdirs into the AppDir. Verified on Arch with no GTK and no WebKitGTK: a terminal session opens, both helpers execve from inside the AppDir, no helper is reached outside it, and the chdir stays invisible to the user's shell. Three mutations each go red; the same gate goes red on the published v0.2.0. ADR-0035 records the decision.

title: The release's macOS build has never run: wails3 build-assets is called with flags it does not define
description:
## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run release.yml on main (`gh workflow run release.yml --ref main`) — the
   dry run, which builds and verifies everything and publishes nothing.
2. `build-macos` fails in its FIRST step, "Generate macOS bundle assets":

   ```
   ERROR  Error: flag provided but not defined: -binary-name
          See 'wails generate build-assets --help' for usage
   ```

## Actual

The step passes kebab-case flags:

    wails3 generate build-assets -dir … -binary-name … -product-name …
      -product-identifier … -product-version …

`wails3` derives a flag name from the STRUCT FIELD NAME, lowercased and
nothing else — clir@v1.3.0 command.go:258, `name =
strings.ToLower(t.Elem().Field(i).Name)`, used whenever the field carries no
`name:` tag. `BuildAssetsOptions` (wails/v3@v3.0.0-beta.9
internal/commands/build-assets.go:34) tags only `description:` and `default:`,
so the flags are `-binaryname`, `-productname`, `-productidentifier`,
`-productversion`. Parsing stops at the first one it does not know, which is
why only `-binary-name` is named in the error.

The sibling step is right and shows the convention: `wails3 generate icons`
passes `-input`, `-macfilename`, `-windowsfilename`, which match
`IconsOptions`' fields exactly.

## When it broke, and why nothing said so

Not a regression in the flags — the step is NEW. v0.1.0 (2026-08-12) shipped
before the Wails v3 migration (8004fd72), and its release.yml had no `wails3`
in it at all. So the macOS half of the release pipeline has never once produced
an artefact: five dry runs since have all failed in build-macos (four on
release/pr91-home-projections on 2026-08-19, one on main on 2026-08-20).

`ci.yml` does not build the .app, and release.yml only runs on a `v*` tag or an
explicit dispatch — so the whole macOS packaging path is outside the gate that
runs on every PR. That is the reason a broken step sat on main for eight days
with every PR green.

## Expected

`gh workflow run release.yml --ref main` reaches `sign`, so a tag can produce a
macOS artefact.

## Acceptance Criteria

Given main, when release.yml is dispatched as a dry run, then `build-macos`
completes and its Smoke checks pass (universal Mach-O carries both slices, the
plist and the linked binary agree on the version, the ad-hoc signature
verifies) — asserted by the run reaching `sign`, which is skipped only for
want of a tag rather than for want of an artefact.

title: Settings intermittently fails to render, taking a third of the e2e suite with it
description:
## Steps to Reproduce
1. On feat/workspaces, run: PW_PROJECTS=chromium e2e/run-in-container.sh e2e/connection-password.spec.ts --repeat-each=5
2. Some repeats fail; which ones changes between runs.
3. Every failure is the same: expect(locator('.ui-page__scroll')).toBeVisible() — 'element(s) not found', raised from the spec's setupVault/openAIEndpoints helper. The Settings page did not mount.

## Expected
The Settings tab renders its page every time it is opened.

## Actual
It intermittently mounts with no content. Twelve e2e files reach Settings to get at vault, secrets, connections or AI endpoints, so each fails at its first step and the failure is attributed to whatever that spec was about — which is why the suite's failing set looks like a vault problem and is not one.

## Evidence
This was the first CI run in feat/workspaces' history: every prior run skipped, because the PR was a draft and every job in ci.yml is guarded on !draft. 143 commits went unchecked by e2e.

- CI, chromium: 132 passed / 35 failed / 4 did not run. webkit: 117 / 47 / 5.
- Local containerized run, same image, at HEAD b17cf7cf: 134 / 33 / 4.
- Same, at b39e78e6 (before the nocx-l21ib.1-.7 batch): 139 / 28 / 4.

So about 28 failures pre-date that batch. The rest is flake rather than regression: with --repeat-each=5 on connection-password.spec.ts, HEAD gave 6 passed / 4 failed and b39e78e6 gave 3 passed / 7 failed. The baseline is worse. Which spec inside a file fails also changes between runs of the same commit (:195 in one, :299 in the next) with the identical symptom — a race in the render, not a defect in whichever spec catches it.

## Why it matters beyond the suite
This is the product's Settings page failing to appear. A user who hits it sees an empty panel.

## Where to start
