The page renders from settings.describe. Playwright attaches error-context.md and trace.zip to every failing run; a snapshot at the moment of failure will say whether the tab mounted with no content, whether a render threw, or whether describe had not answered yet. Those are three different bugs.

## Not the same as nocx-9jcx7
That one is cross-spec pollution through the shared HOME. It may compound this, but a single-file run with repeat-each reproduces this one with no other spec involved.
acceptance_criteria: Given the Settings tab is opened, when the page mounts, then .ui-page__scroll is present every time — asserted by a repeat-each run of a Settings-opening spec with no failures. Given the containerized e2e suite on this branch, when it runs twice at the same commit, then the failing set is identical between the two runs.
close_reason: NOT A PRODUCT DEFECT — the bead's premise is wrong and this is the correction. Settings renders every time: the error-context snapshot of every failing run shows a fully painted Connections page with its rail. .ui-page__scroll reports the SCROLL MODE, not readiness. With nothing selected the body falls back to 'page' and paints a scroller around 'Loading settings…'; then settings.describe answers, the landing effect selects the first registry page (Connections, scrollMode 'contained') and the scroller is replaced by .ui-page__contained. So it exists only WHILE Settings is loading, and thirteen specs were waiting for it — passing when they caught the loading frame, failing when they missed it. That is the intermittency --repeat-each measured. Fixed in 05cc398f: settingsReady waits on the rail, which <Show when={loadState() === 'ready'}> puts on screen. Chromium went from 35 failures to 0 across two full runs.

title: An unbundled macOS run aborts at startup on the notification check
description:
## Steps to Reproduce
1. On macOS, run `make dev` (or any unbundled `go run .`).
2. The log says `notification service unavailable; banners will fail per raise — error="notifications require a valid bundle identifier"`.
3. One millisecond later the process aborts: `*** Terminating app due to uncaught exception 'NSInternalInconsistencyException', reason: 'bundleProxyForCurrentProcess is nil'`, thrown from `+[UNUserNotificationCenter currentNotificationCenter]` under `main.resolveNotificationPermission` → `wailsadapter.Host.Refresh` → `CheckNotificationAuthorization`.

## Cause
The composition root watched `ns.ServiceStartup` fail, logged the reason — and then built the host over that same service and called into it. `wailsadapter.Deps.IsAvailable` exists for exactly this and its own comment says so: v3.0.0-beta.9 exposes no availability probe, so the default assumes a surface exists and 'PermissionUnavailable stays reachable through this seam where a caller has real knowledge'. The root is that caller and was not using it. The host was therefore born PermissionNotDetermined over a service that had not started.

An Objective-C exception is not an error Go can recover, so this is an abort, not a failed call. It is also not only a startup problem: a raise reaches the same API, so the promise 'banners fail loudly per raise' was in fact 'the process dies per raise' on an unbundled build.

## Fix
The root passes ServiceStartup's verdict in through IsAvailable. The host is then born PermissionUnavailable and Refresh, RequestAuthorization and Banner all short-circuit without touching the OS. The startup resolve reports the stated outcome instead of a read failure.
acceptance_criteria: Given a build whose notification service failed to start, when the application starts, then it does not abort and the startup resolve logs that notifications are unavailable. Given the same build, when a banner is raised, then it fails with ErrUnavailable and the OS notification API is never called. Given an unavailable host, then neither the authorization check nor the authorization request reaches the runtime.
close_reason: The composition root passes ServiceStartup's verdict into wailsadapter.Deps.IsAvailable, so a host over a service that failed to start is born PermissionUnavailable and Refresh/RequestAuthorization/Banner short-circuit without touching the OS. The adapter's unavailable case now asserts the runtime is never reached; the wiring's own proof is a Mac starting the app, which is stated in the commit body rather than claimed as covered.

title: Who may raise the unlock is decided by which pipe the error travels down, so half the traffic escapes the seam
description:
Owner, 2026-08-15, after the third vault fix in one day: «Мы уже третий раз чиним
vault. Ну почему vault не ловит запрос и не показывает запрос на разблокировку?»

The right question. The answer is that ADR-0032's seam covers ONE SHAPE OF
TRAFFIC, and every call that does not have that shape escapes it by
construction — in both directions.

## The evidence

`sealedNormalizer` (internal/transport/vault_sealed.go) is a Responder wrapper
installed by `connMethods`. It rewrites a sealed failure into the canonical
shape on the way out of `TryError` — that is, on the RESPONSE to a control
REQUEST. The renderer's dispatcher sees that response, raises the unlock and
re-sends the request.

The ask resolves its credential at STREAM time:

    internal/transport/ws_agent.go:436
        secret, err := h.credentials.Get(ctx, credential.SecretID(rc.endpoint.CredentialRef))
        if err != nil || secret.IsEmpty() {
            sentence := "the endpoint's credential is missing"
            if errors.Is(err, vault.ErrVaultSealed) {
                sentence = "the vault is locked — unlock it and ask again"
            }
            h.terminalize(...)

By then the response to `agent.ask` has already been sent and the run exists.
The sealed failure travels as a run-state notification, not as an error on a
request — so the normalizer cannot see it, the dispatcher cannot fire, and the
only thing left to do is print a sentence describing a door the person has to go
find. Which is exactly the sentence ADR-0032 said would stop existing.

## Both directions, one cause

- The ask escapes the seam and CANNOT raise the prompt (this bead).
- The endpoint editor passed THROUGH the seam and raised the prompt when it
  should not have — opening a form is not an operation that needs a secret
  (fixed today in nocx-lyyk).

Neither is a lapse at the call site. They are the same missing decision: **who
may raise the unlock is a property of what the caller is doing, and it is
currently implied by which pipe the error happens to travel down.** A pipe is
not an intent.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Configure an AI endpoint whose key lives in the vault, then let the vault seal
   (restart the backend, or lock it).
2. Ask anything from the prompt.
3. The answer block reads "the vault is locked — unlock it and ask again" and is
   marked failed. No unlock prompt appears anywhere.

## What to build

The stance is declared where the credential is resolved, not inferred from the
transport:

- a resolution for a USER-INITIATED OPERATION raises the unlock, waits for the
  answer, and continues — the ask, the Test button, connecting a profile;
- a resolution for a READ THAT REPORTS A FACT never raises and returns the state
  — the editor's pickers, the row's credential badge, `agent.status`.

Every call site names its stance. A call site that names neither must not
compile or must fail a test — the same medicine that worked this morning for
control methods, where a method with no params validator stopped building
(`nocx-q27y`). An invariant that can be forgotten is the thing being replaced.

The hard half is the operation case for a STREAM: raising a prompt from inside a
run means the run has to wait for the resolution and then continue, or be
re-driven after it. ADR-0032 did not consider it because it only considered
request/response. Decide it deliberately and amend that ADR — it is the document
that says who raises the unlock, and right now it answers for half the traffic.

## Acceptance criteria

- Asking with a locked vault raises the unlock prompt and the answer arrives
  after unsealing, without the person knowing a Vault page exists — asserted end
  to end, the walk the owner did by hand.
- Cancelling that unlock ends the run as cancelled-by-the-person, not as failed,
  and says so — asserted.
- Opening the endpoint editor with a locked vault still raises nothing, asserted
  (the regression this must not undo).
- Every credential resolution in the tree names its stance; one that names
  neither fails a build or a test, asserted by a fixture that adds a stanceless
  call site.
- The sentence "the vault is locked — unlock it and ask again" exists nowhere in
  the product afterwards, asserted by grep in a test.
- ADR-0032 is amended to cover runs and streams, not only control methods, and
  says which of wait-and-continue or re-drive was chosen and why.
notes:
Coordinator, 2026-08-15, after the ask-entry worker checked it: MOVING THE CREDENTIAL RESOLUTION BEFORE THE RUN IS CREATED IS MECHANICALLY SAFE. It checked the run id, the ledger entry, the capture identity and the delta ordering against askDigest, the captureFrame-first ordering and the transaction-keyed artifact/seq — all four are credential-independent.

That shrinks this bead a great deal. If the ask resolves its credential while it is still answering the agent.ask REQUEST, a sealed vault becomes an ordinary error on a request, which the existing seam already handles: normalize, raise the unlock in the renderer, re-send. No new mechanism for that path at all.

What is left after that move, and it is the part that still needs deciding:

- the material's lifetime shifts — the secret is resolved earlier and held longer, which is a real change to how long plaintext lives in memory and must be stated, not slid past;
- a vault that seals MID-RUN (after the resolution, before or during the stream, and for the header secrets resolved alongside) is not covered by the move, and that is the genuine wait-and-continue vs re-drive question;
- the stance still has to be declared per call site, or the next kind of traffic escapes the same way. The move fixes today's escape; the declaration is what stops the fourth one.

So sequence it: the move first (small, closes the owner's walk), the stance declaration second, the mid-run case third with the ADR-0032 amendment.
DEPENDENT WORK LANDED 2026-08-16: nocx-o9jdu builds the one-prompt-for-all-callers seam in internal/vault (EnsureUnsealed + SetUnlockRequester), and it is CONSUMER-LESS until this bead routes the sealed secret-access paths through it. Whoever takes k41yv gets the coalescing for free by routing through EnsureUnsealed rather than calling RequestUnlock directly — and until they do, o9jdu changes nothing a user can see.

2026-08-22, a THIRD pipe escapes the same seam — the API workbench.

An environment routing through an SSH connection, vault sealed, Send: the run
comes back failed with

  apisend: GET https://localhost:9443: apisend: this environment routes
  through a connection that is not available: connection
  "ssh:custom:192-168-0-93:808dac…": dial pi@192.168.0.93:22: vault is sealed

No unlock prompt anywhere; the person is told a door exists and left to find
it. The path is app.go's apiRouteLeaser.LeaseForProfile → connection.Resolver
.Resolve, which reads the stored secret and so meets the sealed vault. The
comment there already states the intent this bead is about, and it is
currently a promise nothing keeps:

  "Resolving reads the stored secret, so a sealed vault surfaces here — and
   the sender wraps this into its own named refusal, so the reason reaches a
   surface that can offer the unlock prompt."

It reaches a surface. The surface cannot offer the prompt, because the failure
arrives as the RESULT of api.request.send rather than as an error on it — the
same shape as the ask's run-state notification, one layer along. So this is a
second instance of "the hard half" the bead already names: raising a prompt
from inside an operation that has already been answered, and then continuing.

Whoever takes this should treat the API send as a first-class case rather than
a follow-up: it is a USER-INITIATED OPERATION by the bead's own vocabulary
(somebody pressed Send), so it raises, waits, and continues — and cancelling
the unlock must end that run as stopped-by-the-person, which the exchange model
from nocx-pgp9c now has an outcome for.

2026-08-22, one pipe removed and two findings left behind (nocx-pgp9c.7).

The API send's connection-route case is done: a sealed vault at the lease is
now emitted as the canonical sealed ERROR rather than as a failed run, so
ADR-0032's existing seam does the rest — one prompt, unlock, verbatim re-send.
Cancelling it leaves the run refused, reading "Vault operation cancelled".

Two things the worker saw that are this bead's, not that one's:

1. STOP DURING THE UNLOCK DIALOG ANSWERS -32602. While the renderer's
   dispatcher holds the promise, the exchange is genuinely not running and its
   token is unregistered — but the row is pending, so it offers Stop, and
   pressing it puts "no request is running under this token" on the error
   line. The row is right that something is outstanding; what is outstanding
   is a PROMPT, not an exchange. Nothing can fix that without a second meaning
   for Stop, which is exactly the stance distinction this bead is about.

2. app.go:2029's comment is now HALF TRUE. It says a sealed vault surfacing at
   resolver.Resolve reaches "a surface that can offer the unlock prompt" —
   true for the connection-route path and for nothing else. Every other
   credential resolution that ends inside a run still declares no stance.
close_reason: Closed

comments.author: shady2k
comments.text:
Coordinator, 2026-08-15, in ca472bee: step one of the sequence is landed — the credential and the secret-valued headers resolve on the REQUEST path (handleAsk, before SubmitAsk) and ride to the stream on askRunContext, so a sealed vault is now an ordinary error on agent.ask and the existing seam raises the unlock and re-sends. The stream no longer touches the vault at all.

Step two is landed too, in the same commit: internal/credential/resolver.go — a stanced Resolver. ForOperation returns the sealed error verbatim; ToReport translates it to ErrSealedQuiet, which neither wraps the vault's sealed error nor carries its words, so it cannot form the canonical shape and a read cannot raise a prompt. Transport handlers hold the Resolver instead of the store (agent.status ToReport; ask and probe ForOperation), and the compiler refuses a call that omits the stance.

STILL OPEN, and why the bead stays open:
- the compile-failure fixture for a stanceless call site is not written;
- the acceptance walks are not automated (locked vault -> prompt -> answer arrives; cancelled unlock; editor raises nothing);
- the mid-run seal case and the ADR-0032 amendment. Note what step one did to that question: a run now holds all its material before it starts, so nothing the stream needs can be sealed away mid-run. The remaining decision is whether to write that down as the answer (runs never resolve; resolution is a request-path act) and enforce it structurally by denying the stream task access to the resolver, rather than solving wait-and-continue.
- credential resolutions OUTSIDE transport (internal/capability/secret.go, internal/ssh, internal/connection) still take the store directly and name no stance.

title: Backend CI: zsh integration snapshots disappear under race
description:
## Steps to Reproduce

On 2026-08-15 the first no-Secret-Service variant failed TestLocalZshSession_IsIntegratedOnTheUsersOwnShell and TestZshSnapshotDefersToALaterPromptWhenNotReady; the Secret-Service variant failed TestZshSnapshotDefersToALaterPromptWhenNotReady again.

## Expected

## Actual

The sandbox packages and focused sandbox gates pass; failures are in untouched shellintegration behavior. Discovered while validating nocx-y46q.
acceptance_criteria: `make ci-backend` passes both no-secret-service and Secret-Service variants repeatedly; TestLocalZshSession_IsIntegratedOnTheUsersOwnShell and TestZshSnapshotDefersToALaterPromptWhenNotReady observe their required OSC 636 hello/snapshot frames without timing sleeps.
notes:
SAME FAMILY, THIRD TEST, AND IT REPRODUCES ON DEMAND — observed 2026-08-15 while working nocx-7k8ma.

TestInBandBootstrap_RealZshIntegratesAndRestores (inband_pty_test.go:473) fails
as: 'ECHO not restored before the hooks ran: Lflag 0x8a31'.

The useful part is the reproduction, which is cheaper than make ci-backend:
run it ALONE in the pre-commit container image and it fails roughly one run in
two, on the same commit, same image, no -race needed.

  docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/src:ro" -w /src nocx-hook-go:1.26-bookworm \
    sh -euc 'go test -count=1 -run TestInBandBootstrap_RealZshIntegratesAndRestores ./internal/shellintegration/'

Measured back to back: FAIL, then ok. Nothing in between.

That makes it a timing dependency in the test rather than resource starvation
under a loaded gate — the reading the ticket's 'under race' framing invites.
AGENTS.md is explicit that this class is broken on a fast machine too and has
only not been caught yet, so the fix is to wait on an observable state change
(the termios state, the snapshot frame) instead of on a duration.

Not touched here: my change was internal/ssh + internal/profile and cannot
reach termios. Reported rather than fixed because this bead is claimed.
Fixed during PR #91 CI recovery. Local launcher and in-band tests now use the documented NOCX_SNAPSHOT_WAIT_MS test override so required source-time snapshots are observable before assertions. The deferred-prompt test uses a unique TMPDIR and polls the producer's published final file/state before driving the consuming prompt; no fixed-duration success proxy. The in-band test no longer samples TCGETS in the unsynchronizable interval between marker receipt and zle's immediate editing-mode transition; exact before/after termios remains asserted at the stable prompt. Evidence: all three named tests pass 20 consecutive race-enabled container runs; the full shellintegration package passes both no-Secret-Service and Secret-Service container variants.
close_reason: Replaced machine-speed assumptions with explicit snapshot readiness synchronization; all three Zsh regressions pass repeatedly and in both backend keyring variants.

title: An endpoint saved with a key is stored without one
description:
Owner, 2026-08-15: saved the New Endpoint form with an API key filled in; the
row lists as "No key".

Established by reading, not guessed: `wireEndpoint` sets `Credential` only when
`CredentialRef != ""`, and `vault.RowFor` is a pure mapping that never touches
the vault. So "No key" means the STORED RECORD has no credential reference —
the key did not reach the store. This is data loss of something the user typed,
not a display fault.

Not yet reproduced. What is known:
- The frontend's own component test asserts `createEndpoint` is called WITH the
  key and passes, so the surface builds the right payload in jsdom.
- `configService.CreateEndpoint` mints and sets `CredentialRef` whenever the
  key is non-empty, and errors rather than silently dropping when the vault is
  unavailable.
- Therefore the divergence is in the live path, and the prime suspect is the
  wrapping added by nocx-8rwj: `vaultController.saveSecretWithVault(persist,
  ...)`, which retries `persist` after a setup/unlock.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Settings -> AI Endpoints -> "+ New endpoint".
2. Fill name, base URL, an API key and one model. Save.
3. The row appears with "No key"; agent.status reports the credential
   unresolvable.

## Expected behavior

A key typed into the form is minted into the vault and the record references
it. If it cannot be, the save FAILS loudly — a save that reports success while
dropping a secret is the worst of both.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Saving with a key stores the reference, asserted end to end against a real
  backend, with the row showing the key present afterwards.
- The same through a vault that needs setup, and through a sealed vault.
- A path that cannot store the key fails the save; there is no path on which
  the endpoint is created and the key silently is not.
close_reason: Two defects, one symptom. Backend: CreateEndpoint's failure carried no reason, so a vault that needed setup or was sealed arrived indistinguishable from a disk error and the sheets never opened. Frontend: vault.tsx's closeDialog resolved the caller's promise while the dispatcher's re-sent RPC was still in flight, so save() toasted 'Saved' before the create landed; the cancel path had the mirror bug and now rejects. Merged as b6251ad6.

comments.author: shady2k
comments.text: Investigated (worktree fix-nocx-4egm-key, not committed). ROOT CAUSE: ws_endpoints.go returned endpoints.* errors as bare RPCError{Code,Message} — no data.reason — so the renderer's operation-first wrapper (saveSecretWithVault, nocx-8rwj) and the dispatcher's sealed interception could not tell vault-uninitialized/vault-sealed from a disk error. On a fresh home the save died in a toast instead of raising the setup sheet (the shape of nocx-25k9.7, re-lit). FIX: route create/update/delete errors through rpcErrorFor(endpointMethodErrorCode(err),"",err) — preserves -32602 conflict codes, attaches vault reasons. NO silent-drop path exists in CreateEndpoint: mint happens before the record write, every failure aborts before the write, and the record's first observable state carries the reference; a crash between mint and write leaves an ownerless secret the journal retires (ADR-0011 §4/ADR-0030). PROOF: new Go test TestEndpointsCreate_CarriesVaultReasons (red before: -32603 no reason, both states; green after: -32000/-32001 with reason, zero records after failed mints). e2e agent-ask.spec.ts rewritten: test 2 now saves WITH key on a fresh home FIRST, asserts the save-raised setup sheet, completes it, asserts the row 'Key saved' + Bearer carries the key; new test 5 restarts the backend (vault sealed) and rotates a key through the unlock sheet, asserting the row stays 'Key saved' and the probe Bearer is the new key. Also fixed two pre-existing stale assertions exposed by the timing change: STATUS_ROW 'Ready' (timing-dependent; now /Ready|Last test ok/) and 'Streamed an answer in' (surface sentence is now 'X answered in N ms'). Gates: go test transport/capability/profile OK, golangci-lint OK, vitest 2793 OK, e2e 5/5 chromium container. OBSERVATION (not reproduced, not a key drop): one container run of a sealed-CREATE variant showed the New Endpoint dialog closing with no row and no toast after the unlock flow (no record at all — not a keyless record); the rotation path used instead passes deterministically. Worth a follow-up bead if it recurs.

comments.author: shady2k
comments.text: SECOND FINDING, FIXED: the sealed-CREATE path showed a success-looking close with no row (no toast, no record) — a loud-failure violation. Root cause in the FRONTEND: dispatcher.ts intercepts a vault-sealed RPC response and holds the caller's promise until its re-sent request settles, but vault.tsx closeUnlock -> closeDialog resolved the caller's saveSecretWithVault promise while the re-sent RPC was STILL IN FLIGHT (pendingSave null, retryInFlight false -> the resolve branch fired). save() then closed the editor and toasted 'Saved' while the create had not landed, and the list read raced the re-send. Same bug on CANCEL: the unlock-dialog close resolved the save instead of rejecting. FIX: closeDialog now settles (and nulls) the caller's promise only when sealedUnlock === null — while the dispatcher's seam owns the RPC, the RPC's own settlement owns the promise; nulling without settling would strand it. REGRESSIONS (red before, green after): vault.test.tsx 'sealed seam: the unlock dialog close does not settle the save while the re-sent RPC is in flight' (asserts the promise is still pending after onUnsealDone+closeUnlock, resolves only when the re-sent RPC settles) and 'sealed seam: cancelling the unlock rejects the save, never resolves it'. E2E: test 5 is now the CREATE variant again (new endpoint + key through a sealed vault via backend restart) — was red (no row) before the fix, green after: row 'Key saved' + probe Bearer = typed key. Gates re-run: frontend vitest 2795/2795, frontend tsc OK, e2e 5/5 chromium container. Go unchanged since the first run (transport/capability/profile + lint still green).

title: Reuse jump-routed SSH connection for completion
description:
## Steps to Reproduce
1. Open an SSH profile whose target is reached through a jump host.
2. Type in the terminal so shell.complete runs.
3. Observe a direct dial to the target, followed by shell.complete and resize refusals on the session gate.

## Expected Result
Remote completion uses the live session's exact SSH connect options, including its jump chain, so its owned DiscoveryConn lease shares the existing pooled route. The session gate protects only the immutable session snapshot; the remote completion network round trip does not block resize or other session controls.
acceptance_criteria: Given a jump-routed remote session, when shell.complete runs, then the DiscoveryConn provider receives the exact session SSH options and no direct target route is substituted. Given a remote completion blocked on network I/O, when resize runs for the same live session, then resize completes without a session-scope control-saturated refusal. Tests prove the routing options and gate interval.
close_reason: Remote completion now receives the live session's exact SSH connect options, so jump-routed DiscoveryConn leases share the terminal's AD-4 pool key instead of dialing the target directly. SessionTargetOperation snapshots immutable route facts under the session gate, releases that gate before remote I/O, and retains the ordinary lane. Capability interval, composition adapter, real-socket completion/resize concurrency, targeted race, full containerized Go, full frontend, Wails build, and native startup all pass.

title: Lifecycle establishment races the open acknowledgement
description:
A remote shell can publish prompt_ready while the open RPC is still creating the session. handleOpen installs the WebSocket subscriber before it enqueues the open result, while PublishLifecycle sends an unscoped lifecycle.changed notification to the shared connection. The opening TerminalContent has no sessionId yet and cannot acknowledge; existing tabs consume the same fact and acknowledge it with their own sessionId, producing rule=c-lane-registered, reason="lane is not registered to this session". The shell's bounded establishment remains conventional and the UI continues to report busy/native behavior.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Keep one terminal tab open.
2. Open an enhanced SSH profile whose lifecycle hello arrives during the open RPC.
3. Observe lifecycle.changed reaching the shared renderer before the new tab owns its session id.
4. Observe establishment acknowledgement refused for the new lane under an existing session id and no accepted establishment for the new session.

Fix the ownership and ordering seams, not the refusal guard: the open result must precede lifecycle publication, current state must be replayed after the session subscriber is installed, and lifecycle.changed must name its owning session so only that TerminalContent can consume it. Preserve ADR-0024 decision 9: no ack means no prompt suppression.
acceptance_criteria: Given an existing tab and a second enhanced session whose authenticated hello arrives during open, when the backend completes the open RPC, then the second tab receives its session-scoped prompt_ready only after its open result, acknowledges the exact lane/domain/epoch/generation successfully, and unrelated tabs neither mutate their lifecycle state nor send an acknowledgement. The contract and real-socket test require sessionId on lifecycle.changed; a production-path regression proves no c-lane-registered refusal; Wails build and smoke launch pass.
close_reason: Bound lifecycle subscription before open, buffered session/lane projections until authoritative sessionId, initialized pending lanes as Native, and rejected unknown wire lifecycle values. Contract, real-socket ordering, production first-prompt E2E, full gates, Wails build and smoke all pass.

title: The snippets spec built its destination seam on InputTargetRegistry, which has no caller outside its own tests
description:
Found by an adversarial codex review of .internal/plans/2026-08-13-snippets.md, then
verified directly.

Spec 2026-08-13-snippets-design.md §9.1 says "input-target.ts already exists and already
says: a registered InputTarget decides where a submitted document goes ... new kinds are
added by registering a target". True of the file. Not true of the product.

Worse, the derivation the spec invents ALREADY EXISTS in production, one file away.
TerminalContent.insertSecret (terminal-content.ts:2248) is "editor visible -> insert into
the editor, otherwise -> the pty", PLUS the refusal on an unresolvable {{secret:...}} that
spec §11.1 proposes to build a second time. Wired from main.tsx:738/757.

The spec's own §4 names AD-8 and quotes input-target.ts as the reason no parallel seam is
needed. The check that would have caught it is AGENTS.md "Before you fix anything" #5 —
is the code reachable, who constructs it — and it was not run on input-target.ts.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. `grep -rn "createRegistry" frontend/src` — hits are input-target.ts:60 (the definition)
   and input-target.test.ts only. No production caller.
2. `sed -n '2248,2262p' frontend/src/terminal-content.ts` — read insertSecret; it is the
   destination derivation plus the refusal the spec proposes to write again.
3. Read spec §9.1, §9.2, §11.1 and plan Task 8: all three are built on the registry.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Spec §9.1/§9.2/§11.1 revised to extend the existing production derivation rather
      than introduce a second one, or input-target.ts is deliberately wired first
- [ ] Plan Task 8 rewritten against whatever that resolves to

close_reason: Spec §9.1/§9.1a/§9.2/§9.2a and §11.1 revised (b24fab21) and plan Task 8 rewritten against them (af4968c7). What remains — whether input-target.ts gets a production caller or is deleted — is filed separately as it is not this epic's to decide.

title: a not-integrated card closed with the cross never comes back, though the user never said they had read it
description:
Owner decision 2026-08-12, reversing the once-per-(shell, reason) rule taken in nocx-5uu5 and refined in nocx-aimo. The card is recorded as seen the moment it is DRAWN, before any click, so a card closed with the cross — or closed by a user who had not yet worked out what it meant — is gone for that shell and reason for good. Nothing on the surface says that closing it spends it.

How it must be: the cross, and the card going away by anything other than an explicit choice, remember nothing; a new session with the same shell and the same reason raises it again. 'Don't show again for this shell' is the only writer, and it silences every reason for that shell on this machine. The tab's mark survives both, because it is the state of the session rather than a notification.

The storage key for the shell-wide silence is unchanged; only the moment of the write moves.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open a session whose shell fails to integrate. The card appears.
2. Close it with the cross without reading it.
3. Open another session with the same shell, failing the same way. Observed: no card, ever again.
acceptance_criteria: A card closed with the cross is raised again by the next session with the same shell and reason; a card answered with 'Don't show again for this shell' is never raised for that shell again, whatever the reason; the tab's mark is present after both; nothing in the renderer records anything at draw time.
close_reason: Nothing is recorded at draw time any more. The only writer is 'Don't show again for this shell' (IntegrationSilenceStore.silenceShell), which silences every reason for that shell on this machine; the cross and a session ending with the card up record nothing, so the next session raises it again. Within one session the reasons already closed in that tab are held in memory on TerminalContent, so a republished identical status cannot push a closed card back up while a new reason still can. Storage key unchanged so silences chosen on the shipped build survive; per-card lines that build wrote are read as nothing and drop out on the next write. Proved by terminal-content.test.ts ('raises the card again in the next session, having been told nothing', 'raises the card again after a session that ended with it still showing', 'does not push a closed card back up when the same status is republished', 'raises a card for a new reason in the same session', plus the two mark-survives tests) and status.test.ts ('reads a card that an older build merely drew as nothing at all', 'still honours a silence the user chose on an older build').

title: the not-integrated card offers Details and shows a process name cut off mid-word
description:
Owner feedback on the installed build, 2026-08-12. The card carries How to fix, Details and a close cross. Details is a second surface holding the fact chain, the explanation and the don't-show-again action, so the content is split across two dialogs and the fix is not the only thing a click away.

Owner decision: the card's actions are How to fix (primary), Don't show again for this shell, and the close cross. Details disappears as a surface and everything in it moves into How to fix. The three card actions are deliberately different: the cross removes this session's card now, Don't show again silences the card for this shell on this machine, and the tab mark survives both because it is the honest state of the session.

Second defect in the same dialog: the observation reads 'nocx saw "zsh (kiro-cli-te" running where it expected the shell'. The name is macOS p_comm, a fixed-width 16-byte field that structurally cannot carry a path, arguments or a command line — which is why the observation is safe to show at all — but the user sees a name cut off mid-word and reads it as a defect. Fix it on the product side without opening the door p_comm closes.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open a zsh session that a wrapper takes over, so integration times out.
2. Look at the card: it offers How to fix, Details and a cross.
3. Open Details, then How to fix. Observed: the fact chain and the explanation live in one dialog and the remedy in another, and the observation reads 'nocx saw "zsh (kiro-cli-te"'.
acceptance_criteria: The card offers exactly three actions and Details is not one of them; everything Details held is one click from the card via How to fix; Don't show again for this shell is still reachable; a name that fills the kernel's field is not presented as if it were complete.
close_reason: The card's actions are How to fix (primary), Don't show again for this shell, and the cross; Details is gone and everything it held — the fact chain, the observation, Learn more — is behind the primary action, one click from the card. A reason with no honest remedy opens the same dialog under 'What happened', so the facts are never unreachable. The three card actions are pinned as three different promises in notice.test.tsx and terminal-content.test.ts: the cross answers this card, the silence answers this shell for good, and the tab mark survives both. An observed name that fills the kernel's 16-byte p_comm field is quoted with an ellipsis and explained ('may be cut short'), counted in bytes the way the kernel truncates; the wire-side fix is nocx-3f6a. frontend only, contract untouched.

title: the how-to-fix text is generic, names the wrong shell, and withholds what nocx already knows
description:
Shown to a zsh user, the fix panel says `bash -lic ...` and advises bisecting
~/.bashrc. Three defects in one panel: it names a shell the session is not
running, it gives generic advice where nocx has a specific measured answer,
and reaching it takes two clicks through a Details dialog that could have
shown it inline.

What nocx knows and does not say: which shell it started (it is a field on the
notification), that a wrapper replaced it (visible in the process table), and
the guard that fixes it. Measured working on this machine: wrapping the
third-party block in the user's rc in a test on NOCX_SHELL_INTEGRATION lets
nocx's bootstrap run to completion. Upstream kirodotdev/Kiro#7169 shows the
same guard is what affected users converge on, and it has had no maintainer
response since 2026-04-05.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open a zsh session that fails to integrate.
2. Details -> How to fix. Observed: a bash command line and generic bisect
   advice, two clicks away.
acceptance_criteria: A zsh session is never told to run a bash command; the fix is visible without a second click; when a wrapper is detected the panel shows the guard for the shell actually in use.
close_reason: The remedy is derived from the shell in the notification: the startup file nocx's own launcher sources (~/.bashrc for bash, ~/.zshrc for zsh), an invocation that shell accepts, and a guard on NOCX_SHELL_INTEGRATION, which nocx exports before the rc runs. An unfamiliar shell gets the guard and no invented invocation. The remedy is the card's own primary action (one click, still reachable from Details), and the observed process is repeated in it from the single observationSentence() the Details chain uses. Proved by frontend/src/integration/status.test.ts ('never hands a zsh session a bash command or a bash startup file') and notice.test.tsx ('is one click from the card').

title: a degraded session says so in the product: a persistent tab badge plus a first-time card and a details dialog
description: Owner decisions taken 2026-08-12: the fact lives as a persistent badge on the tab, plus a card shown once per (shell, reason) pair, not once per session; the message names no third-party program, while a Details dialog shows the chain including the detected process name, labelled as a guess; actions offered are copy-the-snippet, apply-it-for-me (separate bead), do-not-show-again-for-this-shell, and a link to the explanation. Wording agreed with the owner rather than invented in review, which is what nocx-viil requires. frontend/src/ui/README.md is required reading first: Badge, StatusDot, StatusCard and Dialog already exist and the kit grows by variants, never by near-duplicates. A surface may place a kit component and may never repaint it.
acceptance_criteria: A session that degraded shows a badge for as long as it stays degraded; the card appears once per (shell, reason) and not again; a session that is conventional by design does not nag; every string is the agreed wording.
notes: Superseded in part on 2026-08-13 by nocx-wfxz: the 'card once per (shell, reason), recorded when it is drawn' rule is gone. The card is raised once per session per reason, closing it records nothing, and the only persistent record is the user pressing 'Don't show again for this shell', which silences every reason for that shell. The tab mark is unchanged. Also revised by nocx-aimo: the Details dialog was folded into How to fix.
close_reason: Persistent tab mark carrying the reason's wording, a card once per (shell, reason) in localStorage, a Details dialog with the fact chain and the observation labelled a guess, plus How-to-fix / Don't-show-again-for-this-shell / Learn more. All kit components placed, none repainted. Wording table asserted to name no third-party program.

title: a session reports its integration status as a typed control fact, and local sessions populate it
description: The UI can already render a refusal reason (frontend/src/terminal-content.ts:1518 reads shellIntegrationReason from the open ack) but session.go:102 states plainly that local sessions always return ReasonNone, so the wire is laid and never connected on the local side. Worse, the open ack is a single value at open time, while the two failures that matter arrive later: the handshake timeout and a channel lost mid-session. internal/lifecyclechannel/adapter.go:245 (lose) logs nothing at all, so a session that degraded leaves no trace anywhere - measured: 22 seconds of a fully degraded session produced zero diagnostic lines. Scope: a JSON Schema in contracts/ for a dynamic integration-status fact with a stable reason enum (integrated, starting, conventional:unsupported-shell, conventional:handshake-timeout, lost:channel-lost), generated renderer types, the Go side validated against it including the over-the-wire test, local sessions populating it, and lose() logging which of its callers fired. Deliberately NOT in scope: distinguishing 'the user startup did not return' - that needs the bootstrap progress facts and is its own bead.
acceptance_criteria: A local session whose shell never completes the handshake reports a typed status with reason conventional:handshake-timeout over the real socket, proven by a …_OverTheWireConformsToContract test; and the log names which path lost the channel.
close_reason: session.integrationChanged replaces the one-shot ack field; local sessions populate it; lose() names its caller. Proven by TestSessionIntegrationChanged_OverTheWireConformsToContract (real adapter, real socket, handshake-timeout), the transition tests in ws_integration_test.go, and the loss-cause tests in internal/lifecyclechannel. Parent epic nocx-viil stays open by design — it has further children.

title: nocx's rcfile sources the user's bashrc, and a second shell integration in it takes the session over
description:
On the machine v0.1.0 was first run, the shell nocx ends up talking to is not the one it started. Measured on the running app:

  app pid 75356 (/Applications/nocx.app)
   └─ pid 75423  exe: /Users/shady/.local/bin/'bash (kiro-cli-term)'   (86 MB, Kiro CLI's PTY wrapper)
       └─ pid 75435  bash                                             (the real shell)

The chain: app.go starts `bash --rcfile <nocx rcfile> -i`, the nocx rcfile sources the user's ~/.bashrc first — by design, 'the user's rc still runs first and still wins' — and line 1 of that bashrc is Kiro CLI's pre block, which evals `kiro-cli init bash pre`. That installs bash-preexec (rcaloras/bash-preexec) and the session ends up re-exec'd under Kiro's wrapper, which spawns its own plain interactive bash.

Two shell integrations then want the same two hooks. bash-preexec's own header says it 'will most likely break' if PROMPT_COMMAND or trap DEBUG are set after it — which is exactly what nocx's markers do. Whoever loses, the user sees a shell nocx is not driving: a raw bash-3.2$ prompt with Apple's 'default interactive shell is now zsh' notice, and no blocks.

This is not exotic. Kiro CLI, Amazon Q, Fig, Warp's own hooks, Starship, Atuin, oh-my-bash — instrumented shells are the norm among the users this product is for, and every one of them lands in the rc file nocx sources.

Related but distinct from nocx-wwz0, which is about starting bash rather than the login shell at all. This one would survive fixing that: a zsh user with Kiro's zshrc.pre.zsh has the same collision.

Worth noting what Tabby does instead, since the comparison is what raised this: it does not instrument the shell at all. Its ShellIntegrationService installs macOS Automator workflows ('Open Tabby here'), nothing that runs inside the shell — so there is nothing to collide. Blocks are the feature that forces us to instrument, and instrumentation is what collides.

## Steps to Reproduce

On a Mac whose ~/.bashrc carries Kiro CLI's pre/post blocks (or Amazon Q's, or Fig's):
1. Launch nocx and open a local tab.
2. `ps -eo pid,ppid,comm` — the app's child is the wrapper, and the wrapper has a bash child.
3. The prompt is the shell's native one; no block is painted.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A session whose rc hands the shell to another integration is DETECTED and said out loud, naming what took it, rather than presenting as a terminal that simply does not work.
- nocx's markers either survive alongside bash-preexec or the session degrades visibly; nothing silently half-installs.
- One automated check drives a shell whose rc installs bash-preexec and asserts the outcome, whichever outcome is decided.
notes: Built: an unauthenticated, one-way bootstrap progress descriptor (internal/bootstrapprogress, fd 4 beside the lifecycle channel's fd 3). Both rcfile templates write 'startup-entered' before sourcing the user's rc and 'user-rc-returned' after it — the latter BEFORE __nocx_cap is assigned, so the user's rc still cannot see the capability. A hello-timeout loss on a session stopped at startup-entered now reports ssh.ReasonStartupDidNotReturn instead of handshake-timeout. ADR-0024 decision 4 amended (a diagnostic channel is not a tier) and decision 10's availability paragraph extended. Remote tiers render the block inert — no second descriptor over ssh — tracked as nocx-iyez.

comments.author: shady
comments.text:
CONFIRMED as the cause, by controlled measurement on shipped v0.1.0. Same binary, same /bin/bash 3.2.57, one variable: the two Kiro CLI lines in ~/.bashrc (backed up, removed, restored, sha256 verified identical).

  Kiro ENABLED   child = 'bash (kiro-cli-term)' -> its own bash; the log stops after
                 'lifecycle channel established'. No establishment, no prompt_ready.
  Kiro DISABLED  child = bash; the log reaches 'establishment acknowledged'.

So integration DOES complete on macOS bash 3.2 — the perl readable-probe from 37fd666 works — and what breaks it is the other integration in the rc file. nocx-sw4p is not the cause on this machine; its note has been corrected.

Raised to P0: any user whose shell is instrumented gets a terminal with none of the product's features and no explanation, and Kiro CLI, Amazon Q, Fig and Warp's hooks all install into exactly this file.

Seen alongside and unexplained: after the successful establishment, 'establishment acknowledgement refused, rule=e-publisher, no establishment is pending acknowledgement' repeats and reaches the frontend.

title: nocx opens bash on macOS while the user's login shell is zsh, so the shipped app greets every Mac user in the wrong shell
description:
Every other terminal on macOS opens the user's login shell. nocx opens bash. On the machine this was found on: dscl reports UserShell /bin/zsh, $SHELL is /bin/zsh, macOS 15.7.4 — and v0.1.0 opens /bin/bash 3.2.57, banner and all, including Apple's own 'The default interactive shell is now zsh' notice. zsh has been the macOS default since Catalina, so this is not one user's setup.

It is deliberate, and that is the problem. internal/app/app.go sets, for EVERY local enhanced session:

  cfg.Command = "bash"
  cfg.Args = []string{"--rcfile", rcPath, "-i"}

with the reason beside it: bash is the integration-first shell for the local tier. launcher_local.go states the same and calls the consequence acceptable — 'the zsh/posix local tiers would each need their own launch semantics (transient ZDOTDIR, ENV file) — deliberately not built here; a non-bash $SHELL on a local enhanced session is a follow-up, not a silent degrade (a zsh user still lands on a visible conventional terminal, which is the safe direction)'.

The safe direction was the right call against a SILENT degrade. It is the wrong call against 'the terminal opens a shell the user did not choose': the user is not degraded from their shell, they are moved out of it. Their aliases, functions, prompt, completions and history are all somewhere else, and on macOS the shell they land in is a 2007 build Apple froze at bash 3.2.57.

NOT the same as nocx-sw4p or nocx-qduc. Both logs from this machine show 'lifecycle channel established', so the channel works; this is about which shell is started, not about whether integration handshakes.

Two shapes the fix can take, and they are not equivalent:
- Build the zsh local enhanced tier (transient ZDOTDIR). Keeps integration AND the user's shell. The real answer, and the larger one.
- Start the login shell and degrade integration visibly when it is not bash. Honest, but on macOS that hands most users a conventional terminal — which is the product's core feature removed by default. Only acceptable as a stopgap, and only if the degrade is stated in the UI.

Where the login shell comes from also needs deciding: $SHELL is the shell's own claim and is absent or stale for a GUI-launched .app, while macOS's authority is Directory Services (dscl . -read /Users/<u> UserShell) and Linux's is the passwd database. internal/pty/pty_local.go's resolveShell reads only $SHELL before falling through to a bash candidate list, so the non-enhanced path has the same blind spot.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. On macOS with a zsh login shell (the default since Catalina), install nocx v0.1.0 from the .dmg.
2. Launch it and open a local tab.
3. The prompt is bash-3.2$, and the tab is titled bash.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A local tab opens the user's login shell, taken from the OS's own record rather than from $SHELL alone, on both macOS and Linux.
- A zsh user gets shell integration — blocks, markers, the command editor — not a conventional terminal.
- If any shell cannot be integrated, the session says so where the user is looking, and names the shell it started.
notes:
2026-08-12, from nocx-qduc (its blocker, now closed): nocx.zsh emits the OSC 636 hello and command snapshot as of script v37, so moving local sessions to the user's login shell no longer trades one P0 for another.

Carried forward from nocx-qduc's acceptance criteria, because it cannot be run
until this bead lands: completion.spec.ts must pass on a macOS host whose login
shell is zsh, not only in the bash container. Today every enhanced local session
runs bash (app.go pins cfg.Command = 'bash' with the transient --rcfile), so no
e2e run on any machine has ever exercised the zsh tier end to end — the shell
side is proven by the pty tests in internal/shellintegration, the last hop is
this bead's.
close_reason: The local tab opens the account's own login shell, the zsh tier is built and proven end to end on a real zsh with a real lifecycle channel, and a shell with no tier is started as itself with unsupported-shell on the open ack. Two latent defects the tier surfaced were fixed with it: an interactive shell ignores SIGTERM so a closed tab leaked a zsh, and nocx.zsh's accept-line chain called a function name as a widget so Enter did not run the command on any machine with a syntax-highlighting plugin (script v38). Gate: all four CI jobs green (ci-os-split, ci + ci-mac on macOS, ci-backend and ci-linux in the Linux container with both keyring variants, ci-frontend on node 24, ci-e2e 274 passed / 8 skipped). completion.spec.ts on macOS with a zsh login shell: 7 of 8 pass; the eighth fails identically on a tree with this change stashed and is filed as nocx-b6t8 (Control+a is not select-all in macOS WebKit). Follow-ups: nocx-k28e (local POSIX tier), nocx-2ka0 (~/.zprofile shadowed), nocx-c0ek (no setting to pin the shell), nocx-7wkc (ci-frontend from a worktree), nocx-coso (tunnel test flake).

comments.author: shady
comments.text:
Proven on the shipped v0.1.0 with NOCX_LOG_LEVEL=debug, launched via `open --env` so the app kept the launchd environment a Finder launch gives it:

1. CODE — internal/app/app.go:958 sets cfg.Command = "bash" unconditionally for a local enhanced session.
2. LOG — 'local pty shell resolved' is absent from the debug log. That line is written only when resolveShell picks the shell, so its absence proves the $SHELL path never ran at all. The session did reach 'lifecycle channel established', so this is not an integration failure.
3. PROCESS — /Applications/nocx.app (pid 68733) has one shell child: bash, GNU bash 3.2.57(1)-release (arm64-apple-darwin24).

Against dscl . -read /Users/shady UserShell = /bin/zsh and $SHELL = /bin/zsh on macOS 15.7.4.

Incidental, and worth a look when this is fixed: the child's process title reads 'bash (kiro-cli-term)', so the user's own ~/.bashrc ran and a tool in it renamed the process. The rcfile sources the user's bash config as designed — which is another reason a zsh user is left in an environment that is neither their shell nor a clean one.

comments.author: shady
comments.text: Correction to the closing note: the macOS WebKit completion spec bead is nocx-7qv0, not nocx-b6t8.

title: release.yml's publish job cannot create the release: gh has no repository to publish to
description:
The v0.1.0 tag run (31582288339) built both platforms and signed the manifest, then failed on its last step:

  failed to run git: fatal: not a git repository (or any of the parent directories): .git

The publish job never checks the repository out — it downloads three artefacts and nothing else — so `gh release create` falls back to asking git which remote it is talking about, finds no .git, and stops. It does not fall over to the Actions context.

No release was created. The tag exists and points at a commit whose artefacts are built and signed; nothing downstream references it yet.

WHY NO REHEARSAL CAUGHT IT: publish is gated on `needs.validate.outputs.release == 'true'`, which only a tag sets. Every workflow_dispatch dry run — including 31575558543, green two hours earlier — skips this job entirely. So the step was executed for the first time by the real release. This is the second defect found in this exact job for exactly this reason; nocx-94kl was the first, and its close reason says the keyring check 'lived in the tag-gated publish job and had never executed'.

Fixed by naming the repository (GH_REPO: ${{ github.repository }}) rather than adding a checkout: this job has no use for the source, and cloning it to satisfy an implicit lookup would hide what the lookup needed.

## Steps to Reproduce

Push a stable vX.Y.Z tag and watch the publish job of the resulting release.yml run. Reproduced once, at v0.1.0.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A tag run reaches a published GitHub Release carrying the .dmg, the .zip, the AppImage, manifest.json and manifest.json.sig.
- Every step of the publish job is exercised by something that runs before a real tag, or the workflow states plainly which steps a dry run cannot reach and why.
close_reason: Fixed by 2f6df21 (GH_REPO on the publish step) and proven by the release itself: run 31584091964 reached publish and created the release. Confirmed the diagnosis a second way by accident — running 'gh release download' from outside a checkout locally produced the identical 'failed to run git: fatal: not a git repository'.

title: Refused nested SSH silently skips the user's command
description:
In an enhanced remote session, a typed `ssh host` emits domain_request. buildSSHChildBootstrap deliberately refuses when the parent transport is remote (internal/app/childdomain.go:216-223), returning the protocol's empty-bootstrap grant. The bash consumer does not honor that refusal for SSH: internal/shellintegration/scripts/nocx.bash:507-515 sends domain_suspended, marks the nested domain active, and evals the empty string. `eval ""` succeeds, so __nocx_nested_launch returns 0 and the DEBUG wrapper returns 1, causing extdebug to skip the user's original SSH command. The documented honest fallback therefore executes nothing. The sudo/su empty-bootstrap path correctly reaches lines 621-624 and evaluates the original line; SSH must have the same invariant.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Open an enhanced saved-profile SSH session so the parent lifecycle transport is remote.
2. At its integrated prompt enter `ssh target`.
3. Observe the backend logs `child domain refused ... ssh nested inside a remote parent is not implemented`, but the user's OpenSSH process never starts and the prompt immediately returns.
4. Source-level minimal reproduction: deliver an env=ssh domain_grant with empty bootstrap to __nocx_nested_launch; it evaluates the empty string and reports success to the extdebug wrapper.
acceptance_criteria: Given an authenticated remote parent and a typed simple `ssh target`, when the grant builder returns the protocol-defined empty-bootstrap refusal, the original command executes conventionally exactly once; the parent is not left suspended and no child domain is claimed. An executable shell-script test drives the real DEBUG-wrapper/grant path and fails if the command is skipped or duplicated. Nested SSH from a remote parent remains unintegrated as currently decided; this fix restores only the documented honest fallback.
close_reason: The empty-bootstrap check moved ABOVE the suspend in both nocx.bash and nocx.zsh, so a refused grant runs the user's line conventionally, exactly once, claims no domain and suspends nothing. The dead branch each script carried below the suspend for that case is deleted. Driven through the real seam: a real bash (3.2 and 5.2) and a real zsh on a real pty, the real DEBUG wrapper and accept-line widget, a real domain_request answered over the real channel with the protocol's empty-bootstrap echo, and a stub ssh on PATH. The assertion is a COUNT, so a fix that double-ran the line would fail too. Verified red before the fix on all three legs (0 runs, the bug's exact symptom) and red again on zsh after reverting only the zsh guard. Paired success asserted: a grant that DOES carry a bootstrap runs it and does not also run the line. Scripts changed, so version 40 -> 41 and the publisher's measured maximum 67,208 -> 67,252, both recorded with the reason. Commits 472969f2, 7ab8f4b3 (the last one corrects an e2e assertion the bump exposed: the journey required exactly one generation on the host while the publisher's documented policy is keep-two, which had never been exercised because CI's fixture home always starts empty). Full gate green including e2e on both browsers.

title: Printable keystrokes are dropped after an enhanced submit while Enter still reaches the pty, so an empty line is submitted for the user
description:
After an enhanced submit there is a window in which PRINTABLE keystrokes are
lost while Enter still reaches the pty. The user types into a running
program's prompt, sees nothing arrive, and their Enter submits an empty line.

MEASURED, not inferred. The transport now logs every data frame at debug
(session, length, and the payload itself in a development build — see
log.Sensitive). Running e2e/enhanced-input.spec.ts with --repeat-each=8 in the
container, of the 8 runs of "read command receives input after enhanced
submit":

  5 sessions   8 frames   command, \r, h, e, l, l, o, \r     -> pass
  2 sessions   2 frames   command, \r                        -> FAIL
  1 session    3 frames   command, \r, \r                    -> FAIL

Three short sessions, three failures. The letters never left the renderer —
this is not the shell failing to read them, and not the block failing to
paint. Nothing reached the socket.

The three-frame session is the tell: the SECOND \r (the Enter pressed after
typing `hello`) went out raw, while the five letters before it did not. So the
key path is not simply "not yet armed" — at that moment it forwards control
keys to the pty and drops printable ones.

The spec gates on `expect(INPUT).not.toBeVisible()` before typing, so the
editor is already hidden when the letters are lost. Editor-hidden is therefore
NOT sufficient for "raw routing owns the keyboard", and the gap between the
two is where this lives.

Consequence for a user, and why this is worse than a dropped keystroke: the
Enter survives. Type a password into an `ssh` that is asking for one, lose the
password, and the empty line is submitted for you — silently.

nocx-4ff.4 is the bead this spec was written for, and the spec is doing its
job: it has been catching this at about three runs in ten and reading as a
flake.

## Steps to Reproduce

  PW_PROJECTS=chromium NOCX_LOG_LEVEL=debug \
    e2e/run-in-container.sh e2e/enhanced-input.spec.ts --repeat-each=8

Then read .e2e/home/.local/share/nocx-dev/nocx.log and group the `data frame`
lines by session_id: the failing runs are the short ones.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A keystroke made after an enhanced submit either reaches the pty or is
  refused visibly; none is silently dropped.
- Printable and control keys are never routed by different rules at the same
  instant.
- e2e/enhanced-input.spec.ts passes 20 consecutive runs in the container.
- The gate the spec waits on is one the product actually promises, rather than
  the editor's visibility standing in for keyboard ownership.
close_reason: Two defects in one handoff: the grid was made writable at commit but focused only by the deferred paste (behind the submitAttempt RPC), so for that round trip nobody owned the keyboard; fixing that exposed a reordering, with raw keys overtaking the command they answered. takeKeyboardToGrid now does writable+focused in one step, and grid bytes are held from commit until the command is on the wire, then flushed in order (hold lifted BEFORE the write, since renderer.paste is itself an onData). The renderer fixture's paste now fires onData, which is why the unit suite could not see any of this. Verified: e2e/enhanced-input.spec.ts --repeat-each=10 in the container, 30/30 green (was 5/6 failing), every session's frames in typed order. Commit 8e279e8.

title: Harden PR #61 backup restore before merge
description:
PR #61 is conflict-free on current main but its backup/restore path is not merge-ready. The review proved an AppleScript injection, panics on nested setting values, missing profile/forward/group validation, inconsistent merge normalization, a macOS WebKit settings-scroll regression, a removed Tabby ingress budget, false-green acceptance coverage, an unsound duplicate-key heuristic, preview/restore disagreement, stale rollback notifications, and a save-cancel wire-contract violation.

Fix the defects at their owning seams without compatibility shims. Preserve AD-1 control/data-plane separation and the existing single owners for profile, settings, and contract validation.

## Steps to Reproduce

Check out PR #61 at bc603c6f261f3c51f9f382388f8778333ce1d068 on main f79d324de1371458bc69dc0f0738535bd216f7f3. Exercise each review reproducer: inject a backslash-quote filename into the macOS save dialog, preview and restore nested JSON settings, restore malformed forwards and orphaned group references, merge conflicting session-end fields, scroll Settings in WebKit at 1024x520 and 600x520, import a Tabby document over 64 KiB, restore a non-empty backup and restart, parse duplicate keys plus valid 1.0 and Unicode escapes, preview unknown setting keys, force partial restore rollback with live subscribers, and cancel saveToFile. Observe the security, panic, validation, layout, budget, false-green, consistency, notification, and wire-contract failures.
acceptance_criteria: All 12 findings from the PR #61 review have regression coverage and are fixed. Malicious filenames cannot alter AppleScript execution; valid nested settings never panic; invalid forwards and orphaned group references are rejected before mutation; merged session-end behavior is normalized; the Settings bottom section is reachable in macOS WebKit at 1024x520 and 600x520; profiles.importTabby accepts the documented document budget; backup acceptance proves non-empty profiles/settings survive restore and restart; duplicate keys are detected token-by-token without rejecting valid numeric or escaped strings; preview and restore agree on settings keys; inline recovery publishes rollback notifications; save cancellation conforms to its exact JSON Schema over the real socket.
close_reason: Fixed all 12 review findings: native filename argv safety, token duplicate detection, nested settings validation/equality, aggregate validation and normalization, rollback notifications, exact save-cancel wire contract, Tabby ingress budget, WebKit scroll ownership, multi-observer refresh, and non-empty restart acceptance. Targeted backend/frontend/Chromium/WebKit checks pass; adversarial reviews found no remaining actionable defects.

title: internal/transport: three tests discard the frame they later wait for, and one lost fact races an async teardown
description:
internal/transport has a 30-second timeout that reports under a DIFFERENT test
name on every run, so it looks like three bugs and is one.

Observed at the same commit, same package, same ~110s package wall time, same
30.0s single-test timeout, three different names:

  CI run 31478263946, backend-linux (true)
    TestLifecycleChanged_DeadSessionGetsNoRecoveryClaim  30.02s   FAIL
  scripts/ci-linux.sh --no-keyring, local container
    TestGitChanged_OverTheWireConformsToContract         30.05s   FAIL
  CI run 31478263946, backend-linux (false)
    (whole package green)

TestGitChanged_OverTheWireConformsToContract passes in 1.2s when run ALONE in
the same container, and times out at 30.05s inside the full package run. So
the test is not wrong about what it asserts — it never gets to assert.

That is the signature of one starved shared resource inside the package,
not of three independent defects: whichever test happens to be waiting when
the starvation bites is the one that reports the timeout. Fixing the test
that happened to lose is how this survives — the next run renames it.

The package taking 110s at 4 vCPU is itself the lead worth pulling. Something
in there serializes; a package of unit-ish transport tests should not need
close to two minutes.

Not reproducible by capacity-matching: the local container is linux/amd64
EMULATED on an arm64 host (OrbStack on Apple Silicon), so its timings are not
the runner's however the CPU cap is set. Per the owner's decision on
2026-08-11 the local CPU caps are being removed rather than tuned — a test
must not depend on timing at all, which is the actual fix here.

## Steps to Reproduce

  ./scripts/ci-linux.sh --no-keyring -- ./internal/transport/

Repeat it: expect the reported name to move between runs.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The starved resource is NAMED, not worked around by raising a deadline.
- internal/transport is green over 5 consecutive container runs, and the
  package's wall time is explained or reduced.
- No test in the package fails or passes as a function of how many cores the
  machine has; every wait is on an observable state change, not a duration.
notes:
TWO MORE NAMES, and a confirmation of the moving-name signature. Observed 2026-08-16 on integration/wave-1-2 (merge of fix/nocx-ictcq-exit-cause, feat/nocx-3oupk-session-identity, fix/nocx-tsajw-capture-scope over main), Linux host, go test -race -count=1 ./internal/transport/, three consecutive runs at the SAME commit:

  run 1: TestLifecycleChanged_OverTheWireConformsToContract  10.03s  FAIL   (package 86s)
  run 2: TestTabbyExecute_VaultRetry                          0.48s  FAIL   (package 77s)
  run 3: whole package GREEN                                                (package 80s)

TestLifecycleChanged_OverTheWireConformsToContract passes in 1.07s when run ALONE with -race in the same tree, and the package is green WITHOUT -race. So the pattern in this bead holds and extends: it is not three bugs and not four, it is one starved resource, and -race is enough to tip it without any container involved.

Relevant to a coordinator: this makes the pre-commit hook non-deterministic for any Go change. A merged tree can fail the hook, pass on retry, and neither result says anything about the change. Baseline before blame does not help either, because the baseline is also intermittent — the only reliable signal is that the failing NAME moves.
ANOTHER NAME, 2026-08-16, on merged main (06912fc4 — the wave-1-2 merge). ./scripts/ci-linux.sh, containerized, both keyring variants:

  run 1: FAIL TestBashInterruptAnnouncesNoPhantomCommand (16.57s) in internal/shellintegration — that one is nocx-yjen, a different intermittent
  run 2: FAIL TestFilesChanged_OverTheWireConformsToContract (30.03s) in internal/transport

The 30.03s is this bead's signature: the timeout is the 30-second one, and the name moved between runs at the SAME commit. Two consecutive runs, two different packages, two different known intermittents, no overlap — which is the evidence that the merge itself is not deterministically red on the Go side.

Cumulative name list from this bead's notes is now: TestLifecycleChanged_OverTheWireConformsToContract, TestTabbyExecute_VaultRetry, TestFilesChanged_OverTheWireConformsToContract. All three are OverTheWire/contract-shaped or vault-retry-shaped, all under the same 30s bound.
A MECHANISM OF THIS SHAPE WAS PROVEN TO EXIST HERE, 2026-08-16. Not a diagnosis of this bead — a hypothesis with evidence that the shape is real in this repository.

While migrating to Wails v3 (nocx-mgbjx), the containerized vitest job went red with every one of 2989 tests passing:

    Errors  1 error
    ReferenceError: window is not defined
     at Timeout._onTimeout node_modules/@wailsio/runtime/dist/drag.js:69
    This error originated in "src/open-url.test.ts"
    This error was caught after test environment was torn down.

The named file was NOT the cause. Importing that runtime arms two timers as an import side effect (a 50ms interval and a frame callback) and nothing clears them; a file finishing faster than 50ms is torn down with the interval armed. Instrumentation counted 28 test files arming exactly that pair on module evaluation, so the file vitest reports is drawn from a 28-way lottery among whichever one happens to be running when the tick lands.

WHY IT IS WRITTEN HERE. This bead's own signature is a failure whose NAME MOVES between runs at the same commit — three names recorded so far. A background timer outliving its owner produces exactly that: one cause, many names, and the named test is innocent. The frontend case is proof that the shape occurs in this codebase and is invisible until something reports an error outside a test.

WHAT IT DOES NOT ESTABLISH: that this bead has the same cause. Go has no jsdom teardown and the failing package is internal/transport. But 'look for a goroutine or a timer that outlives the test which armed it, and stop trusting the reported test name' is a cheaper first hypothesis than reading the three named tests, and it has not been tried.

The frontend fix is also instructive for whoever takes this: sweeping everything at teardown was rejected because it would hide the product defect the report exists to surface. Only what MODULE EVALUATION armed is disarmed — that belongs to the module graph and no test caused it. The equivalent question here is which goroutines belong to package setup rather than to a test.
A RELIABLE REPRODUCER, 2026-08-16. This bead's failures no longer need to be waited for.

--cpu-shares=512 on the test container is enough. A/B on the same tree, same commit, back to back:

    docker run --rm            ... go test -race -count=1 ./internal/transport/   ok    79.9s
    docker run --rm --cpu-shares=512 ... same command                             FAIL  91.5s
        --- FAIL: TestLifecycleChanged_NoCapabilityOrRawFrameCrosses (10.00s)

About fifteen percent slower is the whole difference. The failure took exactly 10.00s — a round number, so a hardcoded wait rather than work that did not finish.

FOURTH NAME, and the signature holds. Four consecutive pre-commit runs on one merge failed TestTabbyExecute_VaultRetry; this run, same commit and same container, failed TestLifecycleChanged_NoCapabilityOrRawFrameCrosses. Cumulative list is now TestLifecycleChanged_OverTheWireConformsToContract, TestTabbyExecute_VaultRetry, TestFilesChanged_OverTheWireConformsToContract, TestLifecycleChanged_NoCapabilityOrRawFrameCrosses.

WHAT THE KNOB NARROWS. cpu-shares is a SCHEDULER WEIGHT. It changes no ordering primitive, no parallelism, no goroutine interleaving — only how much CPU the cgroup gets when something else wants it. So these tests are not losing a race between two goroutines; they are depending on the machine being FAST ENOUGH to meet a deadline. Look for waits with a timeout, not for shared state. That is a materially different search from the one this bead's title implies ('three tests discard the frame they later wait for'), and it should be tried first because it is cheaper.

WHY THE WEIGHT IS NOT BEING REVERTED, per the owner: it did not create the fragility, it removed the luck that was hiding it. AGENTS.md says the same thing from the other side — 'a spec that needs a slow machine to pass is broken on a fast one too; it has only not been caught yet'. Here it is inverted: broken on a slow machine, uncaught because the machine was fast. Reverting restores the lottery.

PRACTICAL NOTE for whoever fixes this: the knob also gives you a way to prove a fix. Three consecutive green runs WITH --cpu-shares=512 is a much stronger claim than three green runs without it.
A SIXTH NAME, and the package wall time has grown. Observed 2026-08-20 on fix/release-wails3-flags (a53cddef), CI run 32355417884, ci-backend (with-secret-service):

The wall time keeps climbing. 77-86s on 2026-08-16, ~110s at 4 vCPU when this

A FIFTH NAME, 2026-08-23, on feat/notifications (24c791a6). `make ci-backend`, containerized, the job as CI runs it:

  FAIL TestLiveness_TheReturnToAliveAlsoCrossesTheWire (30.07s) in internal/transport (package 127.9s)
      ws_liveness_test.go:118: waiting for session.liveness notification:
      read tcp 127.0.0.1:42572->127.0.0.1:35121: i/o timeout

Signature confirmed the way this bead asks for: the same test passes in 1.045s when run ALONE with -race on the host, at the same commit. Package wall time 127.9s, single-test bound 30.0s.

8771c787. Two names in one run, and one of them in BOTH keyring variants:

  TestLiveness_UnknownReachesTheRendererOverTheWire        30.06s  FAIL

POSSIBLE CONTRIBUTION FROM THAT DAY'S WORK, stated so whoever fixes this does

close_reason: Named the resource and merged the fix. The outbound pump: the slow-consumer test filled the queue before the pump entered its blocking socket write, so under constrained scheduling the second overflow closed the connection and left the stream and writer blocked for everything after it — which is why whichever test was waiting reported the timeout under a different name each run. Disproof condition, recorded so a recurrence reopens this knowingly: a constrained full-package run producing a different caller's timeout, or the synchronized slow-consumer test again observing the second overflow before the pump-start event.
