THE OWNER'S SCREEN, herdr 2026-08-24, as the parity checklist: a rail of host-sessions each with its
command and an ok/status line; a 'spaces' column grouping worktree branches under their repository
with a state dot per branch; an 'agents · grouped' column of agent cards (name, count, kind, state
dot) separate from tabs; a tab strip inside the pane area.

ORDER PROPOSED: layer 0 (merge feat/git-manager, close nocx-ebl4.1) -> layer 2 (the external control
plane: method surface + D13 enrolment) -> layer 3 (worktree create as one call) -> layer 4 (attention
queue + evidence) -> layer 5 (agent-state detection) -> layer 1 (the session service in the helper).
Layer 2 first because every other layer has a manual workaround for a while and this one has none,
because it forces the addressability model layers 3-5 consume, because it extends nocx's existing
JSON-RPC dispatcher rather than creating a second owner, and because it is testable end to end
without the relay.

title: Watch a request go into a folder, end to end
description:
The epic's happy path, written as the check that proves it (AGENTS.md testing rule 2). An
e2e spec against the real backend: a collection, a folder, a request beside it, the menu,
the chooser, and the row where it should now be — plus the file on disk at the new path
and not at the old one.
acceptance_criteria:
- One spec: make a folder, move a request into it, and see the row under the folder.
- The assertion is on BOTH the tree and the bytes: the file is at the new path and absent from the old.
- The request that was open is still open afterwards.
- It waits on observable state, never on a duration.
close_reason: Merged as d308aa97. e2e/api-move.spec.ts drives the real doors — collection row menu → New folder…, request row right-click → Move to folder…, the chooser, Move here — and asserts on both the tree and the bytes: the row under the folder, the file byte-for-byte what it was, the old path absent, and the request still open with its crumb naming the new place. 23 assertions, no waitForTimeout. Written by a worker that did not write the move (AGENTS.md testing rule 4). It also re-aimed e2e/api-tree.spec.ts, whose whole-list assertion on the request menu still named two items after nocx-8aczn.2 added a third.

title: Move to folder…: the act is in the menu the request row already has
description:
The gesture. The request row's right-button menu already carries Duplicate and Delete request… — nocx-rmjj8 put the acts on a request there deliberately. This is one more item, and a chooser for where.

The chooser lists the folders of THIS collection plus its root; the store already holds them (`collection.folders`). It also offers making one, because `api.collections.createFolder` exists and a person moving something into a folder that does not exist yet is the ordinary case on a young collection.

Two states the surface must not get wrong, and neither is an error: the request in the form is the one being moved (its path changes under the form), and the draft has unsaved edits (moving the file under them is a choice, not a default — say which one it is and why, in the code).
acceptance_criteria:
- From the request row menu a person chooses "Move to folder…", picks a destination and the request is there: the tree draws it under that folder and no longer beside it.
- The chooser offers the collection's own folders and its root, and a way to make a new folder from the same place.
- Moving the request that is OPEN leaves it open: the form still holds it and the header names the new place.
- A refusal from the backend reaches the person on the chooser and the request does not move.
- An unsaved draft is handled deliberately and the code says which rule it follows.
- Kit only: the chooser is a kit component or a new one added to `ui/`, placed and not repainted.
- A test drives it from the MENU — the item exists in the state a person starts in, choosing a folder reaches the client method, and the row is under the folder afterwards.
close_reason: Merged as c4b0bc7c. The act is in the request row's menu beside Duplicate and Delete request…; the chooser lists the collection's folders and its root and can make a new one. The worker caught after its first report that the chooser kept chosen/newName across openings — the dialog outlives one ask — and fixed it with a reopen-after-cancel regression. CSS is placement plus the surface's own two elements; no kit component is repainted.

title: api.request.move: one rename, one owner for the path, and a refusal that names the collision
description:
The backend half. One method that moves a request file from one relative path to another inside ONE collection — which is also the rename, because a rename is a move whose destination differs only in the leaf.

It is a rename on disk, not a read-write-delete: the failure modes of two writes are what this method exists to avoid. Path validation is the one `apicoll` already has (`validateRequestPath`, `validateFolderPath`), and whether a NAME is usable as a path at all has a single owner since nocx-9a22b — ask it, do not write a second answer.

State the invariant with both ends (AGENTS.md testing rule 3): the file is readable at exactly one of the two paths from before the call until after it, and there is no instant at which it is at both or neither.
acceptance_criteria:
- A request moves from the collection root into a folder, and from a folder to the root, and the bytes at the destination are the bytes that were at the source.
- A move whose destination already holds a file of that name is REFUSED, and the error names the collision. Nothing is overwritten and the source is still there.
- A destination outside the collection is refused by the path rules that already exist, not by a new check written beside them.
- A destination folder that does not exist is refused — this method moves, it does not create. Making a folder is `api.collections.createFolder`.
- The result carries the new relPath, so the caller does not have to derive it.
- The result shape has a schema in `contracts/` and both conformance tests, including the over-the-wire one.
- For every "returns an error when…" there is a paired assertion that the ordinary move succeeds.
close_reason: Merged as c4b0bc7c. api.request.move is a no-replace rename at the syscall, per platform (rename_linux.go / rename_darwin.go / rename_other.go) rather than an exists-check followed by os.Rename — that closes the window between the check and the move. A platform with no such syscall is refused by name instead of approximated. Schema in contracts/, generated type regenerated, 200 lines of move_test.go plus 165 in ws_contract_test.go.

title: A request can be put into a folder, and its file renamed, from the panel
description:
A request lands where it was created and stays there forever. There is no move and no
rename: the whole `api.*` surface is `collections.{close,create,createFolder,list,open}`,
`environment.{bindSecret,read,write}`, `import.{curl,postman}` and
`request.{cancel,delete,read,send,write}`. Dragging a row does nothing because there is
nothing to drop onto — the product has no intra-tree drag at all — and the header's rename
deliberately renames the NAME and not the file, which `request-crumbs.tsx` states in as
many words: "Renaming a file is a different act — it is a move, with a collision to
resolve and a git rename behind it — and there is no method for it yet."

So a person who makes a folder cannot put anything in it. The owner made one, watched the
whole collection appear to fall into it, and then found there was no way to actually move a
single request there.

THE ACT IS ONE OPERATION, not two. `request.write` to the new path followed by
`request.delete` of the old one has a window in which the request exists twice and a
window in which it exists not at all, and a failure between them leaves whichever half
landed. It is one rename on the backend, under the path rules `apicoll` already owns
(`validateRequestPath`, and `pathname` for whether a name is usable as a path at all —
nocx-9a22b put one owner on that question deliberately).

ONE METHOD, TWO ACTS. Moving a request into a folder and renaming its file are the same
call with a different destination, so they are built together or the method ships
half-used.

THE GESTURE IS THE MENU THAT ALREADY EXISTS. A request row already has a right-button menu
carrying Duplicate and Delete request… — where nocx-rmjj8 deliberately put the acts on a
request, "where the tab strip and the Files panel already put theirs". Move to folder…
is one more item in it, it is reachable from the keyboard, and it needs no new interaction
vocabulary. Drag is an ACCELERATOR on the same call and is deliberately out of this epic:
a drop grammar is its own design (into a folder versus between rows, the highlight,
autoscroll, what a drop on another collection means) and it would need this menu as its
keyboard equivalent anyway.
acceptance_criteria:
DONE WHEN a person can, with no file editing at all: right-click a request in the tree, choose "Move to folder…", pick a folder of that collection (or make one from the same place), and find the request inside it — the tree draws it there, the file is at the new path and nowhere else, and the request they had open is still the one in the form. One automated check watches exactly that, end to end.

The same method renames a file, reached from the header where the request is already named.

Deliberately out: dragging a row (an accelerator on this method, filed separately), moving a request between COLLECTIONS, and moving a folder itself.

title: Five frontend files on feat/api-testing are not Prettier-clean, so the frontend CI job is red
description:
The containerized frontend job fails at format:check on five files under frontend/src/api — api-client.ts, api-client.test.ts, api-store.test.ts, api-tree.test.ts, api-workbench.test.tsx. They landed unformatted through some path that did not run the hook (--no-verify, or a merge that resolved into unformatted text). The pre-commit hook now refuses every commit on the branch until they are fixed, so this blocks all work, not only CI.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. cd frontend && npx prettier --check .
2. Five files are reported.

## Acceptance Criteria

- prettier --check is clean at the repo root and in frontend/.
- The fix is the formatter's own output, with no hand edits riding along.
close_reason: Formatter run over the six files; prettier --check clean at the root and in frontend/. The pre-commit hook no longer refuses on format.

title: a-later-import-brings-its-own-report-back is red on the branch
description:
`api-workbench.test.tsx > the import report says whose it is and can be ended > a later import brings its own report back` fails deterministically on feat/api-testing at 7f981475 — baselined at HEAD with the surrounding change reverted, so it is not caused by whatever is on top of it.

The second `convertCurl` in that test never brings the panel back: `notImportedPanel()` stays null after the dismiss. The first import's report appears and dismisses correctly, so what is broken is the *re-arming*, which is the one thing the test's own comment says it exists to prove — "a panel that stayed dismissed would be the silent degrade the panel exists to prevent".

The test and the panel both arrived in a326e912 (nocx-q2cx5), so either the dismissal is remembered across imports or the second import's report never reaches the panel.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. `cd frontend && npx vitest run src/api/api-workbench.test.tsx -t 'a later import brings its own report back'`
2. It fails at line 4399: expected null not to be null.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The test passes because the behaviour it names is real: a dismissed report is re-armed by the NEXT import, asserted on a second import carrying different words.
- The fix is in the panel or the store, not in the test's expectations.
close_reason: NOT the panel. nocx-86wvw taught importCurl to ask before discarding unsaved work, and the second import in that test is exactly that case — the first import leaves a request with no file behind it, so unsavedWork() is true. The ask went up, the test never answered it, the awaited promise never resolved and the report was never re-armed. The test now answers it the way a person does rather than mocking showConfirm away, with a 'discarding' parameter so 'was the person asked' stays a fact each test asserts. 400/400 green in src/api.

title: The Auth tab's only field is a variable name, so a token pasted there can never be sent
description:
The Auth tab offers one field, labelled "Secret variable", and the model behind it is a
NAME and nothing else. `apicoll.Auth.Var` is a variable name by definition
(collection.go:100), `apicoll.Substitute` deliberately does not expand it
(substitute.go:223 — "That field IS a variable name, not text containing one"), and
`internal/apisend.resolveAuthVar` looks it up through the Lookup on its own. There is no
way in this model to say "the token is this".

So a person who pastes a token into the only field there is gets a request that can never
be sent: the token becomes a variable name nobody bound, and Send refuses with `the auth
variable "88730fee…" is not bound in this environment`. Observed 2026-08-23 on the
owner's own collection, with "No environment" selected, where the tab does not even draw
the door that would bind a value.

The owner's decision of 2026-08-23 (nocx-tg9l8's closing reason) is that the product does
not hide or move a credential a person typed. nocx-5dfa5 carries the obligation that
follows from it — the vault must be the EASIER path from wherever a person is, offered
rather than imposed. Postman is the same model: the Bearer field takes a value; a
`{{variable}}` or a `{{vault:key}}` reference is simply text one may type into it; what
protects a shared collection is an offer plus a detector, never a refusal.

Design §8 is NOT in the way and does not change. It forbids a file naming ANOTHER
credential by identifier — "there is no syntax in which a file names a secret" — which is
an attack on the reader of a pulled collection. A literal the person typed is not that:
it is their own value, in their own file, and it is what they asked for.

So the defect is narrower than it first looked: auth is the one field in the product that
is not text. Making it text also removes a second owner of "what does this text resolve
to" — the substitution already answers that for the URL, the query, the headers and the
body, through the same `apicoll.Chain` that decides plain-vs-vault by construction rather
than by heuristic (capability/api.go:151).

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open a request in the API workbench, Auth tab, scheme Bearer.
2. Paste a token into the "Secret variable" field — the only field there is.
3. Press Send.
4. The run answers `the request could not be built` / `the auth variable "<the
   token>" is not bound in this environment`, and the token is now written into
   the request file as `auth.var`.
acceptance_criteria:
- A literal pasted into the Bearer field is SENT: the request goes out with `Authorization: Bearer <literal>` and the run reports the answer.
- The same field holding `{{name}}` resolves through the SAME substitution the URL uses — a plain environment value and a vault-bound one both. `resolveAuthVar` no longer exists; there is one resolver, not two.
- A vault-bound value placed in auth is still elided in the raw diagnostic and still reaches Send as a NamedSecret. A literal is NOT elided — that is the decision of 2026-08-23, and a test asserts both halves so it cannot later read as a reversal.
- Basic behaves the same way: a literal password sends, a `{{name}}` resolves.
- An unresolved `{{name}}` in auth reports through `apicoll.UnresolvedError` like every other field, naming the variable and the field it was used in. The bespoke sentence "the auth variable %q is not bound in this environment" is gone.
- A scheme with an EMPTY field is still a blocked send, never a silent downgrade to anonymous (the rule §6.5 already states).
- The file records what was typed, and any schema in `contracts/` that carries auth moves with it in the same commit; the generated renderer types are regenerated, not hand-edited.
- A test drives it from the FORM: a token is pasted into the Auth tab, Send is pressed, and the value is on the wire — not a test that hands the model an Auth struct.
- Deliberately out: the picker and the create-a-secret door from any field (nocx-5dfa5), and the body editor, which is its own shape.
close_reason: Merged as 12a7711e. Auth.Var is gone for Token/Password; Substitute expands them; resolveAuthVar deleted, so one resolver. A literal is sent and shown, a {{name}} resolves through the same lookup as one in the URL, and the plain-vs-vault split is derived field-wise from the RAW file text against the names the binding document answered (SendInputs.RawRequest + AuthSecrets) — no value is ever compared against recorded text. The e2e asserts both halves over the real wire: the pasted literal reaches the server as the header and shows unelided in Raw. Gate green on the merged tree, including go test -race and vitest in their containers.

title: A raw Go error sentinel is shown to the user verbatim
description:
Reported by the owner with a screenshot, 2026-08-23: a toast reading

    content stub: not implemented

That string is `ErrNotImplemented` in internal/content/content.go:31 -- an
internal Go sentinel, surfaced to a person word for word. It names an
implementation detail (a "stub"), uses developer vocabulary ("not implemented"),
and tells the reader nothing they can act on.

Two separate faults, and the second is the one that recurs:

1. Whatever produced it should not reach a person in that form. An error
   crossing the wire needs a message written FOR the person, or a mapping at
   the surface -- the same discipline frontend/src/ui/operation-row.tsx applies
   to enums ("they differ on the wire and they do not differ to a person").
2. The content store being a stub is itself a soft degrade. AGENTS.md: "A soft
   degrade must be visible in the product, not only in a log" -- but visible
   means a sentence a person understands, not the sentinel. If history is
   unavailable in this build, the product should say what is unavailable and
   what it means, once, not leak the reason it happened.

Related in shape to nocx-a9gf4 (the notification row renders wire enum slugs to
a person). Same defect class -- an internal identifier reaching a human
surface -- in a different place. They are separate beads because the fix sites
are unrelated.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run a build whose content store resolves to the stub.
2. Do something that reaches it.
3. A toast shows `content stub: not implemented`.

## Acceptance Criteria

- No Go sentinel text reaches a rendered surface. Whatever gate proves this
  should be able to fail: a test that asserts a known sentinel is not in the
  toast is worth more than an eyeball.
- If the store is genuinely unavailable, the product says so in a sentence a
  person can act on, and says it once.
- Whether the stub should be reachable AT ALL in a shipped build is answered,
  not left implicit -- if it should not, the fix is upstream of the message.

title: The notification row and its filter show wire identifiers to a person
description:
Reported by the owner with a screenshot, 2026-08-23: a notification row reading
"Uploaded log.txt" carries a badge that says `transfer.finished`. "Why should a
user see transfer.finished? Why does it look so crude? Look at how it is done in
Operations." And: "a user must not decode our identifiers."

frontend/src/notify/notifications-panel.tsx:271 passes the WIRE ENUM straight
through as the badge label:

    kind={{ label: o.kind, tone: toneOf(o.level) }}

So a person reads block.finished, pane.workFinished, transfer.finished --
dotted internal slugs.

The same defect a second time in the same file (~line 142): the kind filter uses
optionLabel: (o) => o.kind, so the dropdown lists slugs too. The comment there
requires the filter to say the same word as the row, which is correct -- so both
move together.

THE KIT ALREADY SOLVES THIS and the owner named it. frontend/src/ui/
operation-row.tsx maps kind to an ICON (KIND_ICON: upload -> ArrowUpIcon), state
to human words (PHASE_LABEL: written/sent -> "Done", not the wire word) and
colour to a third map. Its comment states the principle exactly: written and
sent "differ on the wire and they do not differ to a person". The notifications
panel is a second surface that never joined that vocabulary.

NOT a wire defect. The slug is correct ON THE WIRE and in contracts/; it is
wrong only in front of a person.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Cause any notification (finish a transfer, run a command).
2. Open the notification centre.
3. The row badge reads the wire kind, e.g. `transfer.finished`.
4. Open the kind filter: it lists the same slugs.

## Acceptance Criteria

- No wire slug is rendered anywhere in the row or the filter. Asserted on
  rendered text: a dotted identifier in the row IS the defect.
- The mapping lives in the kit vocabulary the way OperationRow does, not as a
  string built inside the panel -- a surface may place a kit component and may
  never repaint it.
- An unknown kind degrades to something readable, never to the slug and never
  to blank.
- Any existing test that asserted the slug moves with it: it was asserting the
  defect.

title: A secret can only be made on the Auth tab, and using an existing one means knowing its name by heart
acceptance_criteria:
Follows the owner's decision of 2026-08-23 (see nocx-tg9l8's closing reason):
the product does not hide or move a credential a person typed. The obligation
that falls out of it is the other one — if we will not push people into the
vault, the vault has to be the EASIER path from wherever they are, not a
detour.

Today it is neither, in both directions.

MAKING ONE HAS EXACTLY ONE DOOR AND IT IS ON THE WRONG TAB. `AuthSecret`
(request-form.tsx) lets a person type a value and press Store, and it is
reachable only from Auth. A person pasting a token into a HEADER — which is
the case the decision above is about — has no door at all: they must leave for
the environments page, find the row, mark it secret, paste, and come back. The
write itself is not the problem: `store.bindSecret` is the one call in this
product that carries a credential and it is already scoped to the collection
and the environment. It has one caller.

USING ONE MEANS REMEMBERING ITS NAME. Substitution already resolves `{{name}}`
through the binding document in the URL, the query, headers and the body — the
capability is complete (capability/api.go:151 records exactly those
placements). What is missing is any way to SEE what exists: nothing lists the
variables of the active environment where a person is typing, so `{{` is a
guess against memory, and a misspelling is refused at send time rather than
prevented at the keystroke.

## Acceptance Criteria

• From a header value, a query value and the URL, a person can insert a
  variable chosen from what the ACTIVE environment actually holds — without
  typing the name from memory and without leaving the request.
• The list says which entries are secrets and which are plain values, in the
  vocabulary the environments page already uses. It is not a second
  description of the same rows.
• From the same place, a person can create a secret: a name and a value,
  written through `store.bindSecret` — the SAME call the Auth tab uses, not a
  second minter and not a second scoping rule. The Auth tab's create path and
  this one are one seam; two would be two owners of "what does storing a
  credential mean here".
• After creating, the field holds `{{name}}` and never the value, and the
  request file never holds the value — asserted on the bytes on disk.
• Absence is the capability, in the vocabulary that exists: `SecretTarget`
  already distinguishes no-collection from no-environment and says which. This
  extends it rather than answering the question a second time; no control is
  drawn that would fail when pressed.
• Nothing here rewrites, refuses or sanitises a credential somebody typed as
  text. It is an offer, and the decision it follows from is that the value
  stays where they put it.
• Kit only: the picker is a kit component or a new one added to `ui/`, placed
  and not repainted.
• A test drives the seam from a HEADER row: the door exists from the state a
  person starts in, choosing an existing secret puts `{{name}}` in the field,
  creating one reaches `bindSecret` and puts `{{name}}` in the field, and the
  saved file contains neither value.
• Out, and named rather than silently missing: the body editor. CodeMirror
  owns its own input and a picker inside it is its own shape — filed
  separately once this lands, because a token in a JSON body is a real case.

title: The collections panel promises a folder is safe to commit, and a pasted credential makes that untrue
description:
Split out of nocx-tg9l8, whose other half the owner decided against on
2026-08-23 (see that bead's closing reason). This half stands and is the one
with the real blast radius.

api-pane.tsx:1364 and :1379 tell a person a collection folder is a folder they
can commit: "It is safe to commit: no secret value is ever written into it."
That was true while every credential arrived as a variable name resolved from
the vault. It is not true now: the owner decided deliberately that a
credential a person pastes stays where they put it (nocx-14exx), so an
imported curl line keeps its Authorization header AS TEXT, in the request
file, in the folder the sentence is talking about.

So the product prints a promise about git that the product itself breaks, and
the person reading it is exactly the person about to `git add`.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Import `curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" https://example.test/x`.
2. Save it into a collection and open the collection folder on disk — the
   token is in the request file, in full.
3. Look at the collections panel: it says the folder is safe to commit.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The sentence says what it actually covers: a value bound to a variable is
  never written into the folder, and a credential typed or imported straight
  into a header is.
- It does not frighten a person away from the ordinary case, which is a
  collection with no pasted credential in it at all.
- If the surface can say WHETHER THIS collection has one — the request files
  are read already — it says that rather than stating a general caveat. A
  warning that is always shown is one nobody reads.
- Nothing here rewrites, refuses or sanitises a header. The decision it
  follows from is that the value stays where the person put it.
- A test asserts the sentence in both states, from the state a person starts in.
close_reason: Merged into feat/api-testing (w-notimported). q2cx5: the importer half was already on the branch (9574c197 — curl.go's three-valued disposition table, so -sS itemises nothing); this adds the missing half, the report naming its import and being dismissable. flidy: the ask now says what it covers — a value bound to a variable never reaches the folder, a pasted credential does. Brief premise corrected by the worker: api.collections.list carries no headers, so the surface answers about the request in the FORM rather than about the collection, and says so. The predicate mirrors authFromHeader's grammar rather than re-deriving internal/secrets.Detect, and the default sentence promises nothing about headers it did not inspect. Nothing rewrites or sanitises a header.

title: The tree never says which request is open
acceptance_criteria:
The header says `Playground › test`, and in the tree the row `test` is drawn
exactly like the thirteen rows around it. There is no way to find, in a list of
requests whose names are often near-identical, the one the form is showing —
and after a duplicate there are two rows one word apart.

The kit already answers this. `TreeRow` takes `selected` and paints it
(`data-selected`, tree-row.css:46), and this very panel uses it two hundred
lines below for the environment list, where the chosen row carries an accent
bar. The tree passes `selected` for COLLECTION rows only (api-pane.tsx:1574) —
a request row is never handed it, whatever is open.

## Success Criteria

• The row of the request in the form is marked as selected in the tree, and it
  is the only request row that is.
• Opening another request moves the mark; closing the collection, deleting the
  open request, or a curl import that detaches the form from any file leaves NO
  request row marked rather than a stale one.
• The mark is the kit's `selected` on `TreeRow` — placed, not repainted, and
  the same vocabulary the environment list already uses.
• A request the tree cannot show — filtered out — does not resurrect a mark
  elsewhere.
• A test opens a request, asserts its row is the marked one, opens another and
  asserts the mark moved.
• Out: distinguishing "this collection is where new requests go" from "this
  request is open" — the collection row's own marking is unchanged here, and if
  one treatment for two facts reads wrong it is its own bead.
close_reason: afb6ec70 on feat/api-testing. One request-action list behind two doors (row right-click, header ⋮); the row's Duplicate IconButton is gone; the open request's row carries the kit's selected mark. 342 api unit tests green, eslint and the css/two-owners/row-grammar/menu-icons ratchets green.

title: A tree row has no right-click, and the header's ⋮ offers one thing
acceptance_criteria:
Duplicate arrived as an IconButton drawn on every request row (api-pane.tsx),
beside the method badge. It is a second control competing with the name for a
line that is already narrow, and it is the third different way this surface
answers "what can I do with this row" — a hover plus on collections, a ⋮ on
collections, and now an always-drawn copy on requests.

The answer the product already has is the kit's ContextMenu, whose own
docstring says what it is for: "a small, non-modal popover of actions anchored
at a point (the row the user right-clicked)". The files panel wires exactly
that (files-view.tsx:501) and the tab strip too (tab.tsx:164). The API tree
wires no contextmenu handler at all, so right-clicking a request offers the
webview's own menu — reload, save image as — about a request.

And the header's ⋮ holds one item, Delete request…, while the only other thing
the open request can do is drawn somewhere else entirely.

ONE LIST, TWO DOORS. The actions of a request are one list, built in one
place, and reached both by right-clicking its row and by the ⋮ over the open
one. Two hand-written lists would be the two-owners defect with a menu as the
thing they disagreed about.

## Acceptance Criteria

• Right-clicking a request row opens a menu at the pointer with that row's
  actions, and the webview's own menu does not appear.
• Right-clicking a collection row opens the collection menu that its ⋮ already
  opens — same items, same code, anchored at the pointer instead of the button.
• The request row's Duplicate IconButton is GONE; duplicating is a menu item.
• The header's ⋮ offers the same request actions as the row menu, acting on
  the open request.
• The two menus are built by ONE function taking the request it is about;
  nothing re-derives the list.
• A menu item that destroys still asks, by name, the way Delete does today.
• Items carry icons from the registry (the menu-icons ratchet), and the menu is
  placed and never repainted.
• A test right-clicks a request row that is NOT the open one, picks Duplicate,
  and asserts the copy appears; another picks Delete on it and asserts the
  confirm names that row rather than the open one.
• Out: a folder row's menu (nothing to put in it until nocx-8v1fu wires
  folders) and renaming from a row (there is no move method — request-crumbs.tsx
  states this).
close_reason: afb6ec70 on feat/api-testing. One request-action list behind two doors (row right-click, header ⋮); the row's Duplicate IconButton is gone; the open request's row carries the kit's selected mark. 342 api unit tests green, eslint and the css/two-owners/row-grammar/menu-icons ratchets green.

title: The tab bar holds one tab's controls, so the row carries what the section should
description:
The tab bar's `actions` slot carries controls that belong to ONE tab and are switched by which tab is active (request-form.tsx:542): `Format` and the body-mode select appear when `tab() === 'body'`, the auth-scheme select when `tab() === 'auth'`. So a row that names the sections also holds one section's contents, and what it holds changes under the tabs as a person moves between them.

The kit's slot is not wrong — its comment says it is for "the section's own control" — but a control that is present only for one section IS that section's content, and putting it in the shared row has three costs, all of them observed:

- **It is what made the row overflow.** The bar was 566 wide in a 496 column because `Format` plus the mode select sit in it; the overflow travelled up and the request column drew a horizontal scrollbar under the whole surface (nocx-kdawd). The kit now clips and shrinks, but the pressure only exists because the controls are there.
- **It puts the controls far from what they govern.** The mode select decides how the editor below reads; `Format` acts on it. Both sit above the tab row, separated from the editor by the tabs themselves.
- **It reads as chrome rather than as the section.** Postman, the owner's reference, puts the tabs in one row and the body's own controls — raw/form-data/binary, the JSON mode, Beautify — in a second row INSIDE the Body panel.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The body-mode select and the Format control render inside the Body panel, above the editor, not in the tab bar.
- The auth-scheme select renders inside the Auth panel, for the same reason and in the same shape.
- The tab bar no longer takes controls that are conditional on the active tab. If nothing tab-independent remains, this surface passes no `actions` at all — and the kit's slot stays, because other surfaces may still have a genuinely section-independent control.
- Absence keeps its meaning: Format is not drawn where the body kind has no formatter, and the mode select is not drawn on a tab it does not govern. No greyed-out control appears anywhere as part of this.
- Kit only: the new row places kit components and repaints none; no hand-rolled control, no inline SVG.
- The existing tests that reach these controls keep reaching them — by role and label, from the state a person starts in. Where a test addressed a control through the tab bar, it now addresses it in the panel; say which ones moved and why.
- The geometry guard in e2e/api-testing.spec.ts still passes: nothing from the editor up to the pane is wider than its own box.
close_reason: eabc0874 on feat/api-testing (w-tabctl). Body kind + Format inside the Body panel above the editor; auth scheme inside the Auth panel; the surface passes the kit's actions slot nothing. tabs.tsx changed only in its prop CONTRACT — the slot is for what belongs to the whole set of sections, and a child wrapped in a Show on the active tab does not belong in it. 4 new tests (3 red first); 351 api unit tests + 1111 with src/ui green, tsc x2, eslint, kit-identities and css-colors clean. Geometry: the row carries both bounds (min-width on the wrapper, max-width on the select), which is the pair nocx-kdawd needed.

title: Watch a multi-step turn end to end, live and after a restart
description:
The epic's happy path (AGENTS.md testing rule 2). cmd/devharness runs the real backend
headless; e2e/run-in-container.sh is how it is run here, and CI is the source of truth.
acceptance_criteria:
- An e2e spec drives one turn through prose → run → prose → a non-block tool call → prose,
  asserts the children's order and their text, restarts the backend, restores the pane, and
  asserts the same order and the same text.
- The spec fails if the arrangement regresses to one body at the bottom.
close_reason:
Landed in 173001b9 and green in the container. e2e/agent-turn.spec.ts drives one turn through prose, an assistant-run command, more prose, a non-block tool call and the answer, then restarts the backend, restores the pane and asserts the same order and the same text. The order is asserted POSITIONALLY by comparing the children's tops, because the failure it guards against is a layout claim — all the prose sliding below all the children is what DOM order alone cannot see.

This task earned the rule that put it here. Six task-level suites were green while three real defects sat in the branch, and this one check found all three: a prose body that never reached the renderer (handleGet flattened only execution artifacts), a kind enum that made ledger.get violate its own contract on a text row, and a restored assistant-run command drawn as prose, which turned out to be the kind/source conflation and became nocx-dc2fr.8. Each hid in a seam that the two suites either side of it did not cross.

Delivered over three worker windows with two WORKER_BLOCKED reports in between, and both blocks were correct: the worker refused to weaken an assertion or to invent a passing state, and each refusal named a product defect with evidence.

The screenshot observation the brief demanded was finally taken, and the coordinator read the image too — the first time in this epic anyone looked at the arrangement in a browser. It renders as designed: question once, children in causal order, the command block between its two sentences with its own output, ok chip and agent badge, the tool block quieter than the command. Two cosmetic notes were passed to the owner rather than acted on: the indent and left rule are subtle at this size, and a tool call's header repeats sessionId even though the whole turn is in that pane, which crowds out the argument that matters.

Carried forward as nocx-dc2fr.9: with a call that carries no id, a turn still merges its two runs of prose and draws them after the command. e2e/agent-restore.spec.ts is its reproduction and lands with that fix rather than red here.

title: A restored turn and the live turn it came from are one list
description:
Restore reads the turn's children in `pos` order and draws them. There is no projection to
share with the live path any more (scrollback/turn-flow.ts is deleted) — the two paths draw
the same stored list, which is what makes agreement structural rather than tested-for.

ADR-0019: this is a projection of the ledger and stores nothing of its own.
acceptance_criteria:
- ONE test builds a turn through the live handle and the same turn through restore, and
  compares the two DOM trees — not two tests each asserting a shape.
- A dangling child (older than the page limit, or evicted) costs the turn that child and
  nothing else; nothing is invented to stand in for it.
- A restored `tool` block names the same tool and the same arguments the live one did,
  read off the stored row.
- A restored turn's chips (duration, completed/failed) are on the turn block, once.
close_reason: Landed in dcc3031a. The parity between a live turn and a restored one is structural now rather than held by keeping two cutters in step, and restored-turn-order.test.ts is back under its old name asserting it: one test builds a turn through BlockManager and the same turn through the restore and compares the two DOMs, never a fixture, with what is compared and what is deliberately excluded stated in the file. The evicted-prose sentence finally reaches the screen: ledger.get carries Entry.ProseEvicted (the detail read the restore already makes per entry, deliberately not ledger.query so there is one owner), asserted off the real socket with a pinned turn as the paired negative; the renderer reuses the wording a command whose body was evicted already had rather than growing a second vocabulary, and says it once for the turn rather than once per hole. The worker found and fixed a latent restore bug the tree made load-bearing: a restored block chose its grammar from WHICH ARTIFACT SURVIVED, so an ADR-0037 turn, which owns no artifact at all, had quietly become a command; the kind is read from the entry's own kind now. Verified by the coordinator on the merged tree: 3809 frontend tests, both tsconfigs, contracts:check, go build, internal/transport and internal/content green, and the full pre-commit hook including the containerised race and vitest gates. Two coordinator edits: a shadowed err in ws_ledger_query_test.go, and a dead ANSWER constant that concatenated the two halves of the prose — replaced by a comment saying why joining them would be the test re-inventing the cut it exists to prove nobody makes. First task run on an omp worker rather than claude.

title: The turn draws its children in order, and a call names its arguments
description:
The live renderer. Much of this is already built on branch feat/ai-assistant under
nocx-lfxi6 — the `tool` block kind, `scrollback/tool-call-title.ts`, the child region, the
`args` field on `agent.runToolCall`, and the deletion of ui/tool-call-line.ts,
ui/tool-call-group.ts and scrollback/turn-flow.ts. What changes is the source: the turn
stops holding one answer body and draws the ordered children it is sent.

Before touching the child region, read turn-flow.ts's rejected-arrangements note as
ADR-0036's second amendment restates it: hoisting a command above the question stays
rejected, and nesting a VT grid INSIDE reflowing prose stays rejected — a child block
beside the prose is not that.
acceptance_criteria:
- A turn that wrote prose, ran a command and wrote more prose draws, in document order:
  the prose, the command block with its output, the prose. Asserted on the DOM order, not
  on presence.
- Two calls to one tool with different arguments render differently — the case the whole
  epic started from (`blocks.read` twice, same pane, different blocks).
- A `run` command block is a child of its turn, carries the `agent` author badge, keeps its
  own id, selection, ⋮ and exit status, and its `.cmd-output` still refuses to re-wrap.
- The question appears exactly once; no fragment, no `continued` badge.
- A turn that made no calls draws exactly what it drew before this epic: a question and its
  prose.
close_reason: Landed in f626db68. A turn is one block carrying its children in stored order: a headerless prose block, a  block naming the tool AND its arguments, and an ordinary  block for what run opened — keeping its id, header, exit status, agent badge and its refusal to re-wrap. The arguments go on agent.runToolCall and on ledger.get's caused row, so a restored call names as much as a live one; the schema's rationale was rewritten rather than left contradicted. A session is still named and never numbered, with the pane's title injected and the session argument identified by the backend's derived resource rather than by its key's spelling. Deleted with the arrangement they served: ui/tool-call-line.ts, ui/tool-call-group.ts, scrollback/turn-flow.ts, their tests, CSS, README rows, the compaction threshold, and the fragment machinery including markTurnFragment and the continued badge. Worker went beyond the brief and said so: restored-block.ts could not merely be made to compile (it depended on four deleted things), so it now draws the turn and its causes in seat order and its eleven anchor/fragment tests became eight asserting the current claim — nocx-dc2fr.4's scope shrank accordingly and its brief was rewritten. Two coordinator edits: the child region gained the gutter and left rule the owner had asked for and my brief had dropped, and a  alias was replaced by named seams (mintId/own/claim/claimedBy) after eslint refused it — the handle's methods are declared , so the alias was load-bearing and needed replacing rather than deleting. Verified on the merged tree: 3804 frontend tests, both tsconfigs, contracts:check, go build, and the full pre-commit hook including the containerised go test -race and vitest. Not verified: nobody has looked at it in a browser — the worker said so and I am carrying that forward to nocx-dc2fr.7.

title: The run writes prose blocks, and a delta addresses the one it appends to
description:
ADR-0037's streaming half. The backend owns the boundary between prose blocks: a `text`
block opens on the first delta after a call and closes when the next call arrives. The
renderer never decides where a piece begins — that is the whole reason the anchor could
drift between the live path and the restore.

`seq` stays monotonic per RUN so replay after a reconnect is unchanged (agent.runDelta's
own contract note on ordering across a suspension still holds).
acceptance_criteria:
- `agent.runDelta` carries the block id its text appends to; the contract declares it
  required, and a `…_OverTheWireConformsToContract` test reads it off the real socket.
- `at` is absent from `contracts/`, from the ledger payloads and from every Go struct.
- A run that writes prose, calls a tool, writes more prose leaves exactly two `text` blocks
  under the turn, at positions either side of the call's.
- A run that calls a tool before writing anything leaves no empty `text` block.
- Two deltas either side of a call never land in one block — asserted on the stored rows,
  not on the notification.
- An approved-egress resume continues the block it was suspended in rather than opening a
  second one.
close_reason: Landed. OpenProse/SealProse on the ledger: a turn's answer is a run of text children, one per stretch of prose between two tool calls, seated at the next free position; the backend owns both boundaries. agent.runDelta carries blockId (required on the contract, asserted off the real socket); seq stays per RUN so a resumed run keeps numbering (nocx-igu4y). at left contracts/ledger.get and ws_ledger_query with the fact it described, and the placeholder assertion the previous commit left behind was deleted rather than adjusted, exactly as its comment asked. 10 new tests in ws_agent_prose_test.go plus one in ledger_agent_test.go: prose either side of a call is two blocks; no call means one; a call before any prose opens none; a call after the last prose opens no trailing block; an approved-egress resume continues the block it was suspended in; OpenProse refuses an absent parent and SealProse is a no-op on a bodiless block, each with its paired success. Verified by the coordinator uncached: internal/content, internal/assistant, internal/transport green, both tsconfigs clean. Worker's escalation was correct and is resolved here: restored-turn-order.test.ts asserted the at-anchored fragment arrangement and was deleted with this commit; its thesis is commissioned as nocx-dc2fr.4's first criterion. Worker also reported TestConcurrentReadersWithOneWriter flaking with 'database disk image is malformed' — independently measured by the retention worker at 2/12 on a pristine HEAD copy and 0/32 on its own tree, so pre-existing contention, not this change.

title: entries become an ordered tree, and prose is a block
description:
ADR-0037 is the brief; read it first. This is its schema half, landing with the Go read and
write paths so nothing here is unreachable (AGENTS.md: a task that adds code lands with the
wiring that makes it reachable).

Touches ADR-0019 (§7 retention evicts bodies and leaves entries — still true, and it is why
artifacts stay their own rows) and ADR-0020 decision 4 (a retry after approval is an
execution of the same intent — `executions` is NOT collapsed by this).

Greenfield: the schema changes in place, there is nothing to migrate.
acceptance_criteria:
- `entries` has `parent_id TEXT REFERENCES entries(id) ON DELETE SET NULL` and
  `pos INTEGER`, with `UNIQUE (parent_id, pos)`. NULL parent is a top-level block, ordered
  by `ingest_seq` as before.
- `entries.kind` admits `text`, under
  `CHECK (kind <> 'text' OR (parent_id IS NOT NULL AND pos IS NOT NULL AND intent = '' AND phase = 'closed' AND status = 'success'))`.
  A test inserts each violation and asserts the database refuses it — one per clause.
- `artifacts.entry_id` is NOT NULL and references the entry; `execution_id` is nullable
  provenance. A `text` block's artifact has no execution and inserts cleanly.
- `edges`'s CHECK no longer lists `caused-by`; inserting one is refused.
- `conversation_id` and `reviewed_at` are gone from the table and from every Go struct that
  named them.
- The ledger writes and reads a parent and a position: submitting a child under a parent and
  reading the parent back returns its children in `pos` order, and a second child at a taken
  position is refused rather than silently reordering.
close_reason: Landed in 3a773cf1. entries carries parent_id + pos with UNIQUE(parent_id,pos); kind 'text' is admitted under a five-clause CHECK (child, seated, empty intent, closed, success) and each clause is refused separately by its own test. artifacts.entry_id is the owner and execution_id is nullable provenance, so prose has a body without an execution invented to hold it. caused-by left the edges vocabulary with its {pos,at} payload, and at went with it — including its plumbing in internal/assistant (answerLen, answerAt, utf16Len). conversation_id and reviewed_at dropped: neither was ever written with a value. schemaVersion 13 discards dev databases, correct for a greenfield change. 16 new tests in ledger_tree_test.go, every refusal paired with 'and on an ordinary database it succeeds' (AGENTS.md rule 3), and the read-back test submits children 2,0,1 so pos and ingest_seq genuinely disagree. Verified by the coordinator, not taken on report: internal/content, internal/assistant and internal/transport green; internal/app failures measured against a clean-branch baseline and identical (nocx-58gq, nocx-65v6). Coordinator's own edit: the over-the-socket contract test now asserts at == 0 for every cause with a comment saying it must fail and be deleted when nocx-dc2fr.2 takes the field off the contract — the fact is dead in the store and splitting it across two tasks must not leave a placeholder passing quietly. Handed on: nocx-gvey3 (a block can be seated under itself), and ADR-0019's stale conversation_id line amended by the coordinator.

title: A block is a node in an ordered tree: a turn's prose, its calls and its commands are one list
description:
Recorded as ADR-0037 (docs/decisions/0037-a-block-is-a-node-in-an-ordered-tree.md), which
amends ADR-0036 in place. Read the ADR before the first line of code: it names what was
tried (nocx-shxv0, nocx-9sqii, nocx-lfxi6), why each failed the same way, and the four
arrangements that were considered and rejected — an EAV attributes table, a per-execution
event tape, a parent pointing at the execution, and prose as several artifacts merged with
the causes on read. None of those is open for re-litigation without amending the ADR.

The defect in one sentence: the unit that is DRAWN (a run of prose) and the unit that is
STORED (the whole answer) were different things, so something had to translate between
them, and every attempt at that translation was paid for twice.
acceptance_criteria:
## Success Criteria

A person asks the assistant something that needs several steps and reads the turn back —
live, and again after restarting the app — and both times sees ONE block whose children are
the causal sequence exactly as it happened: the sentence the model wrote before a command,
then that command with its real output, then the sentence written from it. Two calls to the
same tool are told apart by their arguments.

The end-to-end check that watches it: e2e drives a turn with prose → run → prose → a
non-block tool call → prose, asserts the children's order and text, restarts the backend,
restores the pane, and asserts the same order and the same text.

Asserted, each of which stops being false exactly once:

- `entries` carries `parent_id` and `pos` with `UNIQUE (parent_id, pos)`, and `kind` admits
  `text` under a CHECK that pins its shape (child, positioned, empty intent, closed,
  success).
- An artifact belongs to its entry; `execution_id` is optional provenance.
- `caused-by` is gone from the `edges` CHECK, and `at` appears nowhere: not in the store,
  not in `contracts/`, not in the renderer.
- `conversation_id` and `reviewed_at` are gone from `entries`.
- A restored turn and the live turn it came from produce the same ordered list — asserted by
  one test that builds both and compares, not by two tests that each assert a shape.
- The conversation sent to the model for a follow-up question contains the turn's prose in
  `pos` order, and a second attempt's prose is not interleaved with the first's.
- Retention evicts the prose of one run as a unit: no turn ever renders a partial answer as
  though it were whole.

## Deliberately out

- Re-running a turn (`rerun-of` already relates two turns; no second mechanism).
- Any change to how `executions` model attempts (ADR-0020 decision 4 stands).
- Addressable tool RESULTS — nothing on the wire reports how a call ended; that is
  nocx-d6gn4.2.

title: Two surfaces still describe a world where a credential cannot be in a header
description:
The owner decided, deliberately, that a credential a person pastes into the product stays where they put it: an imported curl line keeps its Authorization header, and whether to promote it into a secret is the person's choice, not the product's (nocx-14exx). That decision is not in question here. What follows from it is that two surfaces are now saying something that is no longer true, and one of them is saying it about git.

FIRST, THE COLLECTIONS PANEL PROMISES SAFETY IT NO LONGER GUARANTEES. api-pane.tsx:1364 and :1379 tell a person a collection folder is a folder they can commit. With a credential legitimately living in a header, that is true only for collections that happen not to have one. The sentence needs to say what it actually covers.

SECOND, THE CREDENTIAL IS NOT ELIDED IN RAW. A value placed by the sender as a NamedSecret is located in the composed text and elided in the raw diagnostic (§11.2, internal/apisend/sender.go). A plain header produces no NamedSecret (internal/apisend/auth.go:77-81), so a token in a header is printed in full in the run's request view — which is the panel a person screenshots and pastes into a chat when asking a colleague for help.

Neither is a reason to undo the decision. Both are the product describing itself inaccurately, which is the thing AGENTS.md calls a silent degrade the UI contradicts.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Import `curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" https://example.test/x` and send it.
2. Open the run's request view: the token is there in full.
3. Look at the collections panel: it says the folder is safe to commit.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The collections panel's sentence about committing says what it covers and what it does not, without frightening a person away from the ordinary case.
- A run's request view does not print a credential in full merely because it travelled as a plain header. Whichever mechanism is chosen — eliding by header name, or letting the sender treat a recognised auth header the way it treats a placed secret — it is ONE mechanism, and §11.2's existing elision is extended rather than duplicated.
- What IS still shown is enough to debug with: the header is present and named, its value is marked as withheld rather than deleted.
- A person who wants the value can still see it where they put it — the request form — because that is the decision this bead follows from.
- A test sends a request with a credential in a plain header and asserts the value does not appear in the raw diagnostic, and does appear in the form.
close_reason: Split by the owner's decision of 2026-08-23. THE RAW HALF IS DECIDED AGAINST and will not be built: a credential the person typed into a header is already in the renderer — they typed it into the form — so eliding it in the raw diagnostic protects nothing architecturally and costs the one thing that view exists for. The screenshot argument is half-protection at best, because the same value is on the Headers tab two clicks away. Vault-sourced elision is UNTOUCHED and is a different rule for a different reason: those values never cross into the renderer at all (ADR-0011), and printing them would have the vault copy keychain plaintext into a browser engine on every send. The distinction is by construction, not by heuristic — plain environment values are tried before the binding document, so PlacedSecret holds vault values only (capability/api.go:151). The implementation that existed (w-capability-probe 9a765545: CredentialHeader, Withheld) was NOT merged; the branch's other commit was cherry-picked as fc803f3f. THE GIT HALF STANDS and is refiled as nocx-flidy. Follow-on from the same conversation: nocx-4wbwn — a secret must be creatable and usable from any field, not only the Auth tab.

comments.author: shady2k
comments.text: Correction to the closing reason: the follow-on bead is nocx-5dfa5 (a secret creatable and usable from any field), not the id named there. The git half is nocx-flidy.

title: The file-picker capability is probed as a method on a class, so it is present on every build
description:
Two capabilities that must agree are decided two different ways, and one of them is decided wrong.

`filePicker` (frontend/src/api/api-client.ts:352) probes the capability as `'openFileDialog' in client`. The client is a class instance and the method is on its prototype, so the answer is TRUE on every build, including one with no Wails runtime at all. Its neighbour `nativeDrop` is decided by `hasWailsWebview()` (frontend/src/main.tsx:592), which is the question actually being asked.

The consequence is in the import ask, on every Wails-less build — `make dev-web`, `cmd/devharness`, the e2e container, and a nocx reached over a forwarded port. The region draws "Or select a file" as the SYSTEM picker's control, which answers -32601 when pressed; and because `onPick` is present, DropZone does not draw the kit's own FileInput, which would have worked (frontend/src/ui/drop-zone.tsx: the picker halves). So the one route that could answer is hidden by the one that cannot, and the picker only "retires" after a person has pressed it and read an error.

This is the rule AGENTS.md states as "absence IS the capability": a capability that is absent must not be drawn, so it never looks like a fallback from something broken.

Measured, not deduced: e2e/api-import.spec.ts:280 asserts the browser file input exists on a no-Wails stand and fails identically at HEAD with only the reshape's own broken line removed — it predates nocx-hqbv3 and predates the reshape (nocx-ysyy2).

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run the app without a Wails runtime (`make dev-web`, or the e2e container).
2. Open the API workbench and the import ask.
3. The region offers "Or select a file" — the system picker. Press it: nothing opens; the backend answers -32601. The kit's own file input is not drawn.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The file-picker capability is decided by the same question its neighbour asks: a runtime that can serve `dialog.*`, not the presence of a method on a class.
- On a build with no Wails, the import ask draws the kit's FileInput and no system-picker control; on a Wails build it draws the system picker and no FileInput. One control, either way.
- The probe lives in ONE place; nothing else re-derives "can this build open a system dialog".
- e2e/api-import.spec.ts's assertion at :280 passes without being weakened, and the test that currently carries it stops being expected-to-fail.
- Every other consumer of `filePicker` is checked and named in the commit body: whatever else probes this way is either fixed with it or stated as deliberately left.
close_reason: fc803f3f on feat/api-testing (cherry-picked from w-capability-probe).

title: A turn is one block that carries the blocks it caused, and a tool call is one of them
description:
## Steps to Reproduce

1. Ask the assistant a question that needs several reads, e.g. "what can I conclude
   from this?" after running `ls` and `top` in the pane.
2. Wait for the turn to finish and read the block it drew.

## What happens

The four calls are drawn as lines inside the answer, compacted behind a
`4 tool calls · blocks.read` disclosure. Each line carries the tool name and the
DERIVED RESOURCE only — which for every one of these tools is the sessionId, so
three of the four read `home/dev` and nothing else. `blocks.read` appears twice
and there is no way to tell which finished command each one read: the arguments
are deliberately absent from `agent.runToolCall` (schema §"the raw arguments blob
is absent") and from the line.

A turn that DOES run a command is drawn as several blocks — the fragment
machinery of nocx-9sqii — each fragment repeating the question in its header with
a `continued` badge.

## What should happen

A turn is ONE block that CARRIES the blocks it caused: the question in the header,
an indented region of child blocks between the header and the answer body, and the
prose below them. A tool call is a child block of a new `tool` kind whose header
names the tool and its arguments; a command the `run` tool opened is an ordinary
`command` child block with the `agent` author badge it already carries.

This retires the fixed-order projection of turn-flow.ts along with the anchor that
fed it: with the calls in a region of their own there is no prose to cut.
acceptance_criteria:
A person reading a finished turn sees, in one block: the question in the header,
every tool call the turn made as an indented child block naming the tool AND its
arguments, and the answer's prose below them. No call is drawn as a bare line, no
run of calls is compacted behind a disclosure, and the question is never repeated.

- Two calls to the same tool with different arguments are distinguishable on screen.
- A command the `run` tool opened is a child block of its turn, carries the `agent`
  author badge, and its VT grid does not re-wrap inside the indent.
- One turn is ONE block: no continuation fragments, no `continued` badge.
- The restored view of a turn and the live view of the same turn agree.
close_reason: Subsumed and delivered by the epic. The original defect — four tool calls rendered as the same three words, two blocks.read of different commands indistinguishable — is fixed by nocx-dc2fr.3, which put the arguments on agent.runToolCall and drew each call as a tool block naming them. What this bead proposed (a turn carrying children, with the whole answer as one body below them) was superseded by ADR-0037 before it shipped: the owner saw that a sentence written before a command was printed after it, and the fix was to make the prose blocks too rather than to keep one body. The interim implementation was deliberately reverted rather than built on.

title: A request cannot be duplicated
description:
There is no way to duplicate a request. A person who wants the same call with one header changed either retypes it or edits the original and loses it.

Everything needed exists: `freePath` allocates a name that does not collide, and `writeRequest` writes a request into a collection. This is a door to them from the tree.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A request can be duplicated from its row in the tree; the copy appears beside the original with a name a person can tell apart, and is selected so the change they came to make is the next thing they do.
- The copy carries everything: method, URL, headers, query, body, variables and auth — including the auth VARIABLE NAME, and never a credential value, which does not live in the file at all.
- Duplicating twice gives two copies, not a collision and not an overwrite.
- The copy is a file like any other: it appears in the tree from the collection listing, not from renderer state.
- A test duplicates a request with headers and a body, and asserts the copy's file contents equal the original's but for the name and the id.
close_reason: Merged into feat/api-testing as 65dc0b00 (w-request-doors). Duplicate's placement on the row is superseded by nocx-rmjj8 — the act itself is unchanged.

title: A request names itself from what you typed, until you name it yourself
description:
A new request is called `Untitled request` (api-store.ts:1020) and stays called that until somebody renames it, so a tree fills with rows that are identical to read — the owner has two side by side. Meanwhile the crumbs above the form already show what the request IS: `POST broker-access`.

The name should be offered from what the person types: the method and the last path segment of the URL. `POST http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/broker-access` is `POST broker-access`.

AN OFFER, NOT A DERIVATION — the rule api-paths.ts states at the top and this obeys. The moment a person names the request themselves, the offer stops: it is never renamed under them, not when the URL changes, not ever.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A request the person has not named takes its name from the method and the URL's last path segment as the URL is typed.
- A request the person HAS named is never renamed by this, whatever happens to the URL afterwards.
- A URL with nothing to take a name from leaves the request named the way it is today; the offer is absent rather than wrong.
- The file's name follows the same allocator that already gives a saved request its file (freePath), so two requests offered one name do not collide.
- The derivation lives in ONE function, beside the existing name and path helpers, and nothing else re-derives it.
- A test types a URL into a fresh request and asserts the name; then renames it, changes the URL, and asserts the chosen name survives.
close_reason: Merged into feat/api-testing as 65dc0b00 (w-request-doors). Duplicate's placement on the row is superseded by nocx-rmjj8 — the act itself is unchanged.

title: New request needs a fixed door, not a plus that appears under the pointer
description:
Making a request means aiming at a collection row and hitting a plus that is only there while the pointer is over it (api-pane.tsx:1562), or opening that row's context menu. Both doors are on a moving target, and both are in the panel a person is not looking at when they want to type a URL.

There is a fixed place that already names the collection: the editor's header, where the crumbs read `Playground › POST broker-access` and Save sits. A control there needs no aiming and asks nothing new — `store.newRequest()` already writes into `activeCollection` (api-store.ts:1013).

## Acceptance Criteria

- A control in the request editor's header, beside Save, makes a new request in the active collection and puts it in the form, with no dialog — the "NO ASK" rule the store already states.
- Where no collection is open the control is ABSENT, not present and refusing: absence is the capability, the rule every picker in this surface follows. The empty state already tells a person how to open one.
- The existing doors stay: the row's plus and the row menu are how a person makes a request in a collection that is NOT the active one.
- Kit only: an IconButton with an icon from the registry, placed and not repainted.
- A test drives the seam a person reaches: with a collection open, the control exists, is enabled from the state a person starts in, activating it reaches the client method, and the new request appears in the tree and in the form.
close_reason: Merged into feat/api-testing as 65dc0b00 (w-request-doors). Duplicate's placement on the row is superseded by nocx-rmjj8 — the act itself is unchanged.

title: Your API runs survive a restart, and any of them can be repeated
description:
Everything a person sent today is gone when nocx restarts: `runs` is a signal in the renderer (frontend/src/api/api-store.ts:475) and nothing on the backend keeps an API exchange. So the one record that holds a request EXACTLY as it went out — the Raw panel already renders it — lives for as long as the window does.

Persisting it answers two things at once, and the second is why this is worth an epic rather than a chore. A person can look at what they fired an hour ago and what came back. And, because the record IS the request as sent, a person can put it back into the form and fire it again — which removes the reason to think about Save at all: an experiment that went out can always be recovered, whether or not anybody named it.

THE HOME ALREADY EXISTS AND NO SECOND ONE IS BUILT. ADR-0018's ContentDB is the encrypted SQLite store for unbounded private content, and the terminal's history already lives in it (nocx-rtg0). This is another writer to that store, not a store of its own. Read AGENTS.md's account of nocx-rtg0 before starting: that epic shipped a store whose write path had no caller, the acceptance criterion was "deadcode is empty", and it was — a reachable read path hid an unreachable write path in the same package.

Deliberately NOT this epic: versioning the request FILE. The file is in git and git already answers "how was it before"; a revision list beside it would be a second owner of that question, disagreeing somewhere nobody looks.

## Success Criteria

- A run survives a restart: send a request, restart nocx, and the run is in the list with its request, its response, its timings and its status.
- Any run can be repeated: one control puts that exact request back in the form and sends it, including a request whose file was later edited or deleted.
- A repeated run says what it is — the list shows the exchange it was repeated from, so a person reading the list is not told two different stories about one request.
- No credential is written into the store. A secret placed by the sender is recorded as a reference the way the Raw view already renders it, and reading the database back shows no credential — asserted on the bytes, the way the vault's tests already do it.
- The store degrades VISIBLY: if the run store cannot be opened, the list says the runs are session-only rather than silently losing them while the surface goes on looking permanent.
- A retention bound exists and is stated, so the store cannot grow without end.
- `deadcode -tags gtk3 -whylive` on the run store's WRITE method prints a path from main(), contrasted with an unwired symbol. A filter run proves nothing here.
- One e2e watches it: send, restart the backend, see the run, repeat it, see the second exchange.

title: Auth asks for a variable name when the person is holding a token; it must be able to create the secret
description:
The Auth tab asks the wrong question. It asks for the NAME of a variable that must already exist and already be bound somewhere else, and offers no way to make one. A person holding a token — which is the only reason they opened this tab — has nothing to do here except type a name, go to the environment editor, find the row, mark it secret, paste the value, and come back. Most people instead paste the token into the name field, and the product accepts it (see nocx-qoavg): the value lands in the file that goes into git, and Send then refuses with

    apicoll: the request uses a variable with no value: the auth variable
    "88730fee0a6657e83badfb6f420ba76fadc4f1bedc337ac5d7506c68b4a7e85a" is not
    bound in this environment

which is the product describing its own field's contents back to the person as a missing variable.

THE MECHANISM ALREADY EXISTS AND IS NOT RE-IMPLEMENTED HERE. nocx-ew3uv.1 gave the environment editor a real mint: a row is marked secret, the VALUE goes to the vault through the binding write, the FILE keeps only the name. What is missing is a door to it from the surface where a person actually holds the credential. This bead adds that door and nothing else — one owner for "a secret is created", reached from two places.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open a request, Auth tab, kind Bearer, with a token in hand.
2. Look for a way to give the product the token.
3. There is none — only a field asking for the name of something that does not exist yet.

## Acceptance Criteria

- From the Auth tab a person can create a secret: they give the value, the product names it (offering a sensible default) and binds it through the SAME write the environment editor uses. No second minting path.
- After creating it, the request sends without any further step, under the environment it was bound to.
- The value never reaches the request file or the environment file: reading both back shows the name only, asserted on the bytes.
- The value is never echoed back into the field, into a chip, into a run's request preview, or into a log.
- Where there is no environment to bind into — "No environment", or a request not in a saved collection — the surface says which of those it is and what to do, instead of offering a control that cannot work. This is the same hole nocx-14exx reports from the curl-import side; whichever lands first states the answer and the other follows it.
- An existing bound variable can still be referenced by name: creating is an addition to the tab, not a replacement of it.
- A test drives the seam a person reaches: from a request with no auth, create a secret with a value, press Send, and assert the exchange carried the credential and neither file contains it.
close_reason: landed in 5d636b55: the Auth tab reaches the existing bindSecret; a new kit component secret-value-field carries the value-in-never-out rule

title: The Auth tab prints the variable name twice, and the second one dresses a pasted secret as protected
description:
The Auth tab shows the variable NAME twice: once in the "Secret variable" field, and again immediately under it as `Sends 🔒<name>` (request-form.tsx:609). When the field holds the name — which is what the field is for — the chip is the same string a line lower, and says nothing the field did not.

The chip's real job is elsewhere and is worth keeping: in the run view (run-list.tsx:430) it renders a secret SEGMENT of a request that was actually sent, showing where a credential sat without showing it. In the form there is nothing to reveal, because nothing is hidden.

AND IT LEGITIMISES THE WORST THING THAT CAN BE TYPED THERE. `Auth.Var` is not validated anywhere — grep finds no check in internal/apicoll; substitute.go:223 only says the field IS a name. So a person who pastes a TOKEN into it gets no refusal: the value is written into the request file, which is the file that goes into git, while the field's own description promises "The value lives in the vault and never in this file — there is no field here it could be typed into." The chip then renders that pasted token inside a padlock, so the surface looks like it is protecting a secret at the exact moment it is committing one. Observed with a 64-hex string pasted into the field.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open a request, Auth tab, kind Bearer.
2. Paste a credential (not a name) into "Secret variable".
3. The chip below renders the credential in a padlock; nothing refuses it; Save writes it into the request file.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The Auth tab does not print the variable's name twice. Either the chip goes, or it earns its line by showing something the field does not — the composed header shape, or that the name resolves to a bound value in the current environment.
- A value that cannot be a variable name is refused where it is typed, with the backend's own sentence, and never written to the file. The rule lives in one place and the wire enforces it — the renderer refusing alone is a renderer promise.
- No surface renders text a person typed into a name field as though it were a protected secret.
- A test drives the seam: type a credential-shaped string into the field and assert it is refused; type a name and assert it is accepted and sent as a reference.
close_reason: landed in 651a7d43

title: The Not imported panel reports things that were not lost, and never goes away
description:
The "Not imported" panel is the import's `unsupported` list, deliberately moved out of the dialog that closes (api-pane.tsx:1651) so a soft degrade is visible in the product rather than only in a log. That decision is right and stays. Two things about it are wrong.

FIRST, IT REPORTS NON-DEGRADES. Importing `curl -sS …` itemises `--silent` and `--show-error`, each with the reason "it does not change the request that is sent". A channel that exists to say "something you asked for did not come across" is being used to say "nothing was lost". A person who reads it twice and finds nothing actionable stops reading it, and the next entry — a dropped pre-request script, a saved response, a header — is the one they will not see.

SECOND, IT HAS NO END AND NO ATTRIBUTION. It stays under the tree until the next import replaces it, with no date, no name of what was imported, and no way to dismiss it. Nothing says which of the requests in the tree it is about.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Import `curl -sS -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/claim -d '{}'`.
2. Look at the sidebar's "Not imported" panel: two entries, both saying the option does not change the request.
3. Do anything else. The panel stays.

## Acceptance Criteria

- An option that cannot change the request that is sent is not itemised as unsupported. The rule is stated once, in the importer, next to the flag table that already knows which flags are output options (internal/apiimport/curl.go).
- A curl line whose flags are all of that kind imports with an EMPTY unsupported list, and the panel is therefore absent — not present and reassuring.
- What is still itemised keeps its current vocabulary: the feature named, and why, never a value.
- The panel says which import it is about, and a person can dismiss it. Dismissing loses nothing that the run's own record does not keep.
- A test asserts the empty list for `-sS` and a non-empty one for a flag that genuinely changes the request and is not carried.
close_reason: Merged into feat/api-testing (w-notimported). q2cx5: the importer half was already on the branch (9574c197 — curl.go's three-valued disposition table, so -sS itemises nothing); this adds the missing half, the report naming its import and being dismissable. flidy: the ask now says what it covers — a value bound to a variable never reaches the folder, a pasted credential does. Brief premise corrected by the worker: api.collections.list carries no headers, so the surface answers about the request in the FORM rather than about the collection, and says so. The predicate mirrors authFromHeader's grammar rather than re-deriving internal/secrets.Detect, and the default sentence promises nothing about headers it did not inspect. Nothing rewrites or sanitises a header.

title: A collection cannot be given a folder from the tree
description:
A collection is a folder and it may contain folders (design §6.2, and the Postman import writes them), but the tree offers no way to make one: nothing in the Collections header menu, nothing on a collection's row, nothing on a folder's. So a collection built inside nocx is flat, while an imported one has structure — two grammars for one concept, and the one a person can reach is the poorer.

Confirmed by grep: there is no folder-creation call site anywhere in frontend/src/api.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A person can create a folder inside an open collection, and inside a folder, from the tree — without editing any file.
- A new request can be saved into it.
- The name is refused by the backend on its own terms (a single path component, §13.1), and the refusal is shown in the ask rather than sanitised away.
