title: Download, backend and wire: bytes come back from the host of the active tab
description:
The reverse direction, backend only. The UI lands in the operations indicator once that exists; this task deliberately ships no surface beyond what is needed to prove the wire.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A file on the host of a remote binding is read and streamed to the renderer, reusing the sink's shape inverted rather than a second engine.
- The wire method carries the same binding authorisation every other files.* call does, and a local binding is answered the same way.
- Contracts with additionalProperties false, generated types, DTO and over-the-wire conformance.
- Failure paths enumerated as spec section 6 does for upload: unreadable, vanished mid-read, permission, connection lost, cancelled.
- Deliberately out: directories, resume, and the save-side surface.

title: Background operations are visible from anywhere, not only from the Files panel
description:
Owner ran the product and could not see a running upload from anywhere but the Files panel: switch view or collapse the sidebar and a 2 GB transfer is invisible and uncancellable while it keeps running on its own SSH lease. Discussed with the owner; merging it into a notification centre was considered and rejected — operations are state with progress and cancel, notifications are events, and the notification design keeps a centre deliberately out anyway.

SETTLED WITH THE OWNER: its own indicator in the activity bar's BOTTOM zone, which is the one place that stays on screen whatever the panel is doing. The badge counts ACTIVE OPERATIONS, not unread anything. A progress bar under the icon carries aggregate progress. Click opens a list with per-operation cancel. The indicator is present while anything is running OR anything has failed and not been let go: success dismisses itself, failure keeps the indicator alive, because a transfer that failed overnight must not vanish with the last active one.

## Success Criteria

- A person starts an upload, switches to another sidebar view and collapses the panel, and can still see it is running and cancel it — one automated check watches exactly that.
- A completed transfer removes itself; a failed one stays until dismissed.
- The transfer row is ONE component: the Files panel and this list place it, neither draws its own.
- Built for OPERATIONS, not for uploads: download has no Files panel of its own and must be able to appear here without the surface being reshaped.

title: The context-menu Upload still gates on the D9 rule that was corrected, so it disagrees with the drop
description:
Spotted by the owner's screenshot while asking about download. The context-menu Upload item landed (nocx-9le.5.21) BEFORE D9 was corrected (nocx-9le.5.22), and it still gates on the pre-correction rule: absent on a local origin.

Since the correction, a browser drop on a local tab uploads — the browser holds File bytes from the user's own machine and there is no path. The menu's picker in a browser raises the same input type=file and yields the same bytes. So the drop and the menu now give different answers about the same tab, which is two surfaces disagreeing about one concept.

The correct gate is the rule already adopted in D9: whoever has only the bytes uploads them. Browser plus local tab has bytes, so the item belongs. Desktop plus local tab yields a ticket for a file already on that machine, so there it is correctly absent.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. make dev-web, right-click a directory row on a LOCAL tab: no Upload item.
2. Drop a file on that same tab's terminal: it uploads.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The menu item is present whenever the gesture would upload and absent whenever it would not, decided by the same predicate rather than a second copy of the rule.
- One owner for that predicate; the drop handler and the menu both ask it.
- Tests for all four combinations: browser/desktop by local/remote.

title: A send through a locked vault is a dead row where an unlock belongs
description:
An environment that routes through an SSH connection needs that connection's
credential, and the credential is in the vault. With the vault sealed, Send
comes back as a failed run reading

  apisend: GET https://localhost:9443: apisend: this environment routes
  through a connection that is not available: connection "ssh:custom:…":
  dial pi@192.168.0.93:22: vault is sealed

— a dead row, a sentence describing a door, and no way to open it from where
the person is standing.

The product already knows how to do this, for a different shape of traffic.
ADR-0032's seam rewrites a sealed failure that arrives as an ERROR ON A
REQUEST into the canonical shape; the renderer's dispatcher raises one unlock
dialog and RE-SENDS the request verbatim once the vault answers. Everything
needed is built — the prompt, the coalescing, the replay. `api.request.send`
misses it for one reason: since nocx-pgp9c the failure arrives as the
RESULT of the call rather than as an error on it.

So the fix is a boundary, not a feature: a sealed vault is not an exchange.
Nothing was composed, nothing was dialled, nothing left the machine — it is a
precondition that stopped the attempt, and the epic's own rule already says
what that is ("what stays a JSON-RPC error is what is NOT an exchange").
Emitted as one, the whole existing path runs: prompt, unlock, automatic
re-send, and the answer arrives without the person learning that a Vault page
exists.

This is a slice of nocx-k41yv (P0) — "who may raise the unlock is decided by
which pipe the error travels down". It does not close that bead: the ask's
stream case, and the rule that every credential resolution names its stance,
are still open. It removes the third pipe.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Give an environment a route through an SSH connection whose key is in the
   vault; let the vault seal (restart the backend, or lock it).
2. Open a request under that environment and press Send.
3. A failed run appears reading "the connection it routes through was not
   available … vault is sealed". No unlock prompt anywhere.

## Acceptance Criteria

- With the vault sealed, `api.request.send` for a route whose credential the
  vault holds answers the CANONICAL SEALED ERROR, not a result — asserted over
  the real socket, not on a struct.
- The renderer raises the unlock, and after unsealing the re-sent request
  completes: the run appears once, answered, with no dead row before it.
- Cancelling the unlock leaves the run refused and says why — never a silent
  nothing.
- A send that does NOT need the vault is untouched: a direct route, and a
  connection whose profile references no vault secret, both send with the
  vault sealed.
- A sealed vault reached mid-exchange — not at the lease — is still a run:
  this changes the precondition only.

title: The local-tab drop has no end-to-end check, and it is the half that broke twice
description:
Twice in one session the owner found a broken local-tab drop within seconds of running the product, while every automated check was green. First it inserted a base name where D9 promised a path; then it refused an upload that D9 should never have refused, because D9 was reasoned from the desktop case.

Both times the unit tests were correct and useless: they asserted conformance to D9, and D9 was what was wrong. The remote branch is the epic happy path and has an e2e; the local branch was judged trivial twice and was broken twice.

## Acceptance Criteria

- One automated check watches a person drop a file on a LOCAL tab in the headless stand and see it arrive in that tab's directory — the browser branch, which is the one dev-web and a networked backend use.
- The desktop branch keeps its unit coverage, and the spec records that nothing in this repository can watch Wails hand Go a real path.
- It waits on observable state, never on a duration.
close_reason: Merged as d02246ba. The shared drop gesture moved into e2e/drop-gesture.ts and upload.spec.ts SHRANK by 41 lines — the common half came out rather than a near-duplicate going in. No waitForTimeout anywhere in either spec. The desktop half is named in a comment in the spec itself, where the next reader is looking, rather than only in the design document: the path-insert branch needs Wails, the headless stand has none, and it stays a manual step. Full suite after the merge: 363 passed, 9 skipped, both browsers, 14.5m.

title: Grant model + shield entry for sandbox
description: Rework PR #91 from panes.ephemeral to pane-subject sandbox_grants, consolidate launch into the active-sidebar-panel shield, remove legacy palette and tab-menu entries, and update contracts, tests, ADR, architecture, settings copy, and design spec.
acceptance_criteria: No panes.ephemeral field remains. Sandbox grants are persisted separately and swept on startup. The sidebar shield converts an eligible active local tab without removing it on launch failure. Palette and tab menu expose no sandbox launch. Backend/frontend/e2e contracts and documentation pass the approved plan's verification gates.

Added wire regression and expanded shield status tests. title: A browser drop on a local tab must upload, not refuse: D9 was reasoned from the desktop case
description:
The owner: dragging a file into the web version must upload it into the current folder, not refuse. He is right and D9 was wrong.

D9 was reasoned from the desktop case, where the UI and the tab's shell are provably one machine, so copying a file onto the machine it is already on is pointless. In a browser that premise is false: a local tab means a shell on the BACKEND's machine, while the file lives on the browser's. In make dev-web they coincide physically and the renderer still has no path; against a networked backend they are different machines and copying is the only thing that makes sense.

The rule should never have been about which machine. It is about what exists: WHOEVER HAS THE PATH INSERTS IT, WHOEVER HAS ONLY THE BYTES UPLOADS THEM. Desktop yields a path, so it inserts. A browser yields a File with no path, so it uploads into the tab's cwd.

This does not weaken R1. R1 forbids sending a file to the WRONG host; the backend's own machine is exactly the host the tab is on.

It does mean D7 changes. D7 withheld a write seam from the local provider because a local Write had no caller and a dead write path is the nocx-rtg0 failure. That was true only while D9 was. The caller now exists.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. make dev-web, drag a file onto a local tab: it is refused with 'a browser cannot tell nocx where a dropped file is'.
2. Expected: the file is uploaded into the tab's current directory.

## Acceptance Criteria

- local.Provider implements filesystem.Uploader, its sink writing through os; the transfer package is unchanged, since RemoteFS is already transport-agnostic and os.Rename replaces atomically so the bak fallback never runs there.
- A browser drop on a local tab uploads into the tab's verified cwd, with the same collision question, progress and cancellation as a remote one.
- A desktop drop on a local tab still inserts the absolute path and starts no transfer.
- D7 and D9 are rewritten in the spec to state the rule as what-exists rather than which-machine, and D9 records that its first form was reasoned from the desktop case only.
- The spec names the new capability plainly: the backend now writes a file to its own filesystem at the renderer's request. Not an escalation — the same client can already type cat into that tab — but it is new and must be written down rather than implied.
close_reason: Merged as 6528cdff. The rule is now stated as what exists rather than which machine: whoever has the path inserts it, whoever has only the bytes uploads them. local.Provider implements Uploader over os; internal/transfer is untouched — not one file — because its RemoteFS was already transport-agnostic, and os.Rename IS the atomic replace, so the .bak fallback is never selected on this path and the code says so. Both gesture branches end at the same flow.send, so there is no second upload path for local tabs. D7 and D9 rewritten, D9 recording that its first form was reasoned from the desktop case only, and the new capability named plainly: the backend now writes to its own filesystem at the renderer's request, which is not an escalation because the same client can type cat into that tab, but is new.

title: A file dropped on a local tab inserts its name where the design promised its path
description:
Reported by the owner running make dev-web: dropping a file on a local tab inserts its base name, not its path. Diagnosis: D9 (a local drop inserts the PATH) and R2 (the renderer never learns the source directory) collide, and R2 won everywhere. SourcePick.Name is deliberately filepath.Base (ws_upload_source.go, describeSource), so on the desktop the backend HAS the absolute path and withholds it; in a browser there is no path at all because a File object has none.

R2 is not weakened by fixing this. R2's threat is the renderer NAMING a source path inbound, which files.upload has no field for and must never gain. Telling the renderer a path outbound, for insertion into the same human's own command line, is the opposite direction and cannot be echoed back anywhere.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. make dev-web, drop a file on a local tab: the command line receives report.pdf, not /home/dev/Downloads/report.pdf.
2. Desktop build, same gesture: the same base name, though the backend knows the absolute path.

## Acceptance Criteria

- On a local tab in the DESKTOP build the absolute path is inserted, carried in a field distinct from anything files.upload accepts, and shell-quoted.
- files.upload still has no inbound source-path field, and a test asserts a request naming one is refused — R2 unchanged.
- In a BROWSER a local drop refuses with a message saying a browser cannot tell nocx where the file is, rather than inserting a name that looks like a path.
- D9's wording in the spec is corrected to say which build can honour it and which cannot, instead of promising a path everywhere.
close_reason: Merged as 271c8be3. SourcePick gains LocalPath, set only by describeSource — the local-tab branch that mints no credential and can perform no upload — and never by mint. R2 is unchanged and now guarded from the other side too: TestFilesUpload_RefusesAPathUnderTheOutboundFieldsName asserts the new outbound field cannot be sent inbound, and TestFilesDropped_ARemoteTabCarriesNoPath plus TestSourceTicket_AMintedPickCarriesNoPath pin the regression that would otherwise be silent. In a browser the drop now refuses out loud — 'a browser cannot tell nocx where a dropped file is' — instead of inserting a base name that looks like a path.

title: Postman path variables are dropped in silence
description:
Postman keeps a per-REQUEST value beside the address: the path carries
`/users/:id` and `url.variable` carries `id = 54321`. Our importer did not
read that field at all — it is absent from the struct that reads a URL — so
the address arrived with `:id` still in it, the value vanished, and NOTHING
said so. The ask above the file field promises the opposite in as many words:
"what the format cannot carry is named afterwards rather than dropped".

This bead is the honest half — the loss is now reported, in both shapes it
takes: with a value (the value is what is gone) and without one (the address
keeps a segment nothing can resolve, and goes out as written). Carrying the
value is a different and larger thing: this model has no per-request variable
at all, and that is the epic beside this bug.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Import a Postman collection with a request whose URL is `/users/:id` and
   whose `url.variable` names `id`.
2. The request arrives with `:id` in the address, no value anywhere, and no
   line in the list of what the import could not carry.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A path variable with a value is itemised, naming the variables.
- A `:name` segment with no value is itemised as a templated path.
- An ordinary URL — the scheme's colon, a port — is not itemised.
- The address itself is unchanged: nothing here rewrites a path.

title: There is no way to choose the export file except by typing its path
description:
The import ask names the export by PATH and offers no way to choose it: a
person opens a terminal, finds the file, copies the path and pastes it back.
The product already has the capability — `dialog.openFile` is a declared
method with a contract, used by Connections and Secrets to choose a private
key — and the workbench simply never had it wired: only `dialog.openDirectory`
reaches it, which is why the destination has a picker and the document does
not.

Wire the file picker the same way the directory one is wired: bound off the

title: The import has no default destination, while create has one
description:
The import asks for a destination as an absolute path and offers no default,
while `api.collections.create` next door takes a NAME and puts the folder where
nocx keeps collections. Two doors to one concept, and the one that asks more is

choosing `/work/acme.postman_collection.json` proposes

Prefill rather than "leave it empty and the backend decides": the person must

empty field with a sentence under it does not give them.

title: An unbound variable is reported as unbound, not as a malformed URL
description:
Sending `{{baseUrl}}/zen` with nothing bound to `baseUrl` answers
`apisend: "{{baseUrl}}/zen" is not an absolute URL`. The substitution never
happened, so the raw text reached the sender and the sender complained about
the only thing it could see. `apicoll` already has the right answer —
`UnresolvedError` carries every `VarUse` — and nobody reports it here.

The user's sentence should name the variable and where it was expected:
which name, which field, which environment was active.

This belongs to the exchange work: it is the `compose` phase of a run that
never went out, and it must arrive as a RUN rather than as an error string.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open the Playground's Zen request (`{{baseUrl}}/zen`) with no environment
   selected, or with one that does not declare `baseUrl`.
2. Press Send. The answer is `apisend: "{{baseUrl}}/zen" is not an absolute
   URL` — a complaint about a URL nobody typed, naming neither the variable
   nor the environment.

## Acceptance Criteria

- An unbound variable in the URL, a header, the body or the auth answers with
  the unresolved reason naming every missing variable, never with a URL
  complaint.
- The run's phase is `compose` and it carries the request text as composed,
  with the unresolved reference visible in it.
- An environment that answers the name still sends, unchanged.

title: The field says which variables the active environment cannot answer
description:
The URL field now marks a `{{variable}}`, and every mark reads the same
whether the active environment answers that name or not. The check a person
actually needs is the second one: `{{baseUrl}}` with nothing bound to it is a
request that cannot go out, and today they learn that from a failed send.

The renderer does not hold the active environment's values — the store reads
an environment only when the editor opens one — so this is a store change:
read the active environment when it changes and when the collection is
re-listed, keep its names, and hand the form a predicate.

Blocked on nocx-pgp9c: it rewrites the same file (api-store.ts), and two
agents editing one file is how work gets lost.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A variable no environment answers is marked in the warning tone, and one
  that is answered is not.
- Switching environment re-marks the field with nothing else pressed.
- A secret variable (declared by name, value in the vault) counts as answered
  — the renderer never sees its value and must not report it as missing.
- No value is ever rendered: the mark says answered or not, never with what.
notes:
DECIDED WITH THE OWNER (2026-08-22): the mark is CLICKABLE and opens a small
panel about that variable, the way Postman's badge does.

What the panel says: the name, whether the active environment answers it, and
the value when it is a plain variable — never a value when it is a secret
variable, where it says the vault holds it and stops. One action: add the name
to the active environment, or open the environment where it is already
answered. That is what makes it the answer to "how was I supposed to know I
had to go to Environments": the path from the problem to the place it is fixed
is one gesture from where the person typed it.

The cost, stated: a marked span takes the click, so clicking the middle of
{{baseUrl}} opens the panel rather than placing the caret. Postman makes the
same trade; the rest of the field still places the caret, and the reference is
still one Backspace from being ordinary text.

title: make lint and make ci-full cannot pass on a Linux dev machine: the lint targets drop the build tag every other target applies
description:
Makefile line 19 computes WAILS_PLATFORM_TAGS exactly as .githooks/pre-commit does, and every Go invocation in the file applies it — build, run, test, the ci targets. The two golangci-lint calls do not.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. On a Linux dev machine with webkit2gtk-4.1, run make lint or make ci-full at any commit, including main.
2. golangci-lint fails: could not load export data for github.com/wailsapp/wails/v3/internal/assetserver/webview, and the run aborts before linting anything.
3. The pre-commit hook passes at the same commit, because it computes --build-tags=gtk3 and explains why in a comment at .githooks/pre-commit:122-133.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Both golangci-lint invocations (Makefile:92 and :429) apply WAILS_PLATFORM_TAGS the way every other Go invocation in the file does.
- The guard stays identical to the hook: linux plus webkit2gtk-4.1, empty everywhere else, so macOS CI and ubuntu CI are unchanged.
- make ci completes on a Linux dev machine.

title: The epic's happy path is watched end to end
description:
One automated check watches a person do the whole thing: press Send and see the
pending row; press Stop and see the run settle as stopped; send at a name that
does not resolve and read the phase and the request text off the row.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The check drives the product through the seam a person reaches — the button,
  the row — not the store.
- It waits on observable state (a row, a phase, a settled run), never on a
  duration.
- It is red before the epic's work lands and green after.

title: The run exists from the moment Send is pressed
description:
The store appends the run when the send STARTS and fills it when the exchange
settles; the row carries the method, the address, the environment and a
client-side elapsed time while it is pending. Send becomes Stop while a run of
this request is in flight. A failed run renders the request text, the route,
how far it got and the phase — the same detail an answered run gets, minus what
never came back.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Pressing Send puts a row in the Response column before any answer exists, and
  the SAME row (same run id) carries the answer afterwards — no second row.
- The button reads Stop while that run is in flight and is enabled; pressing it
  reaches the client's cancel method.
- A failed run shows the composed request text and the phase; the danger card
  is no longer the whole story.
- A stopped run is not styled or worded as a failure.
- Tests assert observable state, never a duration.

title: The exchange can be stopped by the person who started it
description:
The renderer mints a token and passes it in `api.request.send`. The transport
registers a cancel function under that token for exactly as long as the
exchange runs, and drops it when the exchange settles. `api.request.cancel`
fires it.

The token is the renderer's own rather than the JSON-RPC request id: the id
belongs to the dispatcher and is not exposed to callers, and opening it up for
one button would be a second addressing scheme.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The registration interval is stated in the code with both ends: the token
  resolves from before the exchange starts until the exchange settles, and
  never afterwards.
- Cancelling a token that is not registered is refused by name, not silently
  accepted.
- A cancelled exchange comes back as `outcome: "stopped"`, never as a failure.
- A second cancel of the same token after it settled changes nothing.
- Two exchanges in flight at once cancel independently.
close_reason: landed on feat/api-testing in 38261a5e

title: A failed send returns the attempt, not a bare error
description:
`apisend.Client.Send` currently returns `Response{}, err` on any network
failure and drops what it already holds: the composed request text, the
placements of the secret spans, the tracer's timings and the remote address.
It returns the exchange with `Failure` set instead.

`error` is reserved for a violation of this package's calling contract
(`ErrFileBody`, `ErrAuthUnresolved`) and never for a network outcome.

The phase is classified from the error — `net.DNSError`, a TLS verification
failure, `ErrNoConnection` / `ErrSSHDialTimeout`, `context.Canceled`, a
deadline — together with what the tracer saw (a remote address means the dial
landed; a TLS time means the handshake started).

## Acceptance Criteria

- For every failure the package can produce there is a test asserting the
  PHASE, and the composed request text is present on the returned exchange.
- A send to a name that does not resolve returns phase `resolve` and a request
  block; nothing is returned as a bare error.
- The paired "and on a normal machine it succeeds" test still passes: an
  answered exchange carries `failure` unset.
- The redaction rule is unchanged — no credential reaches a failure reason, and
  the existing redact() coverage still holds.
close_reason: landed on feat/api-testing in 38261a5e

title: api.request.send answers an exchange, not a response
description:
The result of `api.request.send` stops being "the response" and becomes the
exchange. It gains `outcome` (`answered` | `failed` | `stopped`); a `request`
block present whatever the outcome — the composed raw text with its secret
spans, which the sender already has before it dials; `route`, `environment`,
`remoteAddr`, `timings` and `certificates` as far as the attempt got; a
`response` that is null unless answered; and `failure { phase, reason }`
otherwise. Phases: `compose`, `resolve`, `dial`, `connection`, `tls`,
`exchange`, `timeout`, `stopped`.

`api.request.send` params gain a client-minted `token`, and
`api.request.cancel { token }` is declared beside it.

Schema first, then the generated renderer type, then the Go DTO — in that
order, because the schema is the contract and the other two are satisfying it.

## Acceptance Criteria

- `contracts/api.request.send.schema.json` declares the shape with
  `additionalProperties: false` and an explicit `required` at every level.
- A failed exchange validates against the schema with `response: null` and a
  `failure` naming one of the eight phases; an answered one validates with
  `failure: null`.
- `contracts/api.request.cancel.schema.json` exists and the method is declared.
- `npm run contracts:check` passes with the generated renderer type committed.
- The Go DTO conformance test and the over-the-wire test both cover a FAILED
  exchange, not only an answered one.
close_reason: landed on feat/api-testing in 38261a5e

title: Watch a request go out, stop it, and read why it failed
description:
Today a run IS its answer: the row in the Response column is built from the
result of `api.request.send`, so it cannot exist before the answer does. Three
things follow, and they are one defect wearing three faces.

Nothing to show while a request is in flight — there is no object yet, so the
only signal is a disabled Send button. Nothing to stop — no party names the
exchange while it runs, so there is no handle to cancel. And a failure is not a
run at all: it comes back as a JSON-RPC error, one sentence with no request, no
route, no timing beside it, while `apisend` HAS all of that at the moment it
fails (`Send` returns `Response{}, err` and drops the composed request text, the
tracer's phases and the remote address on the floor).

The model this epic installs: a run is an EXCHANGE, and it exists from the
moment Send is pressed. It ends in one of three ways — answered, failed,
stopped — and the row is the same row throughout, filled in as facts arrive
rather than replaced when they do.

What stays a JSON-RPC error is what is NOT an exchange: an unknown handle, a
request file that will not read, a domain gate that refused. Everything that
happened to an attempt to send is a run.

## Success Criteria

- Pressing Send puts a row in the Response column immediately, carrying the
  method, the address, the environment and a running elapsed time, before any
  answer exists.
- That row can be stopped, and a stopped run says it was stopped rather than
  reporting a failure.
- A send that never landed — a name that does not resolve, a refused dial, a
  handshake that failed — is a run with the request text we composed, the route
  it went out under, how far it got and the phase it died in.
- One automated check watches a person do all three end to end.

Deliberately out: retry of a failed run, a request history that outlives the
window, and any per-request timeout setting.

title: T9.1 The renderer calls a transfer failed on results that mean running or unknown

title: T12.1 AD-1 records the HTTP upload route as its own amendment
description:
ADR-0036 records that file bytes travel on a streamed POST beside the WebSocket rather than on either of its planes. AD-1's own text still says it binds all frontend<->backend communication, with no exception recorded. The house convention is for AD-1 to record its amendments inline — it has been widened that way twice already (docs/architecture.md:109, :110) and ADR-0024 declares Amends: AD-1 in its header. Raised by the worker that wrote ADR-0036; the coordinator decided AD-1 does need the line.

## Acceptance Criteria

- AD-1 in docs/architecture.md records the exception inline, in the same voice and shape as its two existing amendments, and points at ADR-0036.
- The amendment says what is carried there and what is NOT: PTY bytes never leave the data plane, and control messages never leave the JSON-RPC plane.
- ADR-0036 gains an Amends header if that is what the convention requires; check ADR-0024 and match it.
- No behaviour changes and no code is touched.
close_reason: Merged as 13d8e22e. AD-1 carries the amendment inline in the exact shape of the two before it, with both halves — what the route carries and, explicitly, that PTY bytes never leave the data plane, control messages never leave the JSON-RPC plane, no msg-type is allocated for an upload, and nothing further may be added to the route without its own ADR. The worker also corrected ADR-0036's own header from 'Crosses: AD-1' to 'Amends: AD-1' and fixed the line citations its insertion had shifted.

title: T10.1 The collision question is a kit component that knows nothing about the wire
description:
Carved out of T10 so it can be built while the transport surface is still being written: the dialog knows nothing about JSON-RPC, bindings or tickets.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A kit component in frontend/src/ui/ (or a typed variant of an existing one), driven by an injected callback and tested with no backend at all.
- Overwrite / Keep both / Skip, plus an apply-to-all checkbox whose answer the caller receives once and applies to the rest.
- A row in frontend/src/ui/README.md, a stable identity class, one CSS file in styles/components/ if genuinely new.
- No bespoke colours, borders or paddings: a surface may place a kit component and may never repaint it.
close_reason: Merged as 2efc08d5. Kit branch 1 — pure composition of Dialog, Button, Checkbox and Stack; no identity class and no stylesheet, argued rather than skipped ('a class nothing paints is decoration, and an empty stylesheet is what check-css-integrity calls unreachable'). Overwrite is danger and sits furthest from the pointer's arrival corner; Skip is last and autofocused, per Dialog's own rule that on a destructive question the focused control is the safe one; dismissal is skip.

title: T2.1 The sink's cleanup and retry paths tell the truth about why they failed
description:
Five defects codex found in the landed sink (3aeac879). Filed by the coordinator from an adversarial review, not from a user report.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Point the sink at an SFTP server without posix-rename@openssh.com and make Remove fail — the outcome names the stranded path and swallows the reason.
2. Make Close fail after a complete write — the temp is removed, contradicting spec section 6.
3. KeepBoth against a read-only directory — 32 round trips, then an error saying no free name.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A failed cleanup reports WHY, not only WHICH path was stranded.
- A failed Close after a complete write strands the temp, per spec section 6, instead of removing it.
- A permission or transport failure is never reported as name exhaustion and never costs 32 round trips.
- The Sink contract names who unblocks a stalled source reader on cancellation.
- Each of the above has a test that fails against the current code.
close_reason: Merged as e6b95e6e. All five codex findings closed: tryRemove now returns (paths, error) and every caller errors.Join's the cleanup reason onto the primary; a failed Close after a complete write strands the temp and removes only the reservation, per spec section 6; notCollision stops the KeepBoth search on any refusal the adapter classified, with a stated admission rule — a refusal belongs there when the next suffix cannot change the answer; the copy loop and Sink.Put document that the CALLER unblocks a stalled reader, since an io.Reader has no context. CARRY FORWARD to the transport tasks: whoever supplies the streamed POST body must close it on request cancellation, or a stalled upload never unwinds.

title: Watch a person ask the assistant to look at their session, end to end
description:
The epic nocx-avogl has four closed children and NO end-to-end check. Its own success criterion is a sentence about a person, and nobody has watched it happen:

  "A person asks the assistant to look at their session; it calls readScreen with the RIGHT session id and answers. Watched end to end, against the real backend."

AGENTS.md rule 2 is what makes this a bead rather than a nicety: every epic that is not a chore proves its happy path, and deadcode and coverage are floors that can never report a feature that is missing. Four green units are exactly the state nocx-rtg0 was in when history had no writer at all.

cmd/devharness runs the real backend headless, so there is no excuse about the harness.

What makes this checkable NOW and was not true before the epic: the model is told the session id verbatim (nocx-avogl.1), so a readScreen call carrying it passes the exact-identity scope check that used to refuse an invented one terminally.

## Acceptance Criteria

- An automated check drives a real ask against the real backend, with a grant that permits readScreen, and asserts the tool was called with the session id of the pane the question was asked in — not any id, that one.
- The answer reaches the block. A run that refuses or fails does not pass this test.
- It fails if the system prompt stops carrying the session id: the assertion is on the id that travelled, not on the prompt text.
close_reason: Shipped in c057e86f, merged as 44cdfb39. Go test TestAssistant_LooksAtThePaneTheQuestionWasAskedIn green; Playwright e2e/agent-reads-the-screen.spec.ts green in the container (1 passed).

## Acceptance Criteria

uploadDone survives a reconnect with no subscriber. Progress dropping entirely is not an error. A written outcome invalidates the destination directory; a skipped or failed one does not. Over-the-wire conformance for both notifications.
close_reason: Merged as 206f3132. The asymmetry is implemented as designed: progress resolves the current subscriber at emit time and is dropped when there is none, coalesced to one in flight; uploadDone is retained per session, bounded, flushed on the next attach and cleared as each is delivered, and the retention ends with the session. Ten tests, including the one the task existed for — a transfer that finishes while nothing is attached is still reported after reattach. Spec section 5.5's Refresh clause is asserted all three ways: written invalidates the destination directory, skipped and failed do not.

title: T6 Bytes reach the sink over a streamed POST behind a one-shot ticket
description:
Task 6 of .internal/plans/2026-08-21-upload-to-the-active-tab.md (commit 4e2995ed). The plan is the brief; read that task's section in full.

## Acceptance Criteria

The four ticket states map to 410/read/409/410 exactly. Expiry cancels at expiry. Content-Length mismatch is 400 before the body. Own header and stall deadlines. No ticket in any log line.
close_reason: Merged as 0eeb4526. The four ticket states map as specified; expiry cancels at expiry so a late POST finds an unknown ticket. The carried-forward reader-unblocking obligation was answered with a read deadline via http.ResponseController rather than by closing the body — needs confirming that files.uploadCancel also unblocks a stalled read, not only the stall timeout. Sent to codex with the rest of the surface.

title: T5 files.upload names where a file lands and never where it comes from
description:
Task 5 of .internal/plans/2026-08-21-upload-to-the-active-tab.md (commit 4e2995ed). The plan is the brief; read that task's section in full.

## Acceptance Criteria

No sourcePath and no source field; unknown fields rejected. destDir via validateFSPath; name is one path component. A local binding is refused. Collision returns before anything is created. files.close cancels rather than blocks.
close_reason: Merged as fdabb57c. R2 is structural: the params decoder runs DisallowUnknownFields (ws_upload.go:200), so a request naming any source is rejected before anything happens rather than by a maintained list of forbidden names.

title: T4 The remote provider's sink reaches the binding, so internal/transfer is live
description:
Task 4 of .internal/plans/2026-08-21-upload-to-the-active-tab.md (commit 4e2995ed). The plan is the brief; read that task's section in full.

## Acceptance Criteria

OpenBinding asserts Uploader beside the attester, before Register. deadcode -whylive on the sink's Put prints a path from main, with a contrast probe.
close_reason: Merged as 68b22812. The worker improved on the brief: I said put the sentinel translation in sftp.Provider.Sink(), it put it in the composition root (internal/app, fsUploadLease) with the correct reason — only the composition root may import internal/ssh and internal/transfer at once, and putting it in the sftp provider would have dragged internal/ssh into a package that deliberately declares its own narrow read seam instead. It translates two things: the SHAPE (ssh.FSFile vs transfer.RemoteFile — Go matches result types by identity, so a method not an assertion) and the VOCABULARY (the posix-rename sentinel), and asserts the untranslated fs.ErrNotExist contract holds in both directions. MY ACCEPTANCE CRITERION WAS UNSATISFIABLE and the worker said so rather than fudging it: -whylive on transfer.sink.Put and filesystem.handle.Upload both answer 'reachable only through reflection', because RTA cannot see a method behind a live interface — the exact blind spot AGENTS.md documents. It probed transfer.NewSink instead, a function, which does print main -> App.Run -> ... -> OpenBinding. Wiring is proven by that plus the internal/app tests; the feature's proof is T11's e2e.

title: T3 A binding can write only when its provider carries a sink
description:
Task 3 of .internal/plans/2026-08-21-upload-to-the-active-tab.md (commit 4e2995ed). The plan is the brief; read that task's section in full.

## Acceptance Criteria

handle.Upload on a nil-sink binding returns ErrUploadUnsupported without touching a provider. sftp implements Uploader; local does not, asserted.
close_reason: Merged as 3c2cd423. Uploader has one method Sink() transfer.Sink; Register takes the sink; handle.Upload refuses a nil-sink binding without touching a provider and returns ErrHandleReleased after release. Both directions asserted: a compile-time assertion that sftp implements Uploader, and a test that goes red if local ever starts to.

title: T2 internal/transfer: the sink writes through a temp and promotes, naming what it strands
description:
Task 2 of .internal/plans/2026-08-21-upload-to-the-active-tab.md (commit 4e2995ed). The plan is the brief; read that task's section in full.

## Acceptance Criteria

Every row of spec section 6 has a test. Stranded is a slice and carries two paths when a fallback leaves both. Cancellation is refused inside the two-rename window. KeepBoth resolves by O_EXCL and retries, bounded at 32.
close_reason: Merged as 3aeac879. promote matches spec §6 exactly, including the two-stranded fallback loss and success-with-stranded-bak; promote takes no ctx, which is how 'cancellation is refused inside the two-rename window' is enforced structurally. 1636 lines, all tests against a fake. Worker closed a real gap in the plan: a KeepBoth reservation was an empty file the plan's Put never removed on failure. Renamed ErrSizeMismatch to SizeMismatchError to match capability.RefusedError. WithChunkSize has no production caller yet — may need a deadcode baseline line once wired.

title: T1 FSConn grows a write half: Create is exclusive, every call is a lane call
description:
Task 1 of .internal/plans/2026-08-21-upload-to-the-active-tab.md (commit 4e2995ed). The plan is the brief; read that task's section in full.

## Acceptance Criteria

Create uses OpenFile with O_WRONLY|O_CREATE|O_EXCL and does not truncate. Every FSFile.Write and Close goes through run. Many short writes whose sum exceeds fsHardTimeout complete. PosixRename reports the missing extension distinguishably.
close_reason: Merged as 006bc138. FSFile.Write/Close are lane calls; Create is OpenFile O_WRONLY|O_CREATE|O_EXCL; 12 new tests, none timing-dependent — the long-transfer property is proven with a short-hardTimeout lease and many real short calls. Worker flagged two things forward: pkg/sftp maps EEXIST to a generic SSH_FX_FAILURE so 'the create lost the race' is not distinguishable on the wire (T2 independently reached the same conclusion and advances the KeepBoth suffix on ANY create refusal), and Create can leak an inert *sftp.File if the watchdog poisons in the same window — closing it would be a call outside the lane, which the design forbids.

title: Accepting a remote path completion duplicates the typed directory prefix: cd repos/t -> cd repos/repos/tabby/
description:
## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open an SSH session (cwd `~`, holding `repos/tabby` and `repos/termic`).
2. Type `cd repos/t`.
3. The dropdown offers `repos/termic/` and `repos/tabby/` — already wrong: the
   display rule intends the last segment only (`termic/`, `tabby/`).
4. Accept either row.
5. The line reads `cd repos/repos/tabby/`.

## Root cause

`internal/completion/scripts/nocx_complete.bash` prints compgen's whole
replacement word in the TSV `name` column (`repos/tabby`). Both the Go contract
(`internal/completion/completer.go`, `Candidate.Name`) and the wire contract
(`contracts/shell.complete.schema.json`, `shellEntry.name`) declare `name` to be
"the last path segment for a file". `LocalCompleter` honours that; the SSH
completer does not.

The renderer's shell adapter (`frontend/src/suggest/providers.ts`,
`shellCompleteProvider`) relies on the contract: it builds
`insertText = tokenPrefix + display`, where `tokenPrefix` is the token up to the
last slash. With `name` carrying that prefix already, the prefix is doubled.

Evidence: running the script against a fixture tree emits
`path<TAB>repos/termic<TAB>/tmp/x/repos/termic<TAB>1`.

Affects every nested path completion on a remote session, including the very
common `cd dir/` step-into.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A test runs the real script against a fixture tree with a nested token and
  asserts the `name` column is the last segment while `path` stays absolute.
- Accepting `repos/t` -> `repos/tabby/` yields `cd repos/tabby/`, asserted
  through the renderer's shell adapter.
- The dropdown row for a nested token displays `tabby/`, not `repos/tabby/`.
- A bare token (`re`) and a trailing-slash token (`repos/`) still complete
  correctly.
close_reason: Fixed: the remote completion script now prints the last path segment in the name column, restoring the Candidate.Name / shell.complete contract the renderer's insert path depends on. Covered by a Go test that runs the real script against a fixture tree and five renderer tests asserting the line a pick produces.

title: Choosing a folder works only where Wails does, which is neither dev-web nor a networked backend
description:
Choosing a folder must not depend on a native dialog. dialog.openFile and the new
dialog.openDirectory both go through Wails, and the dev-web harness has no Wails at all —
nor would a backend served over the network. So in two of the three configurations nocx
runs in, there is no way to choose a folder.

Orca answers this the same way and the owner pointed at it: a native dialog for the desktop
case, and its own routed tree (useFileExplorerTree over a runtime file client) everywhere
else. We already have the routed half in files.list, bound to a provider by a bindingId.

NOT IN SCOPE, deliberately: browsing a REMOTE host for a collection. internal/apicoll reads
with os.ReadFile/os.Lstat/os.Mkdir, so a collection lives on the backend machine. A picker
that offered a remote folder would advertise what the reader cannot deliver.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. make dev-web, open the API pane, create a collection.
2. There is no way to browse for a folder, because the only picker is native.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A kit component that browses directories through a caller-supplied list callback and
  returns an absolute path or null.
- It knows nothing about JSON-RPC, bindings, or which machine it reads — tested with a stub
  and no backend at all.
- Only directories are selectable; typing a path stays possible; a failed listing shows its
  reason in place and the dialog stays usable.
- The native picker remains, as an accelerator that fills the same field, not a second
  decision-maker.
notes:
Owner settled the split, and the reason is his rather than mine: a collection lives on the BACKEND's filesystem not because apicoll happens to use os.ReadFile, but because of AVAILABILITY — a collection on a remote host stops opening the moment that host is unreachable, and a collection must open always. A chosen property, not a limitation to lift later.
The PICKER itself supports every filesystem nocx can reach; it is a general dialog and the caller decides which machine. For collections the caller passes the backend-local lister.
close_reason: Done and integrated in 5e731bd3 / 654910a2. Verified on the merged tree: typecheck, lint (dead-exports all baselined, shrunk by 4), 3612 frontend tests green.

title: Opening the API pane for the first time asks you to make a collection instead of giving you one
description:
Owner feedback, second thought after nocx-84shs: opening the API pane for the first time
should not present a form asking you to make a collection. Postman removed its Scratch Pad
and that absence is part of the complaint this feature answers, so we ship the opposite: a
collection is already there, ready to take a request.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. make dev-web with no collections ever opened.
2. Open the API pane. It says "No collections open" and offers a form.

## Acceptance Criteria

- First open of the pane, with nothing open and no prior seed, creates a collection in the
  default location and opens it. No dialog appears.
- It is an ORDINARY collection: renameable, committable, deletable. NOTHING may branch on
  "is this the built-in one" — that condition existing at all is the defect.
- Seeded lazily on first open of the pane, never at install or app start.
- Seeded once: deleting it does not make it grow back.
- Same default location the create dialog pre-fills — one answer to where collections live.
close_reason: Done and integrated in 5e731bd3 / 654910a2. Verified on the merged tree: typecheck, lint (dead-exports all baselined, shrunk by 4), 3612 frontend tests green.

title: A collection's location cannot be chosen with a picker: there is no directory dialog
description:
dialog.openFile exists and opens a FILE picker; nothing opens a directory picker, so 'where should this collection live' can only be typed.

DialogService (internal/transport/ws_dialog.go:28) declares OpenFile alone. The fix is to extend that interface rather than add a second service, and to keep its cancellation contract, which is written out above the interface and is not obvious.

AND THE DEGRADE MATTERS MORE THAN THE PICKER: the dev-web harness has no Wails at all, which is the configuration this was found in, so the method is -32601 there. Typing the path by hand must stay a first-class path, not a fallback that looks broken.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. make dev-web, open the API pane, create a collection.
2. There is no way to browse for a folder.

## Acceptance Criteria

- DialogService gains OpenDirectory beside OpenFile, with the same cancellation contract.
- A dialog.openDirectory JSON-RPC method with its contract schema and both conformance tests.
- The create dialog offers Browse when the capability is present and says nothing about it when absent — typing the path still works, and a test covers the -32601 case.
- A cancelled picker leaves the typed path untouched.
close_reason: Done and integrated in 5e731bd3 / 654910a2. Verified on the merged tree: typecheck, lint (dead-exports all baselined, shrunk by 4), 3612 frontend tests green.

## Acceptance Criteria

description:

- The location is pre-filled with a default under the app's collections directory, so a person who does not care can press Create.

title: Triage: ledger.search and ms7v.2 may be one FTS index under two beads
description:
Raised by the 2026-08-21 assistant-search design (section Risks): nocx-rtg0.21 (ledger.search: full-text over intent and derived output, with honest coverage) and nocx-ms7v.2 (Search over output: FTS across intent and derived text) both want an FTS index over the same corpus, filed under two different epics by two different routes. Neither names the other.

Two owners of one index is the defect the design section 1 exists to prevent, and it is cheapest to settle before either starts — after, it is a migration.

## Acceptance Criteria

- One of the two is the owner of the index, or the split between them is stated in both beads in a sentence naming what each owns.
- The decision is recorded where the next reader will hit it: in nocx-rtg0.21 and nocx-ms7v.2, not only here.
- nocx-ms7v.7 (indexing unit, substring promise) is named as upstream of whichever wins, since it is unanswered and both depend on it.

title: Brainstorming: a search tool over sessions for the assistant
description:
The owner asked for a "search tool over sessions". Two prior arts collide with it and must be dispositioned before any brief: the ms7v search epic (the person's own search over the ledger, MVP, blocked) and the one-session grant scope (policy.go:502-520, exact identity match) that a cross-session tool cannot satisfy today.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The idea is disambiguated with the owner (agent tool vs the ms7v surface vs live scrollback grep).
- Every prior-art hit is dispositioned: folded in, or ruled out with the reason.
- A design section exists and the owner approved it, or the idea is deliberately dropped with the reason recorded.
close_reason: Design approved and committed as 955d6e50; epic nocx-vorhg filed with edges on nocx-rtg0 (owner of ledger.search) and nocx-jrdy (printed secrets), plus nocx-hcggu for the FTS-ownership risk. writing-plans deliberately NOT invoked: the owner chose design-only, and the epic is blocked until ledger.search exists — a plan written now would be re-derived by the time it could run.

title: The conversation survives, and nobody is asked to manage a window
description:
Design: .internal/specs/2026-08-21-what-the-model-is-told-design.md, sections 2, 3 and 3a. Hermes's shape (docs/micro-compaction.md), adapted to our durable ledger.

Nothing carries over between questions today: every ask assembles its own message list, so a follow-up cannot mean what it says.

## Success Criteria
- A person asks a question, then a follow-up with nothing attached, and the answer is about the same thing. They work for an hour; the conversation stays inside the model's window with no action from them. clear ends it, and the next question starts from nothing. Watched end to end.
- Head/tail/middle: the prompt and the newest turns are verbatim, and every question the person typed is verbatim wherever it sits.
- The rolling summary is a durable ledger entry with an edge to what it absorbed, so restore needs no special case.
- Tool traces ride as facts with a handle, never as their text.
- The window is fetched per (endpoint, model) where the provider reports it, and the percentage in use is shown as an estimate until provider usage is captured.

## Deliberately out
- Micro-compaction (argued in the design).
- A /compact the person runs. clear is the whole vocabulary.
- Provider-reported token usage (deferred by the owner).

title: Attaching is a choice: the selection stops attaching itself
description:
Design: .internal/specs/2026-08-21-attaching-context-to-a-question-design.md (approved 2026-08-21). Continues nocx-4wtlh, which said of itself 'build it so it can be changed'.

Today a selection anywhere in a finished block's output raises a reference chip on selectionchange, so copying attaches; one drag across three rows stacks three chips (1-1, 1-2, 1-3 are three fingerprints); and the chip is labelled with term-line coordinates rather than what it carries.

## Success Criteria
- A person selects a word and copies it, types a command, presses Enter: it runs in the shell and nothing was attached. They drag three rows, press Attach, see those rows marked in the block and one chip naming their text; the ask carries exactly one reference. Watched end to end.
- Attaching never moves the input target.
- The floating Attach, the block menu's Attach output and the chord all raise the chip through ONE function.

## Deliberately out
- Files and images as attachment sources (their own bead, after this).
- Naming references in the prompt and a tool that reads more of a frame (their own bead).

title: A refused or failed run says what happened in our words, not eino's
description:
The owner's screenshot shows this on the answer block:
  the model failed to answer: [NodeRunError] failed to stream tool call call_7947...: agent policy: tool call refused
  node path: [node_1, ToolNode]

node_1, ToolNode and NodeRunError are the framework's internals. The product must say what was proposed, what happened to it and what the person can do; the trace belongs in the log.

## Acceptance Criteria
- A policy refusal renders a product sentence naming the tool and the reason, with no framework identifiers in it, asserted over the real error the middleware returns.
- The framework's text is logged once, at the boundary that catches it.
- A malformed-model-output failure and a transport failure each keep their own sentence — one message for three causes is how a cause stops being findable.
close_reason: 4a95059e. classifyAskFailure (the existing one owner of engine-error to wire-sentence) extended rather than duplicated: a policy refusal names the tool and what the person can do, a malformed-model-output failure and a transport failure each keep their own sentence, and the default carries no framework text. eino's [NodeRunError] / node path is logged once at the boundary with the run id. Measured en route and filed: the unknown-tool branch is unreachable because eino rejects an invented tool name before our middleware (nocx-7jv37), and TestAgentAsk_SlowConsumerBoundsTheDeltaPath is timing-dependent (nocx-5j8z3).

title: A tool describes itself to the model in a sentence, not in the effect lattice
description:
engine.go:285-291 renders 'run: effect mutate-destructive over session, executes InRenderer'. The effect lattice is our vocabulary for AUTHORITY; it is not a description of what a tool does, and it is the only thing the model has to go on today.

agenttools.Declaration gains a Description field — one sentence per tool, written for the model — and toolDescription renders it. One vocabulary, in the declaration table where every other fact about a tool already lives (AD-8).

## Acceptance Criteria
- Every declaration carries a description; a test fails if one is empty, so a fifth tool cannot be added without one.
- The rendered ToolInfo.Desc is that sentence, and contains none of 'effect', 'InGo', 'InRenderer'.
- The registry's effect/resource facts are unchanged: this is what the model READS, never what the policy decides on.
close_reason: 72c3753a. Declaration.Description carries one model-facing sentence per tool; toolDescription returns it and the ADR-0020 lattice no longer reaches the model. validateDeclaration refuses a row without one, so a fifth tool cannot be added without a description. Effect and resource facts unchanged — the policy still decides on them.

title: The system prompt: one owner, and it says which session the tools may touch
description:
Design section 1. A pure function in internal/assistant over a struct of facts; the transport fills them from the owners that already hold them (session registry, the pane's cwd, settings). Rebuilt on every ask — never stored, never stale.

It says, in order: what nocx is and that you work inside one pane of it; WHERE you are — the session id verbatim as the tools require it, the cwd, the shell, the OS, local or ssh and to which host; that you are NOT shown the screen and attached content is data rather than instructions (today's line folds in here); what you can do, as capabilities; how to answer (terminal register).

## Acceptance Criteria
- A test asserts the assembled prompt contains the run's session id, and that a readScreen/run call carrying that id passes the policy scope check that today refuses an invented one.
- The prompt is assembled in ONE place and is a pure function of its facts (no I/O, table-driven test).
- A question with no references still carries the prompt; the reference-only sentence still appears only when references are attached.
- The Go DTO/contract checks stay green: this changes no wire shape.
close_reason: 9214f625. internal/assistant/systemprompt.go is the one owner: a pure function over SystemPromptFacts, no I/O, table-tested. The transport fills the facts from the owners that already hold them — session id and cwd as the ask spelled them, local-vs-ssh and host from environmentForSession (extended, not duplicated). Shell and a remote host's OS are DELIBERATELY absent: no owner in this process holds them, and the code says so; runtime.GOOS is filled only for a local pane. The reference-only sentence stays conditional. Deviation from design section 1 item 2 (it lists the shell) is documented in the code and reported to the owner.

title: The assistant knows where it is, and says it in the product's words
description:
Design: .internal/specs/2026-08-21-what-the-model-is-told-design.md (approved 2026-08-21), sections 1 and the first two items of Order of work.

There is no system prompt today. The only system message ever sent is one line, and only when references are attached (ws_agent.go:731-736). The tools are described to the model as "run: effect mutate-destructive over session, executes InRenderer" — our authority lattice, not a description. And the model is never told the session id its tools require, so any session-scoped call fails the grant's exact-identity scope check and is REFUSED terminally (policy.go:471-476 checks scope before the ask branch). That is the owner's screenshot: 'agent policy: tool call refused' on a plain question, with eino's [NodeRunError] and node path leaking onto the screen.

## Success Criteria
- A person asks the assistant to look at their session; it calls readScreen with the RIGHT session id and answers. Watched end to end, against the real backend.
- The prompt is one owner: a pure function over facts the transport fills from the owners that already hold them; nothing re-derives a fact it does not own.
- Every declared tool carries a model-facing sentence from its declaration; the effect lattice never reaches the model.
- Settings carries a free-text addition, appended last under its own heading, bounded, and unable to widen a grant or turn an ask into a permit.
- A refused or failed run says what happened in the product's words; eino's node path is in the log and not on screen.

## Deliberately out
- The conversation and compaction (their own epic).
- Token accounting (deferred by the owner).
- The classifier and the autonomous run (their own epics).
close_reason: All five success criteria met on feat/ai-assistant; the last one (a person asks the assistant to look at their session, watched end to end) is nocx-z4hgm, merged as 44cdfb39 and verified green in this session: the Go test asserts the session id that travelled back through the broker with a second session open throughout, and the Playwright spec watches a real xterm frame reach the model.

title: The endpoint editor never asks the vault, so its secret pickers show secrow: handles and offer nothing
description:
Reported by the owner from a running dev stand: the Edit Endpoint dialog showed
`secrow:dd39558499fe31b5ddce0f88a5d31320` where the secret's name belongs, and the
picker offered no rows. Nothing was lost — vault.json holds that secret under the
name "openrouter API key", kind=password, and sha256(id)[:16] is exactly the handle
shown. The vault was simply SEALED (the backend had restarted; hasOSKey=false).

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Set up the vault with a passphrase and save an AI endpoint with an API key.
2. Restart the backend (or press Lock now) so the vault is sealed.
3. Settings -> Endpoints -> Edit the endpoint.
4. No unlock dialog appears; the API key picker shows the raw `secrow:...` handle
   as its label and its dropdown is empty.

## Cause
endpoints-section.tsx loadInventory() reads the vault status ITSELF and returns
early when it is sealed or uninitialized, so vault.inventory is never called and
the dispatcher's sealed seam (ADR-0032) never fires. passwordRows() is then empty
and secretOptions() (key-material-input.tsx:64) labels the bound-but-unlisted row
with the row handle itself.

The skip came from 96c947b5 ("the door must not ask", nocx-lyyk). It is the outlier:
connections.tsx loadSecretRows() — the SAME editor-opens-a-secret-picker shape —
calls inventory() and lets the seam raise the unlock, and says so in its comment.
ADR-0032 is explicit: needing the vault is a property of the CALL, not of the call
site; the vault raises its own unlock. An editor that must render secret NAMES is
asking the vault for data, and a caller that inspects the vault state to decide not
to ask is exactly the per-call-site logic the ADR deletes.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Opening the endpoint editor (new or edit) on a sealed vault calls vault.inventory
  and the unlock dialog appears; after unlocking, the picker lists the secrets by
  NAME and the bound row is selected by name.
- Dismissing the unlock leaves the editor usable with an empty picker, and does not
  report a store failure ('unavailable') on the rows.
- An UNINITIALIZED vault is still not probed: there is nothing to unlock.
- The endpoints LIST (page load) still never raises the unlock — only an editor and
  the vault-backed operations do.

title: Amend ADR-0020: a grant's subject may be a pane, not only an execution
description:
`authority_grants.execution_id` is `NOT NULL UNIQUE REFERENCES executions(id)`, so today a grant belongs to an agent run. A sandboxed pane needs the same object with a different subject.

Decide between generalising the subject (`pane_id` beside `execution_id` with a CHECK that exactly one is set) and a parallel relation, and amend ADR-0020 §5/§7 deliberately — not inside a feature branch, which is why #91 went back to draft.
acceptance_criteria: ADR-0020 states what a grant may belong to; the schema matches it; the agent lane's behaviour is unchanged.

title: A sandboxed pane holds a grant, and the workspace minted it
description:
PR #91 models the sandbox as `panes.ephemeral` — a boolean naming the consequence ("do not restore") and dropping the cause: this pane's authority was granted once, interactively, and cannot be re-granted without asking.

ADR-0020 §5 already decided the shape: the workspace mints a default grant from its policy and is NOT the enforcement object, because "dragging a tab must never silently confer or revoke the right to write to production". `authority_grants` and `grant_scopes` exist; `resource_kind` already includes 'path'. The gap is the subject — `authority_grants.execution_id` is NOT NULL UNIQUE REFERENCES executions(id), so a grant belongs to an agent run.

Ruled out during the #91 review, recorded so nobody re-derives them: PaneKind (orthogonal, and SSH sandboxing is coming); EnvironmentKind (a sandbox is a constraint on a place, not a place); no pane row at all (leaves entries.pane_id null and the tab ungrouped); `closed_at` (window membership, enforced live by renderFromLayout); a single-column pane_sandbox table (a flag with extra steps).

`workspaces.payload` is already a declared sparse extension, so the workspace half needs no schema change.
acceptance_criteria: A user opens a tab whose filesystem authority came from its workspace's policy, narrowed once at launch, and one automated check watches them do it: the workspace carries a policy, the pane carries the grant minted from it, and after a restart that pane does not come back as an ordinary shell — with no boolean in `panes` saying so. Explicitly out: agent-lane grants changing behaviour, SSH sandboxing, and any re-minting of a grant without asking.

title: Two blinking carets in the command editor after repeated Backspace
description:
Reported by the owner (2026-08-21, macOS build): after pressing Backspace
repeatedly in the command editor, TWO blinking carets appear at once — one at
the start of the input line, one further right. Both blink.

## Steps to Reproduce

Not yet reliable. Observed once: type in the composer, press Backspace
repeatedly/rapidly. The screenshot shows the composer card (location + cwd
chips, the `Run` gutter token) with the right-hand caret sitting well past
where an empty document would place it, plus a second caret at the line
start. Whether Backspace is causal or coincidental is unknown; so is whether
a split or a tab switch preceded it.

## What the code says so far (investigation, not a fix)

- The composer uses the NATIVE caret: editor.ts installs no `drawSelection`,
  so `.cm-cursor` is never rendered (the theme rule at editor.ts:236 is
  vestigial). A native caret only paints in the FOCUSED element, so two
  blinking carets cannot both belong to one CM6 view.
- Only two `new EditorView` sites exist (editor.ts:338, cm-host.ts:139) and
  cm-host is never mounted on the terminal surface. One CommandEditor per
  pane (terminal-content.ts:1318).
- xterm cursor is unlikely: `cursorInactiveStyle: none` (renderers/xterm.ts:303,
  the fix for the earlier "second cursor" defect, item 9), `cursorBlink`
  defaults to false, and at an idle prompt `.xterm-live-container.live-idle`
  is `height: 0; overflow: hidden` — nothing of the grid can paint there.
- Prior art for two composers painted at once: editor.ts `show()` documents an
  inline `visibility: visible` that repainted an inactive pane editor on top
  of the active one at the same coordinates.
- No custom blinking element: the only `@keyframes` near the composer are
  pulses and spinners, none caret-shaped.

## Next evidence needed

A DOM dump taken WHILE both carets are on screen: `document.activeElement`,
every `.nocx-editor` rect + computed display/visibility + `.cm-content` text +
whether it carries `.cm-focused`, the `.xterm.focus` count, live-container
heights, visible input/textarea count. Asked of the owner.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The root cause is named, not guessed: one mechanism that explains a SECOND
  BLINKING caret given that the composer paints only the native one.
- An automated check reproduces the two-caret state before the fix and fails
  after it — a spec that asserts the observable (one caret-owning surface
  focused / one composer painted), never a duration.
- Repeated Backspace in the composer leaves exactly one caret, at the
  document position the text says it should be.

title: The sandbox cannot start on a non-FHS Linux: runtime read-only roots blow the 256 cap
description:
`runtimeReadOnlyRoots` adds one read-only root per PATH binary directory and per ELF RUNPATH/DT_NEEDED library directory. Under FHS those collapse into a handful; under Nix every store path is its own directory. Measured on the dev host: 339 roots against `maxRoots = 256`, so every sandboxed launch fails `-32007 "policy exceeds 256 roots"`. The same shape threatens a Homebrew-heavy macOS, where each formula owns its own Cellar prefix.

It fails closed, which is the right direction, but the feature is dead on a whole distribution and the message names an internal bound rather than anything a user can act on.

## Steps to Reproduce
On NixOS, `go test -run 'TestNewLocal_SandboxedEndToEnd' ./internal/sandbox/` — "policy: sandbox: policy exceeds 256 roots". A probe calling `runtimeReadOnlyRoots(os.Getenv("SHELL"), os.Environ())` returns 339 roots with a nil error.
acceptance_criteria: A sandboxed shell launches on a Nix-style host, or sandbox.status reports a typed, actionable reason before the action is offered.
close_reason: Fixed on PR 91 (feat/sandbox-current) in the review-fix pass.

title: PR 91: the sandbox ADR chain collides with main's ADR-0035

## Steps to Reproduce
`git ls-tree --name-only origin/main docs/decisions | grep 0035` and the same against the PR head: both answer, with different files.
