title: The lease and awaiting-takeover: a wedged agent command ends, and says how
description:
ADR-0020 decisions 2 and 3, deferred out of nocx-tjppv deliberately and named here so the gap
is a recorded fact rather than a discovery.

WHAT A WEDGED AGENT COMMAND DOES TODAY, measured by the worker who built run: the tool call is
held on the broker s ten-minute bound, and then the command KEEPS RUNNING in its lane. Nothing
stops it, nothing reports it, and the only thing that ends it is a person noticing.

DECISION 2 — every execution runs under a lease: a wall-clock deadline (renewable, bounded
ceiling), a SEPARATE inactivity deadline because silence is a different failure from slowness,
an output budget, a terminal-size contract, an interactivity policy, and cancellation that
escalates INT -> TERM -> KILL with each execution in its own process group so cancellation
reaches the children.

DECISION 3 — interactivity is a protocol transition, not a failure. A program that activates
the alternate screen or blocks on stdin puts the lane in awaiting-takeover: the agent is
DEMOTED, not evicted — it loses write authority and keeps the right to read the screen and
advise — and the human takes over, answers, detaches or kills. That is the answer to "the
agent could get stuck forever", and it is better than a timeout in the case that matters: the
program is still there and still usable rather than killed for being interactive.

NOTE THE SPLIT that already exists and must not be re-litigated: keyboard-equivalent acts go
through the renderer, supervisory acts (signals, deadlines, teardown) stay in Go, because a
human does not do those with the keyboard either. So the lease lives in the backend even
though the command it bounds was submitted by the renderer.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A command that never finishes is terminalized by its deadline, and the ledger says which
  deadline ended it — wall-clock or inactivity. Both asserted, separately.
- Cancellation reaches a child process, not only the shell. Asserted by spawning one.
- A program that takes the alternate screen puts the lane in awaiting-takeover and the agent
  keeps reading and loses writing. Asserted by trying to write.
- The output budget bounds what one execution can produce, and the block says it was bounded
  rather than silently truncating.
- Both ends: an ordinary short command runs to completion untouched by any of this.
close_reason: Lease and awaiting-takeover shipped: wall-clock and inactivity deadlines recorded separately on the attempt, INT->TERM->KILL over the process group so a child outlives nothing, the broker request cancelled before signalling so a late resolution cannot report the killed run as completed, and an alt-screen program demotes the agent to read-and-advise rather than being killed. Merged a6f7367f.

title: The agent runs a command, through the same submit path a person uses
description:
The epic headline, and the last tool of the catalogue that acts: design §4.1 run(lane,
command), §2.2 for who executes it.

WHAT EXISTS: the policy narrows and escalates, the approval surface asks, the egress gate
screens, the classifier raises suspicion, readScreen proves the renderer can execute an
effect the backend asked for, and a command block already carries the author that submitted
it. What does not exist is a path by which the agent can submit a command at all — which the
author slice reported honestly rather than faking: the only agent-authored target is
routesToShell=false, so its submission is a question and opens no block.

THE RULE FROM §2.2, and it is why this is not a new executor: everything a human does with
the keyboard, the agent does through the same surface. The command goes through the
renderer submit orchestration — the same InputTarget, the same handoff, the same ledger
record, the same running block, the same attempt. The backend does NOT write to the PTY
directly even though it can (session.Write exists): that bypasses the orchestration and the
command would exist as bytes with no entry — a second input surface, and an invisible one.

THE LANE: ADR-0020 decision 1 — the agent never takes the user PTY and never waits for it.
It gets its own session. Because the renderer executes, that session is necessarily a
RENDERED one, so invisible agent work has nowhere to happen.

DELIBERATELY OUT, and filed separately rather than skipped: the lease (deadlines, output
budget, INT->TERM->KILL) and the awaiting-takeover transition of ADR-0020 decisions 2 and 3.
Say in the report what a wedged agent command does today without them.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A person asks the assistant to do something that needs a command; the command appears in
  the block flow MARKED AS THE AGENT unctions, its output is read back, and the answer names
  something that appeared in it. Asserted end to end. This is the epic headline.
- The agent lane is a session of its own: the user PTY receives nothing, asserted.
- The command produces a ledger entry, an attempt and an output artifact because it went
  through the ordinary path — asserted on the ledger, not on the DOM.
- A grant that does not name the lane refuses the run before anything is submitted.
- Both ends: a human command in the same window is still attributed to the human and is
  unaffected.
close_reason: The agent runs a command through the renderer's own submit orchestration: a second broker RequestKind, the grant narrowing the lane before any request leaves, the author minted at submit, the block frozen and the output windowed back to the model. The backend still never writes to the PTY. Merged 26dd4391. The lease and awaiting-takeover are nocx-4azzq.

title: Two tests fail under load and pass alone: a vault-retry import count and an unrestored ECHO flag
description:
Two tests fail under load in the containerized gate and pass in isolation. Neither
is covered by an open bead: nocx-kqw6.1 and nocx-pu4.3 are closed, and nocx-2y35j
is about zsh snapshots disappearing, not about either of these.

OBSERVED 2026-08-16, both in the same pre-commit run of the containerized
`go test -race`, on a heavily loaded machine (6 cores, several agents and
containers active):

    --- FAIL: TestTabbyExecute_VaultRetry (0.69s)
        ws_import_test.go:1294: profilesImported=1, got 0
        ws_import_test.go:1308: expected error on third execute (plan consumed after success)

    --- FAIL: TestInBandBootstrap_RealZshIntegratesAndRestores (0.89s)
        inband_pty_test.go:473: ECHO not restored before the hooks ran: Lflag 0x8a31

MEASURED, not assumed:
  - TestTabbyExecute_VaultRetry alone, 3 consecutive runs on the host: 3 passes.
  - The whole internal/transport package on the host: ok, 50.8s.
  - So it needs the container, -race, all packages at once, and contention.

NOT THE SAME AS nocx-2h08, and this is the reason for a separate bead. That bead's
signature is a THIRTY-SECOND TIMEOUT whose test name moves between runs. These two
fail in under a second with concrete assertion failures — a wrong count and a
terminal flag not restored. Same class (load-dependent), different mechanism.

WHAT THE FAILURES SUGGEST, offered as a starting point rather than a diagnosis:
  - VaultRetry: "profilesImported=1, got 0" plus "plan consumed after success"
    reads like the import-plan store being observed before a write lands, or a
    plan consumed by something else. planStore lives on the WSServer with its own
    mutex; a test that races its own setup would produce exactly this.
  - InBandBootstrap: ECHO is a termios flag on a real pty. "not restored BEFORE
    the hooks ran" is an ordering assertion, and under load the shell simply had
    not got there yet. The question is whether the test waits for an observable
    state or for the scheduler to be kind.

COST TODAY, which is why this is filed rather than shrugged at: five extra
pre-commit runs across one session, roughly twenty minutes, and three separate
occasions where a red gate had to be proved innocent before a merge could
proceed. The owner's instruction was explicit: fix them rather than work around
them.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Load the machine — several containers or agents running.
2. Commit anything touching Go so the pre-commit hook runs the containerized
   `go test -race` over all packages.
3. Either test fails perhaps one run in three. Both failed in the same run once.
4. Run either alone (`go test -count=1 ./internal/transport/ -run TestTabbyExecute_VaultRetry`)
   and it passes every time.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Each test waits on an observable state change rather than on the scheduler
  being kind — AGENTS.md's rule, and the fix must not be a longer timeout or a
  sleep, which is the same bug with a bigger number.
- The failure is reproduced BEFORE it is fixed: run the package under artificial
  contention (`-race` with the machine loaded, or GOMAXPROCS pinned low) until it
  fails, so the fix is verified against a failure rather than against silence.
- Three consecutive full containerized runs green afterwards.
- If either turns out to share a cause with nocx-2h08, say so and merge the
  beads rather than fixing the same thing twice.
notes:
SHELLINTEGRATION HALF DIAGNOSED AND FIXED, 2026-08-16. The two halves of this bead do NOT share a cause and the bead should be split or the transport half tracked separately.

THE ZSH/ECHO FAILURE WAS A TEST SAMPLING A STATE THAT IS MEANT TO VANISH. 'ECHO not restored before the hooks ran: Lflag 0x8a31' — 0x8a31 is ZLE'S OWN MODE. The wrapper restores the terminal, the hooks are sourced, and moments later zle (or readline) takes the terminal back and clears ECHO BY DESIGN. The test waited for the hello OSC and only then read termios, which races the shell's forward progress from a 20ms poll loop. Under contention the read lands after the window it meant to observe.

WHICH MAKES A LONGER TIMEOUT STRICTLY WORSE, and that is the part worth remembering: a later read is a worse read, not a better one. This is the one flake shape where the usual instinct actively harms.

FIXED BY HOLDING, NOT SAMPLING. A two-line POSIX probe is streamed ahead of the payload so it lands at the top of the file the wrapper sources — after stty "$saved" and before the dispatcher, exactly what fence 2 in inband.go claims. It emits a private OSC and parks on a file only the test creates; between the marker and the release the shell executes nothing, so the termios is HELD rather than caught. Bash and dash carried the identical latent race and got the same treatment.

REPRODUCER, and it is sharper than the one on nocx-2h08: docker run --cpus=0.5 (a hard cap, not a share weight) fails this 1 run in 5, instantly, on an idle machine. --cpu-shares=512 was not enough for it.

AFTER: 30 runs at --cpus=0.5 and 175 inband runs at --cpus=0.25 with three competing containers, zero failures. No production code changed.

THE TRANSPORT HALF IS UNTOUCHED: TestTabbyExecute_VaultRetry with profilesImported=1, got 0 in internal/transport is still open and is being worked under nocx-2h08, whose four recorded names now include it. If that turns out to be the same cause as 2h08, this bead's transport half folds into it and this bead closes on the shellintegration fix alone.
MECHANISM FOUND AND FIXED AT ONE SEAM, 2026-08-17. It was a population of twenty, not two tests, and the cause is the opposite of the one everybody looks for.

NOT a shared wait helper with too short a deadline — the tests that go through a wait were the SAFE ones. channelShell carries TWO INDEPENDENT TRANSPORTS: a TCP socket to the fake kernel, and the pty. Every wait the type offered (waitForAccepted, waitForPromptAfterComplete, waitForHandshake, the kernel's own flags) waits on the SOCKET. A test that waited on one of those and then read s.output() was reading a buffer fed by the OTHER transport, filled by a pump goroutine nobody had waited for. Not a short deadline: NO deadline.

One defect, twenty faces. Which face goes red is whichever assertion the scheduler catches — which is exactly why it kept arriving as 'two more unrelated tests'.

MEASURED AT THE READ POINT under contention: 3 of 60 rounds read the pty before the fence had been pumped. In one round 123 bytes were visible while 4095 sat unread in the kernel and 7264 more were still to come, and the channel had already reported complete and prompt_ready.

THE FIX: run() returns only when the command has finished on BOTH transports, anchored on the product's own render fence — 32 random bytes minted per command and written after that command's output, which is the rendezvous the protocol already defines for this question. Unique per command, so no baseline is needed, and it pins a position rather than a count. 15 of 20 sites covered by that alone; the other five wait for the substring they assert.

A DEAD END WORTH THE INK, now in the code: anchoring on 'more prompt markers than before' STILL FAILED, because the baseline is sampled from the same lagging buffer — under lag it misses the current prompt's own marker, which then arrives and satisfies 'one more than before' while the command has not started. A BASELINE SAMPLED THROUGH THE RACE CANNOT ANCHOR THE RACE. Any fix that compares against a count or a snapshot taken from the racing side will not hold.

DETERMINISTIC REPRODUCER, and it is worth more than the fix. NOCX_TEST_PTY_PUMP_LAG_MS (new, off by default) delays each pty pump between the read that empties the kernel buffer and the append that makes bytes visible — exactly the window a descheduled pump occupies:

    NOCX_TEST_PTY_PUMP_LAG_MS=150 go test -race ./internal/shellintegration/

On an IDLE machine that failed 8 tests per run, every run, and the set matched the static inventory. A test that passes with the knob open does not depend on the pump being prompt. The class stops being a coin flip and becomes a property checkable in one command.

INVENTORY, so the size is known rather than discovered one red gate at a time: 20 unwaited positive pty assertions across 10 test functions, all now covered. Not at risk: ~46 already-waited assertions (all of inband_pty_test.go), 9 negative assertions (which got STRONGER — they no longer pass by reading an empty buffer), and 14 functions that io.ReadAll after the shell exits, structurally immune.

VERIFIED green at lag 150ms and 500ms, three concurrent whole-package runs at --cpu-shares=512, and two waves of the natural contention shape that used to fail. Committed as 1defea08 on fix/shellint-flakes; the pre-commit containerized run passed first time, where it had failed twice before.

title: The deadcode ratchet now runs nowhere: Wails v3 ended its no-cgo cross-GOOS trick, and CI never ran it
description:
The deadcode ratchet ran in the pre-commit hook and nowhere else — it appears in
no workflow and in no Makefile target, which check-deadcode.mjs says itself:
"CI, which never runs deadcode at all, said nothing (nocx-0odm)". The Wails v3
migration (nocx-mgbjx) removed it from the hook, so right now NOTHING runs it.
This bead puts it back, in CI.

WHY IT LEFT THE HOOK, and it is not a preference. The ratchet analysed BOTH
darwin/arm64 and linux/amd64 from whatever machine it ran on, and that was only
possible with CGO_ENABLED=0 — the file states this as its design: "it is what
makes a cross-GOOS analysis possible without a cross-compiler at all". Wails v3
requires cgo for both targets. Its own cross-platform guide is a table: macOS
"CGO required: Yes / Docker with macOS SDK", Linux "Yes / Docker, or native if a
C compiler is available". Measured here rather than taken on faith:
CGO_ENABLED=1 with -tags gtk3 exits 0; CGO_ENABLED=0 fails with the same tag.
There is no no-cgo mode to find.

THE FIX IS CHEAPER THAN EVERY WORKAROUND, and it comes from noticing why the
trick existed. Analysing two platforms from one host was necessary because a
developer machine cannot be both a Mac and a Linux box. CI already has both.
So each job analyses its OWN platform, natively, with cgo on:

  backend        (macos-latest)   deadcode for darwin, native
  backend-linux  (ubuntu-24.04)   deadcode for linux, native

No Docker cross-image, no Zig, and no macOS SDK — the wails-cross route would
have made a mandatory gate depend on Apple's SDK licence terms, which Wails
explicitly does not distribute and asks each user to review.

THE BASELINE NEEDS NO NEW FORMAT. deadcode-baseline.json is the UNION of the two
platforms. A single-platform run produces a subset of it, so a violation absent
from the baseline still fails the job, and the only thing lost is that a stale
baseline entry from the other platform goes unreported on that job. A ratchet
fails on new violations; it does not need to notice shrinkage.

WHAT THIS PROTECTS, so nobody reads the hook removal as "we stopped caring".
nocx-rtg0 shipped an encrypted store, a key lifecycle, a retention policy and
five Settings controls where ContentDB.Add had no caller outside its own tests —
behind an acceptance criterion of "deadcode is empty", which was true. AGENTS.md
keeps the ratchet as a floor for exactly that. It must not stay unrun.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. `grep -rn deadcode .github/workflows/ Makefile` on a tree carrying the Wails
   v3 migration — no hit. `grep -n check-deadcode .githooks/pre-commit` — no hit
   either. Nothing runs it.
2. Add an unreachable exported function anywhere in internal/ and commit. The
   hook passes, and no CI job objects.
3. For the cause rather than the symptom, on the migration branch:
   `CGO_ENABLED=1 deadcode -tags gtk3 ./...` exits 0, while
   `CGO_ENABLED=0 deadcode -tags gtk3 ./...` fails inside wails' own package
   with "undefined: pointer" — the no-cgo path the ratchet was built on.

## Acceptance Criteria

- deadcode runs in CI on both platforms: darwin on the macos job, linux on the
  linux job, each natively with cgo enabled and the platform build tags the
  rest of those jobs already use (-tags gtk3 on Linux).
- check-deadcode.mjs accepts the platform to analyse instead of hardcoding
  TARGET_PLATFORMS, and its long comment is rewritten — the CGO_ENABLED=0
  paragraph documents a design that no longer exists and would mislead the next
  reader completely.
- A deliberately unreachable function added in a scratch commit fails the
  correct job, on both platforms. Prove it once rather than assuming the wiring.
- The hook stays free of it: the point was that a commit does not pay for this.
- nocx-0odm is re-read before starting and updated after. Its bug was the
  ratchet answering differently per host; per-platform CI jobs are a different
  answer to the same question, and its notes should say so rather than leaving
  a closed bug that appears to have been undone.
notes:
ADDED 2026-08-17. Before restoring the ratchet, know what deadcode can and cannot see, because it changes what the gate is worth.

deadcode's RTA marks every method reached through an interface as REFLECTION-REACHABLE. For internal/content that means `deadcode -filter 'nocx/internal/content'` prints nothing and has always printed nothing, whether or not the package's write path had a production caller. An acceptance criterion written on the filter form there is unfalsifiable — and that is the very package where a dead write path shipped once (nocx-rtg0's ContentDB.Add).

Two consequences for this bead. First, whatever you restore must be checked against a package where you KNOW the answer, in both directions: it has to stay quiet on a wired symbol and speak on an unwired one. A ratchet that cannot go red is furniture. Second, AGENTS.md now tells workers to ask `deadcode -whylive <symbol>` rather than `-filter <package>`; if the ratchet's baseline mechanism has the same blind spot, say so in the commit rather than restoring a gate that looks like one.

Note also that every Go command on a Linux dev host needs -tags gtk3 now (Wails v3 defaults to GTK4/webkitgtk-6.0), and CGO_ENABLED=1.
close_reason:
Merged into feat/workspaces at c9cbc368 (2b084105). Each CI job now analyses its own platform natively with cgo on — ci-mac for darwin, ci-linux for linux — so the cross-GOOS trick Wails v3 killed is not needed at all.

Proven in both directions rather than asserted, which was the added acceptance criterion: a plain unwired function is named and the run exits 1; the byte-identical shape with one call site from main() is not reported; a clean tree exits 0. The updater's growth guard refuses with a probe present.

AND IT MEASURED ITS OWN BLIND SPOT, which is worth more than the restoration. A dead METHOD on a type reached only through an interface is NOT reported — the exact shape ContentDB.Add had. So the ratchet catches a dead function and cannot catch a dead method behind a live interface, which on an AD-8 codebase is most of the code. That is now in AGENTS.md (449bdc8a) with the conclusion it forces: deadcode is a floor for 'is this symbol dead' and can never answer 'is this feature wired'.

Also fixed in the same commit, and it had been silently red since the Wails v3 migration: nocx-mgbjx added 'sudo apt-get install libgtk-3-dev libwebkit2gtk-4.1-dev' to the macOS job as well as the two Linux ones. macos-latest has no apt-get, so that step exits 127 and EVERY step after it never ran — Build, the OS-split check, the OS tests, the -tags release test. The macOS half of CI has been reporting nothing.

Unproven from here and needing a watch on its first PR: the darwin run itself. This host is Linux, and cgo is precisely what makes trying darwin locally impossible.

title: Specs leave records behind and the next one finds two: the stand keeps one home for the whole run
description:
Two webkit specs in e2e/notes.spec.ts fail in the FULL suite and pass when the
file is run alone. Measured 2026-08-16 in the CI container, four runs:

    merged main (06912fc4), full suite, webkit   FAIL notes.spec.ts:43 and :127
    merged main (06912fc4), full suite, webkit   FAIL notes.spec.ts:43 and :127   (repeat)
    merged main (06912fc4), notes.spec.ts alone  4 passed (41.3s)
    pre-merge main (7366d1d6), alone             4 passed (21.5s)

Same specs pass on chromium in every run. The failure is webkit-only AND
full-suite-only.

THE MECHANISM IS VISIBLE IN THE ERROR. From the first full run:

    Error: strict mode violation:
      locator('.notes-panel .ui-record-row__title').filter({ hasText: 'Standup notes' })
      resolved to 2 elements

Two notes with the same title in the library. A spec that runs earlier leaves a
note behind, and the notes spec then matches both its own and the leftover. That
is state crossing a spec boundary, not a defect in what notes do.

NOT THE WAVE MERGE, and this is why the bead says so up front. The merge that
surfaced it (06912fc4 — notifications, session identity, exit cause, credential
scope) touches nothing in the notes library. The alone-vs-alone comparison above
is the proof: identical result at both commits.

WHAT IS NOT PROVEN, stated rather than glossed: the full suite was never run on
pre-merge main, so "this already failed before the merge" is inferred from the
mechanism, not measured. The cheap way to settle it is one full webkit run at
7366d1d6.

AND THERE IS NO CI TO DEFER TO. The last CI run on main is 2026-08-10 and it is
red; the release run of 2026-08-12 is green. Nothing has run CI on main since,
including PR #93 which introduced these specs. So the usual rule — the container
is for iterating, CI is the source of truth — has no source of truth to consult
here.

RELATED, and possibly the same shape: e2e/snippets.spec.ts:208 failed in the
second full run and not the first, and three other webkit specs
(connections-settings, notification-osc, quick-connect) failed in the first and
not the second. Those move; the two notes ones do not. Whoever takes this should
check whether the movers share the leaked-state cause or are ordinary flakes.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. ./e2e/run-in-container.sh on any recent main. Observe notes.spec.ts:43 and
   :127 fail under webkit.
2. PW_PROJECTS=webkit ./e2e/run-in-container.sh e2e/notes.spec.ts. Observe 4
   passed.
3. The difference between 1 and 2 is the whole bug.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The notes specs pass in the full webkit suite, three consecutive runs.
- The fix is isolation, not a more specific locator: a `.first()` or a tighter
  filter would hide the leak and leave the next spec to trip on it.
- Whatever leaves the note behind is named in the fix, and a test asserts the
  library is empty at the start of the notes spec rather than assuming it.
- The three moving webkit specs are checked against the same cause and either
  folded in or explicitly ruled out.
notes:
THIRD OBSERVATION, 2026-08-17, on feat/workspaces at fb383d09 after the tab->pane rename. Full containerized e2e: 3 failures, all in the known population, NONE caused by the rename.

  notes.spec.ts:43  webkit  strict mode violation ... resolved to 2 elements
  notes.spec.ts:127 webkit  strict mode violation ... resolved to 2 elements
  snippets.spec.ts:172 webkit  timeout of 60000ms exceeded while running afterEach

The two notes failures are the CROSS-PROJECT LEAK, now confirmed three ways: they fail when both browsers run in one invocation, pass in a webkit-only run, and pass in a chromium-only run. globalSetup runs once per invocation rather than per project, so chromium's notes are still in the library when webkit starts.

snippets.spec.ts:172 belongs to the OTHER half — the webkit timeout population — and this is its second appearance. Per AGENTS.md that half must be checked against the CI webkit job before anything is fixed: the container runs Linux WebKit at a container-default viewport and the shipped app is macOS WKWebView, and 'never fix a test that is only red in the container without checking which one is lying'.

Note for whoever takes this: notes.spec.ts:127 is titled 'asking twice focuses the tab already open'. It does NOT fail on tab focus. It fails at line 141 clicking a row locator that matched two rows. The title will mislead you.

WIDER THAN NOTES, 2026-08-18. The same shape appeared in snippets.spec.ts:215 on CHROMIUM — strict mode violation, locator('.ui-record-row__title').filter({hasText: 'e2e fill'}) resolved to 2 elements. So it is not a notes bug and not a webkit bug; it is that e2e/stand.ts keeps ONE home for the whole run and any spec writing a named record hands it to the next reader of that list.

Retitled accordingly. The webkit-only appearance of the notes cases was an artefact of ordering, not of the browser: notes.spec runs in both projects against one library, so the second project is the one that finds two. Snippets finds two inside a single project because two of its own cases share a name.

stand.ts already records the limitation in words — 'it does NOT reset WITHIN a run; that needs a home per test and a backend to match'. That sentence is the bead.

Not in scope for nocx-isoph.4, which added a LAYOUT reset (tabs and panes) before each test for a different reason. Whoever takes this should read that reset first: it opens the control plane the way the renderer does rather than clicking, because a click cannot reach a row the renderer does not draw — the same lesson applies to any record a spec leaves behind.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
RESTORED 2026-08-18. The notes above were overwritten by a
coordinator using `bd update --notes`, which REPLACES the field
rather than appending to it. Recovered verbatim from the tracked
export at 08172a0a. What follows below is what was written over
them, kept because it is also true.
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

REPRODUCED UNCHANGED at e25262c0 (2026-08-18), on the merged tree carrying
nocx-rtg0.29, .12, .15 and .28's failure test: 330 passed, 2 failed, and the
two are the same pair as ever — notes.spec.ts:43 and :127, webkit only.

Worth recording because of what changed around them and did not move them: a
new transport method and notification (history.status), a widened
history.query source enum, a schema bump to 8, and the renderer now naming its
pane on every open. None of that touched the count in either direction, which
is what a cross-spec pollution failure looks like and is not what a regression
looks like.
close_reason: Fixed in d4206f77 and ae2b181b. The cause was named correctly in the bead — state crossing a spec boundary through the shared home, not a defect in what notes do — and the fix is in resetStand, which now clears the notes library and the snippet library alongside the pane chain and the UI state. Notes was the CI-visible half (webkit, full-suite only, 'resolved to 2 elements'); snippets was the same disease one store further along, invisible on CI because CI starts from a fresh home and visible the moment the suite runs twice on one machine. Both stores had been relying on each spec's own tidy-up, which a spec that fails mid-way never reaches. Full containerized suite on a clean home: 340 passed, 0 failed, chromium and webkit.

title: The policy gets scopes and configuration, and ADR-0020 §7 is amended to say so
description:
Owner, 2026-08-16, declining the three-preset flip: "нужна более гибкая политика. Нужны scope.
Нужна гибкая настройка."

THIS REVISES A DECISION, AND THE REVISION IS THE FIRST DELIVERABLE. ADR-0020 §7 says in as many
words: three presets on top of the policy function, and the full effect lattice is "the enum we
grow into, not a policy engine we build now", because "a policy engine nobody has needed yet is
how this decision would turn into a research project". Somebody now needs it. That is a
legitimate reason to revise — and it is revised by amending the ADR deliberately, not by the
policy quietly growing settings until the ADR is false.

So: write the amendment first, get it approved, then build what it says. A brief that crosses a
boundary names the ADR and what it already decided before it says what to build.

WHAT THE POLICY ALREADY HAS to build on, rather than beside: content.Grant carries Effects and
Scopes (GrantScope{Kind, ID} over the ledger closed ResourceKind set) and a GrantPolicy preset;
internal/assistant/policy.go evaluates permit/ask/refuse over exactly that. The scopes exist. It
is the POLICY over them that is three fixed presets.

THE RULE THAT MUST SURVIVE ANY AMOUNT OF FLEXIBILITY: the grant is over resources and effects,
never over tool names. A configuration that lets a person permit "readScreen" rather than
"observe on these sessions" reintroduces the --no-tools mistake at the settings layer.

## Acceptance Criteria

- ADR-0020 §7 is amended, saying what changed and why the earlier deferral no longer holds.
  Owner-approved before the code lands.
- A person expresses a policy finer than the three presets — at minimum per effect class and per
  resource scope — and a run is permitted, asked or refused accordingly. Asserted end to end.
- No configuration path can express a rule over a tool NAME. Asserted by trying.
- Both ends: the three presets remain expressible in the new form, and a run under each behaves
  as it does today.
- An unstated or unparseable policy fails toward asking, never toward permitting. Asserted.
close_reason: Policy is a matrix over the seven effect classes with resource scopes, ADR-0020 §7 amended and accepted by the owner the same day. The presets survive as named matrices; a rule over a tool name is unexpressible by construction; an unstated policy fails toward asking. Merged 330203ef.

title: Model roles: a feature asks for a role, never for a model id
description:
Owner, 2026-08-16: "у нас сейчас нет возможности задать какую модель для чего использовать.
Можно взять пример из omp" — with omp's model picker attached: providers on the left, models
with context window and price, and at the bottom a ROLE row (default / smol / designer) with
"Enter assign roles".

Today an endpoint carries Models []EndpointModel (internal/profile/endpoint.go:59), so the list
of models a provider offers already exists. What does not exist is the layer above it: a NAMED
ROLE that resolves to one (endpoint, model) pair, so a feature asks for a role and never for a
model id.

WHY IT IS A PREREQUISITE AND NOT A CONVENIENCE: the classifier (its own bead) cannot even be
stated without it — "classify with the cheap model" has nothing to say it with. Every feature
that wants a different model for a different job needs this first.

ONE OWNER: a role resolves in one place. A feature that reads an endpoint and picks a model
itself is the second answer, and the two will disagree the first time a role is reassigned.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A person assigns a model to a role in the product and the feature using that role picks up
  the change without naming a model anywhere. Asserted end to end.
- A role with no model assigned is a VISIBLE failure where the feature is used, never a silent
  fallback to some other model — a silent fallback means a person cannot tell which model
  answered.
- A model or endpoint that disappears leaves the role unresolvable and says so; it does not
  resolve to a neighbour.
- Both ends: the existing ask path keeps working, resolved through a role rather than through a
  hardcoded endpoint choice.
- The wire shape is declared in contracts/ with additionalProperties:false plus explicit
  required, asserted over the socket.
close_reason: Model roles shipped: a closed role set the product defines, assigned to endpoint+model pairs in Settings, resolved in one place. An unassigned role fails visibly where it is used rather than falling back. Merged ac5e866e.

title: A sealed vault raises one unlock per caller: restoring eight ssh panes asks eight times, and seven are already answered
description:
transport.RequestUnlock registers a NEW ask per call and broadcasts its own
vault.unlockRequest each time (internal/transport/unlock_requester.go:215-226):

    rid, ch, err := s.asks.register()
    s.broadcastAsk("vault.unlockRequest", map[string]any{"requestId": rid, ...})

Nothing checks whether an unlock is already pending. N callers meeting a sealed
vault produce N requests with N distinct requestIds, each blocking its own
caller until it is answered or its context ends.

WHY NOBODY HAS SEEN IT. Today the unlock is raised by one user action at a
time — open an ssh profile, read history — so the concurrent case does not
arise in normal use. Session restore is what produces it: a user with eight
restored ssh panes reconnecting on startup meets a sealed vault eight times at
once, because the vault is ALWAYS sealed right after a start.

AND SEVEN OF THE EIGHT ARE POINTLESS. The first successful unlock opens the
vault; the remaining callers would now succeed if they simply retried. So this
is not "many dialogs", it is many dialogs of which all but one ask for
something that has already happened.

SHAPE OF THE FIX, not prescribed: one pending unlock at a time, with later
callers joining the pending ask rather than raising their own, and every
joiner resolved by the single answer. The reason string then has to name more
than one need, or name the first and count the rest — a dialog that says "ssh
srv-01 needs the vault" while seven other panes wait behind it is still a lie
by omission.

RELATED BUT NOT THE SAME: nocx-k41yv (P0, open) is about WHO may raise the
unlock — half the traffic escapes the seam because the raiser is decided by
which pipe the error travels down. This bead is about HOW MANY are raised once
the seam is right. Fixing k41yv does not fix this and may make it worse, since
a wider seam means more callers reach the raise.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Configure two or more ssh profiles whose credentials live in the vault.
2. Open a session on each, so a restore would bring them back.
3. Restart the backend so the vault is sealed.
4. Trigger a reconnect on all of them at once (once session restore exists this
   is simply "start the app"; today, open both profiles in quick succession).
5. Observed: one vault.unlockRequest notification per caller, each with its own
   requestId. Expected: one pending unlock that every waiting caller joins.

## Acceptance Criteria

- N concurrent callers meeting a sealed vault produce exactly ONE
  vault.unlockRequest, and one successful unlock resolves all of them.
- A test asserts the count over the real socket, with N >= 3 callers racing —
  not a unit test of a helper, since the defect is in the broadcast path.
- A caller arriving while an unlock is pending joins it rather than raising a
  second one, and is resolved by the same answer.
- The reason shown to the user accounts for every waiting caller, rather than
  naming the first and silently representing the rest.
notes:
SHARPER, from the owner 2026-08-16, and it relocates the fix.

The defect is not in the broadcast. The broadcast is right and has a reason: the backend does not know WHICH renderer should show the dialog — there may be several clients, and under AD-9 they reconnect — so it asks whoever is listening and takes the first answer.

The defect is that NOBODY HOLDS THE STATE 'I am sealed and one unlock is already pending'. RequestUnlock lives on the WSServer and every caller invokes it directly, so the transport is executing a policy that belongs to the vault. Five callers meet a sealed vault and each independently decides to ask, because the vault was never told it is already asking.

The owner's shape, which is simpler than adding dedup to the transport: five callers make their asynchronous request; the VAULT sees it is locked and raises ONE prompt; unlocked, every waiting caller gets its data; not unlocked, every waiting caller gets the error. One pending unlock, one answer, N resolutions.

So the fix belongs in internal/vault, not in internal/transport, and the transport keeps exactly what it is good for — delivering one prompt to whichever renderer is there. That also makes the reason string easy: the vault knows how many callers are waiting and what each wanted, because it is the thing holding them.
REACHABILITY, reported by the worker 2026-08-16 and recorded before it can evaporate.

The coalescing seam is built and tested in internal/vault (EnsureUnsealed + SetUnlockRequester). The composition root wires SetUnlockRequester, so the vault CAN raise. But EnsureUnsealed has NO PRODUCTION CONSUMER until nocx-k41yv routes the sealed secret-access paths through it — consumer routing is that bead's, not this one's.

So this bead lands a mechanism whose write path is reachable and whose call sites are not. That is the exact shape of nocx-rtg0, where a reachable read path hid an unreachable write path in the same package and 'deadcode is empty' was read as 'history works'. It is named here so nobody reads a green deadcode run as 'one unlock for all callers now ships'.

Until k41yv lands, the user-visible behaviour is UNCHANGED: callers still reach RequestUnlock directly and still get one prompt each.

The worker also notes the seam makes k41yv EASIER rather than harder: with the coalescing state in the vault, whoever k41yv decides may raise the unlock routes through EnsureUnsealed and gets the dedup for free.

STATED LIMITATION, the worker's own: the dialog reason is fixed at broadcast and names every waiter joined at that instant. A waiter that joins after the frame is on the wire is resolved by the same answer but is not named in the already-sent text. Naming it needs a second frame or a mutable reason on the wire, both out of scope here.
close_reason: Fixed on feat/nocx-o9jdu (7652d2cc + b5f76c47) and merged into feat/workspaces at db4ca33e: a sealed vault now raises one unlock for every caller waiting on it. Verified by ancestry, not by report. Unblocks nocx-9y4ku.

title: Approval resumes at the same attempt, while the design says a new one
description:
Found by wv6-approval while blocked, and it contradicts a bead already closed (nocx-lndv).

Design §7.2 and ADR-0020 decision 4 both say an approval resumes as a NEW ATTEMPT rather than
widening the running one — attempts are first class precisely so that "a retry after approval"
is an execution of the same entry rather than a new intent.

The implementation resumes at the SAME attempt number. So either the code is wrong, or
"attempt" in the design means something other than the ledger attempt column — and if it is the
latter, the design says so, or the word is doing two jobs.

WHY IT MATTERS beyond bookkeeping: the blast-radius query ADR-0020 exists for is answered per
execution. An approved call recorded under the attempt that was refused cannot be told apart
from the call that was refused.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Read internal/assistant/policy_test.go:429-443 — the test approves {Attempt: 1} and the
   middleware at attempt 1 accepts it.
2. Read ledger_agent_sqlite.go:498-501 — the agent run row is inserted at attempt = 1, and
   re-submitting the same askId is a replay returning the original run.
3. Compare with spec 2026-08-16 §7.2 and ADR-0020 decision 4.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The word attempt means one thing, stated once, and the ledger agrees with the design.
- An approved call is recorded as its own execution, distinguishable from the escalation that
  preceded it. Asserted against a real content store.
- Both ends: a run with no escalation still records exactly one execution per call.
close_reason: Settled by the epic's own criterion — proposal, decision, attempt and result are one readable thread — so an escalation is recorded, the approved call runs as its own subsequent attempt of the same entry, and a refusal terminalizes as agent-declined.

title: The approval surface: an escalation reaches a person and their answer resumes the run
description:
AMENDED 2026-08-16 after wv6-approval traced the chain and stopped rather than guessing.

THE SURFACE IS NOT THE WHOLE JOB. Four links are broken and all four are the seam, not
decoration. Each is verified with file and line in the worker report:

1. The transport CANNOT SEE the suspension. errApprovalRequested is unexported and its request
field with it, so the transport cannot errors.As into anything. Today classifyAskFailure
terminalizes an escalation as FAILED with the sentence "the model failed to answer: agent run
suspended for approval" — a live lie waiting for the first named grant policy.

2. The transport CANNOT RECORD the answer. newApprovalStore is unexported, ApprovalStore has
unexported maps so a zero value panics, and the client stores its own privately with no
accessor. There is no pending-query, so "a stale or unknown approval id" has no source of truth.

3. THE RUN STATE CANNOT SAY A QUESTION IS OUTSTANDING. RunAwaitingApproval is declared and
unreachable: TransitionRun refuses everything except prepared -> streaming. A suspended run
rests in streaming, indistinguishable to a reconnecting renderer from a run mid-answer.

4. The resume attempt semantics contradict the design — split out as nocx-5dldy.

SO THIS BEAD NOW CARRIES THE WHOLE CHAIN: the exports and the pending-query in
internal/assistant, the awaiting_approval transition in internal/content and
internal/capability, the wire, and the surface. It is sequenced AFTER nocx-0p7y2 because that
slice owns internal/assistant this wave and its finding shape is what the surface renders.
close_reason: All four links closed and merged: the transport can name the suspension, the store is reachable and answers honestly on a stale id, awaiting_approval is reachable and distinguishable from a run mid-answer, and the question is drawn from the kit. An escalation is no longer reported as a model failure.

title: internal/lifecycleremote: a test waits for Send to refuse, then asserts the listener is closed
description:
internal/lifecycleremote/adapter_test.go:504 asserts a state it never waited for.

TestTunnelConnDoneStopsServing waits for one observable and then asserts a
DIFFERENT one as though the first implied it:

    waitFor(t, "adapter closed after loss", func() bool {
        return errors.Is(a.Send(lifecycle.Envelope{}), ErrClosed)
    })
    if c, derr := net.Dial("tcp", "127.0.0.1:"+strconv.Itoa(cfg.Port)); derr == nil {
        t.Fatal("listener must be closed after transport loss; a dial succeeded")
    }

Send refusing with ErrClosed and the listener being closed are two events, and
nothing in the adapter orders them. The test blocks until the first and then
takes a single shot at the second. When the listener has not yet closed, the
dial succeeds and the test reports the product broken.

The doc comment above the test names the sequence — "Send refuses, the listener
is closed" — as if it were guaranteed. That sentence is the assumption, written
down and never enforced.

NOT THE MERGE. The wave it surfaced under (fix/nocx-ictcq-exit-cause,
feat/nocx-3oupk-session-identity, fix/nocx-tsajw-capture-scope,
fix/nocx-jiwq-policy) touches no file under internal/lifecycleremote,
internal/lifecycle, internal/lifecyclechannel or internal/tunnel:
git diff --name-only origin/main...HEAD over those paths is empty.

WHY THIS IS FILED RATHER THAN RETRIED. AGENTS.md: "a test may not depend on
timing. Wait on an observable state change — a frame, a record, a DOM state —
never on a duration. A spec that needs a slow machine to pass is broken on a fast
one too; it has only not been caught yet." This one is subtler than a sleep and
has the same cost: it reds the gate for whoever integrates next, exactly as
nocx-2h08 did on the same tree this morning.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. ./scripts/ci-linux.sh on a tree at or after 7f931a5e — the script runs
   internal/lifecycleremote twice, once per keyring variant, in one invocation.
2. Observed 2026-08-16 on integration/wave-1-2, both variants at the SAME commit
   in the SAME container, one invocation:

     variant 1, no Secret Service:   FAIL internal/lifecycleremote  0.335s
       adapter_test.go:504: listener must be closed after transport loss; a dial succeeded
     variant 2, with Secret Service: ok   internal/lifecycleremote  1.343s

   Same code, minutes apart, opposite verdicts — and the FAILING run is the
   FASTER one, which is the signature of a race won rather than a behaviour lost.
3. Under load the failure is likelier: the box was running the containerized
   gate with other worktrees active. go test -count=5 ./internal/lifecycleremote/
   under parallel load is the cheapest reproduction to try first.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The dial assertion waits on the listener actually being closed, rather than
  taking one shot after an unrelated observable.
- OR the adapter establishes the ordering its comment claims — the listener is
  closed before Send begins refusing — and the test asserts that ordering.
- ./scripts/ci-linux.sh is green across both keyring variants on three
  consecutive invocations.
close_reason: Landed on main in 06912fc4. The test now waits for the listener to close rather than inferring it from Send refusing; adapter.go is byte-identical to before. Proved both ways: with a 200ms sleep between the closed flag and ln.Close the old assertion failed 5/5 and the new one passed 5/5; with ln.Close removed entirely the new assertion still fails at its 2s deadline, so the flake is gone and the test kept its teeth.

title: internal/content: concurrent readers over the encrypted VFS can meet a malformed image
description:
Seen on CI, macOS runner, ci-backend (no-secret-service), 2026-08-16, on PR #93 — a branch that does not touch internal/content. The with-secret-service variant of the SAME run passed, and both variants passed 20 minutes earlier, so it is intermittent.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. go test ./internal/content/ -run TestConcurrentReadersWithOneWriter on macOS.
2. Occasionally: sqlite_test.go:565: reader: sqlite3: database disk image is malformed.

The test runs one writer and several readers against a store opened through the adiantum encryption VFS with a connection pool.

## Why it matters beyond this test

'Malformed image' is not a timeout or a busy error — it is the database reporting that what it read is not a database. Two readings, and both are worth ruling out rather than waiting for:

1. The test's own arrangement races (a reader opening while the file is being created), in which case the test is wrong and the product is fine.
2. Concurrent reads through the encryption VFS can observe a torn page, in which case the product is wrong — and internal/note now stands on the SAME VFS with the same pooled access (a ReplaceAll transaction while List reads), so a defect there is a defect for notes too.

## Acceptance Criteria

[ ] The cause is named — the test's arrangement or the VFS's concurrency — with the evidence that decides it
[ ] If it is the product: a test that fails reliably before the fix, and internal/note is checked against the same exposure
[ ] If it is the test: it stops being intermittent, and the reason is written where the next reader of that file will see it
notes:
SECOND AND THIRD OBSERVATIONS, 2026-08-17, merged in from nocx-zlek8 which I filed as a duplicate without running the 'already filed?' check.

  • The nocx-rtg0.3 worker: 2 failures in 5 runs, Linux container, clean
    feat/workspaces worktree, several agents and containers active. It verified
    its own change to internal/content was comments only, by diff.
  • Me, immediately afterwards, same host, idle, isolated: six consecutive runs,
    six passes.

So it now has three sightings on two operating systems — the CI macOS runner in
the original report, and a Linux container here — and both non-CI sightings were
under load while the isolated runs were clean. That strengthens the second of
this bead's two readings rather than the first: a test whose own arrangement
raced would not care which OS it was on, but it also would not need contention.

URGENCY CHANGED SINCE THIS WAS FILED. On 2026-08-16 the ledger was test-only.
Since 2026-08-17 the ledger's write path is wired (nocx-rtg0.3) and nocx-rtg0.19
is about to make it the ONLY place a command is recorded. 'The test was sloppy'
is the conclusion, never the hypothesis: ADR-0019 makes this file the one
authoritative ledger, so if reading 2 is right it is release-blocking.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
RESTORED 2026-08-18. The notes above were overwritten by a
coordinator using `bd update --notes`, which REPLACES the field
rather than appending to it. Recovered verbatim from the tracked
export at 08172a0a. What follows below is what was written over
them, kept because it is also true.
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

MEASURED 2026-08-18, on the feat/workspaces line, by the nocx-rtg0.12 worker —
and measured at BASELINE first, which is what makes it evidence.

Rate: 1 of 3 runs red on a clean tree at 5c27da2f, and 4 of 12 with an
unrelated internal/content change on top. Same rate, so the change did not
cause it and did not worsen it. Failure text: "reader: sqlite3: database disk
image is malformed".

WHY IT IS NOT COSMETIC. The test exercises only CommandHistory() — Add, Query,
List. It never touches entries, the ledger, or any table added since. So this
is the encrypted VFS under concurrent read/write, not a schema or a caller
problem, and "disk image is malformed" is the shape a reader sees when it
observes a page a writer is mid-way through — which is the failure the WAL and
BEGIN IMMEDIATE discipline exist to prevent.

A 33% flake also means a green gate run is NOT evidence against it: the
coordinator's own pre-change run of the same package came back green at the
same commit.

title: Tool schemas are read from the cwd, so the shipped app silently has no tools
description:
Found by wv3-pgtrh in its own work and reported rather than hidden.

internal/assistant NewClient assembles the tool registry from os.DirFS("contracts/tools"),
a path relative to the process cwd. The shipped Wails bundle carries no contracts/ tree,
so the shipped app assembles the QUIET EMPTY SET: no error, no log a user sees, nothing
distinguishing it from "this build has no tools".

Invisible today because no production caller passes a grant, so the set is empty
everywhere anyway. It stops being invisible the moment nocx-lndv makes a grant real, and
then it presents as "the assistant ignores the tools you granted it" with nothing in the
product saying why. AGENTS.md: a soft degrade must be visible in the product, not only in
a log.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Build and run the app from anywhere other than the repository root (the shipped bundle
   always qualifies — it carries no contracts/ tree at all).
2. Assemble the tool registry.
3. The set is empty, and nothing anywhere says the schemas were not found.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The schemas reach the binary rather than the cwd — go:embed or an equivalent that cannot
  depend on where the process was started. Asserted by a test whose working directory is
  outside the repo.
- A registry that assembles empty when it should not is a VISIBLE failure: the product
  says so where a person can see it. Asserted.
- Both ends: a build carrying schemas assembles them, and the assembled count is
  observable rather than inferred.
close_reason: Schemas embedded into the binary; an assembly that comes back empty when it should not now fails startup instead of degrading silently. Merged 5d233b9b.

title: Wire the request broker into the WSServer, so its functions have callers
description:
The broker built in nocx-e2j1z has no production caller: deadcode reports all 10 of its
functions unreachable, which is correct and is why that branch cannot be committed alone.
The mechanism was deliberately scoped to new files plus tests, with the renderer half
deferred to the first real effect.

This bead is that wiring: the broker is constructed by the WSServer, registered on the
control plane, torn down with the connection, and CALLED by something real — so the
functions gain callers instead of gaining baseline entries. Growing the deadcode baseline
is not an acceptable answer here (see nocx-pgtrh, amended, for why).

## Acceptance Criteria

- The broker is reachable from main: the deadcode ratchet passes with the baseline
  UNCHANGED, and that is the evidence.
- A connection dropping mid-request terminalizes it through the production path, not only
  through the test seam. Asserted.
- The renderer half of the wire contract is declared in contracts/ with
  additionalProperties:false plus explicit required, and asserted over the real socket.
- Both ends: a request that the renderer answers returns its typed result through the
  production path.
close_reason: Broker wired: constructed with the control plane, torn down with the connection, called by the readScreen executor. The acceptance evidence was deadcode passing with the baseline UNCHANGED, and it does. The production grant flip is NOT this bead's criteria and lives on nocx-0p7y2 (egress gate) plus the approval surface; the blocking edge to 0p7y2 was removed as mis-scoped. Merged 14649ff4.

title: A command carries the author that submitted it, minted by the target
description:
Design: .internal/specs/2026-08-16-agent-tools-design.md §3.1.

The durable half exists: entries.kind IN (shell,agent,action)
(internal/content/sqlite.go:570), executions.lane, executions.executor. The gap is
the renderer: CommandRecord (frontend/src/command-ledger.ts:20-33) carries command,
cwd, host, status, exit code and times — and no author at all, while the block is
drawn by the renderer.

THE RULE: the author is minted at submit, BY THE TARGET THAT SUBMITS, and is never
derived afterwards. Deriving it later ("commands during an agent run are the
agent's") breaks exactly where it hurts: a human types while the agent works and
the command is attributed to the agent. That is the interleaving ADR-0019 §2 warns
about, arriving through the back door.

## Acceptance Criteria

- CommandRecord carries an author, set by the submitting InputTarget.
- A human command submitted WHILE another target's submission is in flight is
  attributed to the human — asserted by interleaving two registered targets, not by
  reading the implementation.
- The fact sent up the wire carries the author, and its schema in contracts/
  requires it (additionalProperties:false plus explicit required), with the
  over-the-socket assertion the directory exists for.
- A block whose author is not the human is visibly distinguishable in the flow.
- Both ends of the interval: with only the shell target registered, every record is
  attributed to the human and nothing regresses.
close_reason: Author minted at submit by the target, required on the wire with no default, checked on the ack, marked with the kit badge. Two tests rewritten after review to exercise the router rather than the implementation. Merged 111e28a5.

title: A tool is declared in one row, and tests make the row structural
description:
AMENDED 2026-08-16 by the coordinator, after wv3-tooldecl escalated with evidence.

The first cut of this bead demanded an INERT registry and a commit through the
pre-commit hook. Those are contradictory: the deadcode ratchet fails any commit
staging Go whose functions the baseline does not list, and an inert package has no
production caller by construction. The worker proved it empirically with a scratch
package rather than assuming it, and refused both escapes (--no-verify, hand-growing
the baseline without sanction). Correct call.

THE FIX IS NOT A DEADCODE EXCEPTION. nocx-ng6f set that precedent (grow the baseline,
pair a shrink bead) and it is the wrong instrument here. AGENTS.md testing rule 2 was
bought by nocx-rtg0, where a reachable read path hid an unreachable write path in the
same package and "deadcode is empty" was read as "history works". Answering an
unreachable-code gate by widening the list of sanctioned unreachable code is how that
recurs.

SO THE SLICE MOVES: the declaration table lands WITH its first consumer. The engine
(internal/assistant, reachable from main via internal/app) declares to the model
exactly the tools the run grant permits — today that set is empty, which is the same
observable behaviour as the zero-tool slice and is now produced by the mechanism
rather than by the absence of one. Nothing dangles and criterion 3 becomes assertable
on the real engine instead of a fake.

DROPPED from this slice: the Narrow field (the constructor for the narrowed
capability). There is nothing to narrow until nocx-lndv, and a dangling constructor is
the same defect in a smaller shape. It arrives with its caller too.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A tool whose params schema is absent from contracts/ does not assemble into the set.
  Asserted.
- Effect and ResourceKind are closed enums mirroring the CHECK constraints already in
  the ledger schema; an unclassified tool does not compile, and a table-driven test
  asserts every enum member is covered.
- Given a grant, the set the ENGINE hands the model contains exactly the permitted
  tools, and a forbidden tool is ABSENT rather than present-and-filtered. Asserted on
  what the engine builds, not on a fake registry.
- Both ends: a permitted tool is present and carries its schema. A test proving only
  exclusion would pass over a set that is always empty.
- Every schema carries additionalProperties:false plus an explicit required.
- The deadcode ratchet is NOT grown. If it trips, something in the slice has no caller
  and that is the finding, not the obstacle.
close_reason: Declaration table shipped and wired: the engine declares exactly what the grant permits, asserted on the request it builds. Merged 5d233b9b.

title: Server-initiated requests become a transport mechanism, not a third broker
description:
Design: .internal/specs/2026-08-16-agent-tools-design.md §2.4.

The pattern is already written twice — vault.unlockRequest/unlockResolved and
connections.passwordRequest/passwordResolved, brokered in
internal/transport/unlock_requester.go with minted request ids, closed outcome
enums, timeouts and an honest answer for a stale id. The agent needs it a third
time, and the third time it becomes the mechanism rather than a third copy.
JSON-RPC 2.0 is bidirectional; LSP is the precedent AD-1 names for choosing it.

SCOPE: Go only. Do NOT rewrite the two existing brokers in this bead — show the
mechanism can express one, by a test that drives it. Rewriting them is its own
bead once this is proven.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A backend caller issues a request to the renderer and receives a typed result,
  asserted over a real socket, not a fake conn alone.
- A result carrying an unknown or stale request id is answered honestly and never
  resolves a live request. Asserted.
- Connection loss terminalizes every in-flight request with a terminal reason
  rather than leaking a goroutine or hanging a caller. Asserted with -race.
- Ingress is validated on the read loop with the discipline already applied to
  renderer params, plus an explicit size bound: the model is a LESS trusted source
  than the renderer and gets the same check, never a weaker one.
- A test expresses one existing broker through the new mechanism, proving it is
  capable of replacing both.
close_reason: Broker shipped with 20 tests and five review defects fixed (pre-cancelled ctx, snapshot-to-arm death, unreportable delivery failure, unbound resolve method, non-comparable Conn). Merged 14649ff4.

title: End to end: written, closed, restarted, found by a word from inside it

description:

title: ws.onopen has no superseded-socket guard, so a stale socket can fire onConnect
description:
Found while designing the transport-outage overlay (session bead nocx-cfiul).

dispatcher.ts:145 guards the close listener against a superseded socket --
`if (this.ws !== ws) return`. dispatcher.ts:135 has no such guard on
`ws.onopen`, so a socket that has already been superseded still calls
`this.fireConnect()` and resolves its connect promise.

Unreachable on main today: nothing supersedes a socket while its attempt is in
flight, because the only path to _connectInternal is the backoff timer, which
fires exactly once per scheduled wait.

It becomes reachable the moment `Dispatcher.retryNow()` exists: a manual retry
racing a timer-scheduled attempt is exactly a superseded socket. A late `open`
from the loser would fire onConnect, driving every subscriber -- the session
reattach pass included -- from a socket that is not `this.ws`.

## Steps to Reproduce

Not reproducible on main -- there is no path that supersedes an in-flight
socket. In a unit test the shape is reachable today: call the private connect
path twice so two sockets exist, let the FIRST one dispatch `open` last, and
observe onConnect firing for a socket that is not `this.ws`. With retryNow()
this becomes a live path: drop the connection, then click Retry while the
backoff timer has already started its attempt.

## Acceptance Criteria

- `ws.onopen` fires neither `fireConnect()` nor its resolve when `this.ws !== ws`.
- A test opens two sockets, lets the superseded one open last, and asserts
  onConnect fired exactly once and the reattach ran against the live socket only.
- The paired case: on an ordinary single-socket connect, onConnect still fires.

title: A closed tab's pending credential capture is never destroyed
description:
internal/credential/capture.go:11-14 states the contract of the pending-capture
registry, and it names the triggers separately:

  'A pending capture is scoped to the originating TAB, session and submitted
   history-entry id. It is destroyed immediately on save, dismissal, TAB OR
   SESSION CLOSURE, vault seal or app lock, TRANSPORT DISCONNECT, application
   shutdown, or history-record failure.'

A pending capture holds a credential the user submitted, in backend process
memory, in plaintext, awaiting a save decision. Bounding its lifetime is the
whole reason the registry exists.

TAB CLOSURE NEVER FIRES. Verified 2026-08-15 against the tree — every DestroyTab
call site outside tests:

  internal/transport/ws.go:2431          unregisterConn — TRANSPORT DISCONNECT
  internal/transport/ws_history_record.go:168, :291   history-record FAILURE

That is all three. Closing one tab of several on a live connection fires none of
them. The closed tab's pending capture sits in registry memory, unreachable by
any UI, until the connection drops, the vault seals, or the app shuts down.

AND IT OVER-DESTROYS IN THE OTHER DIRECTION. Both surviving triggers are keyed
on the CONNECTION id — ws.go:2431 passes strconv.FormatUint(wc.id, 10), and the
history-record path passes tabID(wconn), which is the same value (nocx-wyp3p).
One WebSocket carries every tab in a window (ws_lifecycle.go:146), so a masking
or record failure in ONE tab destroys EVERY tab's pending captures. The code's
own comment at ws_history_record.go:136-137 says so: 'destroys the tab's pending
captures' — it destroys all of them.

So one scope is wrong in both directions at once, and both are live today.

RELATION TO nocx-wyp3p. That bead is the NAMING half — tabID(wconn) returns a
connection id. This is the BEHAVIOUR half, and it is why the resolution cannot
simply be 'rename the scope to connection': the contract names tab closure as a
distinct trigger and the renderer already assumes it happens. Found by the
wv1-wyp3p worker while investigating wyp3p; the evidence above was re-verified
by the coordinator against the tree rather than taken on report.

WHY IT NEEDS THE RENDERER. The wire carries no tab identity by design —
historyRecordParams has none, and the seam comments say the renderer's
session-local ids 'never cross the wire' (ws_history_record.go:39-41).
AD-7 gives the backend the session and the renderer the tab, so a real per-tab
scope can only be minted by the renderer and sent. The backend must not invent
a tab id (see .internal/specs/2026-08-15-workspaces-ux-design.md §5.2).

NOT ALL tabID USES ARE WRONG. ws_agent.go:901 uses it as clientID for the agent
ask/captureFrame idempotency binding and is GENUINELY connection-scoped —
'a reconnect mints a new one'. Whatever lands must keep that one connection-keyed
and rename it honestly rather than sweeping it into the change.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open two tabs in one window (one WebSocket carries both).
2. In tab A, submit a credential so a pending capture exists awaiting a save
   decision.
3. Close tab A without saving or dismissing.
4. Observed: no DestroyTab fires. The capture is still in the registry.
5. Then trigger a history-record failure in tab B.
6. Observed: tab B's captures are destroyed AND so are any others on the
   connection.

## Acceptance Criteria

Closing a tab destroys that tab's pending captures and NO other tab's — asserted
by a test with two tabs on ONE connection that closes the first and finds the
second's capture intact.

A history-record failure in one tab destroys only that tab's pending captures —
asserted by the same two-tab, one-connection arrangement.

Transport disconnect still destroys everything on that connection, and a test
says so deliberately rather than by omission.

The connection-scoped consumer at ws_agent.go:901 is named for what it is and a
comment states why it was not moved.
notes: IMPLEMENTED on fix/nocx-tsajw-capture-scope (9567edfd), NOT on main, all thirteen pre-commit gates green including the containerized go test -race and vitest. The capture scope is now the PAIR (connection, tab), so a tab is addressable only inside its own connection and the same tab id arriving on another connection reaches nothing — a case this bead did not name and TestTabClose_OtherConnectionsTabIdIsUntouchable now covers. Destruction splits: DestroyTab for the tab's death, DestroyConnection for the transport's. The tab identity is minted by the RENDERER (a UUID per tab, never reused) and carried on the wire via the new tab.close method and history.record's tabId, because AD-7 gives the backend the session and the renderer the tab. ws_agent.go's clientID deliberately stays connection-scoped with a comment saying why. Every test uses two tabs on ONE connection. Coordinator finished the last mile after the worker's workspace was removed: two Tab constructor call sites, a UUID template-literal type, and — found only by a full go test -race — three history.record acceptance payloads in internal/app that now need tabId, which the brief's package list had not covered.
close_reason: Landed on main in 06912fc4 (9567edfd): a closed tab's pending credential capture dies with it; tab.close.schema.json and ws_tab_close.go with 287 lines of test.

title: The workspaces design asserts a tab-restore path that does not exist
description:
The workspaces/lineage design §4.2 states, as the load-bearing fact under a
scheduling decision:

  'tabs survive a restart through internal/settings — the frontend re-opens
   sessions from persisted tab descriptors and the backend restores nothing'

There is no such path. The tree says so itself, in a comment written by whoever
last resisted adding a fifth writer — frontend/src/file-viewer/index.ts:85:

  'restoreDescriptor is deliberately null. The field is written in four places,
   typed unknown, and read nowhere — nothing serialises the tab list and nothing
   reconstructs a tab from a descriptor.'

Confirmed independently: internal/settings/settings.go carries only TabPlacement
(horizontal vs vertical strip) and nothing about a tab list; internal/session has
no restore path; grep finds no writer of a serialised tab list anywhere in
frontend/src. On start you get one fresh local tab.

WHY THIS IS A BEAD AND NOT A TYPO FIX.

1. §4.2 uses the claim to argue the prepared-to-active session interval belongs
   to epic E rather than epic A. That conclusion SURVIVES and is stronger — there
   is even less to preserve than the argument assumed. So the fix is to the fact,
   not to the decision, and the paragraph must say why the decision still holds.
2. The workspaces UX design (2026-08-15-workspaces-ux-design.md) inherited the
   claim and built an acceptance criterion on it: 'restarts the app, and finds the
   workspace and its tabs intact'. As written that makes epic B build tab
   persistence from scratch. §8.1 and §9 there now record this and drop the
   restart pending the owner's decision — but nocx-isoph's own acceptance still
   says 'restarts the app ... intact' and has to be resolved the same way.
3. AGENTS.md names this exact failure: writing from what the conversation
   remembered instead of reading the binding document — and here, one document
   quoting another rather than the tree.

Found by the worker on feat/notificcations while merging main; verified here.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open three tabs — a local shell, an ssh session, a file viewer.
2. Quit nocx and start it again.
3. Observed: one fresh local tab. Nothing was serialised and nothing restored.
4. Read §4.2 of .internal/specs/2026-08-15-workspaces-lineage-and-orchestration-
   design.md, which says the opposite and builds an epic boundary on it.

## Acceptance Criteria

§4.2 of 2026-08-15-workspaces-lineage-and-orchestration-design.md states what is
actually true — nothing restores tabs — and keeps its conclusion with the
corrected reason.

Every downstream document and bead that inherited the claim is reconciled:
nocx-isoph's acceptance criterion, and §8.1/§9 of the workspaces UX design.

The owner has decided, explicitly, whether workspace membership survives a
restart — because that decision is what sizes epic B.
notes:
OWNER DECISION 2026-08-15 on nocx-qfwrc: restore EXISTS and is a SETTING.
Reference is Warp, which ships two distinct settings and they must not be
conflated: General 'Restore windows, tabs, and panes on startup', and Session
'Enable reopening of closed sessions' with a grace period in seconds (undo-close
while running). What comes back includes BLOCKS and WORKSPACE MEMBERSHIP.

Recorded in the UX design as §8.2. Restoring a tab is NOT resurrecting a process
— D5 stands, workers die with the backend. Blocks are already durable
(content.ContentDB is wired at app.go:449/:523 and reachable from transport), so
what is missing is the tab list, the setting, and the tab->session->blocks map.

Scoped as ITS OWN EPIC rather than part of epic B: it can be handed over whole,
and folding it into 'pure grouping' would make B an area.
close_reason: §4.2 of the workspaces/lineage design now states what is true (d5ce6335); the UX design's §8.1/§8.2 and §9 were reconciled in 84ff8650, and nocx-isoph's acceptance was rewritten. The owner's decision that restore exists and is a setting is nocx-l21ib.
