The headless path, which builds its backend outside Playwright, is now refused by e2e/preflight.ts unless the runner exports NOCX_E2E_HOME_DIR — red until adopted, deliberately.

Proved obeyed, not just handed over: a real devharness started behind the boundary installs ~/.nocx INSIDE the disposable home, and a run without the boundary leaves that home with zero entries, so the assertion has teeth. 12 assertions green on both browsers.

Found while checking the test could fail: the companion real-home mtime check is near-vacuous, because EnsureInstalled is version-gated and reinstalling the same version does not move the mtime. Left in as a labelled tripwire rather than removed, with the limitation written next to it.

REMAINING, and it is the last item: step 5, the OS keychain. system.New() is constructed unconditionally at app.go:108, reached outside the DocumentStore seam, and home-derived on neither platform — so nothing landed here touches it. An ordinary e2e composition must stop registering the system provider at all rather than merely defaulting away from it.

Also unverified by running rather than reading: the wails dev path, because this machine has no GTK or display. CI exercises it on macos-latest.

title: Shell integration scripts ship to nobody when `version` is not bumped
description:
## Context

`EnsureInstalled` writes ~/.nocx/shell-integration.bash only when the installed VERSION file differs from the `version` constant in scripts.go — that short-circuit runs before anything looks at the script's content. So a script edited without bumping the constant reaches no shell: every session keeps sourcing the copy installed the last time the number changed.

Found by the owner: the OSC 636 command-existence hook (nocx-w7h.6, 8d9408f) did nothing in the app. The backend binary carried the new 14210-byte script, go test passed, and ~/.nocx/shell-integration.bash was still the 6504-byte copy from 2026-07-26 because `version` was left at "7".

Nothing connected the script bytes to the number that governs their delivery, which is why two workers and one review all missed it.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Edit internal/shellintegration/scripts/nocx.bash; leave `version` alone.
2. Rebuild and start the backend, open a new tab.
3. `grep 636 ~/.nocx/shell-integration.bash` — the edit is absent, and the app behaves as if the change was never made.

## Acceptance Criteria

- `version` is bumped to "8" so the OSC 636 script actually installs.
- A test hashes the embedded scripts and fails when they change without a version bump, printing the digest to record. Prove it fails: append a line to a script, run the test, see it fail; revert, see it pass.
- The failure message names the consequence (an installed VERSION is never rewritten), not just the mismatch.
close_reason: Bumped version to 8 in dfda66e and added TestScriptVersionTracksScriptContent, which hashes the embedded scripts and fails when they change without a bump. Proven to fail by appending a line to nocx.bash and reverting.

title: The command line says whether the command exists — local bash first
description:
## Context

Owner, three times, with evidence. The last: `sdfsdf` renders green in the input line
before Enter, and `dssdfdsf` ran to `exit 127`. Green now carries ZERO information — it
means "you typed a word first". The old 67-word dictionary at least meant "one of these
67". We traded an arbitrary signal for no signal, which is honest and useless.

zsh-syntax-highlighting solves this by living INSIDE zsh: it reads the live tables of
aliases, functions, builtins, hashed and external commands. We cannot, because ADR-0004
gives our editor the line and the shell never sees it until submit. So we must ask.

Not a daemon. Warp ships a 215 MB remote-server binary (measured: 622 MB and three
processes on this box). We need a list of names, not an agent.

## Scope — deliberately the smallest honest loop

LOCAL BASH ONLY. Prove the whole path end to end on the machine the owner tests on, then
widen to zsh and remote. Do not build per-shell abstraction layers before there is a
second shell.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Type `sdfsdf` at the prompt. It renders as a command, identically to `ls`.
2. There is no way to tell, before Enter, that it does not exist.

## Design constraints — each one was argued and is not up for reinvention

- **Four states, and unavailable is NOT unresolved.** `resolved` (snapshot applies, name
  found), `unresolved` (snapshot applies, is fresh, literal name not found),
  `indeterminate` (expansion/substitution — no literal name to check), `unavailable` (no
  hook, no snapshot, or stale). On a host with no integration everything must render
  `unavailable`, never red — that would be the same lie in the other direction.
- **Not a red foreground.** Red reads as a guaranteed syntax error. Use a subtle underline
  so it reads as a diagnostic remark about one word.
- **The transport is the existing shell-integration hook.** It already emits OSC 133 and
  OSC 7 and already installs on remote hosts. Add a payload type, do not add a channel.
  Follow VS Code's OSC 633 shape, which is documented and in production: a private OSC
  code, typed sub-command letters, `Key=Value` properties with a whitelist on receive
  ("only known properties will be handled"), a nonce against forged sequences from command
  output, and `\xAB` hex escaping rather than base64.
- **Never blocks the prompt.** `compgen -c` is 37 ms here and can be seconds on NFS. The
  snapshot is computed after the prompt is usable, never in front of it.
- **Advisory only.** It never gates submission, never weakens a confirmation, never
  participates in a security decision. Any process can print our OSC.
- **The frozen headers keep their verdict from submit time.** Yesterday's `deploy` must not
  turn red today because the script was deleted.

## Acceptance Criteria

- `pwd` (a bash builtin, not a file — so PATH alone would answer wrong) renders resolved.
- `sdfsdf` renders unresolved, with an underline rather than a red foreground.
- `$TOOL build` and `"$(pick)" arg` render indeterminate, never unresolved.
- With the hook absent, every command renders unavailable and nothing is underlined.
- The prompt appears without waiting for the snapshot — asserted, not assumed.
- Output that prints our OSC sequence cannot replace the snapshot (nonce enforced).
- The snapshot never reaches a log, a diagnostic bundle or ContentDB: the full alias and
  function list is a fingerprint of the user's working environment.
close_reason: OSC 636 command-existence layer landed in 8d9408f: private OSC with H/S sub-commands, per-session nonce, background compgen so the prompt never waits, per-tab store owned by XtermRenderer, four states with unavailable never collapsing into unresolved. Two defects found in review and fixed before commit: a module singleton that judged tab 2 against tab 1's command set, and a staging file named after the nonce (published it to ls /tmp and to ps via mv argv, and leaked on early exit).

title: Replace the shell dictionary with the VS Code grammar via Shiki
description:
## Steps to Reproduce

1. Start the app, wait for the prompt editor.
2. Type `ls` — it is coloured as a command.
3. Type `pwd` — it is NOT coloured.
4. Same divergence in a frozen block header after running each.

## Cause

@codemirror/legacy-modes shell mode colours commands from a hardcoded 67-word list
(commonCommands in shell.cjs): it has ls/cd/grep/make and lacks pwd/cargo/kubectl/docker
and every user script. Arbitrary and unexplainable to a user.

A positional rule of our own was considered and REJECTED as worse: it would colour the
typo `sdf` as a command, which is false precision, while the dictionary at least stays
silent. Silence is honest; a confident wrong answer is not.

## Fix, verified by actually running it

Shiki 4.4.1 with the VS Code shellscript TextMate grammar. Measured output for
`ls -la | grep foo > out.txt`, `pwd`, `cargo test`, `sdf dffd`:

- ls, pwd, cargo, sdf ALL get entity.name.command.shell — positional, no dictionary
- pwd additionally gets support.function.builtin.shell
- -la is constant.other.option.dash.shell, pipe is keyword.operator.pipe.shell,
  redirect is keyword.operator.redirect.shell, out.txt is string.unquoted.argument.shell

It makes NO existence claim, which is what keeps it honest.

- shiki/engine/javascript avoids Oniguruma WASM entirely — no CSP risk in the packaged app
- includeExplanation 'scopeName' returns SCOPE NAMES, not theme colours, so our --color-*
  semantic tokens keep owning the palette
- 0.23 ms per realistic line; the shellscript grammar is a standalone 45 KB module

## Sync vs async (owner, 2026-08-01)

Tokenisation stays SYNCHRONOUS. 0.23 ms is a seventieth of a frame; making it async buys
nothing and adds stale-result and flicker handling. Asynchrony belongs to the LATER
existence layer, where a verdict from the shell arrives after a round trip and must be
layered over already-painted structure rather than repainting it.

## Acceptance Criteria

- ls, pwd, cargo, kubectl, docker and ./scripts/release are styled identically as
  commands. No word is special.
- sdf is styled as a command too and carries NO existence diagnostic.
- Live editor and frozen block headers come from the same tokenizer call and cannot
  diverge.
- No colour literals; the colour and css-integrity linters stay green.
- The commonCommands dependency is gone from the codebase.
- The bundle delta is measured and reported, not estimated.
close_reason: Landed in c5aa4b7. The 67-word commonCommands dictionary is gone; @codemirror/legacy-modes is removed from package.json. Shiki 4.4.1 with the VS Code shellscript TextMate grammar, JS regex engine (no Oniguruma WASM, so no CSP question in the packaged app), scope names via includeExplanation so our --color-* tokens keep the palette. ls, pwd, cargo, kubectl, docker, ./scripts/release AND sdf all resolve to entity.name.command.shell — positional, no list, and no existence claim about any of them. One tokenizer feeds the live editor and the frozen headers so they cannot drift; scopes map to tok-* by innermost scope, longest prefix first. Synchronous by decision: 0.23ms is a seventieth of a frame; asynchrony belongs to the later existence layer, and no seams were built for it. Bundle 286.13 -> 325.58 kB gzip plus 41.48 kB grammar and 26.72 kB theme as async chunks. 1334 -> 1339 tests. NOT verified: the plain-then-decorate path before the grammar resolves (not deterministically exercisable) and per-line timing inside the app.

title: Provenance Recall: why this command, and what changed since
description: Design §8.10 — THE SIGNATURE INTERACTION. Pick a past command and, before it runs, see why this one and what has changed since: the rung it came from, the failure/successor family, and a THEN/NOW diff of the environment facets. Chosen over the alternatives deliberately: outcome ranking alone is INVISIBLE (it looks like odd sorting and earns no credit), the guardrail alone reads as one more warning, search over output is post-hoc investigation. This is the only interaction that puts Environment, confidence, status and edges together at the moment with immediate value — the instant before re-running a real command. Four honesty rules, and they are the feature rather than decoration: the failed original STAYS VISIBLE when a successor is promoted (nocx offered a substitute, it did not rewrite history); unknown renders as unknown, never absent and never guessed; the rung is shown and relaxing it is the user's move, never an automatic widening; accepting inserts, and a significant context diff makes the next Enter open a short review per §10.2. The evidence column replaces Warp's curated descriptions with what happened when YOU ran it — no manufactured substitute, no --help parsing on the keystroke path, no generated prose.
acceptance_criteria: A command with two failures and a successful successor in the same environment shows both, with the successor selected and the failure still on screen. Facets that changed between then and now are marked; a facet at confidence=unknown is marked uncertain rather than omitted. Accepting a candidate from a different environment inserts it and requires one review before execution; accepting one from the same environment does not. Both assertions are needed — the second is what keeps the first from being trained away.

title: The recall overlay: a state machine, and Enter that never executes
description: Design §8.10 (new in v6). Up opens an OVERLAY, it does not cycle the line — a cycled line has nowhere to show the ladder rung, no room for provenance and no way to restore the draft. Boundary v5 never drew: in a multiline document Up stays caret movement first, recall opens on an empty line or when there is no further upward movement, an explicit shortcut opens it from anywhere, and Esc restores draft, selection and scroll exactly. States: closed -> opened-with-draft -> navigating-preview -> accepted | dismissed, each holding draft, selection, scroll, query, scope rung and preview. Also needed and currently absent: the keyboard ARBITER between this overlay and the completion dropdown — who owns a keystroke when both could be open, what Up does inside an open dropdown, what Tab does inside the overlay, whether the palette may open above either. Without it: competing keymaps and z-index defects, which is the risk nocx-2gf already lists and why nocx-0oc exists.
acceptance_criteria: Enter in the overlay inserts the command into the editor and does NOT execute it — asserted directly, because a history of destructive commands crossed with a changed environment makes running from a list unacceptable. Esc after navigating restores the exact draft and caret. In a two-line draft with the caret on line 2, Up moves the caret and does not open recall. With the dropdown open, Up is unambiguous and the test names which surface consumed it.
close_reason: Enter takes the recalled command into the line and never runs it; RecallEditor.submit() and the accepted state are gone, and the test that asserted the old rule is inverted rather than deleted. The owner's reversal of nocx-w7h.5, 2026-08-19. Committed 5fc93b82.

title: Candidate, provider applicability and the merge contract — before any dropdown
description: Design §8.9 (new in v6). §8.4 returns Candidate[] and never says what one holds; a worker given §8.1-§8.8 builds a plausible popup that is wrong in multiline, remote and stale-async. Define: (1) Candidate — stable id for dedup, replacement range, matchRanges for highlighting, displayText SEPARATE from insertText (the evidence column is displayed and must never be inserted), source, scope rung, freshness, outcome/environment evidence, and eligibleForGhostText so §9 sensitivity is expressed in the TYPE rather than in prose a provider can ignore. (2) APPLICABILITY: a provider declares which environments it applies to and is not consulted outside them — the local PATH provider is inactive in a remote session, because 'rm' here may not exist there and a mislabelled candidate is still one the ranker can promote. A label is not safety. (3) MERGE: when first results render, whether a slow provider is waited for, that a late arrival may NOT move the selection, dedup of the same command from history and aliases, one provider's error, the latency budget, and no results after abort. (4) RANKING SEMANTICS with golden cases as assertions — especially that confidence=unknown is NEVER a wildcard, or the exact rung is a lie.
acceptance_criteria: In a remote environment the local PATH provider returns nothing and appears in no ghost text. A candidate whose entry is sensitive cannot be constructed with eligibleForGhostText true. A provider answering 400ms late does not change the current selection. Given two candidates identical but for recency the more recent ranks first — as a test, not a claim. A facet at confidence=unknown does not satisfy the exact-environment rung.
close_reason: Shipped in b9c5cc7. Contracts first (Candidate with separate display/insert text, merge with dedup-by-id and no late-arrival selection moves, ranking golden cases, unknown facet never a wildcard), three providers naming their source (OSC 636 command names, store history, local-only fs.complete with a schema and an over-the-wire test), kit dropdown, ghost text with every §8.7 precondition. Verified by the coordinator in a real browser: typing 'pri' + Tab lists printenv/printf from the shell's own snapshot plus matching history, arrow + Enter inserts, and 'ls /ho' + Tab completes the path.

title: Decide the FTS indexing unit, and whether substring search is promised
description: Design §17.10 (new in v6). External-content FTS does not index artifact_chunks as one document by itself, and the spec never chose. One row per chunk breaks ranking, snippets and phrases spanning a boundary. One row per artifact means rebuilding the document on every append. PROPOSAL: index at SEAL, not per chunk — live output stays visible to the UI, durable search becomes complete once the block freezes; this also stops FTS churn on the streaming path. SECOND, unrelated and equally unanswered: FTS5 matches TOKENS AND PREFIXES, not arbitrary substrings. 'EACCES' is a token and works. A fragment of a hash, a path or a token does not. If the product promises substring search it needs a trigram index, and that costs index size, reindex time and privacy surface (§9.1). Decide what is promised before the schema freezes.
acceptance_criteria: The chosen unit is stated in the bead before code. A phrase spanning two chunk boundaries is found. A search for a mid-token fragment either works or the UI never promised it would — both are acceptable, silently failing is not.

title: Three privacy levels, and a leading space means the entry does not exist
description: Design §9 (rewritten in v6). v5 asked for 'one keystroke for run privately' without saying which. bash has had the answer since forever: HISTCONTROL=ignorespace, zsh spells it HIST_IGNORE_SPACE, and hands already type a space before 'export TOKEN=...'. Level 1 — LEADING SPACE: no row, no metadata, no capture, silent, no prompt. Level 2 — CONFIDENT MATCH: ask before Enter, offering the vault binding so rerun survives. Level 3 — WEAK MATCH: record and capture but do not index. The narrowness of level 2 is the design: a question on every git SHA is trained away in a week and then silent on the one that mattered, which is the same failure §10.2 designs around. We do not depend on the user's shell config — the command line is app-owned (ADR-0008), so nocx sees the space itself. Read Atuin's secrets_filter source before writing our own pattern set.
acceptance_criteria: A command typed with a leading space produces no row, no artifact and no suggestion — asserted by querying the store afterwards, not by inspecting a flag. A weak match produces a stored entry that FTS cannot find. A confident match raises the prompt exactly once and never on a plain git SHA.

title: A secret in a command becomes a sec:v1 binding with byte spans
description: Design §9.2 (new in v6). The reference format is NOT designed here — internal/vault/id.go already mints sec:v1:<provider>:<32 hex>, the provider tags are persisted protocol already embedded in profiles.json (ADR-0017), and only the Vault mints because minting selects a provider. credential.Secret already fails json.Marshal rather than emitting a value. Inventing a second format would be a second vocabulary for one concept. TWO things are new. (1) Bindings are BYTE SPANS stored beside intent, never a text search: the same sec:v1 shape can arrive in a command's OUTPUT or be typed by the user, so substitution applies known spans and text that merely looks like a reference is never resolved. (2) A history entry is a COUNTED REFERRER: a profile's secret dies with the profile, a history entry dies by retention, and neither 'eviction revokes a live credential' nor 'the vault accumulates orphans' is acceptable as a default.
acceptance_criteria: An intent with a bound secret stores the reference plus its span; rerun substitutes from the span and reproduces the original command. A sec:v1-shaped string appearing in captured OUTPUT is never resolved. Evicting the entry does not delete the secret, and the vault inventory still counts that reference.

title: Eviction leaves a watermark, or coverage is unimplementable
description: Design §5.4, invariant 11. The spec promises search states its coverage — 'searched 4 200 of 31 000 entries; output beyond the retention window was not kept'. That number CANNOT be computed from the rows that remain, because eviction deleted the rows it would be counted from. It needs a durable retention watermark: a small journal of what was evicted and to what horizon, written in the SAME TRANSACTION as the eviction. Without it search silently reports full coverage over a partial store — which is exactly the failure the constraint exists to prevent, shipped as a feature.
acceptance_criteria: Evict rows, then read a coverage number that provably could not have come from the surviving rows. Kill the process mid-eviction: no watermark exists without its deletion, and no deletion without its watermark.
close_reason:
Commit fb91938e. Both criteria met, and each proved by making the OLD behaviour
fail rather than by asserting the new one.

Coverage that could not have come from the survivors: the worker temporarily
forced the old MIN(ended_at) path and re-ran — the horizon test failed with
"Coverage = 40000, want 3000" (the survivors' minimum against the true horizon)
and a store evicted empty reported nil. Both green on the watermark. That is
the contrast that makes it evidence.

Kill mid-eviction: the first draft was VACUOUS and the worker said so — with 40
seeded rows two of three delays drained the backlog before the signal, which is
indistinguishable from an untorn store. Raised to 400; now 17/36/78 evicted
across three delays, stable over three runs. It then proved the test CAN fail
by splitting the DELETE and the watermark into separate transactions: "evicted
9 + surviving 390 = 399, want 400".

The shape: one accumulating row rather than the spec's journal of passes,
because eviction runs on the write path and a row per pass is a second history
beside the one being evicted; both questions are accumulators. The horizon is
the newest instant a pass actually removed, never the requested cutoff — under
a cap the store is still complete from somewhere before it, and claiming the
cutoff would assert coverage it does not have.

schemaVersion 7 → 8, retention_watermark in rebuildDropOrder. Six failure-path
tests. Package green here on re-run, -race included.

DELIBERATELY LEFT, and it is size-driven eviction: the watermark's horizon is a
time coordinate and an age cutoff already is one, while a byte-budget pass
would need a per-entry byte sum that does not exist — artifacts.byte_len is
per-artifact and nothing totals it per entry, so building it would put a second
owner on "how big is this entry". It reuses all of retention.go and needs only
a different victim set.

FOLLOW-UPS FILED: nocx-rtg0.30 (the EvictEntries/Watermark seam has no caller
outside internal/content, so a user cannot drive retention), and the measured
33% flake in TestConcurrentReadersWithOneWriter went onto nocx-lc15n, which
already existed — measured at baseline first, so it is not this change.

title: The storage budget is two numbers, and auto_vacuum cannot be deferred
description: Design §5.4 (rewritten in v6). v5 said 'total size — the whole of content.db, the one number people care about'. That conflates two things: DELETE reduces live content and not the file, WAL can exceed the main database, and SQLCipher changes neither. A UI promising 5 GB over a 12 GB file has shipped a defect. Split into a RETENTION BUDGET (logical retained bytes — the user's knob, what eviction acts on) and a DISK CEILING (main db + WAL, with hysteresis, triggering compaction rather than more deletion). Full VACUUM rewrites the whole database, needs free space, takes time proportional to years of history and must never run on a path the PTY depends on — so auto_vacuum=INCREMENTAL is the likely answer and it is DECIDED AT DATABASE CREATION. This blocks the first real database.
acceptance_criteria: After evicting to half the retention budget, the reported logical size halves AND the reported disk figure is a separate number that the UI does not confuse with it. auto_vacuum is chosen, justified in the bead, and set at creation.
close_reason: Landed in 2a98da4 and b6c0985: two-number budget, auto_vacuum=INCREMENTAL set before the schema, surfaced into Settings

title: The loss policy is a product contract, not a writer-goroutine detail
description: Design §17.9 (new in v6). 'The ledger never blocks execution' (§4.5) forces a choice and the spec never made it: lose entries, grow memory without bound, spool locally, or apply backpressure to the terminal. The fourth is forbidden. The second is a leak. The third is almost a second database. So the first, bounded — and then HOW MUCH is lost, WHEN, and HOW the user is told are product decisions that belong in the open before implementation. Note the interaction: an encrypted spool would itself need a key and a format, which is why it is not free.
acceptance_criteria: The bead states a chosen policy as an assertion before code exists. With ContentDB failing every write, N commands still run and the UI has said so exactly once, not N times. Outbox overflow drops oldest, records that it did, and the count is observable.
notes:
THE POLICY, decided 2026-08-18 and stated as assertions BEFORE code, which is
what this bead's first criterion asks for. Everything below is falsifiable.

WHAT WAS ALREADY DECIDED and is not re-decided here: §4.5 forbids backpressure
on the terminal — a command runs before it is recorded, always. §6.4 already
says the outbox is bounded, drops oldest on overflow, and records that it did.
Unbounded growth is a leak and a local spool is almost a second database — it
would need its own key and format, which is why it is not free. So the choice
is bounded loss, and only HOW MUCH, WHEN and HOW THE USER IS TOLD were open.

1. THE BOUND IS TWO NUMBERS, NOT ONE, and for the same reason the retention
   budget is (§5.4: "v5 conflated them" and shipped a defect). An event count
   is what a user reasons about; only bytes prevent the leak. The wire bounds
   one envelope at maxRecordCommandRunes=16384 intent plus maxCwdRunes=4096,
   so 512 events is anywhere between ~75 KiB and ~10 MB — a count alone is not
   a memory bound at all.

   - COUNT: at most 512 unacknowledged events. Three events per command
     (open/bind/close), so roughly 170 commands of disconnected work.
   - BYTES: at most 1 MiB of queued envelope payload.
   - Whichever bites first evicts. In ordinary use the count bites, because a
     typical envelope is a few hundred bytes; the byte cap exists for the
     pathological intent, which is exactly when the leak would happen.

2. OVERFLOW DROPS OLDEST, and the envelope's repetition is what makes that
   safe rather than merely cheapest. Dropping an `open` while its `close`
   survives is not a lost row: §6.3 rule 3 says a close for an unknown id
   CREATES the row, closed, from its envelope, and the envelope carries every
   NOT NULL column. Dropping NEWEST would instead discard the events of blocks
   still on screen and still closable. The cost of dropping oldest is a frozen
   block that loses its open's timing facts; the cost of dropping newest is a
   command the user is watching right now.

3. THE USER IS TOLD ONCE PER EPISODE, NOT ONCE PER LOSS, and the interval has
   both ends: the notice is raised on the FIRST drop of an episode and cleared
   when the outbox has drained to empty and acknowledged. N failing writes
   raise it once; N further failures do not raise it again. That is the
   difference between a degrade the product states and a notification storm.

4. IT USES THE SURFACE nocx-rtg0.15 BUILDS, and does not invent a second one.
   That bead makes "durable history is not running" visible in the product; its
   brief requires the surface to be general enough that a RUNTIME failure can
   raise it later through the same path, and this is that later. Two surfaces
   for one concept is the AD-8 shape this repo has already paid for twice.

5. THE DROPPED COUNT IS OBSERVABLE, not only rendered: it is a number the
   notice carries and a test can read, per episode and cumulative. "Recorded
   that it did" (§6.4) means a count somebody can assert on, not a log line.

NOT DECIDED HERE, deliberately: whether the outbox survives a renderer reload.
It does not today because it does not exist; making it durable is a second
store and belongs with restore (nocx-l21ib) if anyone ever wants it.

IMPLEMENTATION NOTE for whoever takes this: there is NO outbox in the frontend
today. `grep -rn outbox frontend/src` finds only comments in generated contract
types describing one. So this bead builds it, and the clientSeq field the wire
already carries on every ledger envelope is its ordering key, already acked
back on every response — that half is done and must not be rebuilt.
close_reason:
Done. Commits 38a916c3 (the runtime degrade) and 3649474c (the outbox).

ALL THREE CRITERIA MET.

The policy was stated as an assertion before any code existed — that is on
this bead, dated 2026-08-18, and every number below came from it rather than
from what turned out to be convenient.

WITH THE STORE FAILING EVERY WRITE, N COMMANDS RUN AND THE UI SAYS SO ONCE.
Asserted over the real socket: five failing records, five answers, one
announcement. Everything it needed had been built by nocx-rtg0.15 and none of
it was connected — that type's own comment said Raise is idempotent within a
reason "which is what a per-write failure path does", and there was no such
path. history.record raises on failure and clears on the first write that
lands, so the notice ends because a named event ended it rather than because
it faded.

Three boundaries, each of which would have turned a true sentence false, and
each with its own test. A saturation refusal is NOT a degrade — the gate
refusing one call under load says nothing about whether commands are kept, and
treating backpressure as a broken feature puts a permanent notice on a healthy
app. A startup degrade is NOT closed by a runtime success, so ClearReason
closes only the episode it names: one recorded command does not disprove "the
content key could not be read". And every record still answers, which is what
keeps the terminal out of it (§4.5).

OUTBOX OVERFLOW DROPS OLDEST, RECORDS IT, AND THE COUNT IS OBSERVABLE. The
outbox is nocx-rtg0.4 and it is built and WIRED — records go through it and
ipc.ts drains it on connect, with a test that asserts the wiring rather than
only the queue, because a module nothing reaches is the shape this repo has
shipped once already. Bounded at 512 records or 1 MiB, whichever bites; oldest
dropped because the newest are the commands still on screen; dropped and
pending and bytes all readable.

Two behaviours turned out to be load-bearing and are asserted: a drain STOPS
at the first failure rather than skipping past it, or a later command lands
while an earlier one waits and a person's history reorders for a reason they
can never see; and a second drain while one runs is a no-op, or the same
record goes twice.

NOT DURABLE ACROSS A RENDERER RELOAD, deliberately and as the policy said:
that would be a second store with its own key and format, which §6.4 rules
out. The window this covers is a socket drop, which is the failure AD-9 says
will happen.

title: The ContentDB key lives in the OS keychain, outside the vault's seal
description: ADR-0018 §3. A 32-byte random key, its own keychain item through the same platform mechanism internal/vault/system uses, read once at start. NOT the vault root key from internal/vault/keys.go and NOT wrapped by it — a sealed vault must withhold authenticators, never memory. Reachability check applies: grep for the caller, and read internal/app/app.go to confirm it is wired. Per AGENTS.md every dependency-failure path needs a test where it fails: keychain absent, keychain unreadable, item deleted between runs, key present but db missing, db present but key lost.
acceptance_criteria: With the keychain item absent the PTY still starts, ContentDB does not open, the UI says durable memory is unavailable, and no command is blocked. Sealing the vault does not affect any ledger read. The key is never derivable from vault material.
close_reason: Landed in 82d37f2: key minted and read through the provider seam, reference derived not persisted. Superseded in part by nocx-rtg0.14 — the resolution order it chose falls through to the file provider, which sits behind the seal

title: SQLCipher spike: prove an encrypted build before adopting one
description: ADR-0018 §2 gates adoption on this. No Go driver is named in the ADR on purpose — pick by evidence, not by README. Prove on macOS AND Linux, in a PACKAGED app rather than 'go test' on a dev machine: the driver builds SQLCipher with STRICT, JSON1 and FTS5 (read PRAGMA compile_options, do not trust docs); WAL, checkpointing, crash recovery and FTS all behave under encryption; chunk ingest does not produce unacceptable write amplification; eviction followed by compaction returns physical space. If it fails on packaging, the fallback is NOT a more convenient engine — it is shipping without encrypted history until an encrypted build is proven.
acceptance_criteria: PRAGMA compile_options output is captured in the bead and shows SQLCIPHER, ENABLE_FTS5 and ENABLE_JSON1. A packaged build on both platforms opens an encrypted db, survives a kill -9 mid-write, and reopens with FTS intact. Cross-compilation is demonstrated, not assumed.
close_reason: Landed in 2a98da4: SQLCipher rejected (no viable Go driver), ncruces/go-sqlite3 + vfs/adiantum adopted, ADR-0018 amended with the measurements

title: The suggestion provider registry and one ranker per target
description:
Design: .internal/specs/2026-07-31-command-blocks-history-syntax-design.md §8.4, §8.5. The mechanism under both the dropdown and ghost text, and the piece with no bead until now.

SuggestionProvider {id, targetId, suggest(query, env, signal)}. Shipped providers: ledger history (environment-scoped), LOCAL PATH, LOCAL cwd paths, aliases (port the nocx-c2ym.4 prototype).

Two rules that are the whole design. First: the active target selects the provider set, and ONE scoring function ranks within it. Concatenating four pre-sorted lists produces ordering nobody can tune; but ranking a shell command, a destructive action and an agent prompt against each other because their text matches does not reorder results, it changes what Enter does. Cross-target candidates, if shown at all, are segregated and never win a default.

Second: the scorer's features are named and therefore testable — prefix quality, recency, frequency, environment match, outcome (nocx-ms7v.6), provider prior. Providers are cancellable: a keystroke invalidates the query in flight, and remote providers will be slow.

Every candidate carries its source and freshness, because §8.5 ships local PATH only — remote PATH needs a listing channel and a local path must never masquerade as a remote one.
acceptance_criteria: Given two candidates identical but for recency, the more recent ranks first — asserted, not eyeballed. A candidate from a different target never wins the default slot. A keystroke cancels the in-flight provider query. Every rendered candidate shows its source.
close_reason: Shipped in b9c5cc7. Contracts first (Candidate with separate display/insert text, merge with dedup-by-id and no late-arrival selection moves, ranking golden cases, unknown facet never a wildcard), three providers naming their source (OSC 636 command names, store history, local-only fs.complete with a schema and an over-the-wire test), kit dropdown, ghost text with every §8.7 precondition. Verified by the coordinator in a real browser: typing 'pri' + Tab lists printenv/printf from the shell's own snapshot plus matching history, arrow + Enter inserts, and 'ls /ho' + Tab completes the path.

title: Up and Down: recall wired to the ladder, not to a local array
description:
Design: .internal/specs/2026-07-31-command-blocks-history-syntax-design.md §10.6, §8.4. The editor-side half of recall: Up and Down in the CM6 editor walk the ledger, showing which rung of the ladder the result came from (exact environment, then host, then repo, then global) and letting one keystroke relax the scope.

The data is nocx-ms7v.1; this is the binding, the rendering of the rung, and the multi-line behaviour. It must not build its own history store or its own ordering — ledger.query is the only ordering implementation, or the same keystroke returns different results depending on which tab it came from.

The keymap lives inside W2's Prec.highest layer (nocx-f4e) so Up/Down cannot fight Enter/Shift-Enter/Escape/Ctrl-C, and Up inside a multi-line composition moves the cursor rather than recalling.
acceptance_criteria: Up on a remote host returns that host's last command, and the rung is visible. Relaxing the scope is one keystroke and the result set grows monotonically. Up inside a multi-line draft moves the caret and does not recall. No history ordering exists in the frontend outside the ledger client.

title: Rerun with provenance: the environment diff before it runs again
description: Design: .internal/specs/2026-07-31-command-blocks-history-syntax-design.md §10.5. Re-running an entry shows a diff of the environment then versus now — endpoint, user, privilege, branch, k8s context — and demands confirmation only when a meaningful facet changed. The moment: the command that was safe on staging does not silently become a prod command. Unavailable to any design whose context is a host string.
acceptance_criteria: Re-running an entry from a different environment shows which facets changed and requires confirmation. Re-running in an identical environment requires none.

title: The attention queue: what actually needs you
description: Design: .internal/specs/2026-07-31-command-blocks-history-syntax-design.md §10.8. Running too long, failed, disconnected, finished while unfocused, unreviewed — keyboard-reachable. The moment: come back from lunch, press one shortcut, see the three things that matter instead of scrolling four tabs. Backed by lifecycle + status + reviewed_at. 'Resolved' must be an explicit act: inferring it from 'a later command ran' is how such queues become noise.
acceptance_criteria: A command that failed while the window was unfocused appears in the queue. Dismissing it is explicit and persists. Running a later command does not silently resolve anything.

title: Search states its coverage
description: Design: .internal/specs/2026-07-31-command-blocks-history-syntax-design.md §5.4, §10.7. When the retention budget has evicted output, the result says so — 'searched 4 200 of 31 000 entries; output beyond the retention window was not kept' — rather than returning an empty result that reads as 'you never saw that error'. Invariant 11 in §16.
acceptance_criteria: After eviction, a search for a string that was only in an evicted artifact returns no hit AND a coverage report marking those entries unsearchable. Coverage is part of the ledger.search contract, not an optional field.

title: Search over output: FTS across intent and derived text
description: Design: .internal/specs/2026-07-31-command-blocks-history-syntax-design.md §10.7, §5.2. Ctrl-R searches what commands PRINTED, not only what was typed — a question developers ask weekly that no terminal answers. FTS5 with external-content tables so the text is not duplicated a third time. Eviction must delete the index row in the SAME transaction as the artifact, or search keeps answering with content the store no longer has. Nothing doubtful is indexed (§9.1).
acceptance_criteria: A string that appeared only in a command's output finds that command. After eviction removes an artifact, a forced crash mid-eviction leaves no index row without its artifact. A hit pointing at absent content fails this test.

title: Recall as a ladder, not a filter
description: Design: .internal/specs/2026-07-31-command-blocks-history-syntax-design.md §10.6. Up searches the exact environment first, then the host, then the repository, then globally, SHOWING which rung it is on and letting the user relax it. This supersedes the old open question of whether to scope recall to exact cwd — neither answer was right, because the answer is a ladder. Backed by ledger.query{scope}; the frontend cache never answers with its own ordering.
acceptance_criteria: Up on a remote host returns that host's last command. The current rung is visible. Relaxing the scope is one keystroke and the result set grows monotonically.

title: You can find what you did, in the place you did it
description:
Design: .internal/specs/2026-07-31-command-blocks-history-syntax-design.md §2.1, §10.5-§10.8. THE NORTH STAR SLICE — the first moment a user can feel what this design is for.

'nocx is the terminal that remembers the work, not the screen.' The signature moment: close every tab, come back tomorrow, and ask what you ran on prod in /srv/api before the deploy failed — and get the environment, the command, the output, the failure, the correction that worked, and a guarded rerun in the right place.

Search over output is the strongest single item here and the reason retention inverted in §3.5: search cannot find what retention threw away, and 'where did I see that EACCES' is usually about a command that succeeded, ran fast, and was three weeks ago.

A memory that silently forgets is worse than one that admits a horizon, so coverage is reported, not hidden.
acceptance_criteria: After closing every tab and restarting, a user can find a command by a string it PRINTED, see which environment it ran in, and rerun it with a diff of then-versus-now. Search states its coverage when retention has evicted output. Recall on a remote host returns that host's commands, not yesterday's laptop commands.

title: Redact the derived text as it is derived
description: Design: .internal/specs/2026-07-31-command-blocks-history-syntax-design.md §9.1. The raw VT artifact is left alone — it is session-local and replay must stay faithful — but the durable, searchable copy is redacted by the same matchers before it is written or indexed. This has to land before anything indexes output, or the index has to be discarded.
acceptance_criteria: Output containing a token-shaped string is redacted in the derived artifact before it is written, and a substring search for the token returns nothing. Replay of the raw artifact is byte-identical to what the terminal received.

title: Sensitivity is decided before the intent reaches the PTY
description: Design: .internal/specs/2026-07-31-command-blocks-history-syntax-design.md §9. Detection of likely-secret shapes in the composed text flips the pending entry to sensitive VISIBLY, before Enter. One keystroke for 'run privately' — the user knows things the matcher does not. sensitive means: intent stored redacted or not at all, capture suppressed, excluded from suggestions and export by default. Exclusion from suggestions is the main point: an accidental token must not come back as ghost text during a screen share.
acceptance_criteria: A command whose text matches a secret shape is sensitive BEFORE submission, produces no artifact, and never appears as a suggestion. The 'run privately' keystroke works with no pattern match.

title: Nothing is kept that you did not mean to keep
description:
Design: .internal/specs/2026-07-31-command-blocks-history-syntax-design.md §9, §9.1.

A durable ledger is a new secret-bearing store, and it has two halves that fail differently.

Typed secrets: a token in a curl -H, -p<password>, a connection string. The row is not where that leaks — the PTY echoes it and the artifact captures it before any row exists, so the decision has to be made at composition time, before handoff, and govern intent, capture, suggestions, export and agent context as ONE decision.

Printed secrets: env, kubectl get secret -o yaml, a script that echoes a token. Composition-time detection cannot see these by construction. This half was tolerable while output was ephemeral; retaining and indexing output is what makes it reachable by substring, so it is designed here rather than discovered later.

Redaction is best-effort and says so. The boundary is ADR-0011 §2, which keeps real credentials out of this path entirely.
acceptance_criteria: A token typed on the command line is never stored, never offered as a suggestion, and never exported. A token printed by a command is redacted in the durable copy and is not findable by substring search. 'Forget this output' removes the artifact and its index row in one transaction and the entry survives.

title: Retention is the user's budget: four knobs and an eviction path
description: Design: .internal/specs/2026-07-31-command-blocks-history-syntax-design.md §5.4. Total size, age, per-entry output cap, and output-retention on/off, in settings as ordinary public config. Whoever wants a 90-day 5GB memory and whoever wants seven days of commands and no output are both right about their own machine. The default is still ours and is what most people live with: output retained, total size the primary cap, age unbounded until size bites. Eviction is oldest-first by seq, DELETE with cascade, pinned artifacts exempt. Per ADR-0011 §5 the UI says 'removed from nocx', never 'securely erased'.
acceptance_criteria: Lowering the size cap evicts oldest-first and the database shrinks. A pinned artifact survives eviction that removes its neighbours. The settings surface is generated from the kit, not hand-rolled.
close_reason: Superseded by .internal/plans/2026-08-19-output-capture.md. Written 2026-07-31 against the premise the epic's own v6 note withdrew (capture in ipc.ts, a streaming recognizer over the bytes, alt-screen toggles inside it); .3's raw-VT-to-derived chain and .5's retention knobs are both narrowed by what nocx-rtg0.12 and rtg0.30 have since built. Replaced by six children that match the plan's tasks one to one.

title: Head-and-tail cap: bound the budget without a class filter
description: Design: .internal/specs/2026-07-31-command-blocks-history-syntax-design.md §3.5. Derived text is retained for every entry — the earlier class filter (failed, slow, recent, pinned only) silently broke search, because the question 'where did I see that EACCES' is usually about a command that succeeded, ran fast and was three weeks ago. What makes that affordable is the per-entry cap: keep the head and the tail, drop the middle, seal with truncated=cap. Errors live in the tail, the invocation in the head, and a million lines of progress bar between them are of no value to anyone. This bounds the budget almost independently of what the user runs, which a line-count cap does not.
acceptance_criteria: An entry whose output is 10x the cap seals with truncated=cap and both its first and last retained lines are present — the cap drops the middle, not the tail. Chunks are appended, never rewritten.
close_reason: Superseded by .internal/plans/2026-08-19-output-capture.md. Written 2026-07-31 against the premise the epic's own v6 note withdrew (capture in ipc.ts, a streaming recognizer over the bytes, alt-screen toggles inside it); .3's raw-VT-to-derived chain and .5's retention knobs are both narrowed by what nocx-rtg0.12 and rtg0.30 have since built. Replaced by six children that match the plan's tasks one to one.

title: Derived text: application/vt -> text/plain, produced on the frontend
description: Design: .internal/specs/2026-07-31-command-blocks-history-syntax-design.md §3.5, §7.5. Raw VT stays session-local and authoritative for replay; the durable, searchable, copyable artifact is normalized text carrying derivedFrom. Produced on the frontend — AD-6 holds, the backend never parses the stream. blockOutputText, copy, search, diff and agent context all read this, not the escape-sequence stream.
acceptance_criteria: Copying a block yields text with no escape sequences. The derived artifact records derivedFrom. The backend contains no VT parsing code.
close_reason: Superseded by .internal/plans/2026-08-19-output-capture.md. Written 2026-07-31 against the premise the epic's own v6 note withdrew (capture in ipc.ts, a streaming recognizer over the bytes, alt-screen toggles inside it); .3's raw-VT-to-derived chain and .5's retention knobs are both narrowed by what nocx-rtg0.12 and rtg0.30 have since built. Replaced by six children that match the plan's tasks one to one.

title: Alt-screen on the same clock as the bytes, and a declared gap when it is not
description: Design: .internal/specs/2026-07-31-command-blocks-history-syntax-design.md §7.4. Suspending capture on input-state.ts's ALT_SCREEN would reintroduce exactly the two-clock bug the previous task fixes, because that state comes from the parser: under load capture would ingest redraw before the parser announced entry and resume late after exit. The recognizer therefore also matches the alt-buffer toggles (CSI ? 1049 h/l, legacy ?1047, ?47). That is three classes of sequence and it is the ceiling — a fourth means capture belongs behind the parser and this approach is wrong. Ambiguous boundaries seal with truncated=gap and the UI says output was not fully captured.
acceptance_criteria: Given CSI ? 1049 h mid-frame under a lagging parser, no chunk from the alt buffer enters any artifact and the entry reports suppressed. An artifact that admits a gap is usable; one that quietly mixes two commands fails this test.
close_reason: Superseded by .internal/plans/2026-08-19-output-capture.md. Written 2026-07-31 against the premise the epic's own v6 note withdrew (capture in ipc.ts, a streaming recognizer over the bytes, alt-screen toggles inside it); .3's raw-VT-to-derived chain and .5's retention knobs are both narrowed by what nocx-rtg0.12 and rtg0.30 have since built. Replaced by six children that match the plan's tasks one to one.

title: Capture at the binary frame, with boundaries cut in the byte stream
description: Design: .internal/specs/2026-07-31-command-blocks-history-syntax-design.md §7.1, §7.2, §7.3. Capture in ipc.ts on the ArrayBuffer path before UTF8StreamDecoder. Boundaries are cut by a streaming recognizer over the bytes themselves, not by the parser's markers — the parser continues to drive the entry lifecycle and stops pretending to bound the bytes. The recognizer handles sequences split across frames, both BEL and ST terminators, malformed sequences and resets. It is a recognizer over an enumerated set, not a parser: no state beyond a partial-match buffer, and it never interprets what it matches.
acceptance_criteria: Given a frame containing entry A's tail, OSC 133 D, a prompt and entry B's first bytes: A's artifact ends at D and contains none of B's bytes. An escape sequence split across two frames is still recognised.
close_reason: Superseded by .internal/plans/2026-08-19-output-capture.md. Written 2026-07-31 against the premise the epic's own v6 note withdrew (capture in ipc.ts, a streaming recognizer over the bytes, alt-screen toggles inside it); .3's raw-VT-to-derived chain and .5's retention knobs are both narrowed by what nocx-rtg0.12 and rtg0.30 have since built. Replaced by six children that match the plan's tasks one to one.

title: The terminal remembers what commands printed
description:
Design: .internal/specs/2026-07-31-command-blocks-history-syntax-design.md §7 (REWRITTEN in v6), §3.5, §5.4. Supersedes and absorbs nocx-de7.

v6 CORRECTION — read this before starting. Earlier revisions said capture happens at the binary frame in ipc.ts before the decode, and spent three sections solving the resulting two-clock problem (term.write() is async, so OSC 133 handlers fire on the parser clock while bytes arrive on the network clock). THAT PREMISE IS WITHDRAWN. blocks.ts:671 already calls serializeRange(snapshot, getLine, rec.startLine, endLine) from controller.ts:301 on OSC 133 D — the product has produced each block's text from the xterm buffer, bounded by its own markers, since DOM scrollback landed. Buffer and markers share the parser's clock, so there is nothing to reconcile. The streaming recognizer, the alt-screen special case and truncated='gap' are all DELETED: they solved a self-inflicted problem. Capture is the same serializeRange pass in a text mode.

What this costs, and it is the open work: raw VT fidelity leaves the durable path (§3.5 already made it session-local, so this is small), and the HEAD of an output longer than the scrollback buffer can be trimmed before freeze. Either size the scrollback to cover the per-entry cap or serialize the head incrementally — a measurement, not a preference. A cap that returns a tail while claiming head-and-tail is a defect.

Capture is also gated on criticality (§7.4): an environment the user marked critical contributes intent and metadata only.
acceptance_criteria: After a restart, the output of a past command is still readable. Entry A's artifact contains every line between A's markers and none of B's — asserted by freezing two blocks back to back, not by feeding frames. A command run in the alternate buffer produces no artifact, with no alt-screen-specific code in the capture path. An output exceeding the scrollback seals with truncated='cap' and reports its first retained line honestly. An environment marked critical produces a row and no artifact.
notes:
2026-08-19, planned in .internal/plans/2026-08-19-output-capture.md against
the spec .internal/specs/2026-08-19-restore-and-output-capture-design.md,
settled with the owner the same day.

THE FIVE ORIGINAL CHILDREN ARE CLOSED AS SUPERSEDED, not worked. They were
written 2026-07-31 against the premise this epic's own v6 note withdraws —
capture in ipc.ts, a streaming recognizer over the byte stream, alt-screen
toggles inside it. Working them as written would rebuild what was deleted
for being a self-inflicted problem. Six children replace them, one per plan
task.

WHAT THE SPEC ADDS BEYOND THE 2026-07-31 DESIGN: the durable body is SGR
text PLUS derived plain text, not plain text alone. A monochrome restore
reads as data loss, an SGR-only body makes search index escape codes, and
the serialized HTML the frozen block already holds embeds a theme snapshot —
restored blocks would stay in the palette current when they ran while every
live block repainted around them. Two artifacts joined by derived_from is
what that column exists for.

THE rtg0 EDGE WAS REMOVED, deliberately. It encoded 'the ledger must exist
first', which is a 'not yet' rather than a file collision — the shape
AGENTS.md records as having once made bd ready unusable at 68 issues.
Everything it waited for is closed: rtg0.2 (schema v1 with artifacts and
artifact_chunks), rtg0.3 (the write path), rtg0.19 (command_history dies),
rtg0.28 (entries.pane_id), rtg0.29 (the renderer sends paneId). None of
rtg0's nine open children is claimed. Two of them DO overlap these files and
the sequencing is held by whoever coordinates rather than by an edge: rtg0.7
(command-ledger.ts becomes the live cache) touches the same freeze-to-record
path as the capture hook, and rtg0.30 (the retention seam and its knobs)
owns the size and age settings this epic must not also write.

nocx-l21ib now depends on this epic: restore renders bodies capture is the
only writer of, and both touch blocks.ts, serializer.ts and the ledger's
artifact path.




────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2026-08-19, the acceptance criteria read back against what was built.

MET: the output of a past command is still readable after a restart (a round
trip over the real socket with a real store close and reopen, nocx-y0pmn);
entry A's artifact holds none of B's, asserted at the store AND by freezing
two blocks back to back in the renderer; an environment marked critical
produces a row and no artifact (nocx-o9nw0).

AMENDED, deliberately: "a command run in the alternate buffer produces NO
artifact" is built as "produces an EMPTY body". An alt-screen program leaves
no scrollback rows and neither does `true`, and nothing may tell them apart —
a classifier in the capture path is precisely what v6 withdrew this epic's
first design over. An empty body says "this printed nothing into the
scrollback", which is true of both; NO artifact is reserved for "nothing was
captured", which is the different sentence a restored block has to be able to
say.

NOT MET, and not this epic's to meet: "an output exceeding the SCROLLBACK
seals with truncated=cap and reports its first retained line honestly". The
per-command cap is built and seals truncated='cap' with both ends kept, so a
capped body is honest about itself. But an output longer than xterm's
10k-line scrollback has lost its head before the freeze can serialize it, and
nothing here can recover what the buffer dropped. That is nocx-4ff.26, still
open. This epic bounds what it keeps; 4ff.26 owns what was never there to be
kept.
close_reason: Output capture is built and reachable: a frozen block's rows leave as two artifacts (SGR + derived text) through ledger.capture, land in one transaction against the entry's own execution, survive a real store restart, and are refused for output-off, sensitive and critical alike — each as an answer rather than a failure. Eleven children, eight commits b3fa7685..65fca2dc. Two criteria are reconciled in the notes: the alt-screen one is built as an empty body deliberately (no classifier in the capture path, ever), and the scrollback-truncation one belongs to nocx-4ff.26.

title: The environment indicator: the cheapest honest thing in the design
description: Design: .internal/specs/2026-07-31-command-blocks-history-syntax-design.md §10.1. 'prod . deploy@10.0.0.4 . sudo . main' in the surface, always, with explicit 'context unknown' on any facet that is not known. Without it, confidence is an internal field nobody benefits from and every other environment-aware feature appears out of nowhere. Kit rules apply: read frontend/src/ui/README.md before building any control.
acceptance_criteria: A facet at confidence=unknown renders as unknown, never as absent and never as a guess. The indicator is present in RAW, PROMPT_READY and RUNNING_RAW. It is built from ui/ components, not hand-rolled inside the surface.

title: criticality: the user marks what is production, and nothing guesses
description: Design: .internal/specs/2026-07-31-command-blocks-history-syntax-design.md §3.1, §10.2. routine | sensitive | critical as its own column, not a facet, because it gates behaviour (§10.2's confirmation) and a value inside a JSON blob cannot be queried. Set by a checkbox on the connection profile plus a per-environment override. Never derived: inferring production from a hostname is wrong in both directions and the user cannot fix it when it is.
acceptance_criteria: A profile marked critical propagates to every environment derived from it, and a per-environment override wins. No derivation path writes this column.

title: Per-facet confidence, including the nested case we genuinely cannot see
description: Design: .internal/specs/2026-07-31-command-blocks-history-syntax-design.md §3.1. asserted | derived | unknown, per facet, stored and carried to the renderer. A nested shell (NOCX_SESSION_ID gate), a container exec, a sudo shell: the outer facet may be asserted while the inner is unknown, and the model must be able to say so rather than reporting the outer as the whole truth.
acceptance_criteria: An ssh session whose inner context is invisible reports the endpoint asserted and privilege unknown. No code path substitutes a default for an unknown facet.

title: The terminal says which machine you are on, and admits what it cannot see
description:
Design: .internal/specs/2026-07-31-command-blocks-history-syntax-design.md §3.1, §10.1.

Context was keyed on (sessionId, host, cwd), which is wrong twice: sessionId dies with the session so it defeats durable recall, and host collapses user, port, jump route, profile, container and every nested environment into one string.

An Environment is a stable identity for where work happens, with per-facet confidence. With marker-only shell integration, ssh -> container -> sudo -> kubectl is a stack we can only partly see, and a surface that says 'known outer SSH host; inner context unknown' beats one that projects false precision — false precision is what invites running the right command in the wrong place.

RELATED: nocx-pu4 (Warpify) is the mechanism that would raise confidence from unknown to asserted at depth. Disjoint by file; this epic degrades honestly without it.
acceptance_criteria: The surface always shows environment identity. A facet that is not known renders as unknown — never as absent, never as a guess. Recall filters on environmentId and never on sessionId. Two sessions to the same host in the same repo resolve to the same environment id across a restart.

title: Environment identity and derivation
description: Design: .internal/specs/2026-07-31-command-blocks-history-syntax-design.md §3.1, §5.2. The environments table plus derivation from the connection layer and OSC 7: kind, endpoint, profileId, facets (repoRoot, branch, containerId, k8sContext, namespace, privilege), first/last seen. The id is derived from the facets and never from a session. sessionId survives only as an execution facet on the entry.
acceptance_criteria: The same host+repo resolves to one environment id across app restarts. A local shell and an ssh session to the same path are different environments. No query in the codebase filters recall by session_id.

title: Every interval has two ends: nothing stays open forever
description: Design: .internal/specs/2026-07-31-command-blocks-history-syntax-design.md §4.3. Durability creates a failure the in-memory ledger never had — an entry that opens and never closes is now permanent. An entry is open until exactly one of: the driver reports an outcome, the session ends, the app shuts down, or a per-kind timeout expires. abandon() closes interrupted when the cycle was trusted and unknown when it was not. On store open, every row with phase != closed is closed as unknown.
acceptance_criteria: Kill the app with a command running; on next start that row is closed with status unknown. A session that exits without D closes its open entry. The startup sweep uses the partial index and does not scan the table.
notes:
2026-08-18. Two of the three criteria are met; the third cannot be built yet
and this says exactly why rather than leaving it to be rediscovered.

MET: "kill the app with a command running; on next start that row is closed
with status unknown" — closeOpenEntries runs inside Open before the store is
handed out, with TestReopenClosesOpenAndBoundEntriesAsUnknown and the two
agent startup-sweep tests.

MET, commit 1a7caa74: "the startup sweep uses the partial index and does not
scan the table". It was claimed in a comment and checked by nothing; it is now
asserted from EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN, which is the only form that cannot pass
vacuously on an empty test database.

NOT BUILDABLE TODAY: "a session that exits without D closes its open entry."
The hook is easy; knowing WHICH entries to close is not. It needs the entry's
provenance, and entries.session_id is NULL for every row in the product —
nothing writes one, because a session row needs a workspace and nocx-49d4
owns that question. The durable anchor that DOES get written is pane_id, and a
pane outlives the session by design (D5), so it cannot stand in for "this
session ended".

AND THE FAILURE IS UNREACHABLE MEANWHILE, which is why this is a note and not
a defect: the only writer of an OPEN entry is ledger.open, and the renderer
does not call it — history.record writes closed rows. So no session can leave
an entry open in the product today. It becomes reachable with nocx-rtg0.7,
when the renderer starts sending the lifecycle, and the startup sweep is the
backstop until then: an entry left open by anything closes as unknown at the
next start, which is the same answer a session-end hook would give, one
restart later.

Building the hook now would mean inventing the provenance to make it work,
which is the shape AGENTS.md names — a feature written for a state nothing
produces.

title: EntryDriver: take the lifecycle out of the OSC 133 handler
description: Design: .internal/specs/2026-07-31-command-blocks-history-syntax-design.md §4.1, §4.2. terminal-content.ts:283's marker callback currently knows about OSC 133, the ledger, the scrollback and the input machine at once — the module that must not change when a second kind arrives. Introduce EntryDriver; ShellDriver keeps command-ledger.ts's existing rules verbatim (L2 open-while-running finalises, trust from sawCleanA && sawB at C, L1 D-without-exit-code is unknown not failure, B3 finalizeOpen). open() returns a PROVISIONAL entry synchronously — seq and submittedAt are backend-assigned and arrive later, and per §4.5 the command must never wait on the store.
acceptance_criteria: The controller's marker callback contains no phase logic. Every existing command-ledger test still passes against ShellDriver. A command runs with the store returning an error on every write.

title: A client outbox so a socket drop does not lose entries
description: Design: .internal/specs/2026-07-31-command-blocks-history-syntax-design.md §6.4. AD-9 replays PTY bytes and says nothing about control-plane events; a drop between submit and ledger.open silently loses the entry, and a memory product that forgets when the network hiccups is not a memory product. Bounded queue ordered by clientSeq, replayed on reconnect, drained in order, deduped backend-side by (id, phase). Capped — on overflow it drops oldest and records that it did, because a queue that grows without bound to preserve history is how the renderer runs out of memory.
acceptance_criteria: With the socket dropped between submit and open, the entry appears after reconnect with its envelope intact. Overflow is observable, not silent.
close_reason: Built and wired by the same commit as nocx-rtg0.10's overflow half — 3649474c. The queue keeps what the socket refused and ipc.ts drains it on connect; bounded at 512 records or 1 MiB per the policy nocx-rtg0.10 recorded before the code; oldest dropped and counted. A test asserts the WIRING, not only the queue: a refused record is in the shared outbox and a drain delivers it through history.record. See nocx-rtg0.10's close for the full accounting.

title: ledger.open/bind/close: the write path, with the immutable envelope on every event
description:
Design: .internal/specs/2026-07-31-command-blocks-history-syntax-design.md §6.2, §6.3, §6.6. Three events (open/bind/close) and the queries. Every event repeats the immutable envelope {id, environment, cwd, kind, intent, sensitivity, clientSeq} — a few hundred bytes per command that remove a whole class of lost-entry failure, because a close for an unknown id must be able to create its row and the row has four NOT NULL columns the previous design did not send. Phase is monotonic: an event that would move it backwards is dropped and logged. Schemas in contracts/ with all three checks from contracts/README.md.

BLOCKED BY the AD-1 amendment (nocx-m64b) — these events carry marker-derived facts.
acceptance_criteria:
A close for an id never opened creates exactly one row whose environment, cwd, kind and intent come from the envelope — which is why the envelope repeats on every event, and the reason v2's design could not work: the row has four NOT NULL columns and 'create it with empty intent' supplies one of four.

- A bind arriving AFTER a close leaves the phase closed. Phase is monotonic (open → bound → closed); an event that would move it backwards is dropped AND LOGGED, never applied silently.
- Re-delivery of any event for a row already in that phase is a no-op, and a test proves it by sending each event twice and counting rows.
- Every one of the three has a schema in contracts/ with all three checks from contracts/README.md — including the third, which validates the REAL result off the REAL socket rather than a payload the test itself built.
- Every object carries additionalProperties:false plus an explicit required, or the check is theatre.
- deadcode over internal/content afterwards, and READ it: the v1 write path must now have a caller outside its own tests. ledger.go:11-16 says in as many words that it has none, and nocx-rtg0 already shipped that exact shape once — a reachable read path hiding an unreachable write path in one package.
notes: SCOPE NARROWED 2026-08-17. This bead said 'three events and the queries'. The queries moved to nocx-rtg0.20 (ledger.query, ledger.get), nocx-rtg0.21 (ledger.search) and nocx-rtg0.22 (ledger.attention), because the split is real and not cosmetic: the three events map onto repository methods that EXIST — Submit, StartExecution, FinishExecution — while every filter ledger.query needs has no read behind it. LedgerRepository offers ListEntries(ctx, limit) and nothing else. One bead was carrying a wire method over a finished store and a store change wearing a wire method.
close_reason:
Merged into feat/workspaces at d92694ef (434b72a2). ledger.open/bind/close are on the control plane, wired from main, with three schemas in contracts/ and regenerated renderer types. All four §6.3 rules live in one function because they are one decision: seq is the total order, phase is monotonic with a logged drop, a close for an unknown id creates its row from the envelope, and re-delivery is a no-op.

Verified independently, not on the worker's word: deadcode -whylive shows sqliteContent.Submit reaching main through a real path while sqliteContent.AddEdge is still 'reachable only through reflection'. The -filter form the criterion originally demanded prints nothing either way on this package and cannot fail — that is now recorded in AGENTS.md as a rule change, since it is the same package where a dead write path shipped once before.

Three deviations, all recorded rather than assumed: the envelope carries sessionId rather than environment (a second derivation of where a session is would be the AD-8 defect; amended into the design §6.2), ledger.open masks the intent through the existing maskCommandSafe owner rather than writing raw command text to the same database, and the ack shape is a superset carrying outcome ∈ {applied, replay, dropped} so §6.3 is on the wire and not only in a log.

Filed from this work: nocx-rtg0.23 (a close cannot record the exit code or duration of an existing row — blocks nocx-rtg0.19) and nocx-zlek8 (a concurrent-reader test reports the database disk image malformed under load).

title: Schema v1: entries, edges, artifacts, artifact_chunks — and seq as the only total order
description: Design: .internal/specs/2026-07-31-command-blocks-history-syntax-design.md §5.2, §3.2, §3.4. STRICT tables. entries carries a backend-assigned monotonic seq (wall-clock milliseconds are not a key: two windows submit in the same millisecond). edges is the relation primitive (rerun-of, supersedes, caused-by, cites, in-span) — cheap now, and the difference between a log and a memory. artifact_chunks is append-only, not a single BLOB. Partial index entries_open exists for the startup sweep. No FTS in this task.
acceptance_criteria: Two entries submitted in the same millisecond get distinct seq and query returns them in submission order. A string written to duration_ms is rejected by SQLite. Deleting an entry cascades to its edges and artifacts.
notes:
Amended 2026-08-02 by ADR-0019 (one authoritative ledger, disposable projections) and
ADR-0020 (the agent gets a lane, authority is granted per run). Schema v1 delta before this
is built:

- seq -> ingest_seq. It is commit order, not causality; narrative comes from edges only.
- NEW `sessions` (restore key, never a recall filter; entries.session_id ON DELETE SET NULL)
  and `workspaces` (narrative scope). §3.1's refusal of a sessions table conflated recall
  with restore.
- NEW `executions`: entry_id, lane, attempt, lease bounds, interactivity policy, process
  group, start/end, termination reason, executor identity. Artifacts attach to an execution,
  not to the entry — a rerun/retry/takeover is not a new intent, and one status+exit_code
  cannot separate command-failed / executor-timeout / transport-gone / user-killed /
  agent-declined.
- NEW authority grant recorded on the run (versioned, expiring, immutable once execution
  starts). The workspace mints the default; it is not the enforcement object.
- environments mixes durable identity with mutable observation (branch, containerId,
  privilege change at different rates). Split into identity + versioned observations; an
  entry references the observation set known at execution time, or old rows get
  reinterpreted with today's facts. criticality is contextual, not global to a host.
- artifacts need capture provenance: stream, byte offsets, gaps, encoding, terminal
  dimensions, capture method+version, and whether text came from terminal cells or raw
  output. Derived text links to its capture.
- JSON payload is for sparse extension only. Anything used for policy, retention, ordering,
  filtering or joins must be a typed column — otherwise the payload becomes a
  migration-avoidance mechanism nobody can query.
- retention: pinning a reopenable session's tail must be budgeted, or sessions become
  immortal. Keep a compact session manifest after heavy artifacts expire and show the gap.
- client-minted UUIDv7 ids are UNTRUSTED idempotency keys: bind to client identity + payload
  digest, or a replay aliases two different intents.

Still open from the v6 review: CHECK constraints on the closed enums, crash-safe seq
assignment, derived_from ON DELETE, pinned-vs-eviction conflict, cascading edges giving the
incident graph an unagreed retention horizon, byte_len ignoring FTS/B-tree/WAL/free pages.
close_reason: Schema v1: 12 STRICT tables + 8 indexes incl. entries_open, ContentDB.Ledger() seam, 26 acceptance tests through the public seam. Six open review questions decided and named in the bead notes. command_history stays the interim live path — two tables, one writer each. STATED LIMITATION: the v1 write path has no production caller until nocx-rtg0.3. 2fab1f76.

title: ContentDB: implement the SQLite backing behind the existing stub
description: Design: .internal/specs/2026-07-31-command-blocks-history-syntax-design.md §5.1, §5.3, §5.5. internal/content/stub.go returns ErrNotImplemented today; keep the interface, add the implementation. One content.db, WAL, foreign_keys=ON, one writer goroutine with short transactions, concurrent readers. At-rest posture per §5.5: 0600 file in a 0700 directory, excluded from any diagnostic bundle. The database key is a separate 32-byte keychain item (nocx-rtg0.9), NOT the vault root key and NOT behind auto-seal. auto_vacuum is decided at creation and belongs to nocx-rtg0.11, which must land first or the first real database is created wrong.
