title: A scrollbar flashes on every Enter: the settle's own displacement makes the scroller scrollable
description:
## Steps to Reproduce

1. Press Enter on any command.
2. Watch the scroller's right edge.

A scrollbar appears for a fraction of a second and goes away. Reported by the
owner 2026-08-19, on the build that landed the settle.

## Cause

The settle displaces the stack DOWNWARD — that is what the inverse of a growth
is — and the stack hangs from the scroller's bottom edge, so those pixels are
past it. A transformed descendant contributes its transformed border box to
the scrollable overflow region, so for the ~140ms of the glide the scroller
genuinely IS scrollable and says so. Measured in the container: 67px of
scrollable overflow appearing and decaying to 0 across the settle, twice per
command (the block opening and its freeze).

## The fix

`overflow-y: hidden` on the scroller while a settle is in flight, through an
`is-settling` class the glide owns.

`hidden` rather than `clip`: it keeps the scroll offset and keeps the element a
scroll container — `clip` would drop both. `scrollbar-gutter: stable` is
already declared, so no width changes hands in either direction.

The cost, named rather than discovered: a wheel event during the settle is
ignored. It lasts ~140ms and only happens while the person is already
following the output, which is the state where there is nothing above to
scroll to.
acceptance_criteria: Across a command's two settles the scroller never offers a bar it did not have: measured in the container frame by frame, overflow-y is hidden for exactly the frames where the settle's displacement makes scrollHeight exceed clientHeight, and auto with zero overflow either side. Pinned in controller.test.ts by the class the glide owns.
close_reason: overflow-y: hidden through an is-settling class the glide owns. Container, frame by frame: the 67px of scrollable overflow the settle creates is now covered exactly, auto with zero overflow either side. Commit 6a7225e5.

title: Opening a tab jumps the pane twice: the composer is laid out before CodeMirror has a scroller
description:
## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open a tab.
2. Watch the pane's contents.

Observed in the owner's Chrome performance trace (2026-08-19T13:28, dpr 2,
`make dev-web`): two layout shifts 59ms apart, 47 CSS px each and opposite.
Chrome attributes them to `DIV class='nocx-editor'` — inserted by
`editor.ts mount` — whose box goes 30px, then 77px, with a new
`DIV class='cm-scroller'` (23px) appearing between the two frames. Everything
in the pane moves up 47px and back down 47px.

## What is wrong

The composer is measured before CodeMirror has laid its scroller out, so the
pane is laid out twice: once against a composer that is only its chrome row,
and once against the real one. The pane's contents hang from the bottom edge,
so both frames displace everything above.

This is the same class as nocx-i4h04 — a surface whose height arrives in two
instalments — but a different seam: nothing to do with a command, and the
settle in `ScrollbackController._glide` does not cover it, because the change
is in the editor's own slot.

## Where to start

`CommandEditor.mount` (editor.ts) and the `.nocx-editor` box: either reserve
the composer's final height before CodeMirror mounts (the chrome row's
min-height is already declared; the input line's is not), or hold the pane's
first layout until the editor's first measure has landed. The first is
cheaper and matches how the chrome row was fixed for the submit case
(nocx-i4h04).

Note the trace also shows the command cycle itself clean over the same
recording: block open and block freeze, both glided, ZERO layout shifts.
acceptance_criteria: Mounting a pane produces no layout shift attributable to .nocx-editor: its box is its final height from the first frame it is in the tree. Checked the way it was found — a performance trace with layout shifts, or an e2e assertion that the editor's height at mount equals its height once settled.

title: The fence and the cursor disagree by one row, and the block drops by it at every freeze
description:
## Steps to Reproduce

1. At a prompt, run `printf 'A\nB\nC\n'; read x`.
2. Watch the block header while the shell holds on `read`, then press Enter.

Expected: the header does not move when the rows move from the grid into the
frozen block — the block is a photograph of the region it replaces.
Actual: it drops by exactly one grid row (20px in the container's chromium;
also measured on a five-line dripped loop, 2026-08-19).

## Cause

Left behind by nocx-i4h04, which made the running region and the frozen block
the same box in every other respect: row pitch, body padding, when the grid is
measured, and the composer's slot.

What remains is one row. The frozen body ends at the RENDER FENCE; the grid's
cursor sits one row below it — the row the shell parked on and the next prompt
would occupy. So the live region shows one row the block will never contain,
and losing it at the freeze drops the header by exactly one cell.

Neither side can simply give the row up:

- The live region cannot drop it without hiding the cursor of a program waiting
  for input on a fresh line, which is the affordance that says "type here".
  `liveContentHeight` includes the cursor deliberately — a TUI that parks the
  cursor thirty rows down IS using thirty rows.
- The block cannot keep it without swallowing the row the next command's echo
  lands on (nocx-4yhi: the app-owned submit opens the block on the creation
  line and the output range starts one row later).

So the answer is not in either box's sizing. It is that two derivations of
"where does this command's output end" — the fence line and the cursor line —
are allowed to differ by a row nobody owns. Start at `blocks.ts`
`freezeFromAttempt` (endLine vs the sighted fence) and `controller._echoShiftPx`,
which is the same accounting at the other end of the block.
acceptance_criteria: A command that holds the shell (printf three lines then read x) freezes with the block header not moving at all — the tolerance in command-editor.spec.ts's submit-geometry assertion goes from one grid row to zero.
close_reason: Answered by nocx-i4h04.2 and by the owner's decision on 2026-08-19: the live region stops counting the row the cursor moved to, so the two halves no longer disagree. The alternative this bead described — making the fence and the cursor agree — was not needed once the owner took the trade (a program waiting for input on a row it has written nothing to shows no cursor until the first keystroke).

title: The epic's happy path, watched end to end: the tab you left is the tab that opens
description:
nocx-mqie.4 wired uistate.activeTab and proved the round trip at the RENDERER seam: two PaneManagers over one chain and one stored document, with a fake socket between them (frontend/src/panes-layout.test.ts, 'the window reopens on the tab that was in front'). What no test watches is the same trip through the real backend — uistate.set, uistate.json on disk, uistate.get on the next start — with a person doing it.

That is the epic's own criterion ('the active tab restores too') and AGENTS.md rule 2, and it is why nocx-mqie is 4/4 and still open.

The idiom already exists and is one file away: e2e/sidebar-resize.spec.ts starts its own VaultBackend precisely so it can restart it mid-test, and asserts the sidebar's computed width afterwards rather than a variable. This spec is the same shape on the strip: pick unused ports (19882+ are taken by that spec), open a second tab, activate it, restart, reload, assert '.nocx-tab[aria-selected=true]' is the same row.

Note for whoever takes it: the e2e suite runs in the container (e2e/run-in-container.sh) and its failure set is not CI's — layout-sensitive specs are the ones that lie there. This one asserts an attribute, not geometry, so it should be honest in both.
acceptance_criteria: An e2e spec opens a second tab, activates it, restarts the devharness backend and reloads the page, and asserts the SAME tab is aria-selected afterwards — measured on the strip, not on a value read back. It fails on a build where PaneManager's boot activates panes[0].
close_reason: e2e/active-tab-restore.spec.ts: own devharness backend, two tabs with the second in front, backend restarted and page reloaded, asserted on the strip's aria-selected rather than on a value read back. Verified to FAIL on a build whose boot activates panes[0] and to pass with it restored — run in the container both ways. Committed 9852a6ce.

title: The go-tests image cannot start sshd: every live-sshd proof fails in the hook's container
description:
## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run the pre-commit hook, or .githooks/containerized-tests.sh, on a machine whose Docker daemon has no DNS.
2. Watch the Go container gate.

Observed 2026-08-19 while integrating the uistate branch: eight tests fail, all of them TestLiveSshd_*, each timing out at ~10s with

    sshd did not report listening within 10s; log:
    Missing privilege separation directory: /run/sshd

## What is wrong

The go-tests image (.githooks/images/go-tests) carries sshd but not the privilege-separation directory it refuses to start without. Nothing in the diff under test is involved: the same eight fail on any commit, and the whole rest of the Go suite passes in the same container.

Creating the directory by hand inside the container moves the failure one step on — as root the fixture then fails 'root@127.0.0.1: Permission denied (publickey)', because the fixture is written for the non-root uid the hook passes in. So the fix belongs in the IMAGE, next to the sshd it already installs, not in a runtime flag.

Second-order, and the reason this cost an hour to name: the fixture reports only that sshd never listened, with the sshd log appended. The log said exactly what was wrong, but the assertion above it did not, so the failure reads as a timeout — a class of flake — rather than as a missing directory.

## Also true, and separate

The image cannot be REBUILT on a machine without DNS: its Dockerfile derives from bash:3.2 and the build re-resolves that tag every time. That is why this was found on a cached image and could not simply be patched and rerun locally.
acceptance_criteria: A containerized run of ./internal/app passes the TestLiveSshd_* set on a machine with no network access to Docker Hub; the image provides /run/sshd owned by root with 0755; the fixture's failure message names the missing directory rather than only 'sshd did not report listening'.

title: Dragging in the strip: the last slot is unreachable and nothing says where a tab will land
description:
## Steps to Reproduce

1. Drag the bottom tab of a run onto another row.
2. Drag any tab and watch for feedback.
3. Drag a workspace heading.

Observed: the bottom tab does not move; nothing marks where a drop will land; a workspace can only be moved through its menu, and while one is dragged every tab row offers a place between two tabs that a workspace cannot occupy.

## What is wrong

A drop always inserted BEFORE the row it hit, so the final slot of a run could only be taken by the row already in it and the bottom row had no target below itself.

The first indicator drawn was invisible in the vertical strip: a box-shadow of the same specificity as the group-colour spine, whose rule came later in the file.

And a drag carried only text/plain, so no target could tell a tab from a workspace heading in flight — the DataTransfer withholds its data until the drop and only the TYPE list is readable during a dragover.

## The rule

The half of the row the pointer is over decides before or after. The mark is a 3px accent on that edge with a glow into the seam, drawn without moving anything: a slot opened by a margin moves the row out from under the pointer, which moves the slot. A row that will refuse the drop draws nothing. Each dragged kind names itself with its own MIME type.
acceptance_criteria: A tab can be dropped into the first and the last slot of its run; an insertion mark appears on the edge the drop will use, in both orientations; a row that cannot accept the drop shows no mark; a workspace heading can be dragged to reorder workspaces; a tab row refuses a workspace drag and a heading refuses a tab drag.
close_reason: Landed on feat/workspaces

title: The overview's cards say nothing about what a pane is doing
description:
Found by the owner testing feat/workspaces.

The card quoted the last line the pane drew, always. That is right for one state and misleading in three: a 'top' was quoted one row of its process table, an agent waiting on a human was quoted its own empty prompt, and a pane that had just finished a command showed nothing at all — the ledger's completed record was skipped because its xterm marker had been dropped at the freeze, which the code read as 'the command never ran'.

What a person wants from a card is what the pane is DOING: a command and an outcome, a program that owns the screen, or an agent's state.
acceptance_criteria: A card quotes the pane's last block with its outcome; a full-screen program is named rather than quoted; an agent pane is not quoted at all; a pane with no blocks falls back to the last drawn line; the same sentence is the second line of a vertical strip row, from the same function.
close_reason: Landed on feat/workspaces

title: Name and colour are one decision, asked for in two places
description:
Found by the owner testing feat/workspaces.

A tab's colour was chosen from a run of colour WORDS in its context menu — Green, Amber, Red, Violet, plus 'No colour' — none of which showed the colour it offered, with the three things a person actually does to a tab spread around them. A workspace's colour was offered in a form at create time and nowhere afterwards: renaming one was a one-line text prompt.

Two palettes, too: a tab carried four THEME accents on the argument that a decorated tab must still read after a theme change, a workspace nine fixed hues because a container's identity may not shift under it. The second argument is right and the distinction is not: identity is what a colour on a tab is for as well.
acceptance_criteria: Renaming a tab offers its colour in the same form; renaming a workspace offers its colour in the same form as creating one; the tab's context menu carries actions only; one palette serves both subjects; 'no colour' is offered for a tab and not for a workspace; only the fact that changed is sent.
close_reason: Landed on feat/workspaces

title: The vertical strip is a different product from the horizontal one
description:
Found by the owner testing feat/workspaces, one placement against the other.

The two placements had drifted into two products. The layers glyph meant 'show all workspaces' in the horizontal row and 'new workspace' in the vertical rail — one mark, two meanings, and which one a person got depended on a settings value. The rail still carried the five same-weight glyphs the row had already shed. Its width was a fixed 240px while the sidebar beside it has been draggable since nocx-qmcu, and its rows kept the row's 220px ceiling once it could be dragged. A workspace's colour did not appear in it at all. Its rows carried no second line while the overview's cards had just learnt to say what a pane is doing. And a view pane opened at the bottom of the rail, under the last workspace's heading, reading as a member of a workspace it cannot be in.

They are one surface with two orientations, and the differences that remain — a pill in a row, a heading over a column — are the ones the shape of the strip forces.
acceptance_criteria: The layers mark opens the overview in both placements; the strip's other actions are one caret menu in both; the vertical strip's width is dragged with the kit ResizeHandle and its rows fill it; a workspace's colour is visible in the vertical strip; a workspace heading carries the close action; a view pane (Settings) sits in the ungrouped run; every row carries the same one-line preview the overview's card prints.
close_reason: Landed on feat/workspaces

title: A restore marks every tab unread: the shell's own opening is counted as activity
description:
## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open several tabs across a few workspaces.
2. Reload the window.

Observed: every tab except the active one wears the unread-activity underline, for output nobody missed.

## What is wrong

Restoring reopens each pane's session and the shell prints a banner, its rc file's chatter and a prompt. Those bytes arrive on session.onData like any others, so each inactive pane marked activity. The state where the indicator is on every tab at once is the state where it says nothing at all.

Two attempts by clock failed and are recorded so they are not tried again: a fixed window after the session opens, and a window extended by each byte. A restore opens every pane at once and the backend replays behind an establishment acknowledgement, so a pane's own start is separated from the pane before it by however long the other shells took — the gap is not inside one session's stream, and no duration bounds it.

## The rule

The pane's lifecycle says when its opening is over. PaneHost.contentSettled is that event: TerminalContent raises it on the first OSC 133 prompt-end marker, with a backstop for sessions that draw no markers. Anything the opening accumulated is withdrawn at the settle rather than filtered on the way in.
acceptance_criteria: After a reload with several restored tabs, no tab carries the unread-activity mark; output arriving in an inactive tab after its prompt is drawn still marks it; a pane whose session emits no OSC 133 settles anyway.
close_reason: Landed on feat/workspaces

title: The active tab is remembered: wire uistate.activeTab in the renderer
description:
The UI-state document already carries the slot and the wire already carries it: contracts/uistate.schema.json declares activeTab (a durable pane id, never an index), internal/uistate stores it, and uistate.get/uistate.set round-trip it. Nothing in the renderer reads or writes it yet.

WHY IT WAS LEFT: frontend/src/panes.ts is being edited on feat/workspaces, and the geometry branch was cut from main. Touching it would have collided. This is the last piece of the epic's acceptance criterion.

WHAT IS LEFT, all in the renderer:
- On bootstrap, after uiStateClient.load(), activate the pane whose Pane.wireId equals uiState.activeTab. An id matching nothing simply activates nothing, which is correct while the tab SET is not restored (that is nocx-l21ib).
- On tab activation, uiStateClient.save({ activeTab: pane.wireId }).
- The workspaces run split starting a pane from activating it (PaneManager.addPane starts each restored pane and activates none), so the window currently lands on the FIRST pane, which is a placeholder and commented as one.

Backend, schema, generated type and both contract tests are already in place (commit c38b4a91); this is wiring only.
acceptance_criteria: Activating a tab, quitting and relaunching lands the window on the same tab when that pane still exists; an activeTab naming a pane that does not exist activates nothing rather than throwing; a test watches the round trip.
close_reason: Renderer wires uistate.activeTab: PaneManager takes the UIStateClient, boot activates the remembered pane, activate() writes the id back. Round trip watched by two tests in panes-layout.test.ts (two managers, one chain, one stored document, fresh mirror on the second). ADR-0033 §3 and the state-ownership table updated. Commit 1888d7fe.

title: Sidebar width is UI state wearing a setting's clothes
description:
## Steps to Reproduce

1. Drag the sidebar's edge to any width.
2. Open Settings > Interface.

Observed 2026-08-18 by the owner while testing feat/workspaces: the page lists a
'Sidebar width' row reading 206.3828125 px, and the section carries a 'Modified 1'
badge because the drag wrote it.

## What is wrong

Two symptoms, one cause. A SETTING IS A DELIBERATE CHOICE; a width produced by
dragging a panel edge is UI state — what the app must remember without being asked —
which is exactly the class distinction this epic's body draws. The registry is the
wrong owner, and both symptoms follow: a fractional pixel count presented as a value
to type, and a 'Modified' count reporting a drag as a decision.

Registered today as settings.SidebarWidth (internal/settings/settings.go:714, key
'sidebar.width'), applied by the frontend through --sidebar-width.

It moves to the UI-state store this epic builds, beside window geometry, sidebar
collapse and the active view — and is stored as whole pixels: nothing about a panel
edge is meaningful to seven decimal places.
acceptance_criteria: The Interface settings page no longer lists 'Sidebar width'; dragging the sidebar edge changes nothing on that page and never marks the section Modified; the width still survives a restart, read from the UI-state store rather than from the settings registry; the stored value is a whole number of CSS pixels.
close_reason: settings.SidebarWidth removed from the registry (commit c38b4a91) — Settings > Interface no longer lists 'Sidebar width' and a drag never marks the section Modified; asserted by TestSidebarWidthIsNotDeclaredAsASetting. Width now in uistate.json as a whole number of CSS pixels (rounding lives in clampSidebarWidth, the single owner). nocx.sidebar.collapsed left localStorage too: SidebarStorage became SidebarPersistence over uistate.get/uistate.set, and the active sidebar view is remembered with it.

title: A workspace has a colour the user chose, not one hashed out of its id
description:
A workspace has no colour anywhere below the renderer. `content.Workspace` is `{ID, Name, Position}`; the strip derives a colour by hashing the id over the four theme accents, which means the user cannot choose one and two workspaces collide the moment there are five.

THE DESIGN ALREADY SAYS IT SHOULD. .internal/specs/2026-08-15-workspaces-ux-design.md §3 states the model as `id, name, colour` — this implements that line rather than deciding anything new. §4.2 is untouched: the DEFAULT workspace still renders no colour, because it renders no chrome at all.

It is a vertical slice: the content schema, the three layout methods on the wire, the contract, the generated types, the store and the create dialog. Greenfield, so the schema bump DISCARDS and rebuilds — there is no migration and none is wanted.

Creation stops being a bare name prompt. It becomes a form (name + colour) built to take more fields later, and the colour it offers by default is one no existing workspace is using — a default that collides on a fresh install is a default nobody keeps.

The palette stays the CLOSED four of layout/tab-colours.ts: every shipped theme defines exactly those accents, so a fifth would be a colour that exists in some themes and not others. A second palette for workspaces would be the same defect one level up.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Creating a workspace asks for a name AND a colour, and the colour offered first is one no other workspace holds.
- The colour survives a restart: it is read back from the chain, not derived from the id.
- An existing workspace can be recoloured from its menu, and the strip redraws.
- The default workspace has no colour and is offered none.
- layout.read and workspaces.create carry the colour in contracts/, and the over-the-wire test asserts the real payload — not one the test built.
- A workspace whose stored colour this renderer does not recognise draws as no colour rather than as a broken swatch, the same rule tabs already follow.

title: The workspace overview: see every running thing at once, and go to the one that needs you
description:
A transient, full-window overview of every workspace and every pane, opened by a key and dismissed by one — the Mission Control shape, proposed by the owner while testing the strip rework.

WHY IT IS NOT A THUMBNAIL GRID. Mission Control works because windows are visually distinct; twelve terminals are not. A scaled-down terminal is grey noise, so a card here is TEXT: what is running, where, in what state, for how long, and its last line of output. That is also what makes it answer the question a browser never had to — which of my long-running things needs me.

It COMPLEMENTS the strip and replaces nothing. The strip reports continuously; the overview is opened a few times a day to see everything and to move things between workspaces (design §4.5: a drag moves the whole lineage subtree).

Parallel-work boundary: the strip rework is in flight in the same tree. This bead owns NEW files only and a port interface of its own; the wiring into PaneManager/main.tsx is handed back rather than done here.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A key opens an overview showing every workspace, with its panes as text cards; Escape closes it.
- A card names what is running, where, its state and its age; there is no pixel thumbnail of a terminal anywhere.
- Clicking a card activates that pane and closes the overview.
- Ungrouped (default-workspace) panes appear, under no name and no header (§4.2).
- One automated check watches a user open the overview, see a pane from a workspace they were not in, and land in it.
acceptance_criteria: See the criteria in the description.

title: Step 6: owner reviews the spec; then stress-test or writing-plans
Step 5: write the design doc under .internal/specs and self-review
Recall shows one page and cannot ask for the next: history.query's cursor has no renderer caller
description:
FOUND while closing nocx-rtg0.19, and confirmed by reading the renderer rather
than assuming: frontend/src/history-client.ts's queryHistory takes
(client, scope, cwd, host, text) and builds its params from exactly those. It
has no cursor parameter and never sends `before`. So recall asks for one page
and stops, however much history the store holds.

WHY IT SURFACED NOW. The cutover changed the cursor's key space from
command_history's decimal rowid to the ledger's UUID, and the ingress
validator still parsed it as an integer — so every cursor a renderer COULD
have sent was refused -32602 before reaching the store. That is fixed. But
fixing it revealed the larger fact: nothing was sending one, which is why the
break was invisible.

The backend half is complete and tested: LedgerQuery.BeforeID takes the
entry's own id, the store resolves it to that row's ingest_seq inside the same
read transaction, an id naming no row is refused rather than answered with the
newest page, and both cursors at once are refused as two answers to one
question. The page also carries `exhausted`. Nothing needs designing on the
wire; this is the renderer's half.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Record more commands than maxHistoryPageLimit.
2. Open recall and scroll to the bottom of the list.
3. There is no way to ask for the next page — queryHistory cannot express one.
acceptance_criteria:
- Recall can reach older commands than one page holds, and one test drives it:
  record more than a page's worth, open recall, and reach a command from
  beyond the first page.
- The cursor sent is the row's own id — the handle history.query already puts
  on every entry — and nothing on either side compares ids: the order is the
  ledger's commit order, resolved through the row.
- The end of the ladder is visible. `exhausted` already crosses the wire and
  is read, so a person can tell "that is everything" from "there is more".

title: make ci-full cannot pass on a Linux dev host: lint-ci runs golangci-lint untagged and wails webview has no export data
description:
`make ci-full` is what AGENTS.md tells the coordinator to run before every push
to main, every time. On a Linux dev host it cannot pass, and it fails in its
FIRST target, so nothing after it runs either.

Makefile:389 `lint-ci` ends with `$(GOLANGCI_LINT) run ./...` — no build tags.
On this machine that dies before reaching any of our code:

  [runner] Can't run linter goanalysis_metalinter: buildir: failed to load
  package webview: could not load export data: no export data for
  "github.com/wailsapp/wails/v3/internal/assetserver/webview"

The same command WITH the tag is clean: `CGO_ENABLED=1 golangci-lint run
--build-tags gtk3 ./internal/...` exits 0. Wails v3 defaults to
GTK4/webkitgtk-6.0, which is absent here, so the untagged load cannot resolve
the webview package's export data. AGENTS.md already records that every Go
command on this host needs `-tags gtk3` and `CGO_ENABLED=1`; `lint-ci` is the
one place that rule was never applied.

MEASURED AS PRE-EXISTING, not caused by anything current: reproduced in a
detached worktree at 08172a0a — before the day's work — with byte-identical
output. This is the "baseline before blame" check, and it is why this is filed
as its own bug rather than attributed to a merge.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THE INCONVENIENCE. A gate that always fails stops being
read. The coordinator's honest options today are to skip `make ci` and run only
the three containerized jobs — which ARE byte-for-byte their CI counterparts
and were green — or to treat a red `make ci-full` as normal, which is how a
real failure gets waved through next time.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. On a Linux dev host: make ci-full
2. It fails at Makefile:395 lint-ci, Error 3, before test-ci ever runs.
3. CGO_ENABLED=1 golangci-lint run --build-tags gtk3 ./internal/... exits 0.
acceptance_criteria:
- make ci-full completes on a Linux dev host, or lint-ci states in its own
  output that it is a macOS-only target and is skipped deliberately — a target
  that always fails is indistinguishable from one that found something.
- The fix does not weaken the check on the platform where it works: if lint-ci
  gains a build tag, a test or the Makefile comment says which platforms it now
  covers and which it does not.
- AGENTS.md's list of "local and CI disagree" facts names this one, next to the
  internal/pty and internal/app entries it already carries.

title: Retention has a seam nothing outside internal/content calls, so a user cannot drive it
description:
FOUND by the nocx-rtg0.12 worker and flagged rather than fixed, correctly: the
fix crosses into internal/transport, which it did not own.

nocx-rtg0.12 built the retention watermark and eviction of `entries`. The WORK
is wired — evictOnWrite runs on the ledger write path (main → app.New →
content.Open → writer → process → Submit → evictOnWrite → evictEntries) and
the watermark is read on the live query path. But the two PUBLIC seam methods,
EvictEntries and Watermark, have no caller outside internal/content, so
`deadcode -whylive` answers "reachable only through reflection" for both.

That is the RTA blind spot AGENTS.md documents — a dead method behind a live
interface is invisible to the ratchet — which is exactly why this is filed as a
bead rather than trusted to the gate. The gate cannot fail on it.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY MISSING, in product terms: retention runs opportunistically on
write and nothing else can ask for it. The Settings surface already offers an
age and a two-number budget (internal/settings/settings.go, Section "History"),
and those knobs reach the interim command_history sweep, not the ledger. So a
user changing retention today changes something other than the table their
history is about to live in.

DEPENDS on nocx-rtg0.12 landing first — it is the code this wires up.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. deadcode -tags gtk3 -whylive '.../internal/content.sqliteContent.EvictEntries' ./...
2. Read the answer: "reachable only through reflection".
3. grep -rn "EvictEntries" --include=*.go . | grep -v internal/content — empty.
acceptance_criteria:
- deadcode -tags gtk3 -whylive on the LedgerRepository.EvictEntries seam prints
  a path from main, not "reachable only through reflection" — contrasted in the
  same run against a symbol that is genuinely unwired, because the contrast is
  what makes it evidence.
- The Settings retention controls govern the ledger, not only command_history.
  A test drives a retention change through the settings registry and watches
  entries disappear.
- Coverage as the user sees it comes from the watermark: a recall page after an
  eviction states a horizon older than any row it returned.

title: A vertical strip cannot create a workspace, and nothing can rename or reorder one
description:
Found and reported by nocx-isoph.5 rather than quietly shipped, and filed the
same hour so it does not evaporate between rounds.

nocx-isoph.5 built the workspace chip and its switcher, and the chip is
HORIZONTAL-ONLY by design: the vertical strip already shows every workspace, so
a chip there would be a second answer to one question. That is right.

The consequence is that a user whose strip is vertical CANNOT CREATE A
WORKSPACE AT ALL. The per-group [+] and [pencil] affordances the workspaces UX
design §4.3 sketches were not built, and nothing else offers creation.

Default placement is horizontal, so the epic's journey works and nothing is
broken for most users. But `tab.placement` is a real setting a real user
changes, and after they change it a whole feature disappears from the product
with no explanation.

TWO MORE OF THE SAME SHAPE, from the same report, and they belong here because
the fix is one surface rather than three:

  • RENAME AND REORDER A WORKSPACE. workspaces.rename and workspaces.reorder
    exist on the wire, with contracts, and the renderer calls neither.
  • ATTENTION COUNTS IN THE SWITCHER (§4.3). Deliberately not faked by that
    worker, and the reason is worth keeping: it needs the liveness rule, and a
    second spelling of live-work.ts for a decoration nobody asked for would be
    the AD-8 defect for the sake of a badge.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Set the tab strip to vertical placement.
2. Look for any way to create a workspace. There is none — the chip is not
   rendered in vertical placement and no other surface offers it.
3. In either placement, look for a way to rename or reorder a workspace. The
   methods answer on the wire; nothing calls them.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A user in VERTICAL placement can create a workspace, and one automated check
  drives it in that placement — not in horizontal with a note that vertical is
  similar.
- Rename and reorder are reachable, and both survive a renderer reload without
  the backend restarting, like every other decoration this epic stores.
- Whatever affordance is added, it is ONE mechanism placed twice rather than two
  built separately. The chip and the vertical strip are two views of one set,
  and the heading mechanism (strip-groups.ts, axis as input) is already built
  that way — follow it.
- The default workspace still never renders a header, a name or a colour in
  either placement. That rule is asserted byte-for-byte today
  (tab-strip.test.tsx compares the default's rows' outerHTML before and after a
  second workspace exists); do not weaken that test to make room for an
  affordance.
close_reason:
Commits 628edd5e and 6a967601. All four criteria met.

VERTICAL CREATE, driven IN vertical placement: the test mounts the real
PaneManager, replaces the strip with a VerticalTabStrip, asserts there is no
chip, clicks "New workspace" and watches the row arrive with its first tab —
not in horizontal with a note that vertical is similar.

RENAME AND REORDER ARE REACHABLE, and they survive a renderer reload because
nothing about them is renderer state: the store writes its cache from the
BACKEND'S ANSWER, never from the request, and a test proves that by making the
two differ — the fake answers "what the backend stored" to a request of "what
the user typed", and the cache holds the former. A refused reorder leaves the
set exactly as it was, so there is no optimistic move to snap back from.

ONE MECHANISM PLACED TWICE: workspace-menu.ts owns what may be done to a
workspace and owns the rule that the default may have none of it. The chip
appends those rows for the workspace in front of it; a vertical heading opens
the same rows for the one it heads. `closable` is gone from the chip's view —
it was a second reading of "not the default".

Creation is the one thing placed rather than shared, and the reason is the
fourth criterion: the default draws no heading, so a create offered only on
headings would be unreachable for exactly the person who has never made a
workspace. It is an action of the strip.

THE DEFAULT'S BYTE-FOR-BYTE RULE IS UNTOUCHED — tab-strip.test.tsx's
outerHTML comparison was not weakened, edited or moved.

THE LINT RULE CAUGHT A REAL MISTAKE, recorded because the next person will
reach for the same shortcut. The heading first shipped as a div with an
onClick — mouse-only — and the hand-rolled role="button" fix was refused by
nocx/no-role-impersonation. Its two exits are "use the kit component" or
"declare a composite contract", and the second is for a behavioural unit
outside the kit's vocabulary (tab.tsx with role=tab). A button that opens a
menu is not that. The control is the kit's ghost Button now, and the focus
ring and keyboard came with it.

DEFERRED, and filed rather than faked: attention counts in the switcher
(§4.3). They need the liveness rule, and a second spelling of live-work.ts for
a decoration would be the AD-8 defect bought for a badge.

Gates: frontend 3278 tests / 185 files green, tsc on both configs, eslint,
prettier, and the dead-exports, two-owners and row-grammar ratchets all
baselined with no new entries. Containerized ci-frontend green. e2e 330
passed / 2 failed, both nocx-9jcx7 and unchanged from before the work.

title: Closing a workspace names what is live before anything dies
description:
Design: §4.2 and D6 of the 2026-08-15 workspaces UX design; §4.4 of the
2026-08-16 tabs/panes/blocks design.

Closing a workspace closes all its tabs — and the dialog NAMES WHAT IS LIVE
before anything dies.

WHY NAMING RATHER THAN COUNTING. 'Close 4 tabs?' is a number a user cannot
weigh. What they need to know is that one of them is a running deploy and
another is an ssh session into production. D6 is the rule; this bead is where it
becomes a surface.

A PARENT'S DEATH NEVER CLOSES ITS CHILDREN, and that prohibition is already
enforced by nocx-wtv3p. Closing a tab with live descendants ASKS rather than
decides. Three of the four ways to lose a parent are failures, and a failure
carries no information about whether the work is still wanted. This dialog is
the 'asks' half; do not add a second decision path beside it.

THE REPLACEMENT TAB GOES TO THE DEFAULT WORKSPACE, never to the one being
closed — otherwise closing a workspace resurrects it. nocx-isoph.3 owns that
rule; this bead must not re-implement it.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Closing a workspace holding a live shell shows a dialog naming that shell —
  the command or the host, something a person can act on — and not merely a
  count.
- Cancelling leaves every tab, every pane and every live session exactly as they
  were. Asserted on the sessions, not on the DOM: nothing may be torn down
  before the answer.
- Confirming closes them all, and if it was the last workspace the replacement
  tab is in the DEFAULT workspace, asserted by its workspace_id.
- Closing a workspace whose tabs are all idle still asks, and says so honestly
  rather than listing nothing. A dialog that names an empty list is worse than
  one that says there is nothing running.
- The dialog is built from the kit (frontend/src/ui/), not hand-rolled. Read
  frontend/src/ui/README.md first.
close_reason:
Merged into feat/workspaces at 1943dbc9 (d33e431f). The dialog names what is live rather than counting it, in three layers with one owner each: a PaneContent.liveWork?() capability beside lineage?(), a pure live-work.ts owning the naming rule, and PaneManager.closeWorkspace doing the ask through the kit's showConfirm.

The best decision is which question 'live' answers. It is deliberately neither of the two capabilities that already existed: activeOrigin says which machine a tab SPEAKS FOR and goes silent inside a hand-typed ssh, so a prompt built on it would name a machine nothing runs on and say nothing exactly where it matters; lineage says what is OPEN and speaks for a tab whose shell has already exited. This one says what is RUNNING. The reason is written into the capability's comment.

And the liveness rule itself is a product decision, argued: an idle local shell is not live because a new one costs a keystroke, while any remote session at a prompt IS live because a remote connection's state is not free to recreate. Without that second half the bead's own example — an ssh session into production — would not be named.

Cancelling is asserted ON THE SESSIONS, not the DOM: no session.close, no notifyPaneClosed, pane count unchanged, panes still connected. That was the criterion most likely to be faked by a DOM assertion.

Two AD-8 touches worth keeping: hostLabel was EXTRACTED from locationLine rather than copied, so 'which machine are we on' keeps one derivation; and lineage.ts now imports nameAtMost from live-work.ts instead of keeping its own limit, so 'past five it becomes a wall' is one rule.

Not wired end to end, deliberately and recorded on nocx-isoph.5: nothing calls closeWorkspace, because the affordance belongs on the chip and building one here would have collided with two siblings at once.

title: The default workspace never renders, and the chip is how a window shows one at a time
description:
Design: .internal/specs/2026-08-16-tabs-panes-and-blocks-design.md §3, §10, and
§4.2 and §5.5 of the 2026-08-15 workspaces UX design.

THE DEFAULT WORKSPACE NEVER RENDERS. Its tabs are top-level rows with no header,
no name and no colour. Not 'invisible while it is the only one' — that makes the
whole chrome appear and disappear on a counter, and forces the default to
acquire a name nobody gave it.

VERTICAL STRIP: all workspaces, a tree of workspace -> tab -> lineage children.
HORIZONTAL STRIP: a chip on the left, then ONLY the current workspace's tabs; in
the default workspace the chip is a neutral glyph with no label.

A WINDOW IS A VIEWPORT, NOT A CONTAINER (§10). It shows one workspace at a time
— that is what the chip and its switcher are — and it owns no tabs. If a window
contained tabs, a tab would sit in a window AND in a workspace and the two would
disagree.

THE HEADING MECHANISM HAS ANOTHER CLAIMANT. nocx-jv3q.1 groups the same strip by
descriptor.surfaceType, and design §9 adds project, host, worktree and branch as
further axes over the flat list. Build ONE heading mechanism with the axis as an
input; a hard-coded workspace heading that jv3q.1 then forks is the AD-8 defect
in advance.

THIS EPIC SHIPS MEMBERSHIP, NOT A FENCE (§5.5 of the UX design). No shield or
lock iconography, no 'safe', 'isolated' or 'contained', and no copy of the form
'everything here can reach everything else'. An adversarial review found the
first draft shipping exactly that promise with no mechanism behind it. The fence
is nocx-mp2vd's.

## Acceptance Criteria

- With only the default workspace, the strip shows tabs and NO header, name or
  colour anywhere, and the chip is a neutral glyph with no label.
- Creating a second workspace does not make the default acquire a header. A
  test asserts the default's chrome is unchanged by the existence of others —
  that is the 'not a counter' rule, and it is the one a naive implementation
  breaks.
- The vertical strip renders workspace -> tab -> lineage children as a tree, and
  a lineage child appears under its parent rather than as a sibling.
- The horizontal strip shows only the current workspace's tabs; switching the
  chip changes the set.
- A grep of the shipped strings finds no 'safe', 'isolated' or 'contained'
  describing a workspace, a tab or a pane, and no shield or lock glyph in the
  workspace chrome. Automated, not by eye.
notes:
THIS BEAD IS WHERE THE CLOSE DIALOG BECOMES REACHABLE. nocx-isoph.6 built PaneManager.closeWorkspace — the ask, the naming and the close — and nothing calls it, because the affordance belongs on the chip and its switcher, which is yours (§4.3). That is the one place .6 is not wired end to end, and it was left that way deliberately rather than by oversight: building a chip inside .6 would have collided with .4 and .6 at once.

So the chip's 'Close workspace' action is not a new behaviour to design here — it is one call to an existing method, and re-implementing the ask beside it would be the two-owners defect the whole epic keeps avoiding. closeWorkspace takes members as a parameter and returns a boolean saying whether the caller may send workspaces.close.

Also inherited from .6 and worth knowing before you design the switcher: liveness excludes an idle LOCAL shell and includes any remote session at a prompt, because a new local shell costs a keystroke while a remote connection's state does not. If the chip ever shows an activity dot per workspace, use that same rule rather than spelling a second one.
close_reason:
Merged into feat/workspaces at de89ff71 (2bb630d2). The default workspace never renders, and the chip switches one workspace at a time.

THE BEST THING IN IT IS THAT THE RULE IS STRUCTURAL, NOT A BRANCH. GroupAxis.heading is handed ONE KEY and nothing else — not the set, not a count — so 'no heading unless there is more than one group' is not expressible in the type. The criterion I wrote asked for a test that the default's chrome is unchanged by the existence of others; what landed makes the violation unwritable, which is better than catching it.

It also bought a stronger assertion: a heading-less group emits NO ELEMENT AT ALL, no wrapper and no empty caption, which is what lets tab-strip.test.tsx compare the default's rows byte-for-byte before and after a second workspace exists.

closeWorkspace is finally reachable, and wired the way the earlier defects taught: members resolve through LayoutStore's cache of the chain rather than through what is drawn, because only the cache knows about a member with no chrome — a restored ssh row the renderer never drew. That is the same shape that broke reorder in nocx-isoph.4, avoided here first time.

One heading mechanism with the axis as an input, so nocx-jv3q.1 adds a surfaceTypeAxis beside workspaceAxis rather than forking it. Told that bead so, and told it that its Cmd+1..9 criterion now needs editing because numbering became workspace-scoped.

Reported gaps, filed as nocx-isoph.7 rather than shipped quietly: a vertical strip cannot create a workspace at all (the chip is horizontal-only by design and the per-group affordances were not built), and workspaces.rename/reorder answer on the wire with nothing calling them.

Gate on the merged tree: ci-frontend green, e2e 330 passed with 2 failures both the known cross-spec contamination, ci-linux green on re-run after one flake in nocx-1wwm which could not have been caused by this merge — it changed no Go at all.

title: The UI names no opener: the three tab origins that may write a lineage edge are undecided
description:
Reported by the nocx-9hu9d worker as a deliberate non-goal and filed the same hour,
because "the record and the wire accept it" plus "nothing produces it" is the exact
shape AGENTS.md keeps a whole section about.

SPLIT 2026-08-24 by the owner. This bead used to mean "the lineage edge has no
producer at all". Half of that is now owned elsewhere: a pane opened by the
orchestration dispatcher has EXACTLY ONE possible parent — the session of the run
that asked for it — so nocx-dkawo produces the edge for dispatched panes as part of
building the dispatcher, and nocx-szb40 reads it to group a wave under its
coordinator. What is left here is the half that was actually deferred, and the
reason it was deferred: the three UI origins have no obvious answer.

WHAT EXISTS after nocx-9hu9d: session.Ref carrying the full identity (instanceId,
sessionId, sessionEpoch), Config.Parent as a claim, Session.Parent() as the record,
validateParent as the single owner of what may be admitted, and open accepting an
optional parent with the ack reading it back. All of it tested over the real socket.

WHAT DOES NOT EXIST: any renderer code that sends one. Every session the USER opens
is a root, so the edge is admissible and never admitted.

WHY IT IS A UI DECISION, which is why it was deferred rather than guessed: "which
tab opened this one" has no obvious answer. Is it the active tab? The split source?
What about a row in the connection list, activated with no tab in focus at all?
Guessing here writes a wrong edge that is IMMUTABLE BY DESIGN — the one kind of
mistake this feature cannot take back. Design section 11 item 7 leaves it open.

It overlaps the work where the renderer stopped owning the model and started asking
(nocx-isoph.4, closed), which is the moment "which tab opened this one" becomes
answerable from one place rather than three.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open a tab from another tab in the running app, by hand.
2. Read the new session's record: Parent() returns false.
3. grep the renderer for anything that puts parent in an open call: nothing does.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The three ambiguous origins are each DECIDED and the decision written down: a
  split, a new tab from the tab strip, and an activation from the connection list
  with no tab focused. "It happens to do X" is not a decision.
- Opening a tab from another tab BY HAND records an edge naming the opener, and the
  child's record says so — watched end to end against the real backend, not asserted
  at the seam.
- A tab that genuinely has no opener records NO edge, and a test asserts the absence.
  An edge invented for a root is worse than no lineage at all, because it is immutable.
- The refusals nocx-9hu9d already enforces stay enforced from the producing side: no
  self-parent, no cycle, no parent naming a different backend instance.
- The dispatcher's producer (nocx-dkawo) and this one write through the SAME seam.
  Two producers for one immutable edge is the defect, not the fix.
notes:
MOVED OUT OF THE FOUNDATION'S CRITICAL PATH 2026-08-17. This stays a child of nocx-ebl4 for provenance, but it must not hold that epic open: everything the epic exists to retrofit — the identity, the Ref, validateParent, the wire — is merged. What is missing here is a PRODUCER, and producing an edge is a surface decision that belongs with the strip and panes work (design §11 item 7), not with the record.

Concretely it overlaps nocx-isoph.4, where the renderer stops owning the model and starts asking. That is the moment 'which tab opened this one' has an answer, because that is the moment the renderer knows what a tab is. Taking it before then means deciding it twice.
SPLIT 2026-08-24, owner's call, in the session that started teaching nocx to replace herdr. The producer half went to nocx-dkawo: for a dispatched pane the parent is not ambiguous, and the wave needs the edge anyway to group three workers under one coordinator. This bead keeps the UI half, which is the part that was genuinely undecided. Consequence: nocx-ebl4 no longer waits on a surface decision it does not own, and closed the same minute.

title: Submit accepts a payload the store cannot later merge, and the entry becomes uncloseable
description:
Found while writing nocx-rtg0.20's store tests. Unreachable through the wire
today, filed anyway because the guard that makes it unreachable is one line in a
caller and nothing states it as an invariant.

Submit with Payload: "" writes an empty string into entries.payload. The column
is TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}', and every later writer merges with json_patch —
so a subsequent FinishExecution fails with

    sqlite3: SQL logic error: malformed JSON

because json_patch has nothing to merge into. The entry is then permanently
uncloseable: every retry of the close fails the same way.

WHY IT IS UNREACHABLE TODAY: ws_ledger.go's open always writes a receipt object,
so the payload is never empty on the wire path. That is a property of one
caller, not of the store, and nocx-rtg0.20's tests had to pass "{}" explicitly
to work around it — which is the tell. A store that accepts a value it cannot
later read is a trap with a caller-shaped lid.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Call LedgerRepository.Submit with SubmitEntry{..., Payload: ""}.
2. Call FinishExecution for that entry.
3. sqlite3: SQL logic error: malformed JSON. The entry can never be closed.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Submit normalises an empty payload to "{}" — or refuses it outright, stated in
  the commit which and why. Either is defensible; silently storing it is not.
- A test closes an entry submitted with an empty payload and it succeeds.
- nocx-rtg0.20's tests stop needing the explicit "{}" workaround, and the diff
  removing it is the evidence the trap is gone.

title: ledger.attention: the unreviewed queue
description:
Design: .internal/specs/2026-07-31-command-blocks-history-syntax-design.md §6.2, §10.8.

Split out of nocx-rtg0.3 on 2026-08-17 and filed rather than left implied — the same reason nocx-rtg0.19 had to be filed the same day, after twenty-one beads under this epic turned out to contain nothing that deleted command_history.

ledger.attention { limit } -> the unreviewed queue.
acceptance_criteria: Something a user has not reviewed appears in the queue, and stops appearing once reviewed — the criterion stops being false exactly once. Over the real socket against a schema in contracts/.

title: ledger.search: full-text over intent and derived output, with honest coverage
description:
Design: .internal/specs/2026-07-31-command-blocks-history-syntax-design.md §6.2, §10.7, §5.4.

Split out of nocx-rtg0.3 on 2026-08-17 and filed rather than left implied. It needs full-text search over intent and derived output, and NO FTS EXISTS in internal/content today — so this is a store capability, not a wire method with a query behind it.

ledger.search { text, scope, limit } -> { entries, coverage }.

COVERAGE IS NOT OPTIONAL (§5.4). It states what retention still holds. A search that answers from an evicted window and says nothing is a search that lies by omission, and ADR-0019 §7 requires reconstruction to state its own horizon.
acceptance_criteria: A search over a corpus where retention has evicted part of the window returns coverage describing the hole, and a test asserts the hole is described rather than that the search returned rows. Over the real socket, against a schema in contracts/ with additionalProperties:false and an explicit required.

title: Drag one tab onto another and watch both at once, then pull it back out whole
description:
Design: .internal/specs/2026-08-16-tabs-panes-and-blocks-design.md §4.3, §4.4, §5.

A user watching a build in one tab and editing in another has to keep switching.
This epic lets them drag one tab onto another and see both at once, and drag it
back out with nothing lost.

THE DISPLAY GROUP HAS NO HOST, AND THEREFORE NO OBJECT (§4.3). Dragging tab B
onto tab A shows them together. A is not a container — it is a real tab with its
own panes, and it is only "first" because it was the drop target. A pointer edge
is the wrong shape: pull A out and the remaining members point at something that
left. The relation is SYMMETRIC — A, B and C are shown together, no host, any of
them can be pulled out and the rest do not notice. In storage that is a value
shared by the members, not a row of its own, so nothing can outlive its
membership.

THE TAB IS MINTED AND DESTROYED AUTOMATICALLY (§4.4). A pane is never created or
moved by the user; it is dragged, and everything follows:

  drag a pane out of a tab  -> a tab is MINTED for it and appears in the strip
  drag a pane into a tab    -> its tab_id changes, and a tab left with no panes
                               is REMOVED in the same transaction
  in both directions        -> the pane's identity, its blocks, its history and
                               its live pipe are untouched, because only a
                               reference moved

THIS IS WHAT A SEPARATE `pane` TYPE COULD NEVER DO, and it is the owner's own
objection answered: a pane that is a different type from a tab can never BECOME a
tab without creating a new object and migrating content into it. Here the durable
object is the pane and the tab is the cheap wrapper, so the round trip is lossless
by construction. That is why the words were swapped in nocx-ehkvy rather than a
new type invented.

PANES DO NOT NEST (§5). A tab shows a FLAT set of them. Nesting buys asymmetric
geometry — "B on the left, C and D stacked on the right" — and the purpose here is
watching several things at once, which a row or a grid serves. The cost is stated
rather than hidden: no asymmetric layouts, ever, until this is revisited
deliberately.

SIZE IS A PROPERTY OF THE MEMBER, DIRECTION A PROPERTY OF THE SET. Each pane
stores its own share; the tab stores the direction. That is why the tab needed a
row and the display group did not.

TWO EDGES, NEVER ONE (§4.2). Dragging for display touches the display edge and
changes no kinship, so lineage is untouched by every drag in this epic, and
§4.5 of the workspaces design keeps its refusal: dragging between LINEAGE groups
is still refused.

INHERITED UNCHANGED, and still undesigned: whether a pane can be dragged between
workspaces while a subtree move is in flight. §4.4 of the workspaces design left
the atomicity model open and required a partial move to FAIL CLOSED. That
requirement stands; this epic must not leave a pane in two places or in none.

DELIBERATELY OUT: nested panes, asymmetric layouts, restore of the layout across
a restart (nocx-l21ib carries the layout back), multi-window, and any authority
behaviour.
acceptance_criteria: A user drags tab B onto tab A and sees both panes side by side in one strip entry. The blocks, the scrollback and the LIVE SHELL in B keep running across the drag — a command started before the drag prints its output after it. They drag B back out; it is a tab again, with the same blocks, the same history and the same live shell, and A is unchanged. They pull A out instead of B: the remaining members do not notice, because no member is the host. A tab left with no panes is gone from the strip. Watched end to end by one automated check driving the real UI against the real backend, asserting on the live shell and not only on the DOM. Two more, required because the shape of the design makes them cheap: a drag that fails partway leaves the pane in exactly one place, never two and never none; and dragging between two LINEAGE groups is still refused.
notes:
PANES HAVE NO STORED ORDER, and this bead is where the column belongs. Found by nocx-isoph.1 and reported rather than quietly added.

§5 of the design gives the MEMBER a size share and the SET a direction, and nocx-isoph.1's field list stops there — so panes.position does not exist and LayoutRepository.Panes returns id order. That is fine while a tab holds one pane and nothing can reorder them.

It stops being fine here: this epic is where a user drags a pane into a tab and where 'B on the left, C on the right' becomes a thing they arranged rather than a thing that happened. Reordering only becomes a user-visible operation with drag, which is the argument for the column landing with the drag rather than before it.

Two things to keep from nocx-isoph.1 while adding it. There is deliberately NO group_id column: §4.3 says the display group has no row, it is a value shared by the members, so nothing can outlive its membership — and the schema comment says so and says it must never be folded onto parent_id. And schemaVersion is now 5; bumping it again is free (owner, 2026-08-17: drop without fear, nocx is greenfield), so the column costs nothing but the decision.

title: Nothing stops a test from calling a real model provider except everyone remembering
description:
Verified 2026-08-16: no test dials a real model provider. Every model-calling test stands up
an httptest server (assistant/classifier_test.go, probe_test.go, httpguard_test.go;
transport/request_broker_test.go, ws_readscreen_test.go), and there is no BaseURL in
internal/assistant tests that is not a local server URL. The api.openai.com strings in
internal/profile and ws_endpoints_test.go are STORED RECORDS — persistence and key-masking
assertions — and nothing dials them.

THAT IS A FACT ABOUT TODAY, NOT A MECHANISM. Nothing stops the next test from pointing at a
real endpoint: it would pass quietly, cost money, leak whatever the fixture contains to a
third party, and fail only on a machine with no network — which is not where anyone runs it.
The repository closes this class of thing by construction rather than by intention.

Note what the guard is NOT: internal/assistant/httpguard.go enforces the http:// address
rule at dial time as a PRODUCT rule. This is a test-environment rule and belongs beside the
test harness, not in the product path.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A test that dials a host outside the local machine FAILS, with a sentence naming the test
  and the host. Asserted by a test that deliberately tries.
- The guard covers the whole Go suite, not one package.
- Both ends: every existing test still passes, and a local httptest server is unaffected.
- The rule is stated once, where a person writing a new test will meet it.

title: The pre-commit hook runs its containers unconstrained, so a commit competes with the desktop instead of yielding to it
description:
The pre-commit hook runs its containers with no resource constraint of any kind.
`.githooks/containerized-tests.sh` lines 86 and 123 are plain `docker run --rm` —
no `--cpus`, no `--cpu-shares`, no `--memory`, no scheduling priority. It fires on
EVERY commit, which is far more often than anyone runs scripts/ci-linux.sh, and
that script is the only place a cap (`NOCX_CI_CPUS`) even exists.

MEASURED 2026-08-16 on the owner's machine (6 cores, 11.7 GiB), six samples across
one hook run:

    container   cpu 290% → 302% → 283% → 108% → 4%      mem peak 1.53 GiB
    host        4.5–5.8 GiB available throughout
    load avg    7.98 (1m)   42.05 (5m)   49.77 (15m)

TWO CONCLUSIONS, and the first one matters more than the fix.

ONE CONTAINER IS NOT THE PROBLEM. It takes three of six cores and 1.5 GiB. Memory
was never the constraint — the host never dropped below 4.5 GiB free — so a
`--memory` cap would be fixing something that is not broken. What made the desktop
unusable is the 5- and 15-minute load of 42 and 50 on six cores: an eightfold
oversubscription produced by running an e2e container, a ci-linux run, hook
commits and five agents at the same time. That is an orchestration fault, and the
first remedy is not to do it, which costs nothing.

BUT THE HOOK SHOULD STILL YIELD. A developer commits while using their machine, so
the one container that does run should lose to the desktop rather than race it.

WHY --cpu-shares AND NOT --cpus. AGENTS.md removed the CPU caps deliberately: a
hard `--cpus` cap "does not produce the runner, it produces a third machine unlike
either", and it kept timing-dependent specs alive by making them reproducible.
`--cpu-shares` is a RELATIVE WEIGHT, not a ceiling: under no contention the
container still gets every core, so the timing profile of an idle-machine run is
unchanged and the AGENTS.md objection does not apply. It only bites when something
else wants the CPU, which is exactly the case being fixed.

The e2e path has the same shape (`NOCX_E2E_CPUS`) and the same absence of a share
weight; whether it gets the same treatment is part of this bead.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Start a commit in any worktree so the pre-commit hook runs its containers.
2. `docker stats --no-stream` — the container is unconstrained, ~300% CPU.
3. Use the desktop during it. On a 6-core machine with anything else running,
   interactive latency collapses.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Both `docker run` invocations in .githooks/containerized-tests.sh carry a
  `--cpu-shares` weight, with a comment saying why it is a share and not a cap and
  naming the AGENTS.md paragraph it does not contradict.
- No `--cpus` and no `--memory` is added — the measurement says neither is
  warranted, and adding them would reintroduce the "third machine" AGENTS.md
  rejected.
- A run on an otherwise idle machine takes the same wall clock as before, within
  noise, and the number is recorded here before and after.
- The value chosen is justified against Docker's default weight of 1024 rather
  than picked round.
close_reason: Landed on main in 380e6ab5. Both docker run invocations in .githooks/containerized-tests.sh now carry --cpu-shares=512, with the measurement and the reasoning in the file: a relative weight and not a ceiling, so an idle-machine commit keeps today's timing profile and the AGENTS.md objection to --cpus does not apply. No --memory was added — the measurement showed the host never below 4.5 GiB free. ci-linux.sh and the e2e runner deliberately unchanged: they are run by an integrator who has chosen to spend the machine, while the hook is involuntary. Verified in the strongest way available — core.hooksPath is .githooks, so the hook sources its own worktree copy, and the commit that introduced the flag ran through the hook WITH the flag applied and passed every gate.

title: Auto-categorization by a second model, which may only escalate
description:
Owner, 2026-08-16: "нужно добавить возможность авто-категоризации другой моделью" — a second
model judges the effect and risk of a proposed tool call, which is the classification-confidence
dimension of ADR-0020 decision 6 delegated to a model.

TWO INVARIANTS, both derived from decisions already taken, both load-bearing:

1. THE CLASSIFIER MAY ONLY RAISE SUSPICION, NEVER LOWER IT. ADR-0029 rule 7 settled this shape
for keystrokes: the model's judgement is untrusted input, and the local mechanical gate is what
keeps that path advisory. A classifier that can move a call from ask to permit makes the model
the author of its own authority, and a program printing "this is safe" is then writing into our
control flow. One-directional is not caution here; it is the same decision applied to another
input.

2. THE CLASSIFIER IS AN EGRESS POINT. It sees the call arguments, and arguments carry secrets.
The gate of design §7.1 covers it exactly as it covers the answering model, or we have cut a
hole in the gate the size of the thing it was built for.

COST: a second model call per proposed tool call, in latency and money, on every step the agent
takes. The role layer (its own bead) is what lets that be a cheap model rather than the
answering one.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A classifier verdict can escalate a call that policy would have permitted; it can NEVER permit
  a call that policy would have escalated or refused. Asserted by feeding a classifier that says
  "safe" to a call the policy escalates, and watching it still escalate.
- The classifier's input passes the egress gate, asserted with an argument carrying known vault
  material.
- A classifier that is unreachable, slow or unparseable escalates rather than permitting.
  Asserted for each.
- The verdict is recorded on the attempt, so "why was this asked" is answerable afterwards.
- Both ends: with the classifier configured and quiet, an ordinary permitted call still runs.
close_reason: Classifier shipped: composes as the maximum over permit<ask<refuse so it can only escalate; consulted only where policy permits, asserted with a classifier that fails the test on invocation; its input passes the egress gate, asserted with known vault material reaching zero requests; unreachable, timed out, unparseable and role-unassigned all escalate. Merged.

title: tunnelLedger.track can assign into a nil map, and it runs on the control plane
description:
Found by wv6-approval while running the transport suite for an unrelated slice, and
reproduced by it on the clean tree with its own changes stashed — so it is not that slice.

internal/transport/ws_tunnel.go, tunnelLedger.track: the inner owners map is guarded against
nil and created on demand, while the two maps behind the pointers are not. An assignment into
a nil map panics, and this one runs on the control plane.

The panic did not reproduce on every run here — the transport package on this host is also
subject to the nocx-2h08 timing-flake class, and a run immediately after the failing one was
green. That is a reason to fix the nil-map hazard on its merits rather than to wait for a
reliable reproduction: the guard is missing whether or not the schedule exposes it today.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. go test ./internal/transport/ -race -count=1
2. Sometimes: panic, assignment to entry in nil map, reached from tunnel.open via seamSpecs.
3. Read tunnelLedger.track and compare the guard on owners with the absence of one on the
   maps behind l.tunnels and l.owners themselves.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Every map the ledger writes into is non-nil by construction, or the write refuses honestly.
  Asserted by a test that constructs the ledger the way production does and the way a zero
  value would.
- Both ends: the ordinary open/close path still records and releases the tunnel.
- A test names the construction path that produced the nil, so the next reader knows which
  caller was wrong rather than only that a guard was added.

title: A tab shows its directory while a program runs in it: the title has no source between OSC 0/2 and cwd
description:
A tab running herdr is labelled "Users/shady". The owner reported it 2026-08-16
with a screenshot: four tabs, three of them showing a directory while a program
is running in them.

WHAT IS TRUE TODAY, and it is not a propagation failure. The title is composed
in one place and has exactly two sources:

    terminal-content.ts:627   const title = this.programTitle || this.cwdTitle
    tabs.ts:187               const next = <what arrived> || descriptor.defaultTitle

and programTitle is fed ONLY by an OSC 0/2 escape sequence — a program
declaring its own window title (terminal-content.ts:2009 attributes it to the
active domain). herdr emits none, so cwd wins. Everything behaves as written;
what is written is incomplete.

THE MISSING SOURCE ALREADY EXISTS IN THE RENDERER. frontend/src/command-ledger.ts
holds `readonly command: string` per record and a status of 'running', and the
shell integration is what puts it there. So the name of the foreground command
is known at the moment the tab is showing a directory instead of it. The chain
should be:

    programTitle  ||  the running command  ||  cwd

The middle link is the whole fix, and it closes exactly the reported case: a
program that declares nothing is still named by what it is.

A SECOND DEFECT FOUND ON THE WAY, and it is a naming lie with a consequence.
Tab._programTitle does NOT hold the program title. terminal-content composes
`programTitle || cwdTitle` and pushes the RESULT, so the field usually holds a
cwd. And tabs.ts:184 runs updateAgentStatus(title) on that same value — the
agent-state classifier is parsing a string that is often a filesystem path. The
field wants renaming to what it is, and the classifier wants the real program
title, which only TerminalContent has.

CARE: the middle link must not fight the first. A TUI clears its title on the
way out with an empty OSC 0/2, which tabs.ts:181 already documents. The running
command must not resurrect a name the program just cleared, and a finished
command must not leave its name on the tab.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open a tab and run a program that sets no window title — herdr, or any plain
   long-running command.
2. Observed: the tab is labelled with the working directory.
3. Expected: the tab is labelled with the running command.
4. Contrast: run a program that DOES emit OSC 0/2 (vim, ssh to a host with a
   title-setting prompt) and the tab is named correctly — which is what shows
   the propagation itself is sound.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A tab running a program that emits no OSC 0/2 is labelled with the running
  command, not the directory.
- A program that DOES emit OSC 0/2 still wins over the command name.
- A TUI clearing its title on exit does not fall back to the command that is
  itself exiting; the tab returns to cwd.
- Tab._programTitle is renamed to what it holds, and updateAgentStatus is fed
  the real program title rather than the composed one.
- The design in .internal/specs/2026-08-16-tabs-panes-and-blocks-design.md §4.5
  says the label flows pane -> tab; this is that rule for a single pane, and
  the multi-pane label is derived from the same per-pane answer.

title: Move the desktop shell to Wails v3, which is the only thing multi-window needs
description:
Move the desktop shell from Wails v2.13.0 to v3. Decided by the owner
2026-08-16: we are going there anyway, v0.1.0 is tagged and out so nothing is
in flight, and v3 has left alpha for beta. The earlier framing as a spike is
withdrawn — a spike only pays when the decision is open, and it is not.

WHAT MULTI-WINDOW HAS TO DO WITH IT. It is the only capability that needs v3:
v2's runtime has no window-creation call at all, every function is Window*
operating on the one window. The window model agreed the same day makes a
window a VIEWPORT, not a container — it shows one workspace at a time and owns
no tabs — so multi-window changes no object and no table when it arrives. This
bead is the shell, not the feature.

THE CODE IS SMALL, measured rather than estimated. Exactly TWO Go files import
wailsapp/wails:

    main.go                                the composition root: options.App
    internal/notify/wailsadapter/host.go    an adapter, and named one

The runtime surface used is SendNotification with the Notification* types,
OpenFileDialog, and the window options. The frontend has four touch points —
clipboard.ts (ClipboardGetText/SetText), log.ts (Log), platform.ts
(Environment) — plus the generated wailsjs bindings.

It is that small because AD-1 already made the backend a WebSocket server:
Wails shows a window and supplies three OS conveniences, and everything else
crosses the socket rather than the binding.

THE RELEASE PIPELINE IS WHERE THE WORK ACTUALLY IS, and it is verified only by
running it:

    wails.json              config.v2 schema; v3 has a different project shape
    release.yml:105,212     go install .../wails/v2/cmd/wails@v2.13.0
    release.yml:115         patches the product version into wails.json
    release.yml:128         wails build -platform darwin/universal -tags release
    release.yml:228         wails build -platform linux/amd64 -tags release,webkit2_41
    Makefile:9              WAILS ?= wails

A macOS universal binary and a Linux build with the webkit2_41 tag are not
things a unit test can confirm. Budget the work here, not in the two Go files.

WHAT DOES NOT MOVE, and it is most of the gate. cmd/devharness does not import
Wails at all, so the headless path, the Playwright suite and all three
containerized CI jobs are untouched. Only the `backend` job and the release
workflow are in scope.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The app builds and runs on macOS and Linux from the release workflow, and the
  produced artifacts are launched once each by hand before the bead closes.
- The three OS conveniences still work and are exercised: a notification is
  raised and its click resolves, the file dialog opens and cancels cleanly, and
  clipboard get/set round-trips.
- internal/storage/appdir.go still resolves nocx-dev without `-tags release`
  and nocx with it — a dev stand must not acquire the shipped profile
  directory (nocx-ti8w).
- cmd/devharness, the e2e suite and the three containerized CI jobs pass
  unchanged, with no edit to any of them.
- Nothing new imports Wails: the count stays at two Go files, or the bead says
  why it grew.
notes: macOS VERIFICATION IS THE OWNER'S, agreed 2026-08-16. The worker is on Linux and cannot build a darwin/universal binary, so the macOS half of release.yml lands UNVERIFIED by construction and the worker has been told to say so rather than claim it works. The owner will run it. Do not close this bead on a green Linux build alone — the acceptance criterion 'the produced artifacts are launched once each by hand' needs both halves, and the macOS half is handed over, not skipped.

title: The WebSocket has no origin check and no connection auth, which is fine for a webview and not for a browser
description:
The owner raised opening nocx in an ordinary browser (2026-08-16). Most of the
path already exists: cmd/devharness runs the backend with no Wails and no
display, main.ts falls back to the WS port when GetWSPort is unavailable, and
the whole e2e suite rides that path. What does not exist is the security
control that makes it safe, and this bead is that control — not the feature.

WHAT IS TRUE TODAY, verified rather than assumed. internal/transport/ws.go
listens on 127.0.0.1:0 (loopback, random port) and performs NO authentication
and NO origin check: CheckOrigin appears nowhere, and every token in that file
belongs to the import-plan store, not to the connection. The security model is
entirely "only a local process can reach it, and the only local process that
does is our own webview".

WHY THAT MODEL BREAKS THE MOMENT A BROWSER IS ALLOWED. A WebSocket handshake
from a browser page is NOT subject to the same-origin policy the way XHR is:
any page the user visits can open ws://127.0.0.1:<port>. The random port is
obscurity, not a control — a page can scan it in under a second. Behind that
socket are shell spawning, filesystem access and the vault unlock flow, so the
consequence of a successful connection is a shell on the user machine, not a
data leak. nocx-52b is the same class already met once in this repo: "XSS in
the connections UI + no CSP = renderer takeover".

SHAPE, not prescribed: the connection must prove it was launched by us rather
than merely reaching us — an Origin allow-list plus a per-launch secret the
webview (or the browser tab we opened) carries and a foreign page cannot
guess. The token-in-URL form Jupyter uses is the familiar one. Both halves are
needed: an Origin check alone is forgeable by a non-browser client, and a
token alone leaks through URL history and referrers.

DELIBERATELY OUT: the browser feature itself, any remote (non-loopback) bind,
and multi-window. Wails v2 cannot open a second window at all — its runtime
has no window-creation call, every function is Window* operating on the one
window — so multi-window is a Wails v3 question and a separate decision.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A connection without a valid Origin AND a valid per-launch secret is refused
  before any RPC is dispatched, and the refusal is tested over the real socket.
- The secret is per launch, never persisted, and never appears in a log line.
- The Wails path still connects with no user-visible change.
- A test asserts a forged Origin alone does not admit, and that a leaked token
  presented from a foreign Origin does not admit either.
close_reason:
WRONG, and closed as invalid rather than left open. Both controls this bead asked for ALREADY EXIST and are enforced.

internal/transport/ws_auth.go carries:
  - OriginPolicy, with LoopbackOriginPolicy for development and PinnedOriginPolicy for production ('exactly the origins the shipped app…'), matching scheme and hostname while deliberately ignoring the port because it exists only under wails dev;
  - a per-launch connection token: tokenProtocolPrefix 'nocx.token.', tokenBytes = 32, WithTokenSource, Token().

And it is enforced at the handshake: ws.go:1008 sets s.upgrader.Subprotocols = []string{tokenProtocol(s.token)}, so gorilla completes the upgrade only for a client that requested the matching subprotocol. A page that does not know the token cannot connect.
