title: Your tabs, their blocks and their workspaces come back — if you want them to
description:
Design: .internal/specs/2026-08-15-workspaces-ux-design.md §8.2 and §8.3.
Owner's decision 2026-08-15, with Warp as the reference.

WHAT IS TRUE TODAY, verified rather than assumed: NOTHING comes back.
restoreDescriptor is written in four places, typed unknown, and read nowhere —
frontend/src/file-viewer/index.ts:85 says so in as many words. The only
tab-related setting in internal/settings is TabPlacement. internal/session has no
restore path. On start you get one fresh local tab, whatever you had open.
(The prior workspaces design asserted the opposite; nocx-qfwrc is that fix.)

WHAT A USER CAN DO THAT THEY CANNOT TODAY: quit with eight tabs across three
workspaces, reopen, and find them — with their blocks — exactly where they were.
Or turn it off and get a clean start, deliberately.

TWO SETTINGS FOR TWO FEATURES, and conflating them would give one control
governing two behaviours (this is Warp's shape and it is right):
  - General: 'Restore windows, tabs, and panes on startup'.
  - Session: 'Enable reopening of closed sessions', with a GRACE PERIOD in
    seconds — undo-close while the app is running.

RESTORING A TAB IS NOT RESURRECTING A PROCESS. D5 of the workspaces/lineage
design stands: workers die with the backend. What comes back is the TAB — kind,
endpoint, cwd, workspace — re-opened, plus its BLOCKS. Anything that tries to
resurrect the process is the remote-helper epic (nocx-1p1h4), not this one.
Without this paragraph someone builds that by accident.

THE DURABILITY OF BLOCKS IS CONDITIONAL, AND THIS EPIC INHERITS THE CONDITION.
contentDB starts as content.NewStub(logger) (app.go:449) and is wired to the
transport at app.go:600; BOTH failure paths in between leave it a stub — an
unreadable content key and a store that will not open — each announced by a
slogger.Warn and nothing else. That is AGENTS.md's own named anti-pattern, quoted
with this very feature as its example. Sharper still: content.go:77-82 says the
Ledger() surface has no caller outside tests until the ledger.* cutover, and the
ledger is where sessions and workspaces live.

So the criterion is stated at BOTH ENDS, per AGENTS.md testing rule 3: with a
live store the blocks come back; with a degraded store the product SAYS SO.
Never a restored tab silently missing its history.

WHY ITS OWN EPIC. nocx-mqie persists window geometry, sidebar state and the
ACTIVE tab, and explicitly excludes 'restoring the tab SET and live PTY sessions
across restarts'. This is that excluded deliverable. It uses mqie's UI-state
store rather than inventing a second one — hence the dependency.

DELIBERATELY OUT: resurrecting processes; restoring remote sessions' live state;
any authority behaviour on restore.

## Success Criteria

See acceptance.
acceptance_criteria: With the setting ON, a user with eight tabs across three workspaces (one default, two named) quits and reopens: every tab returns, in its workspace, with its blocks, and the workspace names and colours are intact. With the setting OFF, the same quit and reopen gives one fresh local tab. Watched end to end by an automated check, both ways. AND: with the content store degraded to the stub, a restore returns the tabs and the product states that history is unavailable — asserted by a test, because the degraded path is the one with coverage today. DONE WHEN both settings exist, both directions are asserted, and no restored tab is silently missing its blocks.
notes:
AMENDED 2026-08-17 by .internal/specs/2026-08-16-tabs-panes-and-blocks-design.md §8.
The body above is intact and still right; what follows narrows it to the model
that epic settled, and it must be read before this epic is taken.

THE ANCHOR IS THE PANE, NOT THE SESSION. nocx-49d4 said the ledger's session row
is the restore key; §11 of the new design withdraws that. A block hangs on
block.pane_id — durable, minted by the frontend as a UUIDv7, and what makes
restore possible at all — and remembers block.session_id as PROVENANCE, null once
that pipe is gone. Anchoring only on the session loses every block the moment the
backend restarts, which is exactly what `entries.session_id REFERENCES sessions(id)
ON DELETE SET NULL` does today.

WHAT COMES BACK: the workspaces, their tabs with their decoration and layout,
their panes with their cwd, and the blocks with their output. WHAT DOES NOT: the
process. D5 is unchanged and ADR-0019 requires the difference to be VISIBLE —
"live resumption cannot be synthesized from blocks, and nothing in the UI may
imply it".

RESTORE IS DECIDED BY THE PANE'S KIND, NOT BY A DIALOG. Three cases, and the
third exists only because §6.1's provenance edge exists:

• A LOCAL pane opens its blocks and starts a FRESH SHELL IN THE SAME CWD. There
  is nothing to ask: locally a shell can always be started, and the only failure
  is a cwd that no longer exists, which falls back to home.
• An SSH pane opens its blocks and ATTEMPTS TO RECONNECT. A sealed vault raises
  the unlock automatically — the mechanism exists — and nocx-o9jdu, the defect
  where eight panes reconnecting at once asked eight times, is already fixed on
  feat/workspaces.
• An INLINE `ssh` — one entered inside a local pane — is treated as EXITED. The
  pane returns as its local shell, and the blocks that ran on the far host keep
  saying so through their session provenance. Without that edge the restored pane
  would have to either lie about where those blocks ran or drop them.

A RESTORED PANE MAY HAVE A HOLE, AND IT MUST SAY SO. ADR-0019 §7 requires
reconstruction to state its own horizon: retention evicts artifacts, and a block
whose output is gone renders as a block with an HONEST MARKER, never as a block
that printed nothing. What that marker looks like is undesigned (§12 q. 3) and
designing it is part of this epic.

STILL OPEN, and this epic decides it rather than inheriting a drift: what the
SEEN-MARK restores to (§12 q. 2). A tab that had unseen activity when the app
closed — is it still unseen on the other side?

BLOCKED IN PRACTICE BY nocx-rtg0.28, recorded here because bd refuses an epic-to-task edge.

entries has no pane_id. It anchors on session_id ... ON DELETE SET NULL and nothing else — verbatim the line §6.1 of the 2026-08-16 design quotes as the defect it exists to fix. A session dies with the backend (D5); a pane does not; so after a restart every block hangs on nothing while the pane whose blocks they were sits there with a durable row.

This is not 'restore is unbuilt'. It is that the column making restore POSSIBLE is absent, and every day the ledger records commands against this schema is a day of blocks that can never be re-attached. Do not start this epic before rtg0.28 lands, or its first task will be to add that column anyway, with a week of unanchored rows behind it.

Note also that nocx-isoph.4 already made the strip survive an application restart — tabs and panes come back with fresh local shells. So the visible gap today is exactly the blocks, which is what this epic adds along with cwd and ssh reconnect.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
RESTORED 2026-08-18. The notes above were overwritten by a
coordinator using `bd update --notes`, which REPLACES the field
rather than appending to it. Recovered verbatim from the tracked
export at 08172a0a. What follows below is what was written over
them, kept because it is also true.
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

2026-08-18, from nocx-rtg0.28. The condition this epic inherits now has a
concrete name and half an answer.

DONE: entries.pane_id exists and is the durable anchor. A block written in a
pane is found by that pane after a full backend restart, session_id is nulled
at every start (dropDeadSessions, because a session dies with the backend), and
QueryEntries takes a PaneID filter — the read this epic's restore is made of,
through the one ordering implementation rather than a second statement.

NOT DONE, and restore cannot land before it: nocx-rtg0.29. The renderer never
sends paneId on open, so in the shipped product every entry's anchor is NULL.
There is nothing to restore until that is wired, whatever the schema says. The
dependency could not be recorded as an edge — an epic may only be blocked by an
epic — so it is written here instead.

title: The e2e stand never sees bracketed paste: a program that sets DECSET 2004 still reads as inactive at fire time
description:
Found while writing e2e/snippets.spec.ts (nocx-7ude).

The multi-line snippet policy has two branches: with bracketed paste ON the body is pasted, with it OFF the fire is refused because a newline would be read as Return (design §9.4). The OFF branch is covered end to end and passes. The ON branch could not be arranged in the e2e container at all.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. PW_PROJECTS=chromium e2e/run-in-container.sh with a spec that starts 'printf \033[?2004h; read -r x; printf got-%s $x' in a pane, then fires a two-line snippet with the palette chord.
2. The panel shows 'this snippet has more than one line and the running program has not enabled bracketed paste'.
3. Same result with 'bash -i' as the program — a nested interactive shell whose readline turns the mode on at its own prompt (bash 5.2, enable-bracketed-paste defaults on).

Expected: the fire is delivered, because the destination did enable the mode.

What is NOT the cause: the renderer's own read. frontend/src/renderers/xterm.test.ts now has 'bracketed paste, read from the real parser' — a real XtermRenderer, the real parser, \x1b[?2004h then \x1b[?2004l — and bracketedPasteActive() answers true then false. Every other test of the policy MOCKS that method, which is why nothing caught this earlier.

So either the sequence never reaches xterm in the stand (an OSC 0 title set the same way also had no effect, which points the same way) or something resets the mode between the program setting it and the fire reading it. Worth knowing whichever it is: if a shipped pane behaves like the stand, EVERY multi-line snippet is refused for everybody, always.

## Acceptance Criteria

[ ] The cause is named: the bytes are missing from the stream, or the mode is reset, with the place it happens
[ ] e2e/snippets.spec.ts covers the ON branch end to end — a multi-line body delivered to a program that enabled the mode
[ ] If the product is at fault rather than the stand, the fix has a unit test at the seam that was wrong

title: x
The backend calls a WebSocket connection a tab
description:
Found while the owner was working on notifications (worktree feat/notifications):
the backend has no concept of a tab, and the one place it claims to is lying.

internal/transport/ws_history_record.go:339 —

    // tabID is the per-connection identity captures are scoped to
    func tabID(wconn *wsConn) string { return strconv.FormatUint(wconn.id, 10) }

It returns the WEBSOCKET CONNECTION id. Two comments in the same package say why
that is not a tab: ws_lifecycle.go:147 'one WebSocket owns several terminal tabs',
and sessionIDsOf in this very file 'a tab can hold several sessions'. So history
captures — DestroyTab, the Tab field on a record — are scoped per CONNECTION
while being named per TAB. One renderer window with eight tabs is one scope.

Two surfaces owning one name is the AD-8 shape. The fix is not a rename: either
the scope is genuinely the connection and says so, or the renderer supplies a
real tab identity on the wire and the backend keys on that.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND NAMING. The workspaces UX settled 2026-08-15 makes the
workspace a BOUNDARY on addressing, spawning, observing and input — all backend
operations, and an enrolled external agent (design D13) never touches the
renderer at all. A boundary the backend cannot name is a UI convention. So
workspaceId has to be a fact on the SESSION in the backend, with the tab as the
renderer's projection. nocx-ebl4 already carries the field; this bug is the
reason it cannot be nullable and cannot be frontend-only.

Related: internal/session has no restore path at all — tabs survive a restart
through internal/settings, with the frontend re-opening them (design §4.2).

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open two terminal tabs in one window.
2. Record a history capture from each.
3. Read the Tab field on both records: it is the same value.

## Acceptance Criteria

Either the scope is renamed to what it is (connection) with a test asserting two
tabs in one window share it deliberately, or a real per-tab identity crosses the
wire and a test asserts two tabs in one window get DIFFERENT capture scopes.
The comment at the seam states which was chosen and why the other was not.
notes:
ESCALATED BY THE wv1-wyp3p WORKER, 2026-08-15, correctly and without writing a
line of code. Its evidence was re-verified by the coordinator against the tree.

THE RESOLUTION IS OPTION 2 (a real per-tab identity, minted by the renderer and
sent on the wire), NOT option 1 (rename the scope to the connection). Renaming
would make the backend honest about the granularity it can express, but
internal/credential/capture.go:11-14 names TAB CLOSURE as a destruction trigger
distinct from transport disconnect, and the renderer already assumes it happens.
The smaller change is not the honest one here.

The behavioural half is now nocx-tsajw, which is P1 and is the reason this bead
cannot be closed by a rename: a closed tab's pending credential capture is never
destroyed, and a record failure in one tab destroys every tab's.

FOURTH CONSUMER, not previously noted: ws_agent.go:901 uses tabID(w) as clientID
for the agent ask/captureFrame idempotency binding, and that one is GENUINELY
connection-scoped — 'a reconnect mints a new one'. It must stay connection-keyed
and be renamed honestly rather than swept into the change.

PARKED, NOT FAILED. Both implementation paths cross files owned by the wv1-ictcq
worker in the same wave — frontend/src/terminal-content.ts (the history.record
caller and dispose-time destruction), frontend/src/tabs.ts (the identity source),
and internal/transport/ws.go:2431 (the exit-path DestroyTab). Re-dispatched after
that worker lands. The worktree fix/nocx-wyp3p-tab-scope is unchanged and kept.

title: The cascade's global-defaults rung has no store and no surface, so a per-user answer must be repeated per connection
description:
The effective-profile cascade is profile → group → global → hardcoded. Three of
those four rungs work. The global one is a parameter every production caller
fills with nothing.

`ResolveEffectiveProfile` (internal/profile/profile.go) takes `globalDefaults
SparseSSHOptions` and applies it as FieldSourceGlobal. Every call site in the
product passes `profile.SparseSSHOptions{}`: internal/connection/resolver.go:153,
internal/capability/secret.go:303, :428, :443, internal/transport/ws_groups.go
(four sites) and internal/transport/ws_config_handlers.go:1022. There is no
store behind the layer and no surface that edits it. The renderer already
renders its provenance — connections.tsx:86 returns "from global defaults" — a
label for a source no field can currently have.

What the user loses is one place to answer a question that is per-user, not per
connection: "install shell integration everywhere", "never offer me the helper
binary", "relay on everything". Today the only rungs that can carry such an
answer are the group (which not every connection belongs to) and the connection
itself, so the answer has to be repeated. Ad-hoc and alias destinations have no
profile at all, so for them there is no rung above the hardcoded default.

ADR-0033 fixes what an UNANSWERED destination resolves to (`auto`), which is the
other half of this. It says so explicitly: the default is only half the answer to
"must I edit every connection" — this bead is the half that lets a user answer
once, deliberately, for everything.

nocx-p15s already holds the contract change this wiring owes on the credential
side: ComputeSecretUsage skips the global source today, and the day the layer has
a store that skip becomes silent undercounting in the delete blast radius. That
bead is the consequence; this one is the capability, and it must not land without
it.

Deliberately NOT in scope: relay consent, which is keyed by host-key fingerprint
and never inherited (a group cannot answer for a machine) — see nocx-f4o70.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Settings, and the connection manager: there is no surface that sets a default
   for all connections. Every delivery-mode, port-discovery or behaviour answer
   must be given per connection or per group.
2. Create two connections in no group. Set Delivery mode on each. There is no
   third place that could have answered for both.
3. `grep -rn "ResolveEffectiveProfile(" --include=*.go internal/ | grep -v _test`
   — every production call passes `profile.SparseSSHOptions{}`.
4. The renderer can render "from global defaults" (connections.tsx:86) for a
   provenance no field can ever have.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A user sets a delivery mode once, in one place, and a connection that has
  chosen nothing resolves to it — asserted end to end, not only in the resolver.
- The stored global defaults are a real persisted document, resolved through the
  same SparseSSHOptions layer the signature already takes; no second cascade.
- Provenance is honest: a field taking its value from the global layer reports
  FieldSourceGlobal, and the renderer's existing "from global defaults" string
  becomes reachable — asserted by a test that reads it.
- Precedence holds in both directions: a group overrides global, a connection
  overrides its group, and clearing a connection's value falls back to global
  rather than to the hardcoded default.
- nocx-p15s is closed with this, or by it: ComputeSecretUsage no longer skips the
  global source, and a credential used by every profile through a global default
  reports its real blast radius in the delete confirmation.
- The hardcoded default stays what ADR-0033 says it is; this bead adds a rung
  above it, it does not change what silence means.

title: Coalescing overwrites the first event's body, so both messages are lost
description:
deliverWindow (internal/notify/policy.go:229) builds the delivered event from the
window-opening event and then replaces its body outright:

    ev := s.first
    if s.count > 1 {
        ev.Body = fmt.Sprintf('%d notifications', s.count)
    }

So a session that says 'build finished' and then 'tests failed' inside one window
produces a banner carrying the FIRST event's title and the body '2
notifications'. The first message is overwritten and the second was never
carried, so the user is told that two things happened and none of what they were.

The spec (§6.2) asks for 'one notification naming the count', which this
satisfies literally while losing the only content the notification had. Compare
the platforms that do this well: they keep the most recent message as the body
and put the count beside it, so the banner still says something.

Depends on nocx-jiwq.4 -- once the first event is delivered on the leading edge,
the window-close notification is a summary of what was SUPPRESSED, which changes
what its body should say.

## Steps to Reproduce

In internal/notify: Submit two events for one {session, kind} with distinct
bodies inside one window, advance the window, and read the delivery. Observed:
title of the first, body '2 notifications'. Neither body survives.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The delivered notification carries a body a user can act on, not only a count.
- A test names both submitted bodies and asserts what the delivered one says.
- The count is still present, and is still payload-independent so ADR-0029's
  noninterference property test keeps passing.
close_reason: Fixed on fix/nocx-jiwq-policy (7d3e7bbf). The summary now carries the count in its title and the newest held-back event's content — title and body joined — in its body, so a coalesced window says what happened and not only how often. Accounted for nocx-jiwq.4 having moved the debounce to the leading edge underneath the bead: the closing delivery is a summary of what was SUPPRESSED, not the first event plus a count. A bodyless event falls back to its title. Memory bounded at one extra Event per open window. Reviewed and corrected once by the coordinator: the first version kept only last.Body and dropped last.Title, which for an OSC 777 title;body payload lost the informative half — the same defect one size smaller.

title: A saved endpoint's brand-new key reads as deleted until the page is reopened
description:
The endpoints row derives its credential fact client-side, by looking the
endpoint's credential reference up in the vault inventory the page holds
(rowCredentialState in endpoints-section.tsx). A save that carries a key
MINTS a secret, but the inventory was loaded before that, so the row reports
'deleted' — the page tells a person their brand-new key was deleted, one
second after they typed it. Reopening the page fixes it, which is how it
stayed invisible.

Found by the ask walk's e2e (agent-ask.spec.ts), which creates the endpoint
through the surface and then asserts the row says "Key saved".

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open Settings -> Endpoints with an unsealed vault.
2. Create an endpoint with a key.
3. The saved row reads "The endpoint's key was deleted — add it again".

## Acceptance Criteria

- After a successful save that mints a key, the row says the key is saved,
  with no reopen — asserted end to end.
close_reason: Fixed in 8e667731: a successful save reloads the vault inventory the row's credential fact is derived from.

title: The pre-commit hook lints frontend/ only, so the root config's territory is ungated
description:
The hook's lint step is `cd frontend && npm run lint`, so its scope is
frontend/. eslint.config.mjs at the root owns everything else — e2e/**,
playwright.config.ts, .githooks/**/*.mjs — and deliberately ignores
frontend/, which has its own type-checked config. Nothing in the hook ran
it, and the frontend step is additionally gated on staged frontend/ changes,
so a commit touching only e2e/ ran no eslint at all.

This is the second half of a repair that only landed for one checker. Root
`eslint .` and `prettier --check .` used to run ONLY in this hook, where they
died on EACCES against the e2e container's root-owned .e2e/ — a crashing gate
reports nothing, and 19 lint errors and 15 unformatted files accumulated
behind it (nocx-z9s9.8). The repair added the ignore, gave CI its own steps
(scripts/ci-frontend.sh) and widened the hook's PRETTIER to the root
(nocx-yv37, nocx-pvjj). eslint was never widened back.

Cost, measured on this PR: an unused constant in e2e/vault-sealed-probe.spec.ts
survived from the commit that introduced it until ci-frontend failed a pull
request with it.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Add an unused const to any file under e2e/.
2. Stage and commit it: every gate reports OK.
3. Push: ci-frontend fails on `eslint .` at the root.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A commit that introduces a root-config lint error is refused by the hook,
  whether or not it also touches frontend/.
- The frontend and root lint steps are named distinctly in the hook's output,
  so a failure says which config spoke.
close_reason: Fixed in 3955e3c4: the hook runs the root eslint unconditionally beside prettier, and the two steps are named eslint (root) / eslint (frontend).

title: A refused manifest upgrade leaks a temp file on every connection
description:
commitManifest writes tmp/manifest-<nonce>.tmp before renaming it into place. cleanupOrphans — the sweep that bounds tmp/ — runs only on Publish's success path, and sweepEmptyRoot only fires for an invocation that created an empty root.

PR #87 made sftpFS.Rename refuse to replace an existing manifest on a server without posix-rename@openssh.com. That refusal is deliberate and correct, but the nonce is fresh per attempt, so every connection to such a host leaves another dead manifest behind, forever.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Publish once to a host whose SFTP server lacks posix-rename@openssh.com.
2. Bump the script version and reconnect several times.
3. tmp/ gains one manifest-*.tmp per attempt.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A failed commitManifest removes the temp it wrote; a successful one does not (the rename consumed it).
- Repeated refusals converge: tmp/ holds no manifest-*.tmp afterwards.
- The prior activation still remains byte-identical.
- Covered by a test that fails without the fix.
close_reason: commitManifest sweeps its own temp on failure, not on success (the rename consumed it). The refusal test now asserts convergence over repeated attempts and fails without the fix. Pushed as 3ba6ccd5.

title: Remote integration upgrade refused on a non-atomic SFTP server degrades invisibly
description:
sftpFS.Rename (internal/shellintegration/install_remote.go) refuses to replace an existing manifest.json when the server does not advertise posix-rename@openssh.com — deliberately, because remove-then-rename would leave a window with no activation pointer. The refusal reaches ssh_real.go:773, which is a slog.Warn and nothing else.

The user therefore keeps running whatever integration version was published first, forever, with no indication anywhere in the product. AGENTS.md: 'A soft degrade must be visible in the product, not only in a log.'

The fail-open warn predates this branch; what is new is a second, permanent way to arrive at it.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Connect a saved profile to a host whose SFTP server does not advertise posix-rename@openssh.com and let nocx publish the bundle once.
2. Bump the integration script version (internal/shellintegration/scripts.go) and reconnect.
3. The publish is refused; the host keeps the old generation. The UI says nothing.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A refused upgrade surfaces on the session integration axis with a stated reason, the same surface a launch-time refusal uses — not only a log line.
- The prior manifest still remains byte-identical after the refusal (already covered by TestSFTPFSRename_WithoutPosixExtensionKeepsPriorActivation).
- One automated check watches the reason reach the renderer.

title: The agent has no idea when a command ran, and neither does the person scrolling back
description:
Owner, 2026-08-15: «агенту нужна будет метка времени команды, в UI время и дату тоже можно добавить».

Two halves of one fact, and the first half is the load-bearing one.

## For the model

"When did this run" changes answers. A model reading a block cannot tell whether an error is from thirty seconds ago or from yesterday's session, whether two blocks it was granted are minutes or days apart, or whether "the last time this worked" is before or after the change the person is asking about. Ordering is not enough: the ledger's order is causal, not temporal, and a restored session interleaves.

So whatever carries a block to the model carries when it ran and how long it took. The ledger already records both — this is about the context surface, not about new storage. When the reading tools land (the tools epic) the listing is where it belongs; until then it belongs beside the block's text.

## For the person

A block shows its duration but not its wall-clock time. The editor chrome shows a time chip for the CURRENT prompt, so the vocabulary exists; a finished block does not keep one. Scrolling back through a long session, there is no way to answer "when was that" without counting.

Deliberately open, and the reason it is not decided here: a timestamp on every block is noise in a fast session where ten commands run in a minute. Options are a time on the block, a time on hover, or a day separator in the flow when the date changes — the last being cheapest and quietest. Decide with the owner, and say which was chosen and why.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The context a model receives for a block carries when the command ran and how long it took, asserted on what the engine is handed.
- The timestamp comes from the ledger's own record, not from a second clock read at context-assembly time, asserted — two sources for one fact is the defect this repo keeps finding.
- A restored session's blocks carry their ORIGINAL times, not the restore's, asserted across a restart.
- The person can learn when a finished block ran without leaving the flow, in whichever form was chosen, asserted through the DOM.
- Whatever renders it reuses the existing time vocabulary rather than formatting a date a second way.

title: The endpoints list offers no Test on a saved endpoint — only edit and delete
description:
Owner, 2026-08-15, with a screenshot of the Endpoints page listing a saved endpoint: 'здесь в списке тоже нужна иконка test'.

A saved endpoint row carries a pencil and a bin. To find out whether the endpoint still answers — the credential is still valid, the address still resolves, the models are still there — a person must open the editor and press Test connection inside it. The check exists (nocx-q27y gave Test a connection check that needs no model, and nocx-reu5 made it use the endpoint's own stored credential); it is just unreachable from the place where a person is looking at their endpoints.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Settings -> Endpoints with at least one saved endpoint.
2. The row shows name, schema badge, model count, 'Key saved', and two actions: edit, delete.
3. There is no way to test the endpoint without opening the editor.

## Expected behavior

The row offers Test beside edit and delete, and reports its outcome on the row.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A saved endpoint's row carries a Test action, reachable by keyboard, asserted through the row a person sees.
- Activating it runs the SAME connection check the editor's Test button runs — one owner, not a second call path — asserted by watching the client method the editor already uses.
- The outcome is rendered on the row and names which check ran and what it found, in the vocabulary the editor already uses (nocx-q27y decided those sentences; do not invent new ones).
- A row whose credential cannot resolve says so instead of running a check that cannot pass, using the credential state agent.status already reports (nocx-y7fg's enum).
- The action is a kit control with the icon vocabulary the row's other two actions use; no bespoke button.
close_reason: A saved endpoint's row carries Test, running the same call the editor's button runs, reporting in the sentences nocx-q27y already decided, and refusing to run when the credential state says it cannot pass. Merged with the record-row composite.

title: The ADR-0020 grant path is written and unreachable
description:
internal/content/ has the whole ADR-0020 authority path: GrantPolicy (:151, 'the autonomy preset the workspace mints'), StartExecution{Grant} (:286), Grant 'the authority recorded on a run' (:319), GrantScope (:329), a sqlite implementation (ledger_sqlite.go:279) and a stub (stub.go:164).

Nothing calls StartExecution from outside internal/content/.

## Steps to Reproduce

    grep -rn 'StartExecution' --include=*.go . | grep -v internal/content/    # empty

This is nocx-rtg0's shape returning: 'a reachable read path hid an unreachable write path in the same package'. The package is genuinely reachable, so deadcode is unlikely to report it, and the acceptance criterion 'deadcode is empty' would pass over it exactly as it did for ContentDB.Add — the epic that shipped an encrypted store, a key lifecycle, a budget, a retention policy and five Settings controls while no command was ever recorded.

Found 2026-08-15 while cutting nocx-ebl4 (the foundation epic of the workspaces/lineage design). The first draft of that design put a 'grant source seam' in the foundation, which would have meant adding a parameter to a path with no caller and calling it a foundation. The seam moved to nocx-mp2vd, the epic with the first live minter. This bead is the other half: the path that is already there and does nothing.

Related but NOT the same thing: internal/lifecycle carries a DomainGrant (ADR-0024 lifecycle domains) which IS reachable. Two different concepts share the word 'grant' in this tree, which is its own small hazard.
acceptance_criteria: Either a live caller mints a grant through StartExecution and a test drives it end to end, or the unreachable half is deleted. 'deadcode is clean' is not sufficient evidence either way — the epic that first mints a grant must show a run whose recorded grant came from a real caller.
close_reason: content.StartExecution has its first live caller: the middleware writes the attempt before the tool runs, asserted end to end against a real content store (TestAsk_PermittedReadRecordsTheAttempt). The unreachable half is now reachable rather than deleted.

title: An agent runs workers in sibling sessions, and cannot touch anything it was not given
description:
Design: .internal/specs/2026-08-15-workspaces-lineage-and-orchestration-design.md, sections 5
and 6, and D8/D9/D11/D12/D13/D14. This is the epic the whole design exists for.

WHAT IT CARRIES: Delegation (effects observe | receive-events | send-input | delegate-further |
close, states active | input-suspended | scope-suspended | revoked | expired), AuthorityBinding
and its approval act, the grant-source seam AND its first live minter, enrolment of an external
agent process tree, the evidence model with its five provenances, and the user-editable
detection rules.

WHY THE GRANT SEAM IS HERE AND NOT IN THE FOUNDATION EPIC. StartExecution has no caller outside
internal/content/ (verified 2026-08-15) — the ADR-0020 grant path is written and unreachable.
Adding a source parameter to it earlier would widen a dead write path; it lands here, with the
caller that makes it live.

TWO RULES BOUGHT BY REVIEW, both of which the first design got wrong:

- Lineage proves PROVENANCE, not continuing authority. A created B; B is then taken over,
  re-credentialed and ssh'd into production; B is a descendant of A forever, so ancestry alone
  would leave A reading and driving a session whose operator and context changed. Continuing
  authority is the separate revocable Delegation, and its discriminator is "did the
  authenticated authority context change", NOT "did a human touch the PTY".
- An environment variable is not a capability. A token there is inherited by every descendant,
  so `npm test` hands it to a dependency's postinstall script; it also leaks through
  /proc/<pid>/environ, env, sudo -E, crash reports and agent transcripts. The principal is the
  enrolled process TREE, pinned by a non-reusable handle, and the product says so: "allow this
  agent AND commands it launches". Attempting to attribute subprocesses is a guess we will not
  make.

An inherited control FD was considered and rejected for the external CLI: the agent cannot pass
it to a shim without passing it to every other child, and CLOEXEC stops the shim receiving it
either. It stays useful inside nocx, where we own both ends.

HARD PREREQUISITE THE BACKLOG CANNOT EXPRESS AS AN EDGE: nocx-ms7v.4, the attention queue.
bd refuses a blocks edge from an epic to a task, so this note is the edge. It is load-bearing
rather than nice-to-have: today frontend/src/tabs.ts:52 is ONE boolean per tab, cleared by
activating the tab (:170) and not set while it is active (:265) — so three workers that
finished, asked and failed collapse into one dot that activation erases. Without a durable,
typed, individually acknowledged queue, this epic's headline acceptance cannot be written, let
alone pass.

DELIBERATELY OUT: policy revision editing and migration UI; anything remote (epic E); a manifest
catalogue fetched over the network — rules are local, user-editable, switchable off per agent,
and shipped with a live "what is this agent emitting" view, without which a rule the user must
write blind is a dead rule.

## Success Criteria

See acceptance.
acceptance_criteria:
Watched end to end: a user starts an agent in a tab, asks it for work that needs two machines,
and the agent opens a child session on each; the user walks away; one child finishes, one asks
for approval, one fails. The user returns, sees all three in the attention queue as three
separate entries, answers the one that asked, and dismisses the other two — and dismissing is
an explicit act that survives a restart.

Authority, each asserted rather than reviewed:
- The agent can address its own children and cannot address its parent, a sibling, or any
  session in another workspace. Asserted by attempting each and checking the refusal, and by
  checking that the forbidden sessions are not even enumerable to it.
- A grant is minted only from a GrantSource; a test proves no code path can mint one without.
- A session created in workspace X and moved to workspace Y does not gain Y's authority: the
  next run still mints from the binding approved for X, and the UI says which.
- Human takeover of a child SUSPENDS the coordinator's send-input and PRESERVES its observe;
  handing the same attempt back in the same lifecycle domain restores control under the same
  delegation epoch. Helping a worker past a y/n prompt does not sever it — this is the case the
  first design of this got wrong.
- Takeover that changes the authenticated authority context — new credential, different
  lifecycle domain — moves the delegation to scope-suspended, and control does not resume
  without a human.
- Revoking a delegation stops new control immediately and erases no history.

Enrolment:
- `claude` TYPED BY HAND into a tab can be enrolled and then open children. This is the owner's
  stated case and the acceptance stands or falls on it.
- Enrolment requires human approval naming the executable, and the approval states that it
  covers commands the agent launches.
- No bearer material is placed in the environment: asserted by dumping the spawned environment
  and checking.
- A process outside the enrolled tree, same uid, cannot use the control surface.
- Enrolment does not survive the enrolled root's exit, and a reused pid does not revive it.

State:
- An observation is bound to a session epoch, lifecycle domain, attempt and output offset. A
  late inferred observation describing an earlier attempt does not overwrite a declared one.
- A heuristic observation never reaches a notification target.
notes:
AMENDED 2026-08-15 by .internal/specs/2026-08-15-workspaces-ux-design.md §5, after
an adversarial review. This epic now owns the WORKSPACE FENCE, and it inherits
four questions open BY NAME rather than a finished design.

THE FENCE. A session in one workspace may not reach another — no addressing,
spawning, observing or input, through nocx. Formally:

  effective run authority =
      RunGrant(snapshot from the session's AuthorityBinding)
    INTERSECT current workspace fence

THIS AMENDS ADR-0020 §5 — it does not merely interpret it. The ADR says the
workspace 'is not the enforcement object'; the fence makes it an operand the
backend consults before dispatching, and subtraction is an authorization
decision. What survives is the ADR's actual prohibition, which is on SILENCE:
'dragging a tab must never SILENTLY confer or revoke'. The ADR needs the clause
proposed in design §5.1, and writing it is part of this epic.

WHAT BUYS THE AMENDMENT: a workspace move is a change of authenticated authority
context, so D8's scope-suspended applies — presentation changes at once,
authority does not resume without human approval. Three cases, because suspending
only delegations is not enough: a plain human-driven ssh tab has nothing to
suspend and must stay free; a session with a BINDING but no delegations must have
the binding stop being an eligible grant source until re-approval; a session with
delegations suspends every edge whose context changed.

OPEN BY NAME, all four must be answered before this ships:
1. Whether a subtree move suspends the delegation edges INTERNAL to the subtree.
2. Who may re-approve a suspended binding, and whether per binding or per
   workspace. (The prior design's §11.1 already left this open.)
3. The atomic ordering of membership change and suspension. The requirement is
   stated as an interval in design §5.3; the mechanism is not designed.
4. What happens to work ALREADY DISPATCHED when suspension lands. Immutability of
   the RunGrant is not a licence to keep dispatching: the dispatcher must require
   both the immutable grant AND a currently-active binding or delegation.

D9 LOST ITS MECHANISM. 'Spawning is permitted only into an environment the
workspace lists' has no list any more — the owner withdrew D2's rows. The
candidate, NOT decided, is in design §8.1: derive the reachable set from the
endpoints of the sessions currently in the workspace, so widening it by a drag is
a scope expansion that asks at the next spawn (ADR-0020 §6). This epic owes the
decision.

AND THE DECOMPOSITION CHANGED. The prior design's §10 made this epic independent
of the workspace epic, because D3 allowed workspace-less operation and D9 fell
back to the parent's environment. Both are withdrawn: workspaces are mandatory
and D9's rule is gone. The 'critical path is A -> C' claim is stale.

title: Your tabs group into workspaces, and the backend owns the whole chain
description:
Design: .internal/specs/2026-08-16-tabs-panes-and-blocks-design.md §3, §4, §5, §7, §10.
REWRITTEN 2026-08-17. Supersedes the membership-only version of this epic, which
was itself a rewrite of a rows model.

WHAT CHANGED AND WHY. The membership version put tabs in the renderer and asked
the backend only "which workspace is this in". §4.1 of the new design withdraws
that: an invariant whose two ends live in two processes has no owner, and the fix
is to move the objects rather than to write a protocol. So this epic is now the
one where THE BACKEND BECOMES THE OWNER of workspace, tab and pane, and the
frontend asks it to create, move and destroy them and renders what it is told.

THE CHAIN, and each object exists for a job the others cannot do:

    workspace   flat, never nested, user-created — which tabs are one piece of work
      tab       the strip entry — colour, name, position, pinned, layout, seen-mark
        pane    the durable identity — pipe, cwd, blocks; outlives its shell,
                its tab and the application

A pane's id is minted by the frontend as a UUIDv7 and lives forever; a session id
is minted by the backend and is new every time, because it is embedded in the
remote launcher as NOCX_SESSION_ID before the connection exists (AD-7). Those two
must not be merged: D5 kills the process with the backend and the pane must
survive it.

A FRONTEND-MINTED ID IS UNTRUSTED INPUT and the word is already in the schema.
Three consequences, none optional: the shape is validated and never believed; an
insert on an existing id FAILS rather than overwriting, and a repeat of the SAME
request returns the SAME object (entries.client and entries.digest are what that
is for); and knowing an id confers no right to use it, because UUIDv7 embeds a
timestamp and is guessable by construction. The retry case is not hypothetical —
AD-9 exists because the socket drops, and a create whose answer was lost is
retried.

TWO EDGES ON A TAB, AND THEY MUST NEVER BE ONE (§4.2). `parent` is lineage — who
spawned whom, immutable, never set by hand. The display grouping is the other
edge, symmetric and set by dragging. Carrying both on one column is the failure
AGENTS.md names: the loser goes on advertising what it can no longer deliver.
§4.5 of the workspaces design keeps its refusal intact — dragging between LINEAGE
groups is still refused.

WHAT IS STORED ON A TAB AND WHAT IS ONLY COMPUTED (§4.5). Stored: colour, name,
position, pinned, layout direction, workspace_id, the seen-mark. Computed from
its panes: the activity indicator, the attention indicator, the label. Attention
ARRIVES AT A PANE, so storing it on the tab gives one fact two owners and they
diverge the first time a pane is dragged. The label flows pane -> tab: an unnamed
tab is labelled by its panes' titles, and a name the user types wins.

WHAT LANDS

• Workspaces are flat, never nested; depth in the tree comes only from lineage.
• A tab is always in exactly one workspace. The DEFAULT workspace never renders:
  its tabs are top-level rows with no header, name or colour. Not "invisible
  while it is the only one" — that makes the chrome appear and disappear on a
  counter and forces the default to acquire a name nobody gave it.
• A workspace exists only while it holds at least one tab, and a tab only while
  it holds at least one pane. Both need no lifecycle code: the row goes in the
  same transaction that removes the last member.
• Creation is always creation-with-content: "New workspace" mints it together
  with its first tab.
• Closing a workspace closes all its tabs, asking first, and the dialog NAMES
  what is live. The replacement tab that appears when the last one in the app
  closes belongs to the DEFAULT workspace, never to the one being closed.
• Vertical strip: all workspaces, a tree of workspace -> tab -> lineage children.
  Horizontal strip: a chip on the left, then only the current workspace's tabs;
  in the default workspace the chip is a neutral glyph with no label.
• workspaceId moves from the session to the tab (nocx-fraus). The invariant is
  unchanged — never null, one owner of the default — and the argument for keeping
  it in the backend survives whole, because the backend now owns the whole chain
  and resolves pane -> tab -> workspace itself. internal/workspace already holds
  the Default constant.

THE BACKEND GAINS A TAB ROW; IT GAINS NO TAB ADDRESS (§4.4). §5.2's prohibition
is narrowed, not overturned. Every backend->renderer address stays a sessionId
the renderer resolves, for the reasons §5.2 gives — a tab holds several panes, so
"the tab that spoke" is still not well defined, and the renderer still knows where
a session is.

A WINDOW IS A VIEWPORT, NOT A CONTAINER (§10). It shows one workspace at a time
and owns no tabs. If a window contained tabs, a tab would sit in a window AND in a
workspace and the two would disagree. Multi-window therefore changes no object and
no table here.

THIS EPIC SHIPS MEMBERSHIP AND OWNERSHIP ONLY. The workspace FENCE — the
authorization boundary that consumes membership as one input — is nocx-mp2vd's,
and §5.5 of the workspaces design forbids this epic from advertising it. No shield
or lock iconography, no "safe", "isolated" or "contained", and no copy of the form
"everything here can reach everything else". An adversarial review found the first
draft shipping exactly that promise with no mechanism behind it.

DELIBERATELY OUT: the display grouping and drag (its own epic — dragging a pane
out mints a tab, dragging it in removes an empty one); restore (nocx-l21ib);
blocks and the ledger cutover (nocx-rtg0.3); any authority behaviour; multi-window;
asymmetric or nested pane layouts; and any repository registry outliving a pane.
acceptance_criteria: A user creates a workspace, and it is minted together with its first tab. They open tabs in it and in the default workspace, and the default one never shows a header, a name or a colour. They colour a tab, pin it, rename it and reorder it, and every one of those survives a reload of the renderer WITHOUT the backend restarting — because the backend, not the renderer, is where they were stored. They close the workspace; the dialog names what is live before anything dies, and the tab that replaces the last one in the app is in the default workspace. Asserted end to end by an automated check that drives the real UI against the real backend. Two assertions the shape of this epic makes cheap and are therefore required: sending the same create twice with the same client-minted UUIDv7 returns the SAME tab and creates no second row, over the real socket; and dragging a tab between two LINEAGE groups is still refused. No surface anywhere describes a workspace, a tab or a pane as safe, isolated or contained.
notes:
EDGE REMOVED 2026-08-17: nocx-jv3q no longer blocks this epic. AGENTS.md's rule is that an epic blocks another only when they touch the same code, and that edge was too coarse to be true. This epic's first three children — the store, the wire and the container lifecycle — touch no strip code at all; only nocx-isoph.4 and .5 do. Blocking the whole of workspaces on an unclaimed strip epic meant waiting for row glyphs and a draggable strip width, which is 'not yet' wearing 'overlap'.

The real overlap is recorded where it is real: nocx-jv3q.1 groups the same strip by surfaceType while nocx-isoph.5 groups it by workspace, and both need ONE heading mechanism with the axis as an input. Notes on both say so. nocx-jv3q.2 is where the drop table gets decided once, for all five meanings a drop now has.

nocx-ebl4 still blocks, and correctly: the tab carries workspaceId and the lineage parent edge, and retrofitting session identity afterwards is the wide change §8 exists to avoid. Four of its five children are closed; the last is in flight.

SECOND EDGE REMOVED 2026-08-17: nocx-ebl4 no longer blocks this epic, for the same reason nocx-jv3q stopped. Everything this epic actually needs from the foundation is ALREADY MERGED — session.Identity (nocx-3oupk), session.Ref and validateParent (nocx-9hu9d), liveness (nocx-iarf9) and the non-null workspaceId (nocx-fraus, which had been finished and unmerged for two days). What remains in that epic is two prohibitions, in flight, and a missing producer that overlaps nocx-isoph.4 and is better decided there.

nocx-isoph.1 touches no session code at all — it is three tables and a repository seam. Blocking it on the tail of another epic would be 'not yet' wearing 'overlap', which is the edge AGENTS.md says was wrong 13 times out of 20.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
RESTORED 2026-08-18. The notes above were overwritten by a
coordinator using `bd update --notes`, which REPLACES the field
rather than appending to it. Recovered verbatim from the tracked
export at 08172a0a. What follows below is what was written over
them, kept because it is also true.
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

2026-08-18, from nocx-rtg0.29: the open ack's workspaceId now has a reader at
last — decoded onto SessionHandle and logged — but only as provenance. It
drives nothing, because the contract says it carries no behaviour and design
§5.5 forbids any surface before the fence epic from describing a workspace as
safe, isolated or contained.

TWO THINGS WILL CONSUME IT, named here so the next person does not conclude the
field is decorative. The fence epic is one. The other is a real divergence
nobody owns yet: the renderer CACHES which workspace a pane is in, while the
backend RESOLVES it through pane -> tab -> workspace on every open. Those two
can disagree — a pane dragged between tabs is exactly when — and the ack is the
one message that could reconcile them. It needs a SessionHandle reachable from
the pane layer, which does not exist today. Not filed as a bead because nobody
has yet seen it diverge; if anyone does, this note is where it starts.
close_reason:
Every acceptance criterion is met, and the last of them was proven today by
nocx-isoph.7.

WHAT A USER CAN DO THAT THEY COULD NOT BEFORE: create a workspace and get it
minted together with its first tab; open tabs in it and in the default, and
never see the default show a header, a name or a colour; colour, pin, rename
and reorder tabs and find all four after a renderer reload WITHOUT the backend
restarting, because the backend is where they were stored; close the workspace
and be told what is live before anything dies, with the replacement tab
landing in the default. Asserted end to end against the real backend in both
browsers, plus the two assertions this epic's shape made cheap — the same
create twice with one client-minted UUIDv7 returns the SAME tab over the real
socket, and a drag between two lineage groups is still refused.

The seven children: the rows the backend owns, the frontend that cannot mint
behind its back, containers that exist only while they hold a member, order
and decoration moving out of the renderer, the default that never renders with
the chip beside it, a close that names what is live, and today's — the
affordances that had been horizontal-only.

CLOSED WITH ONE THING DELIBERATELY OUTSIDE IT, and it is not a loose end:
attention counts in the switcher (§4.3) are nocx-taehg, standalone and P3.
They need the liveness rule, and a second spelling of live-work.ts for a
decoration would be the AD-8 defect bought for a badge. Holding this epic open
for it would have turned a finished deliverable into an area of code — the
shape that kept "Persistence" and "Quality gates" from ever finishing.

Gate on the closing tree: frontend 3278 tests green, ci-frontend green, e2e
330 passed / 2 failed with both failures nocx-9jcx7 and unchanged from before
any of this work.

title: A tab knows which tab opened it, and stops lying about whether it is alive
description:
Design: .internal/specs/2026-08-15-workspaces-lineage-and-orchestration-design.md,
sections 4.1, 8 and D6/D7/D8. THE FOUNDATION SLICE, and the only one whose cost rises with delay.

Everything here is SHAPE: fields on the session record, a wire contract, and two prohibitions.
There is no store, no authority model and no agent. The argument for doing it now is nocx-if6
phase A's, reused unchanged — retrofitting session identity after tabs, restore, the ledger and
blocks all key on a bare sessionId is a wide, unpleasant change, while adding it now is
mechanical.

WHAT LANDS

- sessionId plus a backend-instance / session-epoch identity, sufficient to prevent id reuse and
  to tell a restored record from a current incarnation.
- An immutable parent edge using that FULL identity. Bare parentId is not enough: orca validates
  repo, host, project and both endpoint instance ids and strips cycles before projecting
  (src/shared/resolved-worktree-lineage.ts), and it needed all of them.
- NON-NULL workspaceId, carrying no behaviour. Amended 2026-08-16 per
  .internal/specs/2026-08-15-workspaces-ux-design.md §5.2, which supersedes the prior design's
  §8 item 3; nocx-fraus is the bead. It is no longer the weakest item and no longer rests on
  the nocx-if6 retrofit argument alone: a tab is ALWAYS in a workspace (the default one never
  renders, §4.2), and the later fence epic consults this field IN THE BACKEND before addressing,
  spawning, observing or input. An enrolled external agent reaches the backend over its own
  socket and never touches the renderer, so a fence the backend cannot name is a UI convention.
  The retrofit argument still holds on top — a field on every session open and restore shape is
  cheap now and wide later.
- Liveness as {liveness, livenessEpoch, observedAt} over alive | dead | unknown | interrupted.
  `unknown` is the point: a child on an unreachable host is neither alive nor dead, and both of
  the other renderings lie. internal/content/ledger.go:336 already uses `interrupted` after a
  restart rather than asserting liveness — same principle, reused rather than reinvented.
- The rule that no addressability follows from lineage alone, enforced now so that no later epic
  can implement "lineage implies control" as a temporary shortcut.
- The rule that a parent's death never closes its children.

WHY THE RULES ARE HERE RATHER THAN IN THE EPIC THAT NEEDS THEM. Both are free to state now and
expensive to reverse once behaviour ships and habits form. ADR-0020 rejected
workspace-as-security-principal for three reasons; lineage answers only the draggability one, so
"a descendant is addressable" must never become true by default while nobody is looking.

DELIBERATELY OUT, each with its reason:

- Durable session records and the prepared -> active transaction. internal/session/ has no
  restore path at all today and tabs survive a restart through internal/settings/, so this would
  introduce session persistence for the first time — and under the design's D5 there is nothing
  yet for it to preserve, because workers die with the backend and every node after a restart is
  fresh. It belongs to epic E, which has the state that must survive.
- The grant-source seam. StartExecution has NO caller outside internal/content/ (verified
  2026-08-15), so adding a GrantSource parameter here would widen an unreachable write path and
  call it a foundation — nocx-rtg0's defect exactly. It lands in the epic that first mints a
  grant from a live caller.
- Workspaces as a surface, delegation, agent state, enrolment, anything remote.

## Success Criteria

See acceptance.
acceptance_criteria:
Watched end to end by an automated check, not by inspection:

- A tab opened FROM another tab renders under its opener in the vertical strip, and the
  relationship survives a strip swap and a filter.
- The parent edge is assigned by the SERVER (AD-7): a client that proposes a parent for a
  session that does not exist, or that belongs to a different backend instance, is refused —
  and the refusal is asserted, not assumed.
- A session id reused after a restart does NOT inherit the previous incarnation's children:
  asserted by driving two incarnations with the same id and different epochs.
- Killing the process in a parent tab leaves its children running and addressable by the user,
  and the parent's row shows it ended. No child is closed, signalled or reparented.
- Closing a tab that has live descendants ASKS — close this tab / close the subtree / cancel —
  and cancelling leaves everything as it was.
- Pulling the network on an SSH tab renders that tab and its descendants as `unknown`, not as
  alive and not as dead, and restoring the link returns them to `alive` without a reload.
- A late liveness observation stamped with a previous livenessEpoch does not revive a record.
- No code path derives permission, addressability or reachability from the parent edge:
  enforced by a test that would fail if one did, not by review.
notes:
AMENDED 2026-08-15 by .internal/specs/2026-08-15-workspaces-ux-design.md §5.2 and §7.

workspaceId is NOT NULLABLE. The prior design called it 'the weakest item in this
epic', kept on nocx-if6's retrofit argument alone. It is no longer the weakest:
the owner's workspace model makes a tab ALWAYS a member of a workspace (the
default one never renders), and the later fence epic consults the field in the
backend before addressing, spawning, observing or input. A nullable field cannot
carry that.

BUT THE ARGUMENT FOR IT IS THE UX DESIGN'S, NOT nocx-wyp3p'S. An adversarial
review caught the first draft spending an unrelated naming bug as evidence for a
security architecture. wyp3p is real and separate; it does not justify this field.

AND THIS EPIC MUST NOT ADD A BACKEND TAB ID (design §5.2). AD-7 makes the SESSION
the identity the backend owns; a tab can hold several sessions, so 'the tab that
spoke' is not well defined from the backend's side; and the renderer already knows
which tab a session is in. Every backend-to-renderer address is a sessionId the
renderer resolves. This is also the answer recorded on nocx-jiwq.1, which asked
the same question from the notification side.
close_reason: Everything the epic exists to retrofit is merged and tested over the real socket: session identity (instanceId/sessionId/sessionEpoch), the immutable full-identity parent edge with validateParent as its single admitting owner, non-null workspaceId, liveness as {liveness,livenessEpoch,observedAt} over alive|dead|unknown|interrupted, and the two prohibitions (no addressability from lineage, a parent's death does not close its children). The last open child, nocx-ebl4.1, was never about the record — it is a producer, and producing an edge is a surface decision this epic deliberately does not own. Split 2026-08-24 by the owner: the dispatcher's producer is now in scope for nocx-dkawo, where the parent is unambiguous; the three ambiguous UI origins stay open as standalone nocx-ebl4.1.

title: Two ADRs answer to 0029, and a bead cites the wrong one
description:
docs/decisions/0029-a-keystroke-is-bound-to-what-makes-it-meaningful.md is 'A proposed keystroke is bound to what makes it meaningful, not to the frame'. nocx-hz94 says 'Governed by ADR-0029 §2.2 (destination, secret-bearing URLs, retention)' and calls the destination rule absolute — so it means a notification ADR, and it tells the reader to read that ADR first. A reader following the citation lands on keystrokes and either concludes the bead is wrong or that the ADR is, and cannot tell which.

Not the first collision: docs/decisions/ already holds 0006-marker-only-prompt-mode.md AND 0006-reusable-credentials.md. So the number is allocated by whoever writes next, and two branches in flight allocate the same one. With ~15 worktrees live at once this recurs by construction rather than by accident.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. bd show nocx-hz94 — read 'Governed by ADR-0029 §2.2 … read the ADR first'.
2. head -1 docs/decisions/0029-*.md — it is about keystrokes.
3. ls docs/decisions/0006-* — two files.

Found 2026-08-15 while writing .internal/specs/2026-08-15-workspaces-lineage-and-orchestration-design.md, which repeated the bad citation from the bead into a design document. That is the real cost: a wrong ADR number propagates into the next document by being quoted rather than checked, and AGENTS.md's fourth pre-fix check ('Decided in an ADR?') is only as good as the number resolving.

Triage question this bead should answer, not assume: whether the notification ADR exists on a branch under another number, was never written, or is one of the 0029 pair that needs renumbering.
acceptance_criteria: Every ADR number in docs/decisions/ is held by exactly one document. Every bead citing an ADR number resolves to the document it means — nocx-hz94 in particular. A check exists that would have caught this, or the absence of one is a recorded decision.

title: settings.describe can answer null for three required arrays: the capability guard's denied path returns nil, and the new schema forbids it
description:
Found by the coordinator while integrating nocx-dgsp, which gave settings.describe its first JSON Schema.

internal/capability/config.go: settingsService.Descriptors, Declarations, Groups and SectionGroups all return nil when s.guard.ok() is false — the guard that rejects a service handle used outside its operation's Run. A nil Go slice marshals as null and a nil map marshals as null, while contracts/settings.describe.schema.json declares groups as type array, sectionGroups as type object, declarations as type array, and lists all three as required. So on the guard-denied path the server sends a payload its own contract rejects.

Declarations predates this bead — it has returned nil the same way since it was written, and nothing caught it because there was no schema until now. That is the point: the schema is what makes the shape checkable, and the first thing it found is the same defect ADR-era vault.status had (providers marshalling as null rather than []).

## Steps to Reproduce

Not reachable through the UI today: guard.check() fails only when a capability service handle is used outside its Run, which is a programming error rather than a user path. Reproduce it in a test by calling the service handle after its operation has released.

## Expected behavior

Either the denied path returns empty values that satisfy the contract, or it returns an error the handler turns into an RPC error — never a success payload that violates the schema. Decide which, because they are different products: an empty catalogue renders an empty rail, an error says something went wrong.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A settings.describe result produced on the guard-denied path either validates against contracts/settings.describe.schema.json or never reaches TryResult, asserted.
- The assertion covers all four accessors, not only the two the group work added.
- The existing over-the-wire conformance test gains the denied case; the happy path alone is what missed this.

title: The backend's unlock-request machinery has no producer now that the renderer owns the replay
description:
Found by the nocx-y7fg worker and verified by the coordinator: after ADR-0032 moved the replay to the renderer's dispatcher, WSServer.RequestUnlock has no production caller. grep over internal/ (excluding tests) returns the definition, the interface it satisfies and three comments — no call site.

What is now producer-less: RequestUnlock itself, the vault.unlockRequest notification it sends, ErrNoClientConnected and ErrUnlockCancelled, and the pending-request bookkeeping behind them. The consumer half is still live and must stay: vault.unlockResolved is in the closed ingress-critical set that runs inline on the read loop, and the renderer's own unlock dialog is what raises the prompt now.

This is the dead-half shape AGENTS.md names: a package can be reachable and still have a half nothing reaches. The worker left it deliberately rather than widen its own change, and said so — this bead is that report, so it does not evaporate between rounds.

## What to decide

Whether the ask machinery is removed or kept as the seam for a future backend-initiated unlock. There is one candidate caller left: nothing today asks for an unlock without an RPC in flight, but a background task (reconcile on start, a scheduled re-key) would. If the answer is keep, it needs a caller or an explicit comment naming the reserved use — a seam nobody reaches and nobody documents is how the vault shipped unreachable the first time.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Either RequestUnlock and its notification are removed, and the deadcode baseline shrinks by exactly those functions with no new entries; or they are kept with a production caller, asserted by a test that watches the prompt arrive from that path.
- vault.unlockResolved stays ingress-critical and inline on the read loop either way, asserted by the existing seam spec.
- The renderer's replay path is untouched.

title: The pre-commit hook re-checks the whole repo when only a few files are staged: prettier and eslint are ~26s of a ~60s warm commit
description:
Owner, 2026-08-15: 'почему у нас такие долгие коммиты'.

Measured on this tree, 2026-08-15, warm caches, one commit's worth of work:

  containerized vitest        37s   (of which vitest itself 33.7s)
  eslint . --max-warnings 0   15s   host, whole frontend/
  prettier --check .          11s   host, whole repo
  deadcode ratchet            10s   host, Go only (already scoped to staged Go)
  tsc x2 (app + test project)  8s
  solid fixture gate           5s
  containerized go test -race  4s   warm; tens of seconds when Go actually changed
  golangci-lint, gofumpt      ~0s   warm; a cold run is the big variable
  contracts:check             ~0s

The containers already run in parallel and start first, so a warm commit is
roughly max(host ~50s, containers ~37s) plus process startup: about a minute.
The hook is not badly built — it skips the Go gates when no Go file is staged,
the Node gates when no frontend file is, and the e2e tsc when no e2e file is
(.githooks/pre-commit, the CHANGED scan).

## What is actually wasted

Two gates re-examine the entire repository regardless of what is staged, and
neither needs to:

- prettier --check . formats-checks every file in the repo (11s) to prove that
  the two files being committed are formatted. Staged paths are already
  computed by the hook.
- eslint runs over all of frontend/ with no cache (15s). eslint --cache with
  the cache file in a gitignored path cuts a re-run to the changed files. Note
  this one is NOT simply 'lint staged files only': check-dead-exports.mjs and
  check-two-owners.mjs are repo-wide by construction and must keep seeing
  everything.

Expected saving is around 20s of a ~60s warm commit. Both changes are pure
scoping: the same files are checked, nothing is skipped.

## Deliberately out

- Scoping vitest to affected tests. The full suite on every commit is the
  repo's position and 34s is not where the waste is.
- Anything that makes a gate check less than it checks today.

## Acceptance Criteria

- prettier in the hook checks the staged file set, not the repo, asserted by
  staging one file and observing prettier is invoked with that path.
- An unformatted staged file still fails the hook.
- An unformatted file that is NOT staged does not fail the hook — this is the
  behaviour change, and it is intended: the hook gates the commit, not the tree.
- eslint runs with a cache whose file is gitignored and not shared between
  worktrees.
- The repo-wide fixture checks (dead exports, two owners) still see the whole
  tree, asserted by a fixture that only they can catch.
- A warm commit touching two frontend files is measurably faster than today,
  with the before and after numbers recorded in the closing note.

title: TestLocalSession_UnsupportedLoginShellRunsItAndSaysWhy fails under load: it waits on a duration, not on state
description:
Found while running `make ci-full` on the merged tree for epic nocx-457v.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run the whole gate so the machine is loaded: `make ci-full`.
2. Watch `internal/app`.
3. `TestLocalSession_UnsupportedLoginShellRunsItAndSaysWhy` fails after 20.07s.
4. Run it alone: `go test ./internal/app/ -run
   TestLocalSession_UnsupportedLoginShellRunsItAndSaysWhy -count=1` — it passes
   in 0.04s.

Three orders of magnitude between the loaded and unloaded run, and the failure
appears only in the loaded one. The test waits on a duration rather than on an
observable state change, so a busy machine fails it.

Established as NOT a regression: a full baseline of internal/app, internal/pty
and internal/shellintegration on origin/main (e8c3825e) produced 28 failures;
the merged epic branch produced 29; the single difference is this test, and it
passes on the branch in isolation. So the branch does not cause it — the gate
run merely exposed it.

This is the shape AGENTS.md names directly: "a test may not depend on timing.
Wait on an observable state change — a frame, a record, a DOM state — never on a
duration. A spec that needs a slow machine to pass is broken on a fast one too;
it has only not been caught yet." Same family as nocx-2h08, where one starved
resource reported a 30-second timeout under a different test name in every
environment.

Note it hides inside a package that already fails 8 other tests on a developer
machine for environmental reasons (the zsh/login-shell set, nocx-58gq and
nocx-65v6). A ninth failure in that group reads as more of the same, which is
exactly why it survived — it took a line-by-line diff against a real baseline to
separate it from the known set.

## Acceptance Criteria

[ ] The test waits on an observable state change rather than a duration.
[ ] It passes with the machine under load — reproduce with `make ci-full`
    running, or by starving it with `NOCX_CI_CPUS`.
[ ] Any sibling in internal/app waiting on a duration for the same reason is
    fixed with it, or named here as deliberately left.

title: Agent mode: bare Enter and Ctrl-C still reach the pty
description:
Agent mode: bare Enter sends CR and Ctrl-C sends ^C to the pty — shell behaviour for a submission that is not a shell command

## Steps to reproduce

With the ask chip up (agent target active):

1. Press Enter on an empty draft. The editor's submitEmpty path sends '\r' to the pty (terminal-content.ts submitEmpty -> session.send('\r')): the shell at a prompt prints a fresh prompt into the live region while the user is mid-conversation with the model.
2. Press Ctrl-C with no selection. The editor's cancel seam sends '\x03' to the pty.

## Why it matters

This is the SAME defect shape as the two already fixed in this epic: shell behaviour reaching a submission that is not a shell command. The loud half (keyboard handoff, ledger, running block, attempt) was fixed with routesToShell; the quiet half (the commit-time hide) was fixed with the handoffToShell seam. submitEmpty and cancel are two more lines where the editor acts as a shell line editor while the agent target is active. Neither blocks a second ask (a bare CR at a prompt is a harmless fresh prompt; a stray ^C clears the line), which is why nocx-wmy4's acceptance does not require them — but they are the same class, and the per-mode meaning of Enter/Ctrl-C in agent mode belongs to nocx-4ff.7's per-mode editor work.

## Acceptance Criteria

- With the agent target active (chip up), a bare Enter sends nothing to the pty (no '\r' reaches the session; the editor stays visible with its draft empty) — asserted through the real editor submit path in terminal-content.test.ts.
- With the agent target active, Ctrl-C with no selection sends nothing to the pty (no '\x03' reaches the session).
- With the shell target active, both behave exactly as before: bare Enter still sends CR, Ctrl-C still sends ^C.
- The fix uses the same seam as the previous two defects of this class: the composition root consults InputTargetRegistry.active() (the target declares via routesToShell) — no per-mode boolean inside the editor. The per-mode DRAFT and HISTORY are nocx-4ff.7's and are not this bead.
