title: The agent loop is ours; the model client is replaceable (ADR-0028)
description:
ADR-0028 (2026-08-13, Accepted). Doc: docs/decisions/0028-the-agent-loop-is-ours-the-model-client-is-replaceable.md

## Context

nocx is gaining an assistant that reads the terminal and, at the next rung, acts by calling OUR tools — read a block, run a command in the agent's lane, reach a connection or the vault. ADR-0020 requires that authority is a per-run grant checked AT the tool call, that a refusal is a control decision, and that approval mints a new attempt rather than mutating a running grant.

## Decision

internal/agent owns the loop, the policy, the attempts and a single tool dispatcher; no agent framework is a dependency. A refusal terminalizes the run rather than being handed back to the model. An escalation stops the loop before any domain call. The grant is over RESOURCES AND EFFECTS (environments, lanes, paths, destinations, effect classes), never over tool names — one 'run a command' tool is a universal escape hatch, so a grant naming it permits everything. The dispatcher NARROWS rather than checks: it resolves the grant into a scoped capability the tool holds, so the tool cannot exceed the grant because it never holds more. Go package privacy is explicitly NOT accepted as the boundary. Underneath sits one Model interface; the first implementation speaks OpenAI Chat Completions over HTTPS+SSE, which also reaches Ollama and llama.cpp so a frame need never leave the machine. Endpoint credentials are opaque vault references (ADR-0016/0017).

## Rationale

The engine question looked like 'which framework' and was not. For EXPLAIN an agent is not needed at all — one call and a stream. For the agent rung, what a framework offers is the easy half; the hard half is refusal, escalation, attempts, grants and durable run state, all specific to this product. The deciding constraint was the tools: if the tools are our domain objects, a loop in another process turns every tool call into an invented IPC boundary with the grant check on the far side of a pipe from the thing it protects.

## Alternatives Considered

pi --mode rpc as an external engine — REJECTED: its RPC protocol has a CLIENT-callable bash command that executes even under --no-tools (verified by running pi 0.84.1 with every isolation flag), and pi 'intentionally does not include built-in MCP, sub-agents, permission popups' (docs/usage.md:303), so our tools would live as TypeScript inside pi's process calling back into Go; plus Node>=22 and a 307MB package.
pi's Node SDK in a sidecar we author — REJECTED: tools/resources/sessions become structural, but the Node cost remains and our domain tools would still be TypeScript.
google.golang.org/adk/v2 — REJECTED: model implementations are gemini, openaimodel, apigee only; no Anthropic, no Ollama.
cloudwego/eino — REJECTED as the loop: has claude and ollama adapters, but its stock ReAct loop treats a policy refusal as an ordinary tool result and offers no suspend-before-domain-call for approval. NOT rejected as a model adapter layer behind the Model interface; deferred to measurement.
Ship EXPLAIN only, no loop — REJECTED by the owner: asking the assistant to do something is part of the product, and deferring the loop would mean two backends later.

## Consequences

No subscription logins (Claude Pro/Max, ChatGPT via Codex, Copilot) — entry is an API key or a local model, accepted deliberately. We own an SSE client and its whole failure surface. 'OpenAI-compatible' is not one protocol, so capability is verified per endpoint rather than assumed from one readiness probe. No Node runtime and nothing to install. EXPLAIN and agent mode are one driver with two run modes, not two engines.

title: Two connections for one machine, and nothing says so
description:
Nothing stops two connections being created with the same name and host. The owner's
store held two profiles for 192.168.0.93 — one `auth: null`, one `auth: "password"`, both
`port: null` — which is how a connection edited in one and connected from the other looks
like a connection that forgets its settings.

Found while fixing nocx-tmis: the worker reported it rather than fixing it, because
"reject a duplicate" and "merge into the existing one" are different products and the
choice is not a detail. Reported shape: no frontend name-uniqueness guard on create,
consistent with the second one having come from a quick-connect create.

The interesting part is what "duplicate" means, and it is not obvious:

- Same NAME is a display collision — two rows the user cannot tell apart in the picker or
  the connections list.
- Same HOST+USER+PORT is a semantic collision — two records for one machine, which is what
  splits settings and secrets across profiles the user believes are one.

They are not the same question and may deserve different answers: a name is a label the
user chose and may reasonably repeat across groups; a destination is a fact.

Also decide what happens to the existing duplicates. nocx is greenfield and writes no
migrations, so the answer is probably "the user resolves them", which means the surface
has to show that there are two.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Create a connection for a host from Settings → Connections → New connection.
2. Reach the same host again through quick-connect's ad-hoc path (or adopt it), and save.

Observed: two connections, same name, same host, independent auth and secrets. Editing
one leaves the other untouched, and the connections list gives no sign they are the same
machine.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A decision, recorded, on what counts as a duplicate: name, destination, or both, and
  what each does — refuse, warn, or merge.
- Whatever it is, creating one is not silently possible. If duplicates remain legal, the
  surface distinguishes them so a user can tell which row they are editing.
- The path that produced the owner's pair — a saved connection plus an adopted or ad-hoc
  create for the same host — is covered by a test, since that is the one combination known
  to happen in practice.
- Existing duplicates are visible to the user rather than silently reconciled: no
  migration, per the repo's greenfield rule.

title: The sidebar takes width from Settings to say it has nothing to show
description:
A Settings tab carries its own navigation — a search field and a section list down its
left edge — and the app's sidebar sits to the left of that with an activity bar and a
panel that have nothing to do with it. The screenshot the owner sent shows FILES saying
"Focus a terminal tab to see the files of the machine you are on" beside a Settings page:
a rail admitting it has nothing to show, occupying width the settings content could use,
next to a second column of navigation.

Owner, 2026-08-13: "And when settings are shown, let's collapse the activity bar."

Every sidebar view is about the machine a terminal tab is on. Settings is not a place —
Files says so itself, Ports says "No active connection", Git has nothing to track. So on
a Settings tab the whole rail is dead weight, and the user pays for it in width on the
one surface that is already two columns wide.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Activating a Settings tab collapses the sidebar, and the space goes to the settings
  content.
- Returning to a terminal tab restores the sidebar **exactly as the user left it** —
  same collapsed-or-open state, same width, same active view. The collapse is a
  consequence of where you are, never an edit to the user's preference: someone who
  keeps the rail closed must not find it open, and someone who dragged it to 400px must
  not find it at 240.
- A user who deliberately opens the sidebar while on a Settings tab gets it, and it
  stays until they close it. The rule sets what happens on arrival; it does not fight
  the user afterwards.
- The persisted `sidebar.width` setting is not written by this behaviour. Asserted,
  because writing it is the obvious accident and it silently rewrites a preference.
- Whatever the collapse does to the activity bar, the keyboard path to a view still
  works — Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+O reveals-or-focuses Ports (nocx-wzc4.7) and must still do so
  from a Settings tab, or it stops being a reveal.
- Asserted through a tab switch a user performs, in both directions, since a one-way
  test cannot report a state that fails to come back.

Deliberately out: hiding the rail for any other tab kind, and any new user-facing
setting to control this.
close_reason: Shipped in #80: transient collapse on arrival, exact restore on departure, and the persisted width is never written by it.

title: Quick connect offers no way to create a connection
description:
The tab-strip caret's quick connect offers saved connections and, when the typed query
matches none of them, "Connect to <host>". It offers no way to CREATE a connection, so a
user who wants a host they have not saved has to leave the surface, find Settings, and
come back.

Owner, 2026-08-13: "I noticed the create-connection item disappeared from quick connect,
it needs to come back."

**This is not a regression — it is a deliberate decision being revisited, and the bead
says so up front so nobody 'fixes' it twice.** `9820dd0f` (nocx-4t37.1) made the caret a
plain server list on purpose: *"The caret keeps the plain server list, because the two
jobs are different: the caret is 'connect to a machine I already know', and its speed
comes from having exactly one job."* Before that commit quick connect was "a host picker
with a couple of actions bolted onto it", and those actions were removed by that change.
The owner drove that model. They are now asking for one of the actions back.

The mechanism is `QuickConnectDialog`'s per-variant admission
(`frontend/src/quick-connect.tsx`, the `admits` predicate): `variant: 'hosts'` (the
caret) admits only `kind === 'host'`, `'secrets'` only `kind === 'secret'`, and the
palette everything but secrets. `ActionsQuickConnectProvider` does emit the row —
`__new_connection__`, label "New connection", running
`openSettingsTab().startNewConnection()` — it is simply not admitted.

The narrow change, and why it is narrow: admit **that one row**, not commands in
general. "New connection" is about connecting to a machine — one you have not saved yet
— so it belongs to the caret's single job, and it is the same need
`AdHocQuickConnectProvider` already serves from the other end with "Connect to <host>".
"Forward a port" is a different job and stays in the palette; admitting it would undo
the decision above rather than qualify it.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Click the caret in the tab strip to open quick connect.
2. Look for a way to define a new connection.

Observed: saved connections and ssh-config aliases only. Typing an unknown host offers
"Connect to <host>", which opens an unsaved ad-hoc session — not a saved connection.

Expected: a row that takes the user to defining a new connection.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The caret's quick connect (variant `hosts`) lists a row that opens the new-connection
  flow, and activating it reaches `startNewConnection()`. Asserted through the surface a
  user actually touches, not by calling the provider directly.
- The palette (variant `palette`) is unchanged, and the secrets variant still admits no
  command row — one Enter must never mean both "open a connection" and "type a password
  into what is in front of you", which is what the per-variant admission exists for.
- "Forward a port" does NOT appear in the caret. Asserted, because the obvious
  implementation — admitting `kind === 'command'` in the hosts variant — would let it
  in, and that is the decision this bead is deliberately not reversing.
- The first row on open is still "Local shell"'s muscle-memory equivalent for this
  variant: whatever Enter activates on an empty query must not change, or the change
  costs more than it gives.
close_reason: Shipped in #80: admitted per item via allowInHosts, never per kind; e2e asserts Forward a port stays out of the caret.

title: Find the port you want without scanning the rail
description:
A busy host lists dozens of listeners — the owner's Pi shows around sixteen, and a
container host shows many more. Finding the one port you care about means scanning the
whole rail. Connections and Secrets both solved this already; Ports did not.

Owner, 2026-08-13: "and it would probably be great to add a filter?"

The existing answer is in the kit and must be reused rather than rebuilt:
`frontend/src/ui/search-field.tsx`, which `connections.tsx` and `secrets.tsx` drive
through `searchPlaceholder` / `searchLabel`. A hand-rolled input in the ports surface
would be a second vocabulary for one concept, which AGENTS.md names as the defect
itself.

What the filter matches is a product decision, not a mechanical one. A port row carries
an address, a port number and — when the probe could name it — a process name and pid;
a forwarded row also carries a local bind and a destination. Matching only the address
would fail the most natural query, which is a process name ("pihole", "node"). Matching
everything risks a query hitting a pid the user did not mean.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A filter control at the top of the Ports panel, built from the kit's SearchField,
  filters the detected list as the user types.
- Typing a port number, a partial address, or a process name each finds the row a user
  would expect. Asserted as three separate cases — one of them passing does not imply
  the others.
- A query that matches nothing says so, rather than showing a heading with nothing
  under it. An empty section reads as broken; that exact shape is what nocx-wzc4.9 and
  nocx-heum were both about.
- The filter does not hide a RUNNING forward the user cannot otherwise reach: decide
  whether a forward whose row is filtered out stays reachable, and say why. A user who
  filters, forwards, then clears the filter must never lose track of a live forward.
- Clearing the filter restores the full list, and switching tabs does not carry one
  tab's filter onto another host's ports.
- The control follows the kit: a surface may place a kit component and never repaint
  it.

Deliberately out: filtering by "forwarded only" or any other faceted control, and
persisting the filter across restarts. If either turns out to be wanted, it is another
bead.
close_reason: Shipped in #80: kit SearchField over the detected list; live forwards stay reachable whatever the query.

title: A cancelled connection edit strands the password secret it already minted
description:
The connection editor mints a password secret at the moment the user presses OK in the
PasswordEditor (mint-and-bind, ADR-0017), not when the profile is saved. The binding is
held on the draft and marked dirty; the secret itself is already in the vault.

So pressing Cancel on the connection edit afterwards throws away the binding and leaves
the secret behind, owned by nobody: it shows in Settings → Secrets with 0 connections,
and nothing on screen ever mentioned that it was created.

Found by the worker fixing nocx-vczn, which established the mint-and-bind timing with
evidence. Deliberately left out of that fix: the fix there was to make the binding and
its failures visible, and this is a different question — what a discarded edit owes the
vault. It is a lifecycle decision, not a display one.

The interesting part is that both plausible answers have a cost, which is why this is a
bead and not a one-liner:

- **Roll the mint back on cancel.** Matches the user's intent, but a delete against the
  vault can itself fail, and now a cancel has a failure path of its own. It also races
  a second editor that may already have bound the same row.
- **Keep it and make it visible.** Honest and simple, but grows orphan rows on every
  abandoned edit, and the Secrets page has no affordance that explains where a
  0-connection row came from.

Relevant: `internal/vault/journal.go` already models a two-phase create with a
`PhasePrepared` record, which is the shape a cancellable mint would use. Check whether
this is a case that machinery already answers before building a third thing —
AGENTS.md's "look for the existing answer" applies, and the vault is exactly the package
where a second implementation of one concept is most expensive.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Settings → Connections → edit any connection → Authentication → Method = Password.
2. "Set Password", type one, confirm. The password is minted and bound to the draft.
3. Press **Cancel** on the connection editor.
4. Settings → Secrets.

Observed: the secret is listed, against 0 connections. The connection has no password.
Nothing ever told the user the secret was created, so nothing tells them to clean it up.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A decision is recorded — an ADR if it turns out to be one — for what a cancelled
  connection edit owes a secret it already minted.
- Whichever way it goes, the outcome is visible in the product: either the secret is
  gone and the user is told nothing was kept, or it survives and the Secrets page can
  explain a 0-connection row.
- The failure path of the chosen answer is tested. If cancel rolls back, there is a test
  for the rollback itself failing, and it states what is then true in the vault and on
  screen.
- Paired with it, the ordinary case: a cancelled edit on a connection that already had a
  password leaves that existing password untouched.
close_reason: Closed by nocx-tmis in #80 rather than decided separately: the binding is now persisted at the moment of the mint, so there is no window in which a secret exists bound to nothing and a cancelled edit can strand nothing.

title: A forwarded port is two rows in two places, and a stop the user asked for leaves litter
description:
Forwarding a detected port makes a SECOND row for that port appear in a separate
"Forwarded" section far below the list, and stopping it makes a THIRD row appear in a
"Stopped" section below that. The owner has to scroll away from the port to find out
what happened to it, and the row they pressed the button on does not change at all.

Owner, 2026-08-13, on a saved connection to 192.168.0.93: "I pressed forward and it
appeared at the bottom. Why? Let it stay at the top, just add an icon. Or highlight it
somehow. Or move Forwarded up." And then: "I stopped it, and why is there a Stopped at
the bottom?"

Two defects, one shape.

**One port, two owners.** `frontend/src/ports.tsx` renders Detected listeners and
Forwarded records as independent lists. After a forward, `0.0.0.0:8000` on the host and
the forward of it are the same thing to the user and two rows to the panel — so the row
carrying the Forward action never reflects that the action succeeded, and the row that
does reflect it is somewhere else. AGENTS.md names this exactly: "Two surfaces may never
own the same input… the loser goes on advertising what it can no longer deliver."

**A stop the user asked for is not news.** After stopping, a "Stopped" section appears
carrying the reason `user`. The user performed that stop one second earlier. The section
is litter in the one case that is guaranteed not to be informative. A forward that
stopped BY ITSELF is different — `error` and `connection lost` are news, and they are
the two reasons that already earn a Retry button (`ports.tsx:637`).

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open a saved SSH connection whose host has listeners (e.g. 192.168.0.93).
2. Ports view → press Forward on a detected row, e.g. `:::8000`.

Observed: the detected row is unchanged. A new row appears under "Forwarded" at the
bottom of the panel, below the whole listener list.

3. Press Stop on that forwarded row.

Observed: "Forwarded" goes to its "No active forwards" empty state, and a "Stopped"
section appears below it with the row and the reason `user`.

Expected: the port's own row says what is true about that port, where the user is
already looking. A stop the user performed leaves nothing behind.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Forwarding a detected port changes THAT ROW: it shows the local address the port is
  now reachable on, and the row's action becomes Stop. No second row for the same port
  appears anywhere.
- The row's forwarded state is legible without reading text — an icon or a tone, drawn
  with the existing kit, never a hand-rolled control or a repainted one.
- Copy and Open (the actions a running forward currently offers) remain reachable from
  that row.
- Stopping a forward returns the row to its un-forwarded state and adds NOTHING to any
  other section.
- A forward that stops on its own (`error`, `connection lost`) is still surfaced with
  its reason and its Retry action — asserted separately from the user-stop case, since
  the whole point is that the two are different.
- A forward whose destination is NOT in the current Detected list (the host stopped
  listening, or a forward replayed from the connection) is still visible and stoppable.
  This is the case that makes "just merge the lists" wrong, and it must be tested.
close_reason: Shipped in #80: the detected row is the single owner of a port's state; the Stopped section is deleted.

title: AGENTS.md's gate section names four CI jobs; ci.yml has five, under different names
description:
AGENTS.md 'Run the gate CI runs, not a subset of it' lists four jobs — backend, backend-linux, frontend, e2e — and says 'the four names below are the whole of ci.yml'. Since 9527464a, 0f499dd1 and 85e1d192 that is wrong in three ways at once, and the section is the operating contract people follow when they gate a merge.

ci.yml now has FIVE jobs and every name changed: ci-mac, ci-backend, ci-linux, ci-frontend, ci-e2e. The old single backend-linux job was split in two — ci-backend runs the portable package set, ci-linux the OS-specific one — so 'scripts/ci-linux.sh' is no longer the runner for a job called backend-linux; it is the shared runner behind two Makefile targets that pass it different package lists.

The concrete cost, paid on PR #61: the section's command list was followed exactly, ./scripts/ci-linux.sh was run bare, it reported both keyring variants green, and GitHub's ci-linux was red on the same tree. Reading the Makefile rather than AGENTS.md is what found 'make ci-linux'.

The same section also claims the containerized runners are byte-for-byte their CI counterparts in software. For ci-linux that is now false in a way that hides failures rather than causing them: .githooks/images/ci-linux/Dockerfile pre-installs zsh, dash and bash 3.2, while the GitHub job installs only what its own steps install. A missing install step in ci.yml is therefore invisible locally — which is exactly how ci-linux came to fail on every run since the split without anyone seeing it.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Read AGENTS.md, section 'Git authority', the paragraph beginning 'Run the gate CI runs'.
2. Compare its four names against 'grep -nE "^  ci-" .github/workflows/ci.yml' — five jobs, none of the four names.
3. Compare its command list against the ci-full target in the Makefile: ci-os-split ci ci-mac ci-backend ci-linux ci-frontend ci-e2e.

## Acceptance Criteria

The section names the jobs ci.yml actually defines and the local target for each, and it is derived from the Makefile's ci-full target rather than restating it from memory. The byte-for-byte claim is either narrowed to the jobs where it holds or replaced with what is actually true — that the images are a superset of the runners' software, so a missing install step in ci.yml cannot be caught locally.

title: the containerized jobs share one named node_modules volume, so concurrent runs corrupt each other
description:
The container runners mount node_modules as NAMED docker volumes, and the
names carry no worktree in them:

  -v nocx-e2e-node:/work/node_modules
  -v nocx-e2e-fenode:/work/frontend/node_modules

So every worktree's run shares one tree. Measured 2026-08-12 with three agents
running gates at once: a pre-commit hook on the main worktree died with

  Error: Cannot find package '/work/node_modules/debug/index.js'
         imported from /work/node_modules/vite-node/dist/client.mjs

while two other runs held the same volume. Nothing was wrong with the commit —
it succeeded on a retry once the other runs had moved on.

The volumes exist to avoid reinstalling node_modules per run, which is worth
keeping; the defect is that the cache is shared where it is also mutable. Key
the volume by worktree, or take a lock, or make it read-only for consumers and
populated by one writer — decide, do not just widen the name.

Related: nocx-xddu removed the reason three agents were running four jobs each
in the first place, which makes this rarer without making it wrong.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run ./scripts/ci-frontend.sh from two worktrees at the same time.
2. Observed: one of them fails resolving a package that is present for the other.
acceptance_criteria: Two gate runs from different worktrees can run at the same time without either seeing a broken node_modules.
close_reason: Fixed in 3c78fd75. Install trees are keyed by worktree (cksum of the absolute path); content-addressed caches deliberately are not. Caught live: ps showed feat-ai-assistant's pre-commit holding the same nocx-hook-fe volume mid-npm-ci while this worktree's vitest died on ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND. The distinction is what the volume holds, not that it is shared — a node_modules tree is the product of one lockfile and npm ci rewrites it by deletion, whereas gomod/gobuild/npm-cache are content-addressed and concurrent access is their normal mode. Keying those too would cost every new worktree a cold first run for no risk; the owner considered it and the split stands.

title: the gate rule reads as 'all four, always', and agents run it per branch
description:
AGENTS.md said "run the gate CI runs, not a subset of it" without saying which
tree it means, so every agent ran make ci-full on its own branch. Measured
2026-08-12: three branches, each ci-full green on its own tree, roughly an
hour of wall clock apiece. The merge of them was red twice, and neither defect
could have been seen from any branch because neither existed on one.

Fixed in this commit by naming the two gates separately. Filed so the reasoning
survives: the rule was bought by a red push to main (2026-08-10), and that is
exactly where it still binds — what came off is a cost it never bought.
acceptance_criteria: AGENTS.md distinguishes the branch gate from the merge gate, and the distinction is stated where the rule is, not in a commit body.

title: a remote session whose startup does not return still reports only a timeout
description:
nocx-yww2 gave LOCAL sessions a bootstrap progress descriptor: the rcfile writes 'startup entered' before it sources the user's rc and 'user rc returned' after, and the pair lets the product say startup-did-not-return instead of handshake-timeout. Both rcfile templates carry the block, so the REMOTE tiers already render it — but they render it inert, because the block is gated on NOCX_BOOTSTRAP_FD and no such descriptor is ever handed to a far shell. ssh gives us one channel and the lifecycle transport is a forwarded loopback port; there is no second inherited fd.

So a remote host whose ~/.bashrc execs a foreign terminal wrapper is exactly as silent as every local session was before nocx-yww2: ten seconds, then handshake-timeout, which cannot be told apart from a shell that never started.

What it must NOT be: a second authenticated channel, or facts folded into the lifecycle codec, whose rule is that every accepted envelope is authenticated (ADR-0024 decisions 2 and 7). ADR-0024 decision 4 permits an unauthenticated diagnostic channel on three conditions — not the terminal, not the lifecycle codec, no authority — and any remote answer has to meet the same three. Worth checking whether the existing TunnelConn can carry a second, clearly-marked diagnostic connection, and whether the relay (nocx-if6 phase B) makes the question disappear by spawning the shell itself with inherited descriptors, exactly as the local path does.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. On a remote host, put 'exec <a wrapper that keeps the connection and starts a bare shell>' at the top of ~/.bashrc.
2. Open an ssh tab to it in script mode.
3. Observed: ten seconds of nothing, then 'Not integrated — your shell did not answer nocx in time'. The same host with an ordinary rc integrates, and the same rc LOCALLY now says the startup did not return.

## Acceptance Criteria

An ssh session whose far startup file never returns control reports startup-did-not-return, by the same two facts and the same closed vocabulary the local path uses — proven by one automated check against a real sshd whose user rc execs. No fact travels through the lifecycle codec, none carries authority, and a host that cannot carry the diagnostic channel degrades to today's handshake-timeout rather than to a broken session.

title: the integration test harness races the open handler's post-ack emit, so any 'nothing further arrives' assertion is a coin flip
description:
Found while adding the process-observation tests (nocx-cgzc), and it cost a
red containerized run:

    --- FAIL: TestIntegration_ALaterLossDoesNotOverwriteTheObservedAnswer
        a later loss overwrote the observation's answer:
        {"status":"conventional","reason":"handshake-timeout",...}

The 'leaked' frame was not a second answer — it was a RE-SEND of the answer the
test had already read. openSessionOnConn returns as soon as it reads the open
ack, while the open handler carries on to h.sess.emitIntegration(sess.ID())
after that ack (correctly: AD-7 puts it there), on its own goroutine. So the
handler's emit can land at any later point, including after the test has
registered the axis and moved it. On a fast host it lands first and nobody
notices; in the emulated Linux container it landed last.

Every test built on newIntegrationEnv that asserts 'and nothing further
arrives' is exposed to this — TestIntegration_SessionDisposalSaysNothing is
one, TestIntegration_LossOnAnUnknownLaneIsDropped is another — and the
exposure is invisible until a slow machine finds it. The new tests were
rewritten to assert that no frame says anything DIFFERENT (answersAfter in
ws_integration_test.go), which is race-proof and is the invariant the user
actually experiences; the older ones still assert absence.

The durable fix is on the harness side: give newIntegrationEnv a way to know
the open handler has finished — an observable, not a duration — so a test can
say 'nothing further arrives' and mean it.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Add a test on newIntegrationEnv that asserts no further
   session.integrationChanged arrives after moving the axis.
2. Run internal/transport in the emulated Linux container (make ci-backend).
3. Observed: an occasional red naming a frame identical to one already read.
acceptance_criteria: A test built on newIntegrationEnv can assert that no further session.integrationChanged arrives and have that assertion mean it, because the harness waits on an observable end of the open handler rather than on the ack alone.

title: internal/shellintegration goes red under load: three tests, three runs, each a duration the test depends on
description:
internal/shellintegration goes red under load, and it has now done so THREE
times in three different tests during work on nocx-cgzc (2026-08-12), each
time green in isolation and in a package the change under test does not touch:

  1. TestZshSnapshotDefersToALaterPromptWhenNotReady — 'want exactly 1 OSC 636
     snapshot at the later prompt, got 0', on the macOS native job. The test
     runs a real zsh with NOCX_SNAPSHOT_WAIT_MS=250 and hangs its real
     assertion on that 250 ms window.
  2. TestBashInterruptAnnouncesNoPhantomCommand — 'timed out waiting for OSC
     133 A after the interrupt (want 2, have 1)' after 15.84 s, in the
     EMULATED Linux container, where every syscall is slower.
  3. (nocx-91ef is a fourth red in the same package, but a different cause —
     a TempDir cleanup race rather than a duration — and stays its own bead.)

One shape: the package drives real shells and asserts on what arrives inside a
window. AGENTS.md forbids exactly this — 'a test may not depend on timing;
wait on an observable state change, never a duration' — and names the reason:
a spec that needs a fast machine is broken on a slow one and has only not been
caught yet. It is also the shape that destroys a bisect, because the red
lands on a different test each run and looks like a regression in whatever
was being changed.

The fix is per test and mechanical: wait for the state the shell reaches (the
snapshot's payload landing, the prompt marker being emitted) rather than for a
duration to pass. Where a real shell genuinely cannot signal readiness, the
bound must be large enough that it measures boundedness and never machine
speed — which is what these tests' own comments claim they do and what their
inner windows do not.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Run make ci-full (the package runs beside the rest of ./... under -race on
   macOS, and inside the emulated amd64 container on Linux).
2. Observed: an occasional red, on a different test each time, green when
   re-run alone.
acceptance_criteria: TestZshSnapshotDefersToALaterPromptWhenNotReady passes with the rest of ./... running beside it under -race, because its deferred-snapshot assertion waits on an observable state change rather than on a 250 ms window.

title: TestZshNestedChildStillborn's TempDir cleanup races the shell it started, so the suite goes red at random
description:
Seen once in a local 'make ci-full' on macOS (2026-08-12, while working nocx-cgzc):

    --- FAIL: TestZshNestedChildStillborn (1.33s)
        testing.go:1464: TempDir RemoveAll cleanup: unlinkat .../TestZshNestedChildStillborn63797428/001: directory not empty

The assertions in the test all passed; what failed was t.TempDir()'s own
cleanup, because something under the test — the parent zsh, the fake sudo, or
a zsh compdump/HISTFILE write — created a file in the directory after
RemoveAll had listed it. Re-running the test three times with -race passed,
and it passes on a clean tree too, so it is not a regression of any current
change: it is a teardown race that will keep making the gate red at random,
which is exactly the failure that destroys a bisect (see the 'a test that
fails under load and passes in isolation' memory).

The fix is to make the test own the interval: wait for the shell it started
to be reaped before the TempDir cleanup runs (t.Cleanup runs LIFO, so a
cleanup registered after the TempDir is created runs first), rather than
leaving the directory to be emptied while a process may still write into it.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. make ci-full on macOS.
2. Observed: an occasional red on TestZshNestedChildStillborn whose only
   failure line is the TempDir cleanup.
acceptance_criteria: TestZshNestedChildStillborn cannot fail on TempDir cleanup: the processes it starts are reaped before the directory is removed, asserted rather than assumed.

title: a cold start once stalled 70 seconds between Tab.start and creating the renderer
description:
Observed twice in a row on the installed build, then not again. The backend
was up and idle the whole time — no shell had been spawned, so nothing was
waiting on a user's rc:

  19:22:42.612  ws server started
  19:22:42.858  frontend: Tab.start() called
  19:23:53.195  frontend: creating renderer      <- 70 seconds later
  19:23:53.264  session opened

A clean relaunch a minute later opened the session in 3 seconds, and every
earlier launch that evening was immediate, so this is not the normal path.

What makes it worth a bead rather than a shrug: for 70 seconds the product is
a window with nothing in it, and the log cannot say why. Everything between
Tab.start() and creating the renderer is renderer-side and unlogged, so the
next occurrence will be exactly as opaque as this one. Candidates not
distinguished by the evidence: macOS re-verifying a freshly copied bundle,
the two rapid quit/relaunch cycles that preceded it, or something in the
renderer's own startup awaiting a resource.

## Steps to Reproduce

Not reproduced on demand. Seen after copying a fresh build into
/Applications and quitting/relaunching it twice in quick succession.
acceptance_criteria: Either the stall is reproduced and explained, or the startup path carries enough logging that the next occurrence names its own cause.

title: Learn more points at a GitHub blob URL that does not resolve
description:
docs/shell-integration.md exists on the local main and the link points at
github.com/shady2k/nocx/blob/main/..., so it 404s until the branch is pushed —
and stays fragile afterwards, since it breaks on a rename, a default-branch
change or an offline machine. Decide where product help lives: in-app, a
versioned docs URL, or not linked at all.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open the Details dialog on a degraded session and follow Learn more.
2. Observed: GitHub 404.
acceptance_criteria: Learn more resolves from the shipped build, or it is not offered.
close_reason: Decision: product help ships IN THE APP, and there is no URL left to rot. A link needs a network, a system browser (shell.openUrl answers -32601 where there is no native runtime) and a path surviving a rename or default-branch change, to explain a misconfiguration on the machine the user is already at; prose in the bundle needs none of them and is versioned with the build. 'Learn more' now opens an in-app dialog rendering INTEGRATION_EXPLANATION, which lives beside the reason table in integration/status.ts (one owner, AD-8). docs/shell-integration.md is DELETED: it was product help, it duplicated these strings, and the stale copy is exactly how 'bash -lic' survived. Owner may object cheaply — the file is one git revert away. Proved by notice.test.tsx 'explains integration inside the app' and 'opens no browser and needs no network'.

title: TestTunnelConn_CloseIsNotConnectionLoss races the test server's accept and fails under load
description:
internal/ssh/ssh_tunnel_test.go:275 fails intermittently with its own diagnostic: 'killConns: no established connection to close — the loss the test is about to wait for can never arrive; wait for the server to accept the connection first (waitLiveConns)'.

Observed 2026-08-12 during a `make ci-full` on macOS, in the whole-suite `go test -race ./...` pass; the same test passes in isolation and with -count=5 -race, and the whole package passes on its own. So it is load-sensitive rather than broken: TunnelConn returns once the client has its lease, and the test server records the connection on its own accept path, so killConns can run before there is anything to kill.

The helper the message names — waitLiveConns — already exists; the test simply does not call it. This is AGENTS.md's 'a test may not depend on timing' with the fix already written next to it: wait on the observable state (the server has an established connection) rather than on the ordering that usually holds.

Not caused by nocx-wwz0, which touches no tunnel code; found by its gate run.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. `make ci` (or `go test -race -count=1 ./...`) on a loaded machine.
2. internal/ssh fails at TestTunnelConn_CloseIsNotConnectionLoss.
3. `go test -race ./internal/ssh/` alone passes.

## Acceptance Criteria
- The test waits for the server to have an established connection before killConns, so it cannot fail for the ordering.
- It still fails if Done closes on an intentional Close while the connection is shared, and if Done does not close after real transport death — the two things it is actually about.

title: a local login shell with no tier (dash, ash) gets a conventional session; the POSIX tier exists only remotely
description:
nocx-wwz0 made the local session follow the user's login shell and classified it with shellintegration.LocalShellKind: bash and zsh get their local tiers, everything else is started as itself and reports ReasonUnsupportedShell.

The remote side already has a THIRD tier — launcher_posix.go, spec section 6, verified against dash and busybox ash — and it has no local launch semantics: it works by writing a transient ENV file and pointing $ENV at it, a different bootstrap from the bash rcfile and the zsh ZDOTDIR. A user whose login shell is dash or ash therefore gets a conventional terminal locally while the same shell over ssh gets markers.

Not fish/csh/tcsh: those ignore $ENV and the remote dispatcher starts them plainly too, so they are honestly out of scope until someone writes tiers for them.

## Acceptance Criteria
- A local session whose login shell is dash or busybox ash emits OSC 133 markers, proven by a real shell on a real pty the way internal/shellintegration's local zsh tier is.
- shellintegration.LocalShellKind maps them to the posix tier rather than to 'no tier'.
- fish/csh/tcsh still report unsupported-shell rather than being started under a shell they are not.

title: detail.observedProcess is declared, rendered and never populated: the details chain has no observation line
description:
The contract declares `detail.observedProcess` — "the executable the backend observed running in place of the shell it started, by name only" — and the renderer renders it, labelled as a guess, in the Details dialog (frontend/src/integration/notice.tsx, proven by a test). Nothing on the backend ever populates it: integrationStatus.observedProcess exists and is never written.

This is the reachability trap AGENTS.md names (check 5, and the ContentDB.Add post-mortem): a reachable read path over an unreachable write path. The field is optional and the surface handles its absence correctly, so nothing is broken — but the details chain is missing the line that most often tells a user what happened, and the schema currently advertises a capability the product does not have.

The observation must come from the process table (the pty's child, or the foreground process group of the tty), never from the byte stream — AD-6 forbids the backend to interpret it, and ADR-0024 already records why TIOCGPGRP cannot answer "who wrote these bytes". That is fine here precisely because this value is NOT authority: it is a guess, the schema says so, and the product labels it so. The bounded question is which process to name and when to sample it — sampling at the moment the handshake bound expires is the obvious candidate, because that is when the shell demonstrably is not where it should be.

Name only: no path, no arguments, no command line — the schema forbids them, because a command line carries the user's own text into a surface that is not theirs.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Make a local shell fail its handshake (a startup file that never returns).
2. Open the card's Details dialog.
3. Observed: the chain has no observation line, on every machine, always.

## Acceptance Criteria

A local session whose handshake expires while another executable holds the pty reports that executable's name in detail.observedProcess, asserted off the real socket; a session where nothing unusual is observed still sends no detail at all; and no path, argument or command line ever appears in the field.
close_reason: detail.observedProcess is now written: the observation carries the kernel's own p_comm, name only (no path, no arguments, no command line, enforced by the source of the value), asserted off the real socket against the schema. A session where nothing unusual is observed still sends no detail.

title: an unpinned remote session reports its shell as 'auto', so the details dialog cannot say what nocx started
description:
session.integrationChanged carries `shell` — what nocx actually started — because a diagnosis that omits the shell is not actionable: which shell a session runs is the single biggest thing that varies between two machines running the same code.

For a LOCAL session the launcher has a real answer and sends it (the absolute path exec resolved). For a REMOTE session with a profile shell pin, it sends the pin. For a remote session with no pin, nocx genuinely does not choose: the launcher emits a POSIX dispatcher that detects the login shell at the far end, so the honest local answer is the literal string "auto" (internal/transport/ws_integration.go, remoteShellName). The Details dialog therefore reads "nocx started auto", which is true and unhelpful.

There IS an authenticated source for the far shell's real name — lifecycle.Hello carries `shell` and the kernel drops it on the floor today (lifecycle.Domain records BundleGeneration from the same hello and nothing else). Recording it the same way and letting the transport prefer it over the pin would make an integrated-then-lost remote session name its real shell.

What it cannot fix, and the design must say so rather than pretend: a session that never completed its handshake never sent a hello, so a remote handshake-timeout has no better answer than "auto". Do not invent one — the wrong shell name sends a user to edit a file the session never read.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Connect to a saved profile with no shell pin, on a host where integration is declined (any launcher refusal).
2. Open the card's Details dialog.
3. Observed: "nocx started auto".

## Acceptance Criteria

An integrated remote session's status names the shell the authenticated hello reported, and a test asserts it off the real socket. A remote session that never completed its handshake still reports the pin or "auto", and the details surface says what that means rather than showing a bare "auto".

title: zsh and posix shells never send domain_closed, so a closed session's open attempts reconcile only on transport loss
description:
## Summary

nocx.bash's EXIT trap sends a final `domain_closed` envelope before the shell
exits (internal/shellintegration/scripts/nocx.bash, __nocx_exit_cleanup).
Neither nocx.zsh nor nocx.posix does.

Found while adding the zsh command-existence snapshot (nocx-qduc), which gave
nocx.zsh its first exit hook (add-zsh-hook zshexit __nocx_snapshot_cleanup) —
so the seam the send would ride now exists in the zsh tier.

## Steps to Reproduce

    grep -n domain_closed internal/shellintegration/scripts/*

returns exactly one hit, in nocx.bash. TestZshChannel_HandshakeAndLifecycle
drives a real zsh over the channel and never observes a close envelope
because none is sent.

## Why it matters

The kernel marks a domain's open attempts unknown when the domain closes.
With no explicit close it learns of the exit only when the transport dies —
for the local tier that is the descriptor closing with the process (usually
equivalent), for the remote tier it can be later or not observed as an orderly
close at all. ADR-0024 decision 5 still holds either way (nothing marks an
attempt successful, nothing assigns a code it did not report), so this is a
latency and tidiness gap rather than a correctness break, which is why it is
P2.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A zsh session that exits sends domain_closed as its last envelope, asserted
  by a channel exec test (the bash twin is the model).
- The POSIX tier either sends it or records in the script why it cannot.
- The bash tier's behaviour is unchanged.

title: The nocxify journey proves the second connection again
description:
The nocxify journey lost the assertions that watched shell.launcherCommand
and the compact installed carrier when nocx-292k landed: both watched a
deleted RPC and a delivery path selected by an installed fact that has no
production writer, so leaving them would have timed out or preserved a test
narrative for functionality that no longer exists.

What the journey still proves is the user-visible half — the frozen local
block, remote blocks from the first prompt, the exit back to local, the auth
failure, rc files intact, one verified generation. What it no longer proves
is that the SECOND connection is cheaper than the first.

Depends on the installed-fact writer (blocker A): until facts are recorded,
there is no compact path to assert.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The journey asserts, at the wire or filesystem level, that a second
  connection to the same host is integrated from its first prompt by a
  route distinguishable from the first connection.
- No assertion references shell.launcherCommand, shell.environmentObserved
  or the .nocx/run staging directory.

title: Stress-test: consent before a remote footprint
description: Adversarial review of .internal/specs/2026-08-10-remote-footprint-consent-design.md (nocx-i5yl). Branch categories: architecture, assumptions, dependencies, edge cases, scale, failure modes, alternatives not considered, security & risk.
close_reason: Stress-test complete: 9 branches resolved (6 agreed, 3 modified), design materially simplified — fourth consent axis removed in favour of desiredMode=auto, consent keyed by host key, ask rides with host-key trust; confidence medium-high

title: Transition to writing-plans
close_reason: Stress-test ran before writing-plans, as selected at the spec gate

title: Spec self-review, fix inline
close_reason: Self-review: placeholders none; all code citations verified against the tree; criteria restated as intervals

title: The insert toast still asks for the Enter that is now sent with the value
description:
After fc189136 the newline goes with the resolved value — picking a secret at a password prompt IS the answer to it. The toast still read 'Secret inserted — press Enter to send it', which asks for a keystroke that now submits a second, empty line.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. At a password prompt, open the tab-strip key icon and pick a secret.
2. The far side already received the answer, and the toast asks for Enter.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The toast reports a completed send and asks for no keystroke.
- It still says something, rather than nothing: a password prompt echoes nothing, and an answer the user cannot see is an answer they give twice.
close_reason: Landed in 399574d4: the toast reports a completed send.

title: Answer ssh's password prompt through nocx, via SSH_ASKPASS rather than the tty
description:
Owner, 2026-08-10: "can we intercept the password prompt and show a dialog
like the vault one? Or at least let me paste a password from the vault."

Today a hand-typed `ssh` to a password host is answered in the pty by the ssh
client itself. nocx has a password dialog and a vault full of credentials,
and neither is reachable from there — while a PROFILE connection uses both,
because the backend owns that transport.

## Why this is now possible without sniffing the stream

nocx already rewrites the command for a nested ssh (ADR-0022), so it composes
the argv. OpenSSH has a supported seam for exactly this: SSH_ASKPASS plus
SSH_ASKPASS_REQUIRE=force makes the client call a helper program instead of
reading the tty. The composer can point that at a nocx helper, which asks the
backend over a channel and returns the answer.

That keeps the whole thing inside the architecture: no OSC parsing, no
matching "password:" in the byte stream (AD-6, ADR-0004), no timing guess
about when the prompt appears. The client asks; we answer.

It also opens the useful half of the request: the destination is known before
the connection (host/user ride the domain_request, ADR-0025), so nocx can
look for a matching stored secret and offer it — the same lookup the profile
path already does.

## Open questions for the brief

- Where the helper lives and how it authenticates back to the backend. It
  runs on the LOCAL machine as the user, so the lifecycle channel is not
  automatically the right carrier.
- Whether a no-match falls back to the client`s own tty prompt (it must — a
  helper that fails must not make the host unreachable).
- Whether an answer may be remembered, and under whose consent. The vault has
  a named-create surface (ADR-0016/0017) the profile path already uses.
- SSH_ASKPASS_REQUIRE is OpenSSH 8.4+; older clients need the fallback.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Typing `ssh host` for a destination with a stored secret offers it through
  the same dialog the vault uses, and the session logs in without the user
  typing the password.
- With no stored secret, the user gets nocx`s prompt and may choose to
  remember the answer.
- With the helper unavailable or refused, the ssh client prompts on the tty
  exactly as it does today.
- Nothing anywhere matches on the word "password" in the output stream.
close_reason: Merged into nocx-jee1 by owner decision 2026-08-10: same askpass seam, and AGENTS.md gives one behaviour one owner. Everything 5175 carried that jee1 did not — the ADR-0022 argv composition, the ADR-0025 pre-connection destination, the OpenSSH 8.4+ bound, the local-helper authentication question and the tty fallback — is recorded on jee1 as a comment. jee1 covers sudo and ssh together and is P1.

title: A nested ssh session does not say which host it is on
description:
Owner, 2026-08-10: inside a hand-typed `ssh`, nothing on screen says the
session is on another machine. The cwd chip reads `home/pi` — correct, and
indistinguishable from a local /home/pi.

A profile-opened ssh tab carries the destination in its tab title
(root@ct-ziti-tunneler). A nested one carries nothing: same tab, same title,
same chip vocabulary, and the only hint is the shell prompt the far host
happens to print.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. In a local tab, `ssh pi@192.168.0.93`, log in.
2. Run `pwd`. The block chip says `home/pi`.
3. Nothing distinguishes this from a local session in /home/pi.

## Why it matters beyond cosmetics

This is the "which machine am I about to run this on" question, and the
answer is currently the user`s memory. The information exists and is
authenticated — the child domain carries host and user (ADR-0025: the
domain_request carries exactly the destination), so the projection can state
it without inferring anything from the stream.

## Deliberately open

Where it belongs — the block chip, the pane`s capability rail, the tab title,
or more than one — is a design question, not a fix. The rail already states
what is true at the prompt (nocx-4t37.2) and is the natural candidate.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A nested session states its destination somewhere a user reading the pane
  cannot miss.
- It is derived from the active domain, never from the prompt text or any
  other stream-derived guess (AD-6).
- Returning to the parent removes it in the same instant the domain does.
close_reason:
Fixed in 519c46f4. The destination now rides the published fact and the renderer states it.

Where it was stuck: domain_request already carried host/user/port (ADR-0025) and the value stopped at the grant seam. frontend/src/lifecycle/domain-environment.ts said so outright on its 'host' field — a child domain has no authenticated host source and shows none until one exists. This bead is that source.

Boundary: publishing it is inside ADR-0024 decision 7, not against it. What may never cross is the per-epoch capability and raw frames; schema-checked facts crossing is the point of the boundary. It carries no authority — domain id and epoch remain the only authority the renderer gets — and nothing is derived from prompt text (AD-6).

One owner: the publisher records it at the grant seam, the single point where the child's identity and its destination are both in hand. The kernel deliberately does not keep it.

Where it shows: the environment projection seeds an ssh child's record with host, user, isLocal=false and the destination as the tab title — the same thing the lane seed already does for a profile-opened ssh session, which is what the owner asked for ('as for the ssh we get from quick connect'). Everything downstream was already wired to that one projection, so the block header chip, the editor location chip, the tooltip and the tab all name it through the derivation they always shared. It disappears in the same fact the domain does.

Proven three ways: internal/lifecyclepub/grant_test.go drives the real grant seam; TestLifecycleChanged_DTOConformsToContract covers both shapes against the schema; the live-sshd assembly test asserts the destination reaches the fact for a child established over a real ssh client against a real sshd.

title: Transport tests flake at their 5s bound under container load
description:
Observed 2026-08-10 while running the containerized suite repeatedly for
nocx-beib: two runs out of four failed in internal/transport, each at exactly
its 5.00s bound, and a different test each time
(TestLifecycleChanged_DeadSessionGetsNoRecoveryClaim,
TestGitChanged_OverTheWireConformsToContract). Both pass locally and both
pass in the container on a clean tree and on repeat runs, and the change
under test touched only shell scripts, which these tests never execute.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run .githooks/containerized-tests.sh (go_test_containerized) several
   times on a loaded machine.
2. Occasionally one transport test fails after exactly its wait bound.

## Why it matters

A suite that fails at random teaches people to re-run rather than to read,
which is how a real failure gets waved through. The bound is the suspect: a
fixed 5s wait for a published fact is a timing assumption about a machine
under unknown load, not about the code.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The transport waits are condition-based rather than a fixed sleep-to-bound,
  or the bound is derived from something the test controls.
- Twenty consecutive containerized runs are green.
notes:
--- A SECOND PACKAGE, same disease, 2026-08-23 ---

internal/pty, not internal/transport, and the same 5s wait bound:

    --- FAIL: TestLocalPty_SignalForegroundReachesAChildNotOnlyTheShell (5.04s)
        signal_foreground_test.go:172: the execution's child 2826 was not reaped
        after the group signal — cancellation reached only the shell

Seen in scripts/ci-linux.sh during the epic-end gate on feat/ai-assistant. Measured
rather than assumed:

- The change under test never touched internal/pty (`git log 9c730ed3..HEAD --
  internal/pty` is empty).
- On the same machine, quiet, the test runs and passes in 0.05s — three times with
  -count=3. The failing run spent 5.04s, i.e. it sat on its bound and gave up.
- The machine was NOT quiet at the time: another session's e2e run was on the same
  Docker daemon concurrently, which is exactly the serialization AGENTS.md warns
  about.

So the population is wider than "transport": it is every test that waits out a
duration for a state change. Worth deciding whether the fix belongs per test or as a
rule with a lint, because the next instance will be in a third package.

title: Shift+Enter is indistinguishable from Enter, so no program can bind it
description:
Reported by the owner, 2026-08-09: Shift+Enter does not insert a newline in omp, and the same in other TUIs.

Cause: while a program owns the keyboard the keys go through xterm's default handler, and nocx installs no custom key handling — there is no attachCustomKeyEventHandler, no modifyOtherKeys and no CSI-u / kitty keyboard protocol anywhere in frontend/src/renderers/xterm.ts. xterm's default sends a bare CR for Enter and does not encode the shift modifier, so the program receives exactly the same byte for Enter and for Shift+Enter and cannot tell them apart. This is not omp's defect: it is what the terminal does or does not send.

The fix is a choice, and it should be made deliberately rather than by picking the first sequence that makes omp work: the two conventions are the legacy 'ESC CR' that many editors accept, and a proper modifier encoding (xterm's modifyOtherKeys, or the kitty keyboard protocol) which programs negotiate and which also fixes every other unencodable chord rather than this one. Whichever is chosen, say why at the site and say what the other one would have bought.

nocx's own editor is unaffected — it handles Enter/Shift+Enter itself (editor.ts:588) — so this is strictly about the raw path while a program owns the pane.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run omp (or any TUI that binds Shift+Enter to 'insert newline') in an integrated session.
2. Press Shift+Enter.
3. Observed: it behaves exactly like Enter — the message is submitted instead of a newline inserted.

## Acceptance Criteria

A program running in the pane can distinguish Shift+Enter from Enter, proven by a test asserting the bytes nocx writes to the pty for each. The chosen mechanism is recorded at the site with the alternative named. If a negotiated protocol is chosen, the default (nothing negotiated) still behaves exactly as today, so no existing program changes behaviour.
close_reason: Shift+Enter is re-encoded as ESC CR through xterm's custom key handler; Enter stays a bare CR. Legacy convention chosen over modifyOtherKeys/kitty because xterm.js 5.5.0 ships neither and hand-rolling a negotiation beside a library that will have one is what the repo's reuse rule forbids — reasoning and the Alt+Enter collision recorded at the site. Neighbouring chords pinned by tests. Not verified against a real TUI: the proof is byte-level.

title: Transport notification tests time out under container load — three different tests so far
description:
Seen four times during the nocx-u7uh epic's gate runs, always as an exact 5.00s 'timed out waiting for <x> notification' and never as a logic failure:

- TestGitChanged_OverTheWireConformsToContract
- TestLifecycleChanged_DeadSessionGetsNoRecoveryClaim
- TestConnectionsPasswordRequest_OverTheWireConformsToContract
- once, internal/lifecyclechannel as a whole

Each passes in isolation and on re-run; a full 'go test -race ./...' in the pre-commit container passes on the same tree that just failed. So the notification wait (5s) is not generous enough for the container under full-suite parallel load, and the failure is indistinguishable from a real regression at the moment it appears — which is the expensive part: a coordinator bisecting one of these spends a wave measuring noise. It also erodes the gate: a red run that is 'probably the flake' is a gate nobody trusts.

Note TestLifecycleChanged_DeadSessionGetsNoRecoveryClaim additionally fails reproducibly under -count=2 while passing under -count=1, so at least one of these is not idempotent within a process — that is a separate, findable defect rather than pure timing.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run the pre-commit hook's containerized 'go test -race ./...' on a loaded machine, repeatedly.
2. Observed: one of the tests above fails with an exact 5.00s notification timeout.
3. Re-run the same package in isolation: passes.

## Acceptance Criteria

The notification waits no longer fail under container load — either the wait is derived from a documented budget rather than a bare 5s literal, or the tests stop racing the runtime. The non-idempotence of TestLifecycleChanged_DeadSessionGetsNoRecoveryClaim under -count=2 is diagnosed and fixed rather than papered over by a longer timeout. Proven by a repeated full containerized run (>=5 consecutive) staying green on a loaded machine.

title: su nested child domain is wired on both tiers but never proven on a pty
description:
nocx-u7uh.11 (bash) and nocx-u7uh.28 (zsh) both prove the nested child domain end to end for 'sudo' on a real pty, and nocx-u7uh.29 proves 'ssh' as a live assembly against a real sshd. 'su' is wired on both tiers — detected, requested, granted, launched — and has no pty-level proof on either.

su is not sudo: it crosses the privilege boundary differently, many implementations preserve descriptors while resetting the environment, and none promise it. The brief for nocx-u7uh.11 said explicitly 'test it; never infer success from inheritance', and that half is outstanding.

## Acceptance Criteria

A test on a real pty watches a parent enter 'su' and the child establish its own authenticated domain, on both the bash and zsh tiers, the way TestBashNestedChildDomain and TestZshNestedChildDomain do for sudo. Where the platform's su does not preserve the descriptor, the honest conventional fallback is asserted instead — and which platforms fall in which bucket is written down where the launcher decides.
close_reason: Four real-pty tests prove su's nested child domain: bash and zsh happy paths (completion asserted on the CHILD's domain, parent re-activates only through an authenticated activation), an auth-refused stillborn that injects a late frame from the child that never established and counts its rejection, and a descriptor-closed case asserting the conventional degrade. Real su descriptor preservation established by reading util-linux 2.42.2, shadow 4.19.4 and the BSD/macOS lineage AND by measuring the shadow su on this host preserving fd 7 through the exact launcher line — recorded at the launcher decision site, together with the fact that none of them promises it.

title: The ssh child domain is proven in pieces, never end to end against a real sshd
description:
nocx-u7uh.11 proved every piece of the ssh child path separately — the composed command line evals under bash and carries the -R byte-exact (TestComposeSSHChildLine_*), the loopback listener transport works, the in-band installer works, the kernel grant flow works — but never the combination: a real ssh client reaching a real sshd over the composed line, the reverse forward terminating at the listener, and the remote shell's hello establishing the child.

The live_sshd fixture is where this belongs (internal/app/live_sshd_test.go already drives a real sshd through the production composition). The gap that stopped it: the fixture's client key has to reach the composed line's ssh, and domain_request carries only host/user/port — typed options such as -i are deliberately not reproduced, which is a documented limit of the request shape rather than an oversight.

Until this lands, 'ssh establishes an authenticated child domain' is an assembly of proven parts, not a proven assembly.

## Acceptance Criteria

An automated test drives a real ssh client against the live sshd fixture over the composed child line and asserts the child domain reaches Established through its own hello on the reverse-forwarded transport, that the parent is Suspended for the whole interval, and that the parent re-activates only through an authenticated activation. Whether domain_request should carry the user's typed ssh options is DECIDED and written down — either the request shape grows or the limit is stated where a reader of the composer will find it.
close_reason: The ssh child is now proven as an assembly against the live sshd fixture, not as parts: the -R forward terminates at the lifecycle listener and the far shell's own hello establishes the child, parent Suspended throughout, re-activating only via authenticated activation; forwarding-refused, stillborn and late-frame paths covered. Found three defects no per-piece test could see: -t never allocates the remote pty (now -tt), the child's capability was never set on the in-band plan (capability-free integration), and the grant builder captured a nil publisher. Option question decided in ADR-0025.

title: A ready prompt stays unstructured until the first command starts
description:
Found by the nocx-u7uh.25 worker and deliberately left.

After nocx-u7uh.25 the block model is no longer torn down on every fact, but a session sitting at a ready prompt with no command yet is still in the unstructured mode it was left in — nothing moves it to the idle/structured layout until the first command starts and opens a block. The pre-ADR-0024 code called setIdle at that point; the ADR rework dropped it.

Consequence: the first impression of an integrated session is a conventional flat grid, and the structure only appears once the user has run something. Cosmetic rather than functional, which is why it was left rather than folded into .25.

Decide whether a ready prompt with a live domain should present the idle structured layout, and if so restore that call with the same integrated predicate .25 used.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open an integrated session and wait at the prompt without running anything.
2. Observed: the pane is in the unstructured full-pane layout.
3. Expected (to be confirmed): a live domain at a ready prompt presents the idle structured layout.
acceptance_criteria: A decision is recorded on what a ready prompt with a live domain should present, and the code matches it: either the idle structured layout is restored at prompt_ready, or the comment says why unstructured-until-first-command is correct.
close_reason: Decision recorded: YES, a ready prompt with a live domain presents the idle structured layout — ADR-0024 §4 is what entitles it, and flat-until-first-command was an implementation accident of the ADR rework. setIdle restored in the lifecycle onChange prompt_ready branch.

title: Alt-screen exit leaves an integrated session unstructured until the next command
description:
Found by the nocx-u7uh.25 worker and deliberately left, so it does not evaporate.

renderer.onBufferChange in frontend/src/terminal-content.ts calls scrollback.setUnstructured() unconditionally when leaving the alternate buffer. It is the same unconditional shape nocx-u7uh.25 fixed one call site up, and historically it was gated on the OSC-133 integration latch that ADR-0024 deleted.

Consequence: an integrated session that runs an alt-screen program (vim, less, top) comes back to a flat unstructured grid and stays there until the next command starts, instead of returning to the structured block layout its live domain entitles it to.

The fix is presumably the same predicate nocx-u7uh.25 used — shellStateFromLifecycle(state) !== 'integrated' — but confirm that against the fullscreen/exitFullscreen path before assuming it, because the alt-screen exit has ordering constraints setUnstructured declines while an alt-screen program owns the pane.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open an integrated session and confirm blocks appear for a command.
2. Run an alt-screen program (e.g. vim) and quit it.
3. Observed: the pane is a flat unstructured grid; no block framing until the next command starts.
4. Expected: leaving the alternate buffer returns the session to the structured block layout.
acceptance_criteria: Leaving the alternate buffer in an integrated session restores the structured block layout rather than a flat grid, and a conventional session still stays unstructured on the same path. Proven in the real UI.
close_reason: Leaving the alternate buffer asks the one existing integrated predicate: a live domain returns to the structured block layout (idle, or running while an attempt is in flight), a conventional session still lands unstructured. Four tests, both directions.

title: Recovery fence: how a Lost session becomes a conventional terminal
description:
Decided during nocx-u7uh.15. ADR-0024 decision 8 fixes the PROPERTY (restoration must be acknowledged before a session is treated as a usable conventional terminal) and deliberately leaves the MECHANISM open. The mechanism chosen: a composite ACK on decision 1's rendezvous carve-out — the shell emits a one-shot recovery fence, pre-provisioned during the authenticated bootstrap, after restoring its native PS1; the renderer matches the fence without inspecting the grid and acks only once the conventional presentation is also applied; the lane goes Lost -> Native while the domain stays permanently Lost.

Rejected alternatives and why: (a) the renderer OBSERVING a repainted native prompt in the grid — untrusted inference, reintroduces the render-state -> control-plane edge this epic exists to sever; (b) the renderer acking only that it APPLIED the conventional presentation — acks the wrong thing, leaves ADR-0024:439's feared state (suppressed prompt taking raw input) reachable.

Why the pre-shared nonce is not a new stream-derived authority edge: a forged recovery fence can only force a transition to native mode, which ADR-0024:472 already accepts as a bounded availability loss.

This bead is the OPEN QUESTION for the owner: does this belong in docs/lifecycle-protocol.md (worker .15 is writing it there) or as an amendment to ADR-0024 itself? Editing the ADR is the owner's call, so .15 was told not to.
acceptance_criteria: The owner decides whether the recovery-fence mechanism is documented in docs/lifecycle-protocol.md or as an amendment to ADR-0024, and the chosen document says so.
close_reason: Owner decided both: the mechanism stays in docs/lifecycle-protocol.md §12.1, which now says it is decision 8's deferred mechanism, and ADR-0024 decision 8 carries a pointer plus the two rejected alternatives.

title: The shell cannot name its active or last-completed attempt in a snapshot
description:
Found by nocx-u7uh.9 while building the recovery. The protocol says a snapshot carries the active attempt and the last completed one; the shell hooks cannot supply them, so every completion lost inside a gap reconciles as unknown even when the shell knows the exit status. That is SAFE — unknown is never success — but it is lossy, and the loss is invisible to the user.

Also open from the same bead: zsh and the POSIX tier do not yet answer a refresh request; only bash does.

## Acceptance Criteria

Per --acceptance.
acceptance_criteria: A snapshot answering a refresh carries active_attempt and last_completed with the shell's own view, and a completion lost inside a corrupted region reconciles to its real status rather than to unknown — including for app-originated attempts, via a per-domain alias recorded only from an authenticated start (kernel applyStart attach branch). Plus: nocx.zsh answers refresh_request the way nocx.bash now does. POSIX sh is deliberately EXCLUDED: nocx.posix:12-22 and ADR-0024:207-208 say the authenticated channel is not implementable in that tier and it needs its own proven adapter (Tier B) or gets nothing — a POSIX host stays a conventional terminal, and the omission is documented in the script rather than faked.
close_reason: Shell names its own attempts (domain-scoped ids); applyStart records an unexported per-attempt alias; applySnapshot resolves through it so a lost completion keeps its real exit status while unknown ids still reconcile to unknown. zsh answers refresh_request; POSIX deliberately excluded per nocx.posix:12-22 and ADR-0024:207-208. No new field crosses JSON-RPC, contracts untouched. Round 2 fixed a cross-domain id collision that broke nested domains on docker exec. Committed 00c14ceb; full pre-commit gate green.

title: Audit every renderer stale-guard for the shared-counter shape the git store had
description:
## Why

Removing the control plane's implicit FIFO (nocx-sfv6) broke the Git panel in a way no Go test could see and no ordering audit found. git-store.ts kept ONE lastAppliedEpoch across three independent facts — status, log and remote. A remote read issued after the log completed before it, bumped the shared counter, and the log's arriving response was discarded as stale. The panel sat in 'idle' forever: no rows, and not even the 'No commits yet' text, because it never learned anything.

The pre-work audit asked 'does the renderer await its mutations before dependent reads' and the answer was yes. That question cannot find this: the dependency was not an await, it was a counter. Any guard of the form 'drop a response whose sequence number is older than the newest applied' assumes responses land in issue order, which the transport no longer promises and ADR-0024 now says so explicitly.

## What to check

Known siblings, none of them yet judged:

- frontend/src/files/files-store.ts — dir.appliedGeneration is per DIRECTORY, which is narrower than the git store's, but six separate call sites write it (446, 460, 470, 489, 912, 1019) against guards at 420, 477, 887, 992. If two different response kinds for one directory can bump it, the same defect is there.
- frontend/src/settings-observer.ts:45 and frontend/src/settings-domain.ts:138 — revision guards. Settings revisions are server-monotonic, which may make them safe; say so with the reason rather than assuming.

Then sweep for the shape rather than the names: any comparison of a stored 'applied/last/expected' number against one carried by an in-flight response.
acceptance_criteria: Every stale-guard in the renderer is either scoped to one class of fact, or documented with why sharing is safe for it. At least one test per guard that is NOT already per-class drives two responses completing in the opposite order to their issue and asserts the older one does not discard the newer — the discriminating shape, not a smoke test.

title: Prove the remote lifecycle channel against a real sshd, and add the zsh net/tcp adapter
description:
nocx-u7uh.4 landed the adapter and proved it against the TunnelConn seam and its tests. It was NOT run against a live remote host and zsh has no net/tcp adapter — the worker said so plainly rather than letting silence imply coverage, which is why this bead exists instead of a surprise later.

## Acceptance Criteria

Per --acceptance.
acceptance_criteria: A run against a real sshd shows a bash shell on a remote host reaching an accepted domain with nothing installed there, and a host with AllowTcpForwarding no falling back to a visible native prompt. Plus a zsh adapter using zmodload zsh/net/tcp, or a written statement of why zsh cannot have one.
close_reason: landed in fa812fda: real sshd proofs plus the zsh ztcp adapter

title: Research: how often is there no transport?
description:
ADR-0024 accepts that POSIX sh remotes, forwarding-disabled hosts and docker exec shells lose enhanced input until Tier B. Whether that is a footnote or a serious regression is a measurement, and the ADR deliberately refuses to guess it from an armchair.

Independent of every other child — it informs the roadmap, not the implementation.

## Acceptance Criteria

Per --acceptance.
acceptance_criteria: A written finding against real hosts the owner actually uses: how many run a POSIX sh login shell, how many set AllowTcpForwarding no, how many sessions are docker exec. Concludes with a recommendation on whether Tier B moves up the roadmap, and files the follow-up bead if so.
notes: Explicitly NON-blocking: ADR-0024 places Tier B in a later epic regardless, so this informs the roadmap and must not silently expand this epic's DONE WHEN halfway through. If the finding is that no-transport is common, it files a follow-up bead — it does not widen nocx-u7uh.
close_reason: landed in 57c7723e: not estimable from data at rest; Tier B stays deferred, probes listed

title: Saturation is visible in the product: a structured retryable error, one central renderer mapping, and a contract schema
description:
A wire error is not product visibility. `dispatcher.ts:234` turns any RPC error
into a rejected promise, so whether the user learns anything depends on each
call site remembering to show it — which is exactly the "soft degrade visible
only in a log" shape AGENTS.md forbids.

A rejected request answers immediately with a stable error:

    {"code": -32001, "message": "Control plane busy",
     "data": {"reason": "control-saturated", "scope": "connection",
              "retryable": true, "retryAfterMs": 250}}

No secret-bearing parameters in `data`; the transport-wide rule that no control
frame is logged verbatim applies here too. A notification with no id gets a
rate-limited `control.saturated` instead, carrying method class and scope only.

One central mapping in the dispatcher turns `data.reason === "control-saturated"`
into a deduplicated toast, so a surface that forgets still degrades visibly.
Individual surfaces may additionally disable an action or retry.

The result shape gets a schema in `contracts/` in this commit, per the wire rule
— `additionalProperties: false` plus explicit `required`, generated renderer
